sections.text: Your opponent opened with 1.d4 and a fianchetto, and you built a solid centre with 1...d5, 2...e6 and 3...c6. The trouble began with the setup 4...b6?!, 5...f6?! and 6...Nd7?!, which weakened your pawn structure without developing much, and you were slightly worse (-1.8 by move 6).

7.Bh3?? from your opponent was a mistake and brought the evaluation back to level, but 7...Ne7?? let them off the hook (the engine preferred 7...f5). After 8.Bxe6 you were a pawn down, and the bishop stayed uncomfortable for several moves.

There were real chances later. 11.Bxh7?? was a blunder and took the evaluation to +2.7 for you, but 11...Bb7?? gave it right back; 11...Nf8 was the move. The same happened on move 13: 13...Nxg6 would have won a piece, but 13...Qc7?? let it go.
You then fought for activity with 15...Nxe5!, a good practical resource, but the position stayed worse and you resigned after 17.Qf3+, when the engine had you only about a pawn down.

review.turning_point: 13...Qc7 missed 13...Nxg6, which would have won a piece after your opponent's loose 13.e4.
review.focus: When your opponent blunders, as on 11.Bxh7 and 13.e4, stop and list every capture and check before answering; 13...Nxg6 was sitting there.

review.headline: Italian game turned by a pin on the d2 bishop and a trapped knight on e4

sections.text: An Italian Game where you opened the centre with 4.d4 and 5.dxe5?!, then slipped with 7.Nbd2?. The engine preferred 7.Nxe5, a discovered attack that would have won a piece, so that was the chance you missed in the opening.

The middlegame was tactical. After 8.h3 Bxf3 9.Nxf3 Nxe4 10.Bf4 Nxf3+ 11.Bxf3 d5 12.Qe2 Qa5+ you played 13.Bd2??, and that was your one big error: the bishop was pinned to your king by the queen on a5, which left a piece to be won.
Your opponent missed it with 13...Bb4?, since 13...Qxd2+ was available. You then found 14.c3!, and 14...Bxc3?? gave you the chance to recapture with 15.Bxc3!, hitting the queen with tempo.
From there you converted cleanly. 16.Bxe4 won a piece, and after 17.O-O dxe4 18.Qxe4 you stayed well ahead. 20.Rad1 and 21.Rd7 piled up the pressure before 22.Qxe2 ended it.

review.turning_point: 14...Bxc3?? let you recapture with 15.Bxc3!, and the swing from -0.1 to +4.5 left you clearly better.
review.focus: At 7.Nbd2 you passed on 7.Nxe5, which would have won a piece; before developing, check whether an enemy piece is loose.

review.headline: A calm Scandinavian grind with a well-timed trap on the bishop

sections.text: You met the Scandinavian with 3.Nc3 and 4.Qe2, which allowed the queen trade after 4...Qxe2+ 5.Ngxe2. It was a small inaccuracy (4.Be2 was the engine's choice), but the endgame was comfortable for you and you developed steadily with 6.f3, 7.d4 and 8.Bf4.

The key structural decision was 10.Bxa6 bxa6, which wrecked your opponent's pawns, followed by 11.O-O-O. After 13...Bf4? you struck with 14.Nxd5!, taking the knight, and the exchanges that followed left you +1.8.
Then came the highlight. 17...Bc4?? put the bishop on a square where 18.b3! trapped it, and after 18...Bb5 19.axb5 axb5 you were a piece for a pawn ahead. Very good spotting.

From there it was technique: 21.Rde2 and 22.Rxe2 traded a pair of rooks, then 24.Rxg7 and 25.Rxh7 picked up pawns. You missed a quicker finish, though. 26.Rh8+ Re8 27.Rxe8# was a back rank mate, and the same idea worked a move later with 27.Rg8+ Re8 28.Rxe8#.

review.turning_point: 17...Bc4?? allowed 18.b3!, which trapped the bishop and left you a piece for a pawn ahead.
review.focus: At 26.Rg7 you had a back rank mate with 26.Rh8+ Re8 27.Rxe8#; in winning positions, check every forcing move before improving slowly.

review.headline: A cool-headed counterattack that ended in a mating net

sections.text: You answered 1.d4 with a solid 1...d5 and developed with 2...Nf6 and 3...Nc6. White pushed with 6.e5, and 6...Nd7?! was the one slightly passive moment; 6...Nd5 was more active. Still, you got your pieces out with 7...e6 and stayed calm.
Your opponent then overreached. 8.d5?? opened lines, and 8...exd5! was the right capture. After 9.Qxd5 Qe7 10.Bg5 f6 11.Bh4 Ndxe5 you had won a pawn and your pieces were well placed.
12.Bc4?? walked into the best shot in the game: 12...Nxc4+! was a discovered check from your queen along the e-file, and the knight took the bishop at the same time. It put you far ahead, up four.
You kept converting accurately: 13.Kd1 Be6 14.Re1 Rd8 15.Rxe6 Qxe6 and then 16...Qxd5 picked up the queen. The finish with 21...Rd3, 22...Qxc3+ and 24...c6# was clean.

review.turning_point: 12.Bc4 allowed 12...Nxc4+!, a discovered check that won material and decided the game.
review.focus: At 6...Nd7 the engine preferred 6...Nd5; when your knight is attacked by a pawn, look for the square that keeps it central.

review.headline: Petrov Italian where two opponent errors gave you a clean extra piece

sections.text: You answered 3.Bc4 with the flexible 3...d6?! and 4...Be6, and after 5.Bd5 Nxd5 6.Nxd5 c6 the position was roughly level. 7...h6?! was a slow move, though, and it set up your one real mistake.

That mistake came with 8...Nd7??. After 8.d4 the engine wanted 8...Qf6, and 8...Nd7 dropped you to -3.8. Fortunately your opponent answered with 9.dxe5??, when 9.d5 was the strong move, and you got back into the game with 9...Nxe5 and the queen trade on move 11.
The decisive moment was 13.Nc4??. After 12.O-O Bc5, your opponent's knight went to a square where 13...Bxc4! just took it, and you were up a piece (+5.5).
You then converted calmly: 14...Bd4 and 16...Bxe3 traded off White's bishop, and 17.Rxd8+ Kxd8 left you with a clear extra piece. 25.Rc6+ was your opponent's last try before resigning.

review.turning_point: 13.Nc4?? let you play 13...Bxc4!, winning a knight and the game.
review.focus: At 8...Nd7 the engine preferred 8...Qf6; when the centre opens, check which of your pieces are undefended before you commit.

review.headline: A speculative bishop sacrifice that fizzled, then a flag fall in a level position

sections.text: You played the French with a normal 2.d4 and 3.Nf3 setup, and 4.Nc3 dxe4 5.Nxe4 Nf6 6.Bd3 Nxe4 7.Bxe4 f5 left you slightly better (+1.9 after 7...f5). Your development with 9.Bg5, 10.Qd2 and 11.Be3 was sensible.

The first mistake was 12.Bxh6??. After 12...gxh6 13.Qxh6 you had two pawns for the bishop, and the engine's 12.O-O-O would have kept your edge. The sacrifice looked attractive but there was no follow-up that worked.
After 13...Rf6 14.Qg5+ Kf8 you kept the initiative, but 15.Ne5?? dropped you to -2.7 because 15...Qxd4 was strong. Your opponent missed it with 15...Nd7.
16.Ng6+?? Kf7 17.Nf4 left you still worse, but 17...c5?? let you back to level (0.0). The game ended on time after 17 moves, so keep an eye on the clock.

review.turning_point: 12.Bxh6 gave a bishop for two pawns when you were already doing well, and the attack that followed ran out of steam.
review.focus: At 12.Bxh6 the calm 12.O-O-O kept your edge; before sacrificing, count whether your next two moves create real threats.

review.headline: A winning attack that nearly slipped away at move 29 before the clock decided it

sections.text: You chose the Scotch Gambit and 5.Nxd4?! allowed 5...Nxd4 6.Qxd4 c5 7.Qe3, and then 8.f4?! and 9.e5? made the position loose (-1.0). The engine preferred 9.Nc3 with a calm, developing game.
Your opponent's 10...Nd5?? was the break you needed. You found 11.Qf3!, which hit the knight on d5 and led to 14.Bxd5 Bxd5 15.Rxd5, winning a piece.
Your technique after that was strong. 16.Bf4 Rxd5 17.Qxd5, 19.Nc3 and 20.Qxb7 fxe5 21.Qxe7 took more and more material, and by 22.Qe6+ you were well ahead (+4.7).
29.Qe5?? was a major mistake, taking a +5.3 position to -7.3, and you were saved because your opponent ran out of time first.

review.turning_point: 11.Qf3! punished 10...Nd5?? and turned a shaky opening into a winning position.
review.focus: At 29.Qe5 the engine saw 29.h3; with the win nearly secure, check the opponent's checks and captures before moving the queen.

review.headline: Clean win in a Center Game after one hung bishop

sections.text: You met the Center Game calmly with 2...exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qd1 Nf6 5.Nc3 Bb4 6.Bd2 Bxc3 7.Bxc3, and the position was healthy. Your 7...Nxe4?! was a pawn grab that the engine rated at -0.4; castling with 7...O-O first was the quieter option.

Your opponent's 8.Bd3?? was the blunder; 8.Qg4 would have kept things balanced. You found the best answer, 8...Nxc3!, and after 9.bxc3 you came out a clean pawn up and followed with 9...O-O to finish development.
10.Nf3 Re8+ 11.Be2 Qe7 12.O-O Qxe2 picked up a bishop and put you well ahead (+5.0). 13.Qd5 Qxc2 won another pawn, and your queen was dominating the board.

You finished in style: 14...Qg6 and 16...Ne7 kept your pieces coordinated, 17.f5 Qxg5 took the knight, and 19.Qxc7 Bxf5 added another pawn. After 22.Qc6 you took the queen with 22...bxc6, and the game ended on time.

review.turning_point: 8.Bd3?? allowed 8...Nxc3!, which broke White's structure and left you a pawn ahead with the better pieces.
review.focus: At 7...Nxe4 the engine preferred 7...O-O; take a moment to castle before grabbing material in the opening.

review.headline: A French Exchange win built on a poorly timed queen check

sections.text: You chose the Exchange French with 2.d4 and 3.exd5 exd5, then developed with 4.Nc3. After 4...c5 you played 5.Nf3?!, and the engine preferred 5.dxc5 d4, but it was not a big concession.
5...Qe7+?? was the mistake that decided the game. You found 6.Be3!, blocking the check and keeping your pieces working, and after 6...cxd4 7.Bb5+ Bd7 8.Nxd4 you were already clearly better (+2.8).
8...Bxb5? traded off the bishop on your terms: 9.Ndxb5 recaptured and left you with two active knights (+4.3). Your opponent should have played 8...Nf6.
From there 9...Nc6 10.Nxd5 Qe5 11.Nbc7+ brought both knights into the attack and won a pawn along the way, and your opponent resigned after 11...Kd7.

review.turning_point: 5...Qe7+?? was a premature check, and 6.Be3! blocked it and left you clearly better.
review.focus: At 5.Nf3 the engine preferred 5.dxc5; when the opponent's pawn challenges your centre, consider taking it before developing.

review.headline: A winning attack that slipped away just before the finish

sections.text: You took on e5 early with 3.Nxe5 and 4.Qe2, and your opponent's 4...f5?? gave you +3.0. You were clearly better, but 5.d3?! gave some of it back.

6.Nf7?? forked the queen and rook, but the king captured it and you lost a piece for little (-3 in material). The engine preferred 6.Qh5+ g6 7.Nxg6. Luckily 8...g6?? came next and 9.Bc4+! put you back at +6.6.

After 10.Bxd5+ Kg7 you were doing well (+7.1), but 11.b3?? threw it away. The engine's 11.Qe5+ would have set up a skewer on the king and rook, and after your opponent's 11...Bb4+?? your 12.Kf1?? passed up 12.Qxb4, which would have won a piece.
You still had a forced win after 13.Bb2+, 14.Qf4+ and 15.Qf7. The final blunder was 20.f3+??, because 20.Qh3# was checkmate, and the game ended with a loss on time.

review.turning_point: 20.f3+?? missed 20.Qh3#, a checkmate that would have won the game on the spot.
review.focus: At 20.f3+ you missed 20.Qh3#; when you have a big attack, look for forcing moves like checks that finish the game.

review.headline: Level Petrov endgame lost to a passed f-pawn

sections.text: You met 3.Nxe5 with the standard 3...d6 and 4...Nxe4, and the queen trade after 5.Qe2 Qe7 6.Nc3 Nxc3 7.Qxe7+ Bxe7 8.dxc3 led to a balanced middlegame. Both sides traded pieces steadily through move 17 and the evaluation stayed near zero.
The first slip was 19...e5?, when the engine preferred 19...Kf7, and 20.f4 e4?! pushed you further out of balance (-1.2).
You held on until 29.Rxe4+ Kxd5, but 30.f6 created a dangerous passed pawn. 30...Rc8?? was the critical mistake (-3.1); 30...Rc1 31.Re7 was a tougher defence.
31...Kc6?? made it worse, because 31...Rc4 32.f7 was a better try. After 32.f7 the pawn could not be stopped, 38.f8=Q+ decided matters, and you resigned after 49.h8=Q.

review.turning_point: 30...Rc8?? let White push the f-pawn with a decisive advantage; 30...Rc1 would have kept more resistance.
review.focus: At 30...Rc8 and 31...Kc6 you missed more resilient defences like 30...Rc1 and 31...Rc4; against a far-advanced passed pawn, keep the rook active.

review.headline: A Vienna Game where a stranded knight led to a long attack and mate

sections.text: Your opponent played a slow Vienna setup with 3.h3, 5.b3 and 7.g4, and you set up solidly with 2...d6, 3...c6 and 4...Nf6. You were a little better, but 8...h6?!, 9...Qb6?! and 10...Qb4+?! each gave back some of that edge; 9...d5 was the engine's choice.

Your opponent made it worse with 10.Na4? and 11.c3?, and you found 11...Qa5!. Then 13.O-O?? was the blunder: your 13...b5! attacked the stranded knight, and 14.Nc5 dxc5 15.bxc5 Nxc5 won a piece (+3.3).
You kept pressing with 16...b4, 17...bxc3, 18...cxb2 and 19...bxa1=Q, which opened the position against the king, and 20...Nxa6 left you far ahead. 23...Bxe1 and 26...Rexb8 kept the edge intact.
28...Ne4?! was a small slip, but 29.f3? allowed 29...Rb2+!, and the finish with 33...Ng3+, 34...Ra2 and 35...Rb1# was checkmate.

review.turning_point: 13.O-O?? let you play 13...b5!, winning material and tearing open the queenside.
review.focus: At 9...Qb6 the engine preferred 9...d5; avoid bringing the queen out early where it can be chased, as with 10...Qb4+.

review.headline: A wild Bishop's Opening slugfest that ended in mate on the back of a queen-and-rook attack

sections.text: You went for the early queen attack with 2.Bc4 and 3.Qh5, and kept pushing with 5.Ng5?!. Your opponent's 5...Nh6? gave you a chance, but 6.d4?? was an error: after 6...Bxd4 you were a pawn down (-1.7). Black missed 5...Bxf2+, which was stronger.

7.Nf3?! was a retreat that also set up a discovered attack from your bishop on c1 onto the knight on h6. After 7...Bb6?? 8.Bxh6 gxh6 9.Qxh6 you were back in the game, and 11.Bxf7+ and 12.Qf6+! kept the king in the centre.

The game swung again. 13.Ng5?? and 14.Ne6+?? gave the edge back: 14.Ne6+ forked the king and queen, but 14...Bxe6 just took the knight. Worse, 16.Nc3?? missed 16.Qxd6+ Kc8 17.Be6#, a forced checkmate, and 20.Qb4?? and 21.Rxd6?? were more slips.
Your opponent's 21...Rxd6?? let you recover with 22.Qxd6+!, and the finish was crisp: 23.Bxg8, then 25.Qd8+!, 26.Rxd8+ and 27.Rxc8# was checkmate.

review.turning_point: 21...Rxd6?? allowed 22.Qxd6+!, and 23.Bxg8 left you well ahead after a long series of mistakes on both sides.
review.focus: At 16.Nc3 you missed 16.Qxd6+ Kc8 17.Be6#; with the king exposed, check every forcing move before a quiet one.

review.headline: A Philidor Lion where your opponent's queen capture backfired

sections.text: You chose the Philidor Lion setup with 3...d6, 4...Nbd7 and 5...dxe5, then pushed on the queenside with 8...b5, 9...a5?! and 10...a4. After 11...O-O and 12...Re8 you were solid, but 13...Bb7?! and 14...Qb6? loosened things slightly; 14...Bc8 was the engine's preference.

Your opponent had 15.Bxf6 Nxf6 16.Nxe5 available, but 15.Qxd7?? was a blunder, and you took it at once with 15...Nxd7!. That was a discovered attack that also hit the bishop on g5, and it put you a queen for a knight up.
16.Rxd7 Bxg5 17.Bxf7+? Kh8 18.Bxe8 Rxe8 19.Nxg5 liquidated into a position where you were still doing well (+1.1), since your queen was more powerful than their rooks.
20.Ne6?? gave you the finish. 20...Qxf2+! forked the king and rook, and 21.Kh1 Qf1+ 22.Rxf1 Rxf1# was a neat mate.

review.turning_point: 15.Qxd7?? let you play 15...Nxd7!, winning the queen for a knight and turning the game.
review.focus: At 14...Qb6 the engine preferred 14...Bc8; before putting the queen on a loose diagonal, ask which of your pieces become hard to defend.

review.headline: A chaotic Petrov Damiano rescued by a back rank shot

sections.text: You played the Damiano with 3.Nxe5, 4.Qe2 and 5.d3, and your opponent's 6...f6? gave you +1.8. But 6.Bf4? and then 7.Nf7?? let it slip: after 7...Qxf7 you were a knight down until 8.dxe4 recaptured. The engine preferred 7.dxe4 fxe5 8.Qh5+.
9.Bxc7?? grabbed a pawn but 9.exd5 was stronger, and 10.Bxb8 Rxb8 kept things even. Your opponent kept drifting with 8...Be7?, 11...Re8? and 13...Bf5??, which kept you in the game.
13.Nxe4?? and 14.f3? gave a lot back, and 19.Be6?? was another slip, but your opponent missed their chance with 19...Rc7??.
Then 20...Qxg2?? allowed the finish: 21.Qxe8+! was a back rank shot, since 21...Bf8 22.Qxf8# was checkmate.

review.turning_point: 20...Qxg2?? allowed 21.Qxe8+!, a back rank blow that forced mate on the next move.
review.focus: At 7.Nf7 you gave up a piece for little; 7.dxe4 was the move. Before a sacrifice, check that it creates a real threat.

review.headline: A scrappy Petrov where you survived a slow start and won with a knight shot on move 19

sections.text: This Petrov was a game of survival first and attack second. 3...Bc5?! was a little loose and the engine had you around -1.1 straight away, and 7...Bb6?! invited 8.dxe5 and 9.Bg5 with pressure on your f6 knight. You kept your composure with 9...c6 and 10...axb6 and stayed in the game.
Your one real error came at 11...Nxf6. Recapturing with the knight opened the d-file, so the queens met with 12.Qxd8 Rxd8 and you were left at roughly -1.5. The engine's choice was 11...Qxf6.

White gave you something back at once: 13.Rae1 missed 13.Nxe5. You then traded your way into activity with 14...Rxe4 15.Rxe4 Nxe4 16.Nxe5 Be6 and 17...Bxb3 18.cxb3, and 18...Nd2?! set a trap for a tired opponent.

19.Rd1 walked into it. 19...Nxf3+! was a fork of the king on g1 and the knight on e5, and after 20.gxf3 Rxd1+ you were three points up. You then picked up pawns with 22...Rxb2 and 23...Rxa2, pushed the c-pawn, queened with 42...c1=Q and finished with 44...Rb1#.

review.turning_point: 19.Rd1?? Nxf3+ forked the king on g1 and the knight on e5; after 20.gxf3 Rxd1+ the evaluation went from about -0.6 to +5.6 in your favour.
review.focus: On 11...Nxf6, ask what a recapture opens before you make it. The knight leaving d7 uncovered the d-file and forced the queen trade, while 11...Qxf6 was the engine's choice.

review.headline: A winning position against the Petrov thrown away by a queen blunder on move 14, then lost on time

sections.text: You handled the early Petrov trap well. After 3.Nxe5 Nxe4 4.Qe2 d5 5.d3 Bb4+ the engine already had you at +2.5, and 6.c3 and 7.Nf3 were calm, correct responses. Then 8.dxe4 dxe4 9.Nfd2 g6 10.Nxe4 put you a clean piece up (+3.9).

The slide began with 12.Qc4??, which dropped from +3.9 to +1.6 and allowed 12...Bxd2+. The quiet 12.f3 was the engine's choice. After 13.Nxd2 (13.Bxd2 was better) Black replied 13...Be6??, and 13...Re8+ was the move that would have kept Black afloat.
That gave you +4.4, and you only needed a safe queen move. Instead 14.Qb3?? ran into 14...Bxb3, and you gave the queen for a bishop. 14.Qf4 was the engine's choice, with the queen still active.
From there you were fighting at -4 to -6. You kept making sensible moves, like 18.Bf4, 22.O-O and 24.Bd5+, but the position never recovered and the game ended on time at move 31.

review.turning_point: 14.Qb3?? Bxb3. You stood at +4.4 and the queen stepped onto a square the bishop on e6 attacked; the evaluation fell to -4.5.
review.focus: Before moving your queen, check every enemy piece that attacks the destination square. On 14.Qb3 the bishop on e6 covered b3, while 14.Qf4 kept your lead.

review.headline: A messy Petrov you won by punishing a run of White errors, with the key answer on move 18

sections.text: You were worse for a long stretch of the opening. 8...O-O-O? weakened your king, and the engine preferred 8...Be7. Then 10.b3?? was a gift, but 10...Nc5?? let it slip: 10...Qxc3 was the engine's move, and 10...Nc5 took you from +0.8 to -4.1.

12.Nc4?? gave you another chance and 12...Bxc4! was the right answer. After 13.dxc4 you stood at -1.8, and 13...d5?? (the engine preferred 13...Ncxe4) opened the centre while your king was still on c8.

The game turned with 17...Rxd1 and White's answer. 18.Rxd1?? was a mistake (18.Bf5+ was needed) and you found 18...Nxe4!, moving from -2.9 to +1.5. White's 19.Bf4?? (19.Nxf7 was better) met 19...g5 20.Be3 Qe2 21.Rd7 Bg7, and your queen and bishop took over.
The conversion was clean: 23...Bxc3, 24...Bxa1 took the rook, 27...Bxf2+ followed, and your queen mopped up with 42...Qxa5+, 43...Qxc5 and 44...Qxb6 before 50...Qa1# finished it.

review.turning_point: 18.Rxd1?? Nxe4!. After 17...Rxd1 White needed 18.Bf5+; instead the recapture allowed 18...Nxe4 and the evaluation swung from -2.9 to +1.5.
review.focus: 13...d5?? at -1.8: the engine preferred 13...Ncxe4. With your king on c8 and White's pieces active, avoid opening the centre before your pieces are ready.

review.headline: A long Petrov won in the endgame, with several chances to finish earlier

sections.text: A Petrov that stayed balanced for a long time. 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.Nc3 d5?! 6.d3 Nxc3 7.bxc3 gave White doubled c-pawns, and 9.d4? Qe7+ kept you active. You did slip with 13...b6?? (the engine's move was 13...Nb6).

White returned the favour with 16.Bh6??, which took the evaluation to +2.2 for you. 16...f5?? gave most of it back; the simple 16...Bxh6 was the engine's preference. Later 25.h4?? Bxg5! was your high point: the bishops came off with the evaluation at +2.4 and an endgame to grind.

The endgame is where you left value on the table. 29...Kc7?, 31...Ke7? and 32...Ng7? each let White off, and each time the engine wanted the pawn push: 29...c4, 31...c4 and 32...c4, which cramps the bishop on a6. White's 30.Bb5? and 31.a4?? let you back in, going up to +4.1.
From 34...Nxf4+ your knight collected pawns with 36...Nxg5, 38...Nxc3 and 39...Nxb5, then your f-pawn ran with 44...dxc4+, 45...f4, 46...f3, 47...f2 and 48...f1=Q. 55...Qa5# finished it.

review.turning_point: 25.h4?? Bxg5!. White needed 25.Bh6; instead you traded bishops on your terms and the evaluation went to +2.4.
review.focus: Endgame decisions: 29...Kc7? at +2.6 to +1.2. The engine wanted 29...c4 each time, so when you have a pawn push that restricts the enemy bishop, ask whether it beats a king move.

review.headline: A wild Bishop's Opening where both sides blundered and your attack mated on move 17

sections.text: A sharp game from the start. 3...d5 4.exd5 Nxd5 5.Qf3 c6 6.Nc3 Be6 was a natural set-up, and 7...Bb4?! pinned the knight on c3 against the king. White played 8.Ng5 and you grabbed the knight with 8...Nxc3?, though the engine preferred 8...Qf6.
9.Nxe6?? (9.Bxe6 was right) gave you the chance, and 9...Nd5+ was a discovered check. But 9...fxe6 was the engine's choice. After 10.c3 fxe6 11.cxb4 Nxb4?! you were still about 2 pawns worse.
12.Bxe6?? handed you the lead, and 12...Rf8! was the best answer. 13.Qh5+ g6 14.Qxh7?? was another blunder, but 14...Qf6?? let White out: 14...Nxd3+ 15.Ke2 Rxf2+ was the engine's forcing route.
White then missed 15.O-O and played 15.Bh3??, and you hit the right shot: 15...Qxf2+! 16.Kd1 Qc2+ 17.Ke1 Nxd3# was mate.

review.turning_point: 15.Bh3?? Qxf2+! After 14...Qf6?? White could have held with 15.O-O, but missing it allowed 16.Kd1 Qc2+ 17.Ke1 Nxd3# and mate.
review.focus: 14...Qf6: with the king exposed in the centre, look at checks first. 14...Nxd3+ 15.Ke2 Rxf2+ was a stronger forcing line, and you were winning at +8.1 before it.

review.headline: A wild Italian where you were winning and then lost the queen's grip on the game

sections.text: An aggressive game that you started well. 3...Nh6 4.d4 exd4 5.Bxh6?! gxh6 6.Nxd4 Nxd4? 7.Qxd4! put your queen in the centre against doubled h-pawns. When Black played 7...Qg5??, 8.Qxh8! took the rook and you were five points up.

9.Qf6?? began the slide: 9...Qxe4+ forked your king, bishop on c4 and rook on h1. The engine preferred 9.Qe5+. Black even missed 9...Qxh1+, but 10.Kd1?? allowed 10...Qxh1+ anyway and the material went to -2. 10.Kd2 was the engine's move.
12.Qe5+?? (12.Bb5+ was better) dropped you to -4.0, but Black blundered back with 12...Be7?? and 13...f6??, and 14.Qh5+! took you to +7.0. At that point 15.Bxh1 was the strong continuation.
Instead 15.Qf5+?? Kd6?? and then 16.Qxc8?? Qxd5+ left your bishop hanging to the queen on h1, and you resigned. 16.Qf4+ would have kept control.

review.turning_point: 16.Qxc8?? Qxd5+. You were at +7.0 and the black queen on h1 still attacked your bishop on d5; 16.Qf4+ was the engine's move.
review.focus: 16.Qxc8: before grabbing material when ahead, check which of your own pieces are attacked. The bishop on d5 was hanging to the queen on h1, and 15.Bxh1 had already been available.

review.headline: A quick Italian win: you missed 5.d5 but later punished the king with a mating attack

sections.text: Black's 4...Be6?? was a blunder that took the evaluation to +4.7 for you, and 5.d5 was the move, attacking both the knight on c6 and the bishop on e6 (a fork). 5.Bb3?? let it go (+0.5), but it was not a disaster: after 5...Bxb3 6.axb3 you had an open a-file for your rook.
You then built an initiative with 6...Nxd4 7.Nxd4 exd4 8.Qxd4 Qe7 9.Nc3 Qe5 10.Qb4. Black's 10...O-O-O? walked into 11.Rxa7!, grabbing a pawn and lifting you to +6.5.
12.Qxb7+ Kd7 kept Black's king exposed. 13.Nb5?! made things a bit trickier, but after 13...Ke6? 14.Nxc7+! Kf6 15.Nd5+ Ke6 16.Qxf7+ Ke5, you were winning by force.
The finish was a queen sacrifice: 17.Be3 Nh6 18.Qe7+ Bxe7 19.Rxe7# was mate.

review.turning_point: 11.Rxa7! Qc5 12.Qxb7+: after 10...O-O-O? the evaluation went from +3.2 to +6.1, and the black king never found safety.
review.focus: 5.Bb3?? after 4...Be6??: look for forcing moves first. 5.d5 attacked the knight and the bishop at once and was the engine's move.

review.headline: A Vienna where you won a pawn early, then lost the exchange with 12...Qd7

sections.text: A Vienna that started well for you. 3...Bg4?! was a little loose, but White's 7.g5? gave you a chance and 7...Nxe4! was the right shot. After 8.Nxe4 Bxe4 you were a pawn up, and 9...Bg6 and 10...Be7 kept things solid.

Then 11.Nxg6 hxg6 12.Bf3 attacked the b7 pawn, and 12...Qd7?? was the mistake: it ignored the threat to b7 and the evaluation went from +1.0 to -2.6. The engine's choice was 12...d5. After 13.Bxb7 Na6 14.Bxa8 your rook was gone; you got the bishop back with 18...Rxa8.
You kept playing sensible chess: 14...c6, 15...d5 and 17...Qc7 kept the bishop on a8 under pressure, but White's pieces were comfortable, and 19.h5 Qd8?! pushed you into passivity.
20...f6? was a final slip (20...Rb8 was the engine's move), and 21.hxg6 ended the game. The early tactic was great, but the middlegame needs careful piece safety.

review.turning_point: 12...Qd7?? ignored the threat to b7. 13.Bxb7 and 14.Bxa8 followed and the evaluation fell from +1.0 to -2.6.
review.focus: 12...Qd7: before developing, check what the opponent's bishop is aiming at. 12...d5 was the engine's move and blocked the long diagonal toward b7 and a8.

review.headline: A French Exchange you were winning until 26.Nd2 and 27.Qf3, then lost on time

sections.text: A quiet French Exchange. 7.a3 Bxc3 8.Bxc3 gave you the bishop pair, and you built steadily with 9.Be2, 10.O-O and 11.Re1. 13.b4? was the first slip (13.Bd3 was the engine's move), but Black's 13...Ne4 did not hurt you much.
Black went wrong with 20...Nc4??, and you were quick to punish it. 21.Bxe6+ won a piece (+4.2), and 22.Qd3 Qd6 23.Bh3 Rxe1+ 24.Rxe1 Nb2 25.Qb3 Nc4 kept you at +5.0.

Then 26.Nd2?? walked into 26...Nxd2, and the evaluation fell from +5.0 to +1.6 with the material back to zero. 26.g3 was the engine's choice. 27.Qf3?? made it worse: 27...Nxf3+ took your queen (-9); 27.Qd3 Nc4 was the engine's line.
The game ended on time at move 27, in a position that was already lost.

review.turning_point: 26.Nd2?? Nxd2. You were at +5.0, but the knight stepped onto d2 where the black knight on c4 could capture it; the evaluation dropped to +1.6.
review.focus: 26.Nd2: before placing a piece, check what attacks the square. The knight on c4 covered d2, while 26.g3 kept your lead.

review.headline: A French Exchange you were losing until 17...Rb2+ gave you a won endgame

sections.text: A tough game for most of the way. 8.b3? weakened your queenside (8.Bd3 was the engine's move), and 10.Qc2? was another small step in the wrong direction. Black's 10...Qe7?? pinned your bishop on e2 against the king, but didn't make the most of it (10...Bf5 was the engine's move).
11.O-O-O?? allowed 11...Bxc3, and after 12.Bxf6? Qxf6 13.Qxc3 Rxe2 you had lost a piece and were at -4.3. The engine preferred 11.O-O or 12.Bd3.
You kept fighting with 14.Ne5 Qf4+ 15.Kb1 Rxf2 16.Rde1?! Bf5+ 17.Nd3, and Black cracked: 17...Rb2+?? was a blunder (17...Nd7 was the engine's move) and 18.Kxb2! took you from -5.5 to +5.5.
After 19.Re8+ Qf8 20.Rxf8+ Kxf8, you were way ahead. You played safely with 21.Rf1, 24.Nxg6+ and 30.Rxa2, and finished with 37.Rh7+ Kg8 38.Qxg6+ Kf8 39.Qf7#.

review.turning_point: 17...Rb2+?? 18.Kxb2!. Black tried a flashy check at -5.5 for you and the evaluation flipped to +5.5 after you took the rook.
review.focus: 11.O-O-O: it let Black take on c3. The engine preferred 11.O-O, so before castling long ask which piece your move leaves loose.

review.headline: A solid London defence undone by one pawn push on move 7, then lost on time

sections.text: You set up a sensible game against the London: 1...d5 2.Bf4 e6 3.Nf3 Bd6 4.e3 Nf6 5.Bd3 O-O 6.O-O Nbd7 was a normal, solid structure, and the evaluation was close to level.

7...e5?? was the mistake. It dropped the evaluation from roughly equal to -4.5, because after 8.dxe5 the pawn attacked both your bishop and your knight. The engine's suggestion was 7...Bxf4 8.exf4, trading White's best bishop first.
After 8...Nh5 9.exd6 Nxf4 10.exf4 dxc4 11.Bxc4 cxd6 12.Qxd6 you were down material. 12...Qf6 walked into 13.Qxf6, which left you without the queen and the game ended on time at move 13.

review.turning_point: 7...e5??, which turned a normal position into -4.5; 8.dxe5 hit your bishop and your knight at once.
review.focus: 7...e5: before pushing a central pawn, check which of your pieces become targets. The engine's choice was 7...Bxf4 8.exf4, which resolves the tension.

review.headline: A winning Two Knights game that ended in a draw after 48.g6

sections.text: The opening went well because Black cooperated. 4...Nxe4 5.dxe5 Bc5?? and 6...O-O? gave you the chance, and 7.Qd5! was a strong answer, hitting the f7 pawn and the king (a pin on f7). 7...Bxf2+ 8.Rxf2? Nxf2 9.Kxf2 Nb4 10.Qd2 left you comfortable. 6.O-O was a slip (6.Qd5 was the engine's move).

You kept the edge with 12.Bg5 Qd7 13.Bb5?! (13...Qf5? was Black's mistake), and 14.Bxc6 bxc6 15.exd6 cxd6 was fine. 16.Qxc6?? dropped the evaluation to -0.5, but 16...Qc5+?? gave it right back, and 17.Qxc5! dxc5 kept you ahead.
You were winning comfortably through 21.Bxa7, 22.Nxe2 and 25.Bd4. Then 27.Ng5? missed a back rank mate: 27.Re8+ Kh7 28.Rh8# was available. You still held +5 and played on.

The decisive slip came with 48.g6??. Your knight on e6 was attacked by Black's king, and 48...Kxe6 won it. 48.Nf4+ was the engine's move. After 49.g7 Kf7 50.g8=Q+ Kxg8 only kings were left, so the game was drawn.

review.turning_point: 48.g6?? Kxe6. You were at +5.2 but the knight on e6 hung to the king, and the game was drawn after 50.g8=Q+ Kxg8.
review.focus: 48.g6: in endgames, check what the enemy king attacks before you push a pawn. 48.Nf4+ kept the knight safe, and 27.Re8+ would have mated.

review.headline: A Petrov where you were far ahead, then nearly threw it away before White's clock ran out

sections.text: A Petrov where you were comfortable early. 10.Bxf6 Qxf6 11.Re1 Be7?! 12.Ne4 Qg6 was fine, but 13...Qh5? wasted time (13...Nd7 was the engine's move). White's 14.g4? gave you 14...Qa5!, and 15.b3?? 15...d5! put you at +3.2.

16.Ned2 Qxa2 17.Nb1 Qa1 18.Kd2 Bb4+ 19.c3 Qb2+ 20.Ke3 Bxc3 was a strong, forcing sequence. You kept grabbing material with 21...Qxc3 and 23...Qxb3, and 28...Qxe3+ simplified the queens for a clearly better ending.
29...O-O-O?? let White back in (30.Nxc6 was the engine's move), but 30.Nxe6?? fxe6! saved you. Then 36...Rxf2?? low on time threw away +5.7, going to -3.8 (36...Kc7 was the engine's move).
The ending was then a race. 49.Rf1?? Kxd4! and 51...c2! were strong, but 50...c3? gave a chance back. White blundered again with 52.Rc1?? Kd3, and the win came on time.

review.turning_point: 15.b3?? d5!. After 14.g4? Qa5! you were at +0.4, and 15...d5 pushed the evaluation to +3.2 and gave you a lasting initiative.
review.focus: 36...Rxf2?? at +5.7: with little time left, choose the simple move. The engine's 36...Kc7 kept everything safe.

review.headline: A Queen's Gambit Declined where you found 13...bxc5 and finished with a mating attack

sections.text: You played a good, solid opening: 1...d5 2.c4 e6 3.e3 Nf6 4.a3 c6, with 5...Qa5+?! a little loose but harmless. 6.b4 Qc7 7.Bd2 Be7 8.Nf3 Nbd7 and 9...b6 kept your position sound.
13.b5?? was White's mistake, and 13...bxc5! was the right answer. After 14.dxc5 Nxc5 15.Bc3 Nxd3 16.Qxd3 cxb5 you were two points up, and 17.Qxb5 Rab8?! was a bit inaccurate but fine.
22.f3? Bf5! was a skewer on the queen and the knight on b1, and you built up to +5.0 by move 25. 25...Qg3?? was the one slip (25...Qd7 was the engine's move), and 26.Qc3 was the answer, not 26.Rc7??.
26.Rc7?? Bf6 27.Bxf6 Rxd3 won the queen on d3 (+7). 28.Nc4 Rb2?! 29.Be5 Qxg2# finished it.

review.turning_point: 26.Rc7?? Bf6! After 25...Qg3?? White had 26.Qc3; instead the rook move allowed 27.Bxf6 Rxd3, which took the queen.
review.focus: 25...Qg3: you were at +5.0. When ahead, prefer the simple consolidating move; the engine's 25...Qd7 kept the lead.

review.headline: A Scandinavian where you were ahead for a long time before a run of mistakes from move 21

sections.text: The opening was fine for you. 1...Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.c3?! was a slow move, but Black's 7...Bxf3?? gave you 8.gxf3! and a good position. 9.fxe4 Qe6 left you at +3.6.

10.e5?? gave a lot back (10.d5 was the engine's move), and 12.f4?? was another step in the wrong direction (12.exf6 was better). Black's 12...fxe5? let you recover with 13.fxe5!, and 18.Qa6+ Kd7? put you back up at +5.5.

21.d5?? dropped from +4.3 to +1.2 (21.O-O was the engine's move), and 22.Qa6?? turned the game: 22.Qb4+ would have forked the king and the knight on c4. After 22...Ne3 23.Qxa7? Nc2+?? you had a chance with 24.Ke2, but the position was already difficult.
24...Nxa1 and 25.Qxc7+? (25.Rxa1 was better) did not fix things, and you resigned after 26.Qc8 Bg7.

review.turning_point: 21.d5?? Rxd5. At +4.3 you gave up a pawn and left your king uncastled, and 22.Qa6?? followed.
review.focus: 21.d5: you had not yet castled. The engine preferred 21.O-O, so get your king safe before opening lines.

review.headline: A French Bourdonnais that fell apart after 8...Nd7 let the knight reach f7

sections.text: A short game in which you were fine at first. 2.f4 d5 3.e5 f6 4.Nf3 fxe5 5.fxe5 Ne7 was a normal French set-up, and 6.d4 g6?! 7.Bd3 Bg7 8.O-O left you only slightly worse.
8...Nd7?? was the mistake, taking you from -1.7 to -4.3. The engine's choice was 8...c5, challenging the centre. After 9.Ng5 White's knight was aimed at f7.
9...h6?! made it worse. 10.Nf7 attacked both your queen on d8 and your rook on h8, and after 10...O-O 11.Nxd8 Rxd8 you had lost the queen for a knight. You resigned after 11 moves.

review.turning_point: 8...Nd7?? let 9.Ng5 and 10.Nf7 come with threats on the queen and rook; the evaluation fell from -1.7 to -4.3 and then to -6.9.
review.focus: 8...Nd7: before each move, ask which squares the opponent's knight can reach. 8...c5 would have hit the centre first.

review.headline: A Caro-Kann win after both sides dropped the thread, ending in a queen win on move 24

sections.text: A quiet game early. 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Nc3 Bg4 5.d4 Nf6 6.Be2 Nc6 7.Be3 e6 and 10.h3 Bxf3 11.Bxf3 were all fine. 12.Ne2 and 13.b3 Nb4 14.c3 Nc6 kept the position level, with Black pressing a bit.
17.b4 Nc4 created a problem. 18.Qb1?? was the mistake, dropping from +0.2 to -3.4; 18.Bg5 was the engine's move. But Black replied 18...Nxe3??, and 19.Rxe3! got you back into the game.
19...Qc7?? (19...a5 was the engine's move) gave you +4.0. 20.Qb3! was the best answer and kept the pressure, and 21.Nxe4 dxe4 22.Bxe4 Bxb4 23.Qxb4 won material.
23...Qa5 hung the queen, and 24.Qxa5 ended the game.

review.turning_point: 19...Qc7?? 20.Qb3!. After 18...Nxe3?? your 19.Rxe3 was good, and the follow-up took you to +3.9.
review.focus: 18.Qb1: when a knight lands on c4 and attacks your bishop, a developing move like 18.Bg5 beats a passive queen retreat. It would have kept you at +0.2.

review.headline: A Tennison Gambit where you refuted White early, then lost the queen on move 14

sections.text: White opened with the Tennison Gambit, and 2...dxe4! was a good answer. 3.Ne5 f6?? gave it back (3...Nd7 was the engine's move), but 4.Qh5+ g6 5.Bc4?? let you off, and 5...fxe5! won a knight.
6.Qxe5 Nf6 7.g4 Bg7 8.g5 Nh5 9.Qxe4 Bf5?! was a bit loose, and 10.Qxb7 grabbed a pawn. You held on with 10...Nd7 11.Qd5 Ne5 12.Qb5+ Qd7, and the evaluation stayed at about +4 for you.

14.Bb5 hit your queen, which was tied to the king on e8. 14...O-O?? ignored the attack: after 15.Bxd7 Bxd7 you had lost the queen for a bishop, and the engine's 14...Nf3+ would have forced 15.Qxf3 Qxb5.
16.Qxc7 Bf5?? was a final slip (16...Bc6 was the engine's move), and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 14...O-O?? ignored the attack on your queen, and 15.Bxd7 won it; 14...Nf3+ was the engine's move.
review.focus: 14...O-O: when your queen is attacked, look for a forcing check first. 14...Nf3+ was the engine's move.

review.headline: An Italian you won by converting a slow, careful ending, helped by Black's 15...Re7

sections.text: A slow Italian. 8.Bb3?! Qd7 9.Nc3 O-O 10.Nd5? Bxd5 11.exd5 Nd4 was a bit awkward: the engine's choice at move 10 was 10.Bxc5. Then 12.Nxd4?? exd4 13.Bxd4 put you at -4.7 (12.Bxd4 was better).
Black returned the favour: 13...Rae8?? (13...Bxd4 was the engine's move) and your 14.Be3! was the right answer. After 14...Bxe3 15.fxe3 Re7?? 16.e4!, you were back to +0.9.
17.O-O-O c6 18.Rhf1?! cxd5 19.Qf2? dxe4 20.Qxa7 was a risky stretch (19.Rxf6 was better). But Black blundered again with 22...b5??, and 23.Qxd7! Rxd7 24.Rfxe2 Rxe2 25.Rxe2 took you to +3.
You converted carefully, with 28.Rxb5, 38.a8=Q and 50.b8=Q+, and 55.Qh5# was mate.

review.turning_point: 15...Re7?? 16.e4!. Black needed 15...Rxe3; instead the rook move turned -2.6 into +1.2, and you kept the initiative.
review.focus: 12.Nxd4: the engine preferred 12.Bxd4. When a piece is attacked, compare recaptures before taking with the first piece.

review.headline: A lively Bishop's Opening where you were winning at times, but loose moves and the clock undid you

sections.text: You answered 1.e4 with ...e5 and ...d5, trading into a comfortable game. 6...a6 and 7...b5 grabbed queenside space but loosened your pieces, and White's 9.Bg5? was a genuine mistake. You found the best reply, 9...f6!, and later 11...h5! also hit the right note after 11.Bg3 gave you a big edge.

The trouble was that you handed the advantage back. 10...g5 was a blunder that let White off the hook, and 13...Bc5 was the next slip; the engine preferred 13...Qd7. After 14.d4 e4? you lost a pawn to 16.Rxe4+ and were suddenly the one defending (-2.0).

You fought back well. 20.Rxe7?? was a blunder by White, and 20...Nxe7! was the right recapture: the knight left d5 and uncovered your bishop on b7 against the knight on f3, a discovered attack that left you well ahead.

21...Nd5? let some of that evaporate (21...g4 was stronger), and 23...Nxb4?? swung the evaluation from +1.5 to -2.5. Then 26...Qc5?? walked into 27.bxc5 and cost you the queen. The game ended on the clock, though the position was already lost.

review.turning_point: 23...Nxb4?? turned a healthy +1.5 into -2.5; 23...Rde8 kept everything protected. 26...Qc5?? then finished the job.
review.focus: Before each queen move, check which pawns attack the destination square: on 26...Qc5 the pawn on b4 simply took it. 26...Qd5 would have hit the queen on f5 and the knight on b3 at once (a fork).

review.headline: A Colle game decided early by 7...Qb6?? and a series of missed chances to hit back

sections.text: White set up a Colle with Nf3, e3, Bd3 and Nc3, and you built a sound Queen's Gambit-style position. The problem came at 7...Qb6??. After 7.e4 the engine wanted 7...dxe4, when the pawn on e4 attacks both the bishop on d3 and the knight on f3 (a fork). Instead 8.e5 won space, 9.exf6 removed your defender and you were clearly worse (-5.0).

You kept fighting. 11...Bxc3! was the best reply to White's 11.a3?, and 14.Nxe5?? was an error by White, but 14...Re8?? missed the point: 14...Qxe5 would have taken the knight and kept your queen active. After that the attack on g6 and h6 gave White the upper hand again.

White went wrong too, with 17.Qh6?? and 19.Rbd1??, and you found 19...Qg7!, a good defensive resource. The next big moment was 22...Bh5??; the engine pointed to 22...Qxh6 as the stronger move. Then 23.g4?? gave you one more chance, and 23...Nf3+ (a fork of the king on g1 and rook on e1, as well as a discovered attack on the e-file) was the answer. 23...Nf7?? let it slip.
After the queens came off on 24.Qxg7+ you made it to a long endgame, but 33...Nc5 (instead of 33...gxh5) lost more ground, and White converted.

review.turning_point: 23.g4?? gave you the position back and 23...Nf3+ was crushing; 23...Nf7?? let White off the hook instead.
review.focus: Look at checks and captures first. On 23...Nf3+ the knight forks the king on g1 and rook on e1, and on 22...Qxh6 you simply had a strong capture available instead of retreating with 22...Bh5??.

review.headline: You blundered a piece on move 5, but a fine tactical reply won the game and then you dropped two mates

sections.text: A Four Knights Italian started normally, but 5.Nxe5?? was a trick that does not work: after 5...Nxe5 6.d4 Nxc4 you were behind (-2.4). Quieter moves such as 5.d3 kept everything safe.

Black then went wrong. 9.Nd5?! looked risky but set a trap, and 9...dxc5?? fell for it. You found 10.Nxf6+!, a knight check that also unveiled your queen on d1 against the queen on d8 (a discovered attack). After 10...gxf6 11.Qxd8+ Kxd8 12.Bxf6+ and 13.Bxh8 you had won back everything and more (+4.8).

From there you simply played good chess: you castled long, pushed with h4 and g4, and used the open files for your rooks. 27.Bxe7 and the h-pawn run to 35.h8=Q showed clean technique, and you won on time.

Two moments cost you a faster finish. On 40.Qe2+? the engine had a forced mate in two with 40.Re4 c4 41.Qd5#. On 48...Kc5 Black erred and 49.Kc3? missed 49.Re3, again with a mating attack available. Neither changed the result.

review.turning_point: 10.Nxf6+! punished 9...dxc5??: the knight check uncovered your queen on Black's queen and the position turned from -2.7 to +4.4.
review.focus: Check forcing moves before simplifying: on 40.Qe2+? you had 40.Re4 and a forced mate, and on 49.Kc3? you had a similar mating line. Also avoid 5.Nxe5, which gave up a piece for a pawn.

review.headline: A clean, mistake-free win where Black over-pressed early and you punished it

sections.text: 1.Nf3 d5 2.d4 Bg4 3.e3 is a sensible set-up for you, and 3...f6?! (engine suggestion: 3...e6) loosened your king side a little, but it was only a small inaccuracy (-1.0). After 4.c4 e5 5.dxe5 fxe5 you grabbed the centre, and 7...Bxe2 8.Qxe2 traded off your active bishop.

8...Qg5?! (the engine liked 8...Qd6) invited trouble but the real mistake was White's: 9.Ng4?? attacked your queen but hung the knight, and you found 9...h5!, which hit it again. After 10.h4 Qxg4 11.Qxg4 hxg4 you were a clean knight up (+4.7).

13...Rxh4?! was a slight inaccuracy (13...Nf6 was a cleaner move), but you continued calmly. 16.Ng3? was another White slip and you found 16...Bxg3! to trade a strong piece and open the position further.

From then on you kept the initiative: 17...Ne4 centralised the knight, 19...axb4 and 22...Nxd5 took pawns, and you finished with the rook trade 31...Rxf4+. White's king walked into the centre and you won on time.

review.turning_point: 9.Ng4?? gave away the game; 9...h5! swung it from -0.5 to +4.2.
review.focus: Build your pawn structure first: 3...f6?! weakened the e6 and g6 squares for no gain, so 3...e6 would have developed with fewer risks.

review.headline: A short Scandinavian win where Black walked into a mating attack

sections.text: You met the Scandinavian with the standard 2.exd5 and 3.Nc3, then 4.d4 and 5.Bb5, putting pressure on the knight on c6. 6.Ba4?? was the first slip: 6.Bxc6+ bxc6 was the engine move, since 6...b5 now kicked your bishop back.
Black then played 7...b4?? (7...Nxd4 was better). That attacked your knight on c3, but it left the king in the centre and weakened the queenside.
8.Qf3? was a small inaccuracy: 8.Bd5 was the sharper move, but it still worked because Black greedily took with 8...bxc3?? (8...e6 was needed).

Then you spotted the finish: 9.Bxf7+! drove the king out with check, since the queen on f3 protected the bishop, and 9...Kd7 10.Qd5# ended the game in ten moves. Great vision, using every piece on the diagonal.

review.turning_point: 8...bxc3?? lost on the spot; 9.Bxf7+! followed by 10.Qd5# was the finish.
review.focus: On 6.Ba4?? you gave up your advantage (+1.3 to -0.5); 6.Bxc6+ bxc6 first would have kept the initiative, so check exchanges before retreating.

review.headline: A model Scandinavian where Black's queen wandered and you took it

sections.text: You played the standard Mieses-Kotroc line: 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qe5+ 4.Be2, developing with tempo. Black's 4...Bg4 5.h3 Bf5 6.Nf3 Qe6 was a fairly loose set-up, and you kept calm with 7.Nd4, which hit both the queen on e6 and the bishop on f5.
7...Qh6?? was the blunder. It left the bishop on f5 undefended and walked into 8.Nxf5!, which attacked the queen as well, so you won a piece with a threat attached (+5.7).
The rest was efficient. 9.Ne3 and 10.d4 developed the pieces, 11.O-O got the king safe, and 12.Ned5 opened the diagonal for your bishop so that 13.Bxg5 took the queen. Black resigned straight away.

review.turning_point: 7...Qh6?? left the bishop on f5 hanging, and your reply 8.Nxf5! won material and gained a tempo on the queen.
review.focus: A tidy game with no real errors. When an opponent plays a surprising queen move like 7...Qh6??, ask first what it stops defending: here the bishop on f5.

review.headline: An uneven French where you missed a clean winning shot and still won on time

sections.text: You played 1.e4 and 2.d4 against the French, and Black's 2...h6 and 4...Na5? were slow. 4.Bc4?! and 5.Bb3?! lost some time as well, and after 6.Bd2 Bxd2+ 7.Nbxd2 and 8.e5?! the game was fairly level.
Then Black blundered with 11...Ba6??. The engine pointed to 12.Rxa6 as the move: the rook takes the bishop and pins the a7 pawn against the rook on a8 (+5.0). Instead 12.Qg4?? let Black off (+1.4).

You missed it again on 13.Ne4??, when 13.Rxa6 was still available. After 13...Bxc4 14.bxc4 and 14...Nb4? you stayed in the game: 15.O-O-O Na2+? 16.Kb1! was the accurate reply, and the knight had to go back with 16...Nb4.
In the last phase 18.f4?! and 19.h4? were pushed without finishing the plan (19.d5 was the engine suggestion), and 20.h5?? again missed 20.d5. Black ran out of time first and you took the win.

review.turning_point: 11...Ba6?? gave you a big opportunity; 12.Qg4?? let it go from +5.0 to +1.4 and 12.Rxa6 was the move.
review.focus: Look for captures first. On 12.Qg4?? and 13.Ne4?? the rook on a1 could simply take on a6 with 12.Rxa6, and the same on move 13.

review.headline: A wild Petrov where both sides blundered and your counterpunch with the queen won

sections.text: You began with the Petrov, but 3...Bc5?? was a poor choice: the engine preferred 3...Nxe4, taking the pawn. White answered with 4.d4?, a mistake, and you found 4...exd4!. After 5.Ng5? you correctly castled with 5...O-O!.
6.e5 was strong, and 6...h6?? made it worse; 6...d5 was needed. After 7.Nxf7 Rxf7 8.Bxf7+ Kxf7 9.exf6 Qxf6 you were a little worse (-1.8), but White's pieces were still undeveloped.
After 10...d5?! White played 11.Re1?, which missed 11.Qh5+ (a pin against the d5 pawn). You answered with 11...d3??, a blunder (the engine preferred 11...Bf5), hoping for a trick, and White obliged.
12.Qxd3?? was the blunder. 12...Qxf2+! forked the king on g1 and rook on e1, and after 13.Kh1 Qxe1+ you had won the exchange and more. White resigned.

review.turning_point: 12.Qxd3?? allowed 12...Qxf2+!, a fork of the king and the rook on e1.
review.focus: On 3...Bc5?? and 6...h6?? you moved without checking the e-pawn and White's threats. The engine preferred 3...Nxe4 and 6...d5, so put the central pawn first.

review.headline: A solid Petrov with an exact setup, and a late knight trap that won a bishop

sections.text: Against a stronger player you chose the Petrov, and it paid off. 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 gave you the pawn back, and after 5.Qe2 Qe7 6.d3 Nf6 7.Qxe7+ Bxe7 the position was level.
You developed sensibly: 8...d5, 9...O-O and 10...Re8 gave you a compact centre. 11...Bg4 developed your last bishop, and your structure was healthy. White answered with 12.Be2.
12...Nh5?! (the engine suggested 12...Bd6) was the one inaccuracy: it hung the c7 pawn to 13.Bxc7. But it also set a trap. White fell for it with 13.Nc3??, and 13...Nxf4! won the bishop (+5.9).
From there you kept control of the e-file and White resigned a few moves later. Good use of the knight and good calm after the queen trade.

review.turning_point: 13.Nc3?? left the bishop on f4 hanging; 13...Nxf4! took it and the evaluation jumped to +5.9.
review.focus: On 12...Nh5?! you allowed 13.Bxc7. Setting traps is fine, but make sure the trap doesn't give away a pawn; 12...Bd6 was the safer idea.

review.headline: A tactical Italian where Black collapsed and your queen found the finishing blows

sections.text: You played 1.e4, 2.Nf3, 3.Bc4 against 3...h6, and opened the centre with 4.d4. After 5.Nxd4 Nf6 6.Nc3 Bb4 you had a good game, but 7.Bd2?? was a blunder: 7.Nxc6 would have forked the bishop on b4 and queen on d8 (+0.7).
Black returned the favour with 7...Bxc3??, and you recaptured 8.Bxc3!. After 9.Nxc6 bxc6 10.Bxg7?! Rg8 11.Bxh6 you were a pawn up and your bishop was strong.

12.Qf3?? was another slip (12.Be3 was safer), but 12...Nxf2?? was a blunder by Black. Their knight left e4 and unmasked an attack on your bishop on c4, but you found 13.Qxf7+!, a fork of the king on e8 and rook on g8.
After 13...Kd8 14.Qxg8+ Ke7 15.Qf7+ Kd6 16.Qxf2 you had the queen in the centre, and the king hunt ended with 17.O-O-O+, 18.Rhe1+ and 19.Bg5#. An exciting win.

review.turning_point: 12...Nxf2?? let you play 13.Qxf7+!, a fork of king and rook that decided the game.
review.focus: On 7.Bd2?? check forcing captures first. 7.Nxc6 dxc6 would have kept an edge, and a calculation of the knight fork on b4 and d8 would have shown that.

review.headline: A Petrov game where early slips on both sides ended with a crushing queen check

sections.text: You began with ...e5 and ...Nf6, then played 3...Bc5??, which the engine marked as a mistake: 3...Nxe4 was better. White replied 4.d3? and you followed with 4...h6? (4...d6 was needed), but White's 5.h3? gave the advantage back, and you found 5...d6!.
6.O-O O-O 7.c3 Re8 and 8.b4 Bb6 was a quiet middlegame. You kept your pieces ready with 9...c6, 10...Bc7 and the central break 11...d5, which opened the position in your favour.
After 13.Ba2 Nc6 14.d4 e4 you gained space and the e4 pawn cut off White's pieces. 15.Nfd2 Qd6 aimed your queen along the diagonal towards h2.

That diagonal was the key: 16.f3?? left g3 uncovered, and you found 16...Qh2+!, supported by the bishop on c7. After 17.Kf2 Bg3+ 18.Ke3 Qxg2 the king was exposed, and 19...exf3+ and 20...fxe2 won the queen, so White resigned.

review.turning_point: 16.f3?? opened the long diagonal for 16...Qh2+!, a check that made it +8.1.
review.focus: On 4...h6? you spent a move on the rook pawn when 4...d6 was needed. Develop and protect the centre before pushing side pawns.

review.headline: A gutsy knight sacrifice that White could have refuted, and you finished with a fork

sections.text: In the Three Knights Petrov, 3...Be7?! was a bit passive, and after 5.d3 Bg4 6.h3 Bh5 7.O-O Nbd7 the position was balanced. Then 8.g4 invited complications.
8...Nxg4?! was a knight sacrifice for pawns (-1.7), and 9.hxg4 Bxg4 left you behind. 10.Kh1 h5 11.Rg1 and then 11...Nf6? (the engine liked 11...c6) kept the pressure, but the engine liked 11...c6.
White could have met the attack with 12.Qe2 (a pin on the f3 knight). Instead 12.Qd2?? abandoned the defence of the knight, and you found 12...Bxf3+!, winning a knight with check.
13.Kh2 Qd7?! was fine, and 14.Qe3?? fell into 14...Ng4+!, a fork of the king on h2 and queen on e3. After 15.Rxg4 Qxg4 you were well ahead (+6.7) and White resigned.

review.turning_point: 12.Qd2?? left the knight on f3 undefended and 12...Bxf3+! swung the game from -1.9 to +3.0.
review.focus: On 8...Nxg4?! you sacrificed a piece for pawns, and only White's 12.Qd2?? saved it. Try to calculate whether the attack works against best defence before sacrificing.

review.headline: A Scandinavian where you survived an unclear moment and then took the whole point

sections.text: After 3...Qe5+ you played 4.Qe2?!, walking into a pin against the king on e1 by the queen on e5, and 5...Qxe2+ traded queens. 5.Nf3?! was a small slip as well (the engine liked 4.Be2). Still, 6.Bxe2 Bg4 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Bxf3 was a calm endgame.
Black went wrong with 8...Nd4?, hoping for a trap, and you replied 9.Nd5??, a blunder (+2.2 to -0.7) since 9...Nxc2+ attacked the king and rook. 9.Bxb7 was the better way.

You then finished with technique: 12.Nc3, 14.a4 and 15.a5 attacked the bishop on b6, 16.axb6 axb6 opened the a-file, and 18.Ra8+ Kd7 and 21.Rxh8 took a rook.

review.turning_point: 10...O-O-O?? let you play 11.Kxc2!, picking up the knight, from +0.1 to +4.5.
review.focus: On 9.Nd5?? you moved a knight that was guarding c2 and the rook on a1. Before each move ask what your piece was protecting; 9.Bxb7 would have kept everything safe.

review.headline: A near-perfect game: you accepted White's bishop sacrifice and attacked the king to the end

sections.text: You met the Three Knights with ...d6 and ...Be7, a solid Petrov set-up. After 5.Ng5 O-O White blundered with 6.Bxf7+?? (6.d3 was needed). You found 6...Rxf7! and after 7.Nxf7 Kxf7 you were comfortable (+2.1) with White's king still in the centre.
8.d3 Bg4 9.f3 Bh5 10.g4 Bg6 pushed your bishop out, and you replied with 11...d5, a central strike. When White opened with 13.dxe5 you recaptured with 13...Nxe5 and had a strong initiative.
14.Bf4 Nxf3+ 15.Kf2 Bxe4 won pawns and kept hitting the king. 16.Nc3 Nxg4+ 17.Kg3 Bh4+ drove the king into the open; each of your checks removed a defender.
The finish was clean: 18.Kxg4 Qd7+ 19.Kh5 Qf5+ 20.Bg5 Qxg5#. The engine agreed with every move you played, with accuracy at 96%.

review.turning_point: 6.Bxf7+?? was refuted by 6...Rxf7!, after which White's king never got safe.
review.focus: A clean game with no errors. Keep it up: 11...d5 and 13...Nxe5 show the idea of opening the centre when ahead in development.

review.headline: A smooth Italian where you won a bishop by removing its defender

sections.text: Against 3...h6 you opened the centre with 4.d4. Black's 4...Bb4+ 5.c3 Ba5 gave you the choice, and 6.dxe5?! won a pawn but let Black into the game; 6.b4 would have hit the bishop at once.
6...Qe7 7.Qd5 d6 8.Bb5 added pressure. The bishop on a5 was defended by the knight on c6, so 9.Bxc6 Bxc6 removed the defender, and 10.Qxa5 won the bishop (+4.4).
Black snatched a pawn with 10...Bxe4, but 11.exd6 cxd6 12.O-O and 13.Qa4+ Qd7 14.Qxe4+ took the other bishop with check, and you were well ahead. Black resigned.

review.turning_point: 9.Bxc6 Bxc6 10.Qxa5 removed the defender and won the bishop on a5.
review.focus: 6.dxe5?! gave back some of your edge (+2.6 to +1.9), whereas 6.b4 was cleaner. When your opponent's piece is stuck on a5, attack it directly.

review.headline: A messy Petrov that turned into a mating attack after White grabbed too much

sections.text: You played 3...d6, and then 4.d4 Be6?? (4...Nbd7 was the engine move) gave White a small edge. White replied 5.Bg5?, which did put a pin on the knight on f6 to the queen, but you answered with 5...Nbd7 and traded with 6.Bxf6 Qxf6.

Still, 16.Rxb7?? was a blunder and you found 16...Qxa2!. After 17.Rb2?? Qa1+!, the queen checked the king on the back rank, and 18.Rb1 Bxa3# finished the game.

review.turning_point: 16.Rxb7?? Qxa2! brought the queen into the attack and 17.Rb2?? Qa1+ ended it.
review.focus: On 12...a4?? a pawn push left the knight on d7 loose to 13.Rxd7. Before you advance a pawn, check which of your pieces it stops defending.

review.headline: You won a big advantage in the Giuoco Pianissimo, then let it slip into a draw

sections.text: After 4.d3 Nf6 5.Bg5 Qe7 6.Qd2 h6 7.Bh4?! g5 8.Bg3 d6 9.Nc3 Be6 you had a flexible position. 10.Nd5 laid a trap: 10...Nxd5?? (10...Bxd5 was safer) allowed 11.exd5!, a pawn fork on the knight on c6 and bishop on e6.

review.headline: A Four Knights where you were completely winning, then 29.Bxb4?? walked into a forced mate and the clock finished you

sections.text: You played the Italian-style Four Knights and Black answered 4...d5?, a mistake (4...Nxe4 was the engine's choice). You found the best answer with 5.exd5!, and Black's 5...Nxd5?? lost material after 6.Nxd5 Nd4 7.Nxd4 exd4.
You kept the pressure up with 8.Qe2+ Be6 9.Nf4 Be7 and 10.Bxe6 fxe6 11.Nxe6, and by 12.Nxg7+ you were way ahead. 14.Qc4+ Qe6+ 15.Qxe6+ Kxe6 simplified, and 17.Nxe8 Rxe8 kept your large lead.
The endgame went smoothly with 22.Bxd4, 27.Bxc5 and 28.Bxd6, and you were about +9.
Then 29.Bxb4?? was the fatal error. After 29...Rc1+ the engine sees a forced mate, where 29.g3 would have kept the win. The game ended on the clock.

review.turning_point: 29.Bxb4?? grabbed a pawn but allowed 29...Rc1+ with a forced mate.
review.focus: At move 29 you were up about +9, but the bishop capture 29.Bxb4 allowed a check. When far ahead, first ask where the opponent's rook can check your king; 29.g3 gave your king air.

review.headline: A Petrov where a bishop shot to h3 and left you far ahead, before the finish slipped

sections.text: This was a quiet Petrov with White playing slowly. White traded with 6.Bxf6 and you recaptured 6...gxf6, which doubled your pawns but opened the g-file. The engine marked the recapture as slightly inaccurate, yet 7...Rg8 put that open file to work straight away.

The game turned on 8...Bh3, which pins the g2 pawn against the rook on f1, so White could not simply take the bishop. White answered with 9.Nh4, and you found the best reply, 9...f5. That was a discovered attack: moving the pawn opened your e7 bishop onto the knight. 10.g3 then lost even more.

After 10...Bxf1 11.Bxf1 Bxh4 you were about five points up, and you kept it simple by trading queens with 14...Qxf5 15.exf5. The engine had you above +5 for most of the rest of the game, which is why your 93% accuracy is no surprise.
The one real slip came late, when you were low on time. At +6.2, 37...b3 let the evaluation fall to +3.9, and the game ended as a loss by resignation even though your side was still better.

review.turning_point: 9...f5 answering 9.Nh4 uncovered your bishop on the knight, and 10.g3 let the exchange win on f1 happen.
review.focus: With a big lead and little time, choose the simplest safe move. At 37...b3 the engine preferred 37...Rc2, which kept your winning edge intact.

review.headline: A messy Vienna where both sides blundered and your queen and rooks finished the job

sections.text: You were slightly worse from early on. 4...Qe7?! put the queen on a awkward square, and after 8.Ng3 gave you a chance (the engine moved to +1.1 in your favour), 8...Nbd7 handed it straight back. 8...exf4 was the engine's choice there.

The real damage came with 10...Rg8, which allowed 11.fxe6 and left you down material, with the evaluation around -6 after 11...Qxe6. You stayed active, though. 14...Nxh2 and 17...Rxg3 kept White's king under pressure.

Then White cracked. 18.Bxf7+ threw away a better line, and you found 18...Kxf7. After 19.d4 you missed the stronger 19...Rxg2+, but 20.Rf2 Rag8 still kept things dangerous, and 22.Ne2 gave back the advantage.
The finish was great. After 22...Rh6 White grabbed with 23.Rxf6+, and 23...Rxf6 left you comfortably ahead. 24.Qe1 Qxg2 was mate.

review.turning_point: 18.Bxf7+ was a blunder that went from -3.9 to equal, and your calm 18...Kxf7 started the comeback.
review.focus: Look at 8...Nbd7: with White's pawn push on f4 hanging in the air, 8...exf4 was the simple way to keep your advantage.

review.headline: A Scandinavian where a greedy bishop grab opened the door to a queen mate on f7

sections.text: You met the Scandinavian with the usual development. After 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qa5 4.d4 e6 5.Bd2, you had a comfortable, slightly better position with a lead in development.

The opening had a few small inaccuracies. 6.Qf3 and 8.O-O-O were not the most precise, and 7.Bc4 pins the f7 pawn to the king, which was good in principle. But Black helped you with 6...e5 and then 8...Bxc3, a blunder that took the evaluation from +0.7 to +4.3.

You found the right recapture, 9.Bxc3, which also attacked the black queen on a5. After 9...Qb6 you played 10.dxe5, winning a pawn and opening the position, and your queen and bishop were both pointing at the black king's side.
10...Ng4 allowed 11.Qxf7#, the exclamation mark move: the bishop on c4 supported the queen and the king had no escape.

review.turning_point: 8...Bxc3 gave up the bishop pair, and 9.Bxc3 with tempo on the queen set up everything that followed.
review.focus: At 8.O-O-O the engine preferred 8.Qg3, which kept your king safe and still attacked the g7 pawn. Castling long walked into Black's bishop trade.

review.headline: A Petrov slugfest where you survived a wild middlegame and mated on d3

sections.text: You played the Petrov properly with 4...Nxe4, but 5...Bf5 was the first slip, dropping the evaluation from -0.3 to -1.6. The engine preferred 5...Nf6.
White gave it back with 8.Bxe4, and after 8...Bxe4 9.Ne5 Nd7 you traded with 10...Nxe5 11.dxe4. You then pushed your d-pawn with 11...d4 and 14...d3, trying to cramp White.

17...d2 was your blunder, since the engine preferred castling with 17...O-O. White could have punished with 18.Qa4+, but 18.Ne2 missed it, and you found 18...Qxb2. White then compounded it with 19.Bxd2, and 19...Nxd2 left you three points up.
After 22.Nd4 Qxd4 you were winning for good, and 27...Nxe1+ turned your knight into a rook. You kept pieces coming off carefully until 37.g4 Rd3#.

review.turning_point: 18...Qxb2 and 19...Nxd2 punished two White inaccuracies in a row and turned a slightly worse game into a won one.
review.focus: Look at 17...d2: castling with 17...O-O was safer than pushing the pawn to a square White could attack.

review.headline: A Scotch where your opponent's pawn grab let you win a piece and then the queen

sections.text: You opened with a Scotch and after 4.dxe5 Nxe4 5.Qe2 Nc5 6.Be3 Ne6 7.Nc3 Bb4, you had a small edge. 8.O-O-O invited 8...Bxc3 9.bxc3, which damaged your pawns, and 10.g3 was another small slip, so the position was roughly level.

Then Black erred with 11...d5, and you replied with the best move, 12.exd6. After 13.Qb5 and 14.Ne5, the engine disliked both, but 14.Ne5 produced a discovered attack from the bishop on g2 along the long diagonal, and Black missed it with 14...f6.
You took advantage with 15.Nxc6, and after 15...Bxc6 16.Qxc6 you were a piece up. The bishop on g2 and queen were now far more active than anything Black had.
The best moment was 20.Qxh7+, giving up the queen so that 21.Bxd7 could win Black's queen in return. The rest was technique: 26.Re7, 28.Rf7+, and 33.Rh7# finished it.

review.turning_point: 14...f6 missed the engine's 14...Ncd4, and 15.Nxc6 won a full piece.
review.focus: At 14.Ne5 the engine preferred 14.Nh4, which keeps the same discovered attack idea without allowing counterplay. Check what the opponent can do before choosing a good-looking move.

review.headline: A calm win where one careless pawn push at move 11 let you pick off pieces

sections.text: Both sides played slowly in the opening. 2...Nf6 was a small inaccuracy and 6...e4 was another, because the engine preferred 6...Nc6. Even so, you were comfortable after 4...dxe4 and 5...exd3, winning pawns early.

The game was decided by 11.d5. You found the best reply, 11...Nxd5, and from there White's position fell apart. 12.Bxe4 Nxe3 13.fxe3 Qxd2 was a neat sequence, because it dismantled the pieces defending White's king.
After 14.Qxd2 Bxd2 you had lots of material, and 15...Bxe2, 16...Bxe3 and 17...Bxf2 simply collected loose pieces one by one. Your bishop went around the board picking up what was undefended.
From there 20.Bxc6 bxc6 and 22.Rxc7 Rd3 were about technique, and White gave up after 25.bxa5.

review.turning_point: 11.d5 left White's pieces loose, and 11...Nxd5 exploited it right away.
review.focus: Look back at 6...e4, which dropped you from +1.6 to +0.6. The engine's 6...Nc6 developed a piece instead of pushing a pawn that White could challenge.

review.headline: A shaky opening where you lost your queen, but White blundered into a mating attack

sections.text: This one went badly early. 3...d5 was a questionable idea, and after 4.exd5 Nxd5 you lost a pawn. 5...Qe7 and 6...Nb6 followed, and the evaluation sank to about -5.3.

White could have punished you with 7.Bxf7+, but 7.Re1 gave you a chance. You failed to find 7...Nxc4 and played 7...Qc5, which the engine marked as a blunder. After 8.Nd3+ Qe7 9.Rxe7+ Bxe7 you had given up your queen for a rook.
You kept playing well, and 10...Nxc4 won a piece back. White drifted with 13.d3 and 15.Bc3, then threw it away with 16.Bxg7, which you answered perfectly with 16...Rhg8.
17.Bc3 was another gift, and 17...Rxg2+ opened the attack. 18.Kh1 was the final error, and 18...Rg4+ 19.f3 Bxf3# finished the game.

review.turning_point: 16...Rhg8 and 17...Rxg2+ turned a lost position into a mating attack after White grabbed the g7 pawn.
review.focus: At 7...Qc5 you had a simple 7...Nxc4 available. Before you move the queen, check what is on the e-file and whether a piece is already hanging.

review.headline: An Alekhine where tactics swung back and forth and you won on the clock

sections.text: You played the Two Pawns Attack and chased the knight with 3.c4, 4.c5 and 5.Bc4. After 8...Bxc5 you were a pawn down, but the position was playable.
9.h4 O-O was a mistake by Black, since it castled into the pawn storm. But 10.h5 was inaccurate, because 10.Bd3 was better. 12.exf6 and 14.b4 were also not the most precise.
Then Black played 14...Qe4+, a fork of your king and bishop, and you found the right answer, 15.Be2. Black followed with 15...Bd6, which took the evaluation to +6.1 for you.
16.O-O threw most of that away. The engine's 16.Qxd6 would have won a piece. You kept an edge anyway with 18.Re1 and 19.Bxf3, and the game was won on time.

review.turning_point: 15...Bd6 gave you a winning position, and 16.O-O let it slip back to about +1.3.
review.focus: Look at 16.O-O. When your opponent leaves a piece hanging, check captures first: 16.Qxd6 won material.

review.headline: A Steinitz Ruy Lopez where one early pawn push cost a lot and the finish ended on the clock

sections.text: The opening went well until 7...f5, which dropped the evaluation to -3.1. The engine preferred 7...Na5, a normal retreat for the knight. After 8.exf5 you were a pawn down.
You then fought back. 10...Qxg5 was your best move after 10.Bxd5, and 11...Qxf5 won back a pawn. The game became level again after 12.dxe5 dxe5.
13...Rd8 and 15...Ne7 allowed White to get ahead again, and 15.e6 and 16.Qf3 looked dangerous. But you found 16...Nxd5 and stayed in the game.
18...Bxd5 was a clear mistake, since the engine's 18...Bxe3+ would have won material. 21...Kd7 then left a piece to be won, and 22.Rxf7+ ended it. The game finished on the clock.

review.turning_point: 18...Bxd5 let the advantage go, since 18...Bxe3+ was the stronger capture.
review.focus: Review 18...Bxd5: before recapturing, check whether a check like 18...Bxe3+ wins more.

review.headline: A Wayward Queen game where a tactical shot won a lot, but a long ending nearly slipped

sections.text: You played the Wayward Queen Attack with 2.Qh5, and after 3.Qxe5+ Be7 you were a pawn up. Black erred with 4...d6, and you found 5.Qf4. 7.Ne2 was a small slip.
8.Qg3 was a blunder, but Black missed 8...Nxg3 and played 8...Bxc1. You found 9.Qxg7, and after 9...Bd2+ 10.Nxd2 you were up two pieces.
After 11.Nxe4 dxe4 12.Qxh7 you were well ahead. You traded queens with 14.Qxe4 and kept a big edge with 16.Bb5+ and 17.Nd6+.
28.Nc5 and 30.Rxc6 let Black back in, since 30.Rh2 was the engine's choice. 30...Rb1+ was a back rank skewer, but Black missed the better 30...Rexe2+. You held and won with 44.Rxa4 and 47.Rxg8#.

review.turning_point: 9...Bd2+ was a blunder that gave you a winning position after 10.Nxd2.
review.focus: Look at 30.Rxc6, where the engine preferred 30.Rh2. In a winning ending, check your opponent's checks before grabbing a pawn.

review.headline: A Bishop's Opening where you punished a greedy knight and finished with a queen mate

sections.text: 3...Nf6 was the one inaccuracy of your opening, since the engine preferred 3...Nc6. White replied with 4.Ng5, which was an error because it left the knight loose, and you found 4...O-O.
5.Nxf7 looked greedy, but you found the right reply, 5...Rxf7 6.Bxf7+ Kxf7. That left you with a safe king and an extra piece in the position.
7...Nxe4 and 8.Qh5+ Kg8 were fine, but 9.Qxe5 was a mistake by White. You played 9...Bf2+ and after 10.Ke2 d5 11.d3 Nc6 you had developed all your pieces.
12.Qe6+ lost the queen to 12...Bxe6, and you finished with 13...Bg4+ 14.Kf1 Qh4 15.g3 Qh3#.

review.turning_point: 5.Nxf7 and your reply 5...Rxf7 won material after White's overreach.
review.focus: Look at 3...Nf6, which allowed 4.Ng5. 3...Nc6 defended e5 and kept the f7 square covered.

review.headline: A Petrov where a fork on move 9 should have won, but one wrong capture reversed it

sections.text: You played the Petrov well through 5...Qe7 and 7...d5. 8...c5 was a small inaccuracy, but it set a trap: 9.O-O-O walked into 9...d4, a fork of the knight on c3 and the bishop on e3.
That was a strong move, and White's 10.Nd5 gave you a real chance. The engine rated you at +5.0 at this point.
10...dxe3 was the mistake. It won a bishop, but 11.Nxe7 took your queen. 10...Nxd5 was the engine's choice, and after 11.Bd2 Qxe2 you would have won a piece.
The game ended soon after on the clock.

review.turning_point: 10...dxe3 swung the evaluation from +5.0 to -3.2, because the knight on d5 attacked your queen.
review.focus: Look at 10...dxe3. Before capturing, check what your opponent's last move attacked: the queen on e7 was in danger, and 10...Nxd5 solved that.

review.headline: A short Bishop's Opening where a queen sortie and a pawn storm backfired

sections.text: 3.Qf3 took aim at f7, but 3...f6 stopped it, and the early queen move was not ideal. After 4.Nc3 Nge7, Black was fine.
5.g4 was the key mistake, since it weakened your king and the engine preferred 5.Nge2. Black replied with 5...a6, which was inaccurate, and you followed with 6.g5.
6...b5 was a mistake by Black, but 7.Qh5+ was your blunder. The engine preferred 7.gxf6, and after 7...Ng6 the queen was stuck on the edge.
The game was actually near equal after 8...Nd4 (about +0.5 for Black), so resigning was premature.

review.turning_point: 7.Qh5+ took you from +1.6 to -1.6, and the queen had nowhere useful to go.
review.focus: Look at 5.g4. A pawn push in front of your own king before you have castled is risky, and 5.Nge2 would have kept things solid.

review.headline: A Philidor where an early bishop mistake cost a piece and the middlegame never recovered

sections.text: 4.Bg5 and 5.Qd2 were slightly inaccurate, but the position was equal until 6.Bh4. That was a blunder: 6.Bxe7 Nxe7 was safer, while 6.Bh4 allowed 6...Bxh4 with a knight to win on h4.
Black missed it with 6...g5, and you found 7.Bg3. That was a good recovery and kept the game level.
8.Nc3 and 9.Nd5 were both mistakes, though Black misplayed with 8...a6 and 9...Bxd5. After 10.exd5 Nd4 11.Nxd4 exd4 you had regained the balance.
14.f4 was the final blunder, since it lost a pawn to 14...Nxd5, and 15...hxg5 followed. You resigned in a worse position.

review.turning_point: 6.Bh4 allowed a knight to be won, and the slips at 8.Nc3 and 9.Nd5 then added up.
review.focus: Look at 6.Bh4. Before retreating a bishop, count what attacks it: 6.Bxe7 Nxe7 was the simple trade.

review.headline: A Queen's Pawn game where a calm setup was rewarded by a discovered check winning the queen

sections.text: You set up a classical structure with 2...e6, 4...Be7 and 5...O-O. White built a Stonewall-like setup, but you responded with 6...Nbd7 and 7...b6, and everything was solid.
After 10.Ba6 Qc7 11.Bxb7 Qxb7, 12...bxc5 was a small inaccuracy, since 12...Nxc5 was better. You still held the balance with 14...d4.
16.Nf5 was a blunder, and you found 16...Bc5. White then played 17.a3, another blunder.
17...d3+ was a discovered check from the bishop on c5, and it also attacked the queen. After 18.Kh1 dxe2 you had won the queen, and you finished with 20...gxf5.

review.turning_point: 17...d3+ was a discovered check that won White's queen.
review.focus: Look at 12...bxc5. Recapturing with 12...Nxc5 would have developed a piece and kept your pawn structure intact.

review.headline: A Larsen opening that turned into a kingside attack and ended on the clock

sections.text: You started with 1.b3 and 2.Bb2, but 3.g3 was a mistake and 5.e4 gave Black space. By 10.c4 you were worse.
Black erred with 14...g4, and the best reply was 15.Bxh3. Instead 15.b5 was a discovered attack on the knight on e7, but 15...gxf3 won a piece.
You fought back and 17.Bxh3 helped. 20.Rfb1 was a blunder, since the engine preferred 20.Bxf8. Black missed 20...hxg3 and played 20...b6.
21.c5 and 22.Bxc5 were more errors, and the mating attack followed. The game ended on time while you were far behind.

review.turning_point: 20.Rfb1 took the evaluation from -0.5 to -6.1.
review.focus: Look at 15.b5. 15.Bxh3 took the bishop, and it is worth checking captures before pushing a pawn.

review.headline: Quiet Larsen opening, then a tactical blow-out where the opponent kept erring

sections.text: You went for the Nimzo-Larsen setup with 1.b3 and 3.g3, putting both bishops on the long diagonals. It was a slow, flexible start, and the engine felt Black was a shade more comfortable until the position opened up. Castling early and playing 7.Re1 followed by 9.e4 gave you a sensible center, and the trade on f3 left things level.

Your opponent then went wrong with 12...g6, which loosened the kingside and swung the evaluation to +4.1 for you. The engine liked 13.Qxf6 there, taking on the knight that guards Black's position. You chose 13.cxd4 instead, and the same idea was still on offer a move later with 14.Nd2 slipping again.

Black helped with 14...Bc5 (14...Bb4 was the better try), and after 15.Nc4 and 16.e5 your pieces were pointing at the king. 16...Nxe5 was another gift, and from 17.Nxe5 you were clearly ahead in material. 19.Nxf6 and 20.Qxb7 kept it going, and the trades at the end, 22.Rxe8 and 23.Bxe8, finished the job.
A win is a win, but you gave back a lot of advantage in the middle. Three times the engine's first choice was simply 13.Qxf6, 14.Qxf6 or 15.Qxf6, trading into a big edge.

review.turning_point: 12...g6 handed you +4.1, but 13.cxd4 let a lot of it slip; luckily Black kept making it worse with 14...Bc5 and 16...Nxe5.
review.focus: When the opponent weakens the king, look for the forcing queen capture first: at 13.cxd4 the engine wanted 13.Qxf6 straight away.

review.headline: A Scotch with early queen trade where you built a big edge, then lost on the clock

sections.text: After 3.d4 d6 4.dxe5 Nxe5 5.Nxe5 dxe5 6.Qxd8+ Kxd8, queens came off early and Black's king was stuck in the center. You developed with 7.Bc4, 8.Nc3 and 9.Bg5, and it was a calm game until Black slipped.

9...Be7 was the first real error (9...c6 was needed), and after 10.Bxf6 Bxf6 11.O-O-O+ Black's 11...Ke7 got worse. You found the right idea with 12.Nd5+! and then 13.Nxf6+, which drove the king up the board to c5 and put you at about +5.
Then 14.Bb3 threw most of that away (14.Nd5 was the move). The game stayed tricky, and Black's 22...Rg8 gave you a second chance, with 23.Bxg8 the engine's pick. 23.Rf7 let it go again.

Later you played accurately in the rook ending with 34.Rg5, 37.bxc4 and 43.Kd3, and reached +8.1 for you. But with the clock nearly gone, 40.Kc2 and finally 45.Rg6 went wrong. 45.f7 kept control, and you ran out of time in a position where you had been winning.

review.turning_point: 14.Bb3 gave away a +5.3 position; later at 45.Rg6, in a won ending, time pressure produced the final mistake.
review.focus: Time management: by 40.Kc2 you were playing the ending too fast to calculate. The strong move was 40.f6, pushing the passed pawn.

review.headline: Elephant Gambit that survived a slip and finished with a crushing material lead

sections.text: You met 1.e4 with the Elephant Gambit, 1...e5 2.Nf3 d5, and took the opportunity to trade your way out after 3.Nxe5 dxe4 4.d3. It was a sharp opening, and the engine had White slightly better by 6.Qe2+ and 7.Ne5.

8...f6 was the inaccuracy (8...Nc6 was safer) and dropped you to -2.2. But White didn't use it: 9.Nc4 was a big error and left your queen with a free capture, so you played 9...Qxf4! and the material swung to +3 for you.

White made another mistake with 10.Nbd2, and you collected pawns with 10...Bxc2. After 13...Qd4, 14.Ne4 walked into 14...Qxe4!, which brought material to +7. You kept going with 15...Qb1+, 17...Qxb2 and 20...Qxd2, and the lead grew to around +12.
Your opponent ran out of time on move 25 with you winning by a mile.

review.turning_point: 9.Nc4 was the moment: after 8...f6 you were worse, but 9...Qxf4! turned it around.
review.focus: Avoid loosening moves like 8...f6 when your pieces are exposed; 8...Nc6 developed and kept everything protected.

review.headline: Scandinavian where a few loose moves ended in a knight check and a time-out

sections.text: Black played the Scandinavian with 1...d5 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qe6+ 4.Nge2 Nf6. You had a comfortable edge, around +0.9 after 3.Nc3.

5.Nb5 started to drift. The engine preferred 5.d4, taking the center, and the knight trip only invited 5...Na6 and later 6...Qc4. Black's queen move wasn't perfect (6...Bd7 was better), but 8.Bf4 was another small slip. 8.a3 was the move there.

9.a3 was the real blunder, dropping you from -0.4 to -4.7. Black's knight on b4 jumped in with 9...Nxc2+ with check, and material went to -1. The engine's suggestion, 9.Rc1, simply guarded that square.
The game ended on time after only nine moves, so the clock mattered too.

review.turning_point: 9.a3 ignored the threat against c2, letting 9...Nxc2+ in with check.
review.focus: Before every move, check what the opponent's last move threatens. After 8...Nb4 the c2 square needed defending, and 9.Rc1 did that.
