review.headline: An unusual opening, a strong counterpunch, and then a won position slipping away

sections.text: White opened with 2.d4 and 3.d5 and you got a Nimzowitsch-style structure. You played 5...f5 and 6...fxe4 to open lines, and the engine considered the position roughly equal or slightly good for you. Your 8...Bg4 and 10...Bg6 maneuvers were a little slow but not harmful.

Then White blundered with 12.Bg5, and you took advantage by 12...Nxe4 and 14...Bxe7!, finding the best replies. 16.Qa4 was another mistake, and 16...cxd5! made use of it with a discovered attack along the a4-d7 diagonal.

However, 15...Bf7 cost you around three pawns of advantage; 15...Bxe4 was best. Later, 20...Be6 (20...Rhc8+ was right), 25...Ke8 (25...Bg5), and 29...Ra8 (29...Rxb2) let White back in. Your 23...Rxc5! was a nice tactical idea.
By 34...Bc8 you were short on time, and 35.Rxg7 settled it.

review.turning_point: 15...Bf7 threw away most of a +3.2 position; 15...Bxe4 was the move.
review.focus: At 29...Ra8 you could have traded rooks with 29...Rxb2; when you're ahead, simplifying is usually better than keeping the pieces on.

review.headline: A quick win in the Petrov where the opponent walked into a queen capture

sections.text: You answered 1.e4 with 1...e5 and 2...Nf6, then played 3...d5 against 3.Bc4. After 4.exd5 e4 5.Ng5, White's knight left the center and you had decent chances, though the engine called 3...d5 a bit loose.
5...Nxd5 was the mistake; 5...h6 was better and kept things safe. After 6.Nxe4 you were down a pawn in material, but 6...Qh4 and 7...f5 created threats against White's king and kept the game level.
Then White blundered with 8.Nc5 (8.Bxd5 was correct), and you spotted 8...Qxc4! to take the bishop. Material went to +2, and after 9.Qh5+ g6 your opponent resigned.

review.turning_point: 8.Nc5 walked into 8...Qxc4!, and you saw it immediately.
review.focus: At 5...Nxd5 you could have played 5...h6 to ask the knight a question first; check whether the capture hangs anything before you take.

review.headline: A messy Petrov with mistakes on both sides, won by a clear endgame technique

sections.text: The opening was a Petrov-style Three Knights game. You played 6...b6?! and 7...Bb7, and after 8.dxe5 grabbed with 8...Nxe4, which the engine did not like (8...Nxe5 was better). White replied with 9.exd6, and you played 9...Nxc3 (9...Nxd6 was the correct recapture).

White returned the favor: 10.bxc3 was a blunder, and 11...O-O! was a good response. White's 13.Nh4 and 14.f4 pushed further, and after 14...Qxd4+ the queen check hit both the king and the bishop on c4 in a fork. Still, 14...Bc5 was the stronger idea.

You then missed chances with 16...Ng4 and 17...Bxg5, but White's 18.Ne7+ was a big blunder and 18...Bxe7! took the knight. From there you were up material and your rooks and knight did the rest, finishing with mate on move 46.

review.turning_point: 18.Ne7+ was a big mistake by White and 18...Bxe7! put you well ahead in material.
review.focus: Look at recaptures carefully: at 9...Nxc3 the engine preferred 9...Nxd6, keeping your pieces safe and developed.

review.headline: Petrov where White's queen got hunted and you came out well ahead

sections.text: White chose 3.d4 and queen out with 4.Qxd4 and 5.Qe3. You responded with 5...Bb4+ and 6...Ba5 to pressure the position. After 7.b4?, you retreated with 7...Bb6! and the bishop stayed on the diagonal.
10.Qc4 was a clear mistake, and you answered with 10...Rxe4, hitting the queen. After 11.Bd3 Rxc4 12.Bxc4 you came out well ahead in material.

You continued with 12...Bxe3, 13...Qe7 and 14...Qxe3+, with a strong attack. Then 17...Nd3+ was a slip: it was a discovered check, but 17...Nh3+ was a forced mate. You still won because your opponent resigned.

review.turning_point: 10.Qc4 allowed 10...Rxe4, which left you well ahead in material.
review.focus: At 17...Nd3+, look for checks and mating nets first: 17...Nh3+ 18.Kh1 Qg1+ 19.Nxg1 Nf2# was forced.

review.headline: A wild Sicilian where both sides blundered and your attack decided it

sections.text: You opened 1.e4 against the Sicilian with 2.Nf3 and 3.d4. Black replied 3...g6?, which left the engine at +1.7 for you. You played 4.Nc3 and 5.d5, then 6.Bc4. Black's 4...b6?? was another slip.
You were then the one to wobble: 7.Bb3?, 8.Bg5?, 9.Nd2? and 10.Qf3?? let Black take over. After 12...Bxd1 you were down in material, then recovered with 18.Nxb6.

The attack started with 22.h6!, followed by 23.hxg7!. Black's 21...c4?? and 22...cxb3?? helped. You then missed the forced mate: 24.Bxf6+ exf6 25.Qh6+ Kg8 26.Qh8#. Instead 24.Bh6+, 25.Bg5, and 26.Bh6+ repeated.
Black eventually erred with 28...Nxe4, and 29.Qh8# finished the game.

review.turning_point: 22.h6! and 23.hxg7! broke open Black's king, though 24.Bh6+ gave you a chance to find a quicker mate.
review.focus: At 24.Bh6+ the engine saw 24.Bxf6+ exf6 25.Qh6+ Kg8 26.Qh8# mate. Before each check, list all checks and captures.

review.headline: Queen out early, then a sharp attack that cashed in when Black stumbled

sections.text: You played the Bishop's Opening with 2.Bc4 and brought the queen out early with 3.Qf3. Black replied 3...f6?, which weakened things, and you continued with 4.Qh5+ and 5.Qf3. 6.Nc3 and 7.Nd5 added pressure.

Black's 7...Be7 (7...Nd4 was best) and 8...Nh6 let you take over, and 10.Bxc6! bxc6 was a good strike. 11.Nb4 gave it back (11.Qxc6 hit the rook on a8 and was the engine's choice), and 13.Qd5 was another slip.
Black's 13...Rb8 let you play 14.Nc6!, followed by 15.Nxb8 and 16.Nxd7!. Material went up to +9 after 17.Nxf8. From there 19.Bxh6 and 33.Rxg8+ finished the cleanup.

review.turning_point: 14.Nc6! after 13...Rb8 started a run of captures that took you to a large material lead.
review.focus: At 11.Nb4 you could have played 11.Qxc6, attacking the rook on a8; look for the capture that hits two things at once.

review.headline: A quick knight sacrifice and queen attack finished in 13 moves

sections.text: Black played the odd 2...Qf6, and you responded well with 3.Nc3! and 4.Nd5, chasing the queen back. Black's 5...Bd6 allowed 6.Bg5!, another good move.
7.Nxf6+! was a nice shot, a real sacrifice, opening the f-file and taking Black's knight on h6 after 8.Bxh6. 5.d3 was less accurate (5.Nxe5 was better), but you were still way ahead.

9.Nxe5 was a blunder that dropped the advantage from +4.0 to +0.3, as 9.Nh4 was correct. Black replied 9...Bxe5, and after 10.Qh5+ Ke7 11.d4 Bxd4, 12.Bc4 was another error. But 12...d6 missed the defence 12...Qe8, so 13.Qf7# ended it.

review.turning_point: 12...d6 allowed 13.Qf7#, a mate that White's king hunt made possible.
review.focus: Keep your advantage: 9.Nxe5 gave away most of +4.0. Look for the quiet move that keeps everything protected, like 9.Nh4.

review.headline: A clean Scotch Gambit win where rooks took over the seventh rank

sections.text: You played the Scotch Gambit with 3.Bc4 and 4.d4, then 5.Nxd4. Black's 5...d5? opened up the position, and 6.exd5! was exactly right. 7.Nc3 was slightly off (7.O-O was best), but not costly.
Black's 8...Bc5 allowed 9.Nxc6, and after 9...Qxd1+ 10.Kxd1 bxc6 you kept the initiative with 11.Re1+. You traded bishops with 12.Bxe6 and continued 13.Rxe6+, 14.Rxc6 and 15.Rxc7+.
Your rooks were relentless: 16.Rb1 and 17.Rbb7 doubled them on the seventh. Black's 17...h5?? let 18.Rxg7+! come in, and 20.Rxf2 and 23.Rxa7 added up to a huge material lead. 35.Bxg5 finished it.

review.turning_point: 18.Rxg7+! after 17...h5?? cleaned up Black's kingside and put you winning.
review.focus: At 7.Nc3 the engine preferred 7.O-O; castle before trading off pieces in the center.

review.headline: King's Gambit Declined where you won the queen trade but let wins slip

sections.text: White played 2.f4 and you went 2...Nc6 and 4...Bg4, then 5...h5? and 6...exf4. 7...Nf6 was a slip (7...g5 was better) and White got an edge with 8.Bxf4.
Then White blundered with 9.e5?, and you found 9...dxe5!. 10.dxe5 was weak, but 10...Nxe5?? gave it back (10...Qc5+ was best). After 11.Bxe5 Qc5+ 12.Bd4?? Qxc4! you won a piece again.
14.Qd3 Qxd3! led to a queen trade with 15.cxd3 and you were ahead. 23.Bxg7?? was a big mistake and you needed 23...Kxd5 for a clear gain, but 23...Rhg8?? let it go.
The ending fell apart with 32...h4?? and 46...f5??, which turned an equal game into a loss.

review.turning_point: 23...Rhg8 passed up 23...Kxd5, which took the rook and kept a large advantage.
review.focus: At 23...Rhg8 check for free material first: 23...Kxd5 24.Bxh8 Rxh8 was clearly good.

review.headline: Wayward Queen Attack where a loose bishop check ended your game

sections.text: White opened with 2.Qh5 and you played solidly: 2...d6, 4...Be7, 5...Nf6 and 6...c6. After 3.Nf3 the engine liked you slightly. The position got interesting after 8.dxe5 Nxe5 9.Nxe5 dxe5.
10.f4 Nd7? was the first slip (10...exf4 was better). 11.f5 O-O followed, and 12.fxg6? fxg6! was a good reply. 13.Bc4+ Kh8 14.Qh6 hit your kingside.
14...Nb6 and 15...Qd4 were both inaccurate (14...b5 and 15...Bg4 were better). Then 16...Bh4+?? was the blunder, falling to -4.4. 17.g3 Qb4 18.gxh4 left you down in material, and 22.Qg7# ended it.

review.turning_point: 16...Bh4+ threw away a playable game; 16...Qd6 was the move.
review.focus: At 16...Bh4+ ask if the checking piece can be captured or just lost; 16...Qd6 kept everything protected.

review.headline: A fast win when White blundered the queen on move 8

sections.text: White opened 2.Qh5 and 3.d4, and you replied 3...g6?! and 4...exd4. The engine had White slightly better after 4.Qf3 and 6.Bg5, but you developed 5...Nf6 and 6...Bg7 sensibly.
7...Bg4 was a mistake in principle (7...Nbd7 was better), because White could simply take with the queen. But 8.Nf4?? ignored the bishop and missed 8.Qxg4.
You pounced with 8...Bxf3!, taking the queen. Material went to +10 and White resigned.

review.turning_point: 8.Nf4 left the queen en prise and 8...Bxf3 took it.
review.focus: Before 7...Bg4, ask what happens after the capture 8.Qxg4; 7...Nbd7 was safer.

review.headline: A crisp queen trade punishing the Wayward Queen, then a methodical mating attack

sections.text: White tried 2.Qh5, and you played 2...d6 and 3...g6, then 4...Nf6. After 5.d4 Bg7?, 5...exd4 was slightly better, but your setup was fine.
7...Qd4 was active, and 8...Qxe4+ took a pawn. White's 9.Be3?? walked into a pin on the e-file. Then 9...Qxf3! traded queens with a big gain, and 10...Bxh3 added material.

You then played cleanly: 12...Bg2, 13...Bf3, and 15...Bxd1. Through 24...Bxe1 and 25...Bxd2+ you kept increasing the lead, and your rooks swept up with 27...Rxf4 and 30...Rxd4+. The final 42...Ra1# was clean.

review.turning_point: 9.Be3 stepped into a pin, so 9...Qxf3! won heavily.
review.focus: 5...Bg7 was the only real slip; 5...exd4 6.Ne2 c5 gets the pawn trade in first.

review.headline: A Four Knights game with many mistakes, ending in a time-out loss

sections.text: You played 3.Nc3 and 4.d3, then 5.Bg5 against Black's 5...Bg4 and 6.h3 Be6. 7.Nh4 and 8.Be3 pushed the knight to the edge, and the engine called both slightly off.
9.Nd5?? was the first big error (9.g3 was needed), and 9...Nxd5 left you down material. After 10.Bxd4 you were back, but Black's 10...Nf6 was a mistake. 11.Be3! was a good reply.

Black gave it back: 13...Nh5?? and 15...Nh5?? let you play 16.Qxh5!, and you were ahead. 14.Qf3 had missed a chance (14.Qxe5), but you recovered. Then 21.g4?? left a piece to be won and 26.Rxg5 and 27.Rxf5 made it worse.
You lost on time at move 30 in a losing position.

review.turning_point: 21.g4?? turned +3.9 into -0.5, and the rook captures at 26.Rxg5 and 27.Rxf5 sealed it.
review.focus: At 21.g4 the engine wanted 21.Bd2; when ahead, make safe, simple moves.

review.headline: A four-move opening disaster

sections.text: You played the Van't Kruijs Opening, 1.e3 d5 2.Nf3 Nc6. 3.Nc3 was slightly off.

4.e4?? was the blunder. The engine's choice was 4.Bb5, creating a pin on the c6 knight against the king after the d-pawn had left d7. Instead 4...d4 hit your knight on c3 and you resigned on the spot.

review.turning_point: 4.e4 allowed 4...d4 hitting the knight; 4.Bb5 was the pin.
review.focus: After 3...Nf6, 4.Bb5 was strong because the d-pawn had left the king's side; check the pawn move's side effects before 4.e4.

review.headline: A Scotch where you were winning but a rook sortie ended in mate

sections.text: You played the Scotch with 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4, and 5.Be3. Black's 5...Nf6?? gave you +5.0, but 6.Qf3?? threw it all away. The engine's choice was 6.Nxc6, a discovered attack on the bishop on c5.
7.c3 was another miss, again 7.Nxc6. But you recovered with 8.cxd4! after 7...Bxd4 and 9.Bxd4! after 8...Nxd4??, then 10.Bxf6 and 11.exd5 took material to +5 or so.
Then 14.Rh3?? flipped it (14.Nc3 was right), and 14...Qxb2 took advantage. After 15.Rg3+ Kh8, 16.Qh5?? allowed 16...Qc1# mate. Your knight and rook on the back rank were never developed.

review.turning_point: 14.Rh3 threw away a winning position and 16.Qh5 allowed 16...Qc1#.
review.focus: At 14.Rh3 you should develop first: 14.Nc3 brought the sleeping knight out.

review.headline: Early queen trade, a sharp knight raid, one bishop giveaway, and a clean finish

sections.text: This was a Ruy Lopez Steinitz where White opened the centre early. After 4.Bxc6+ bxc6 5.d4, your 5...Ba6 let White open lines, and 7.Qxd8+ Rxd8 traded queens on move 7 with you a little worse.
White's 8.Nc3 was a slip, and you found the best reply with 8...Bd6!, putting the bishop on its most natural square. After 10.O-O-O O-O you were back to level.
Then White blundered with 12.h3??. Your 12...Nxf2! jumped in and hit the rook on d1, and after 13.Bg5 Nxd1 14.Rxd1 you came out clearly ahead in material.

You gave much of it back with 15...Be2??, going from about +4.1 to -2.8, because 16.Nxe2 simply took the bishop for nothing. You regrouped well: 18...Rxb2! used a pin along the second rank, and when White answered 19.Kd1?? and 20.Nxe5??, the finish was ready.

review.turning_point: 20...Bxc3 was a fork of the rook on d2 and the knight on e5, and it swung the game from about +0.8 to +5.7 for you.
review.focus: At 15...Be2 you were close to +4 and moved a bishop onto a square the knight on c3 could take. Before a forcing-looking move, ask what recaptures; the engine preferred the quiet 15...Bc8.

review.headline: A sound Philidor opening, a pleasant edge, and a flag that fell first

sections.text: You opened with 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3, and Black chose the Philidor with 2...d6. Your 3.Bc4 is the classic setup, putting the bishop on the diagonal toward f7 right away.

Black's 3...Bg4 went after your knight on f3. You answered with the sensible 4.O-O, and after 4...Bxf3 you recaptured with 5.Qxf3, which develops the queen and adds to the pressure on f7 together with the bishop on c4.
After 5...Nf6 the engine liked your position at about +1.8, and none of your moves were flagged as errors. You also have the bishop pair here, since the trade on f3 gave up a knight for a bishop.
The game was not decided on the board, though. Your clock ran out after only five moves, so a comfortable opening ended in a loss on time.

review.turning_point: There was no tactical turning point: the position after 5...Nf6 was good for you, and the game was lost on the clock.
review.focus: Your play through 5.Qxf3 was accurate, so the work is time. Know these opening moves quickly so you save minutes for the middlegame, and glance at the clock regularly.

review.headline: A wild Scandinavian where the opponent blundered twice and you missed the answers

sections.text: After 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qd4 4.Nf3 Qg4 5.Be2, Black's queen went hunting. 5...Qxg2 took a pawn and 6.Rg1 Qh3 left the queen far from home, but you were better at around +1.8.

7...Bg4?? was Black's first big error, and you needed to find the strongest reply. 7.d4 was fine, but 8.Bf4? let Black off the hook after 8...Bxf3 9.Bxf3. The engine suggested 8.Rg3 to keep Black's queen under pressure.

Then came 9...Qxh2??, a second blunder, and now your bishop on f4 could simply capture the queen with 10.Bxh2. Instead 10.Bxb7?? let Black's queen take the rook with 10...Qxg1+ and your position fell apart.
After 11.Kd2?! Qxf2+ the queen was running free. 12.Qe2?? stepped into a pin on the second rank against your own king, and 12...Qxf4+ finished off the game. Your clock then ran out.

review.turning_point: 9...Qxh2 hung the queen to your bishop, and 10.Bxh2 would have been winning. 10.Bxb7 let it escape and flipped the game from about +8.1 to -0.7.
review.focus: At 10.Bxb7 you grabbed a pawn when the opponent's queen was en prise. When a piece lands next to your pieces, first ask what it is attacking and whether you can simply take it.

review.headline: A long, bumpy Vienna where you survived early errors and converted a bishop ending

sections.text: This was a Vienna with an early bishop trade, 5.Bxe6 fxe6, and a slow, balanced middlegame. White's 11.Qd3? was a mistake, and you hit back with 11...Nxf3+!, an exchange that brought you back to level.
The next stretch was messy. 13...Qb6?? was a blunder, since 13...bxc6 was better, and after 14.cxb7 you were worse. Later 17...Qxb2?? was another slip, when 17...Qxb7 was the better capture.
White returned the favour with 18.Bxa7??, and 18...Qxb7! was a fork of the bishop on a7 and the queen on d5. After 19.Qxb7 Rxb7 the position was close to equal again.
You then let the pressure rise with 20...Bf6? and 24...Rc8?, but White's 26.Bxb2?? gave you the winning swing. After 26...Bxb2! 27.a4 Rxf1+ 28.Kxf1 you were far ahead.

You nearly spoiled the ending with 37...g5??, which cut a big lead to +0.6, but White replied badly with 38.g4?? and your king and bishop closed in. The passed h-pawn eventually promoted with 50...h1=Q.

review.turning_point: 26.Bxb2?? gave you the chance, and 26...Bxb2! won a lot of material, moving the game from about -1.4 to +3.6.
review.focus: At 17...Qxb2 you took a pawn where 17...Qxb7 kept things safe. Compare your candidate captures before choosing; the one that captures the most is not always the best.

review.headline: A messy King's Knight game where you recovered from errors and mated on the back of a big attack

sections.text: You went for a quiet setup with 3.d3 and 5.O-O, and Black's 6...d5?? gave you a big opening. The engine wanted 7.Bxc5 dxe4 8.dxe4 Nxe4 first; your 7.Nbd2?? let Black take the bishop with 7...Bxe3 instead.

Black's 8...d4?? gave the advantage back, and 9.exd4! was the right reply. Then 11.Nxd4?? was your second error and allowed 11...Qxd4+, dropping you to about -3.3. The engine preferred the quiet 11.Bd1.
Black returned the favour with 12...Ne3?? and 13.Nb3! was a strong reply, uncovering your queen on c1 against the knight in a discovered attack. After 13...Qa4?? 14.Qxe3! you were winning.
From there you kept control: 15.Rf3, 16.Rg3 and the bishop trade with 17.Bxg4 hxg4 18.Rxg4 brought the rook to the attack. 19.Qg5 g6 20.Rh4 and 21.Qf6 ended with 22.Rh8#.

review.turning_point: 13...Qa4?? after 13.Nb3! let you play 14.Qxe3!, taking the knight and turning a worse position into about +5.
review.focus: At 7.Nbd2 you skipped 7.Bxc5, which would have won a bishop. When your opponent pushes a pawn forward, look at captures before developing moves.

review.headline: An Italian where the centre opened, the queen was harassed, and you ran out of time

sections.text: You played the Italian with 3.Bc4 and 4.c3, and Black's 4...Qf6 was an early queen move. After 5.d4 exd4 6.cxd4?! Bxd4? the position was roughly level, and Black's 6...Bxd4 let a bishop be hit by 7.Bg5.
6...Bxd4 was a mistake by Black, since 6...Nxd4 was better, and it gave you a chance. 7.Bg5 was a reasonable try, and Black's queen retreated with 7...Qg6.
Your 8.Qb3? was the mistake: the engine preferred 8.Nxd4, taking the bishop. Instead 8...Qxe4+ captured a pawn with check, and you were two pawns down.
Your clock then ran out after eight moves, in a position that was already difficult.

review.turning_point: 8.Qb3 missed 8.Nxd4, and 8...Qxe4+ took a pawn with check, moving the game from about -0.1 to -1.4.
review.focus: At 8.Qb3 you passed on the chance to take the bishop on d4. When your opponent's piece lands on a square you can capture, look at that capture first.

review.headline: A solid Queen's Pawn middlegame lost to one oversight on move 17

sections.text: You played a normal Queen's Pawn setup with 1...d5 2...e6 3...Nf6, and after 5.Bxd6 cxd6 you built a solid position. Moves like 8...b6, 9...Bb7 and 10...Qe7 developed everything naturally.
Then you pushed 12...e5, and after 13.dxe5 dxe5 the centre opened. White's 14.Ng5?? was a blunder, and your 14...e4! was the best reply, gaining space and giving you about +4.
You then slipped with 15...h6?, where 15...Qe5 was stronger because it forked the knights on c3 and g5. After 16.Nh3 g5?! the advantage dropped but you were still better.
The game turned on 17.Nxd5, which attacked your queen. 17...Rad8?? ignored the threat, and 18.Nxe7+ took the queen with check.

review.turning_point: 17...Rad8?? missed that the knight on d5 attacked your queen; 17...Nxd5 would have kept you clearly ahead, and instead 18.Nxe7+ won the queen.
review.focus: At 17...Rad8 you moved a rook while your queen was attacked. Before every move, list the opponent's last move and what it attacks.

review.headline: A winning Owen Defense attack thrown away by a hanging queen

sections.text: You played the main plan against 1...b6 with 2.d4, 3.Bd3 and 4.e5. Black's 4...Nd7?? was an error, and your 5.Nf3? missed 5.e6, but you kept an edge anyway.
After 8.Re1 f6? you slipped with 9.Nbd2??, but 9...fxe5 10.Nxe5 Bxe5 11.dxe5 left you still ahead. Black's 14...Bxf3? was a mistake and your recapture 15.Qxf3! led to +8.
16.Qa8+ checked along the back rank, and you kept hunting with 17.Ba6+ and 18.Bb5+. 20.Qxb8+ won more material, and by 22.axb5 you were crushing.
Your clock was getting low. 25.Bg3?? let Black off with 25...Kg6??, and 26.Qxe6+ Kh5 still won. But 27.Qf5?? walked into 27...Rxf5, which took your queen.

review.turning_point: 27.Qf5?? hung the queen to the rook on f8, going from about +6.8 to -3.8 in one move.
review.focus: At 27.Qf5 you gave up a winning position. When you are low on time, play the simple solid move such as 27.Rad1, and check whether your queen can be captured before you move it.

review.headline: A Vienna where one missed capture on move 9 left you slightly worse

sections.text: You met 2.Nc3 with 2...d6 and 3...Nc6, and after 5.d4 Nf6 6.dxe5 dxe5 7.Qxd8+ Nxd8?! the queens came off. White won a pawn with 8.Nxe5, and you answered with 8...Bb4.
White's 9.Bc4?? was a blunder, and the engine suggested 9...Nxe4, regaining the pawn at once. Instead 9...O-O?? let White back in, dropping you from about +0.2 to -1.8.
White's 10.O-O? was a mistake, and you found 10...Bxc3!, damaging the pawn structure after 11.bxc3. 12...Rxe4 won the pawn back and the game was balanced.
The rest was a slow manoeuvring fight. 17.Bxe6 Bxe6 18.Ne5 gave White the more active pieces, and after 21.f4 Re7?! 22.Nc6 you resigned, even though the engine did not see the position as decided.

review.turning_point: 9...O-O?? missed 9...Nxe4 and swung the game from about +0.2 to -1.8 for you.
review.focus: At 9...O-O you castled instead of capturing 9...Nxe4. Check loose pawns and captures before routine moves, and avoid resigning when the evaluation is still close.

review.headline: A Wayward Queen game where you survived an attack and finished with 35...Qxg2#

sections.text: White opened with 2.Qh5 and 3.Bc4, and you played the solid 2...d6, 3...g6 and 5...Bg7. 7...Bg4?! and 8...Nc6 got you out of the opening in decent shape, and you then took the initiative with 9...Nd4.
White's 13.Bd5?? was a blunder, but 13...b4 and then 14...bxa3?? gave it back. The engine wanted 14...Nxd5 first, which would have won more material.
You fought back with 17...Nxd5 and 19...exd4+, then 20...Be2+ kept White's king on the run. Some inaccurate moves like 22...Bg4? and 25...Bb5? let the lead shrink.
The decisive blow came after 24.Rxb2? Rxb2!. Then White's 26.Qxd4?? allowed 26...Qxd4+!, winning the queen, and the attack ended with 35...Qxg2#.

review.turning_point: 26.Qxd4?? offered a queen trade you could accept for free: 26...Qxd4+! left you far ahead with a winning attack.
review.focus: At 14...bxa3 you took a pawn and gave up a lot of your lead; 14...Nxd5 was better. Prefer the capture that keeps your pieces working together.

review.headline: A Vienna that went wrong when the queen was left on d2 and you flagged

sections.text: You played the Vienna with 2.Nc3 and 3.d3, then 5.Be3 Bb4. 6.a4?! and 7.a5?! were slow pawn pushes, and 9.a6 bxa6 left you a pawn down.
10.Qd2?! put the queen into a pin: the bishop on b4 pinned the knight on c3 to it. Black's 10...Nd4?? was a blunder, and you found 11.Nxd4!, which brought you ahead.
After 12...Bxe2 13.Kxe2 Ng4?? Black blundered again, and you were around +3.8 at the best moment. 14.h3?! and 15.Ra4?! let the lead shrink.
16.Nd5?? was the big mistake, because moving the knight uncovered the bishop on b4 against your queen in a discovered attack. After 16...Bxd2 you lost the queen, and your clock ran out.

review.turning_point: 16.Nd5?? moved the knight off c3 and let the bishop on b4 take your queen, swinging the game from +1.3 to -4.3.
review.focus: At 16.Nd5 you moved a pinned knight. Before moving a piece that shields another, check what it was blocking; 16.Qf4 was safe.

review.headline: A quick Berlin-style win where White's queen walked into a knight

sections.text: After 1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6?! 3.Bb5?? the opening was unusual. The engine wanted 3...Nxe4, but 3...e5? was still fine and you got a solid game.
5.Nxd4 exd4 6.d3 and then 6...Bd6?? was your mistake, since it allowed 7.e5, which would have forked the bishop on d6 and the knight on f6. The engine preferred 6...c6.
Luckily, White played 7.Qg4?? instead, which left the queen on a square the knight on f6 attacked. That lost to 7...Bxh2+ 8.Kxh2 Nxg4+, which won the queen for a bishop.
White resigned after 8...Nxg4+, and the result was a short win with a lot of luck.

review.turning_point: 7.Qg4?? left the queen undefended against 7...Bxh2+ 8.Kxh2 Nxg4+, moving the game from -3.1 to +6.7 for you.
review.focus: At 6...Bd6 you left your pieces open to 7.e5. Before developing, ask what pawn pushes your opponent has.

review.headline: A wild win where the queen blundered and a pawn took it on d6

sections.text: You started with 1.Nc3 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4, and Black's 3...e5?? gave you a real chance. The engine preferred 4.dxe5, taking the pawn, but 4.Bg5?? pinned the knight on f6 to the queen and let Black keep the pawn.
Both sides then missed several chances. 5.Bh4?? and 6.Bg3?? kept the bishop running, while 5...Nc6?? and 6...Bg4?? helped you back into the game.
8...Bb4?? pinned your knight on c3 to the king, and you played 9.Bxe5?! to trade. 10...Bxc3+?? was another error, and 11.bxc3! was the right capture.
11...Qd6?? hung the queen, and 12.exd6! took it, ending the game.

review.turning_point: 11...Qd6?? put the queen where your pawn on e5 could take it, and 12.exd6! swung the game to about +7.
review.focus: At 4.Bg5 you skipped 4.dxe5 and let a free pawn go. Capture loose central pawns before starting your own plan.

review.headline: A chaotic Caro-Kann where both sides gave away queens and you won on time

sections.text: After 1.e4 c6 2.d4 Qb6?! 3.Bc4 you grabbed with 3...Qxd4??, but 3...e6 was safer. White replied with 4.Nf3??, and you followed with 4...Qxf2+??, where 4...Qxc4 was the engine's choice.
5.Kxf2 e6 left you without your queen, but White gave it back with 6.Qxd7+??, which you took with 6...Nxd7!. The game was suddenly level.
The middlegame was full of errors: 11...Ndf6??, 12.Bd3?? Bb4?? and 19.Nc5?? Rxe5??, which dropped a lot. By 23.Be3?? Rd1+! you had a good position again, with a rook on the first rank.
In the end 26...Rf3+?? and 27...a6?? missed 27...Rxe3. You won on time.

review.turning_point: 23.Be3?? allowed 23...Rd1+!, which won a rook and swung the game to about +4.8 for you.
review.focus: At 4...Qxf2+ you traded a queen for a pawn. Before checks and queen captures, count what recaptures.

review.headline: A wild h-pawn opening that you won when the queen came loose

sections.text: You opened with 1.h4?! e5 2.h5 Nc6 3.h6?!, an unusual pawn storm. 4.g4?? was a mistake, because 4.hxg7 would have forked the rook on h8 and the bishop on f8.
Black's 5...Nb4?? and 6...Na6?? let you back in, and 7.Nxe5! was the right capture. After 7...Qf6 you pushed 8.f4??, which was a mistake, when 8.d4 was better.
Black's 8...Bxg4?? was a blunder, and 9.Nxg4! took the bishop with the knight, attacking the queen. After 9...O-O-O 10.Nxf6 you won the queen and Black resigned.

review.turning_point: 8...Bxg4?? let 9.Nxg4! take the bishop with the knight, moving the game to +4.1 and then to +5.8.
review.focus: At 4.g4 you pushed another pawn instead of capturing 4.hxg7. Don't push on the same wing unless it wins material.

review.headline: A Center Game where you gave up the queen, then Black blundered back

sections.text: After 1.e4 e5 2.d4 Bb4+?? 3.Nc3 Qh4 4.Qd2, you went wrong with 4...Qxe4+??, where 4...Bxc3 would have pinned the queen on d2 to the king on e1.
You got the queen back with 5...Bxd2+ 6.Bxd2 exd4, but you were still behind after 7.O-O-O. White kept the edge until 10.Nf3??, which allowed 10...fxg5!.
11...c6?? and 12...Nf5? gave back some advantage. The engine liked 12...d5, which forked the bishop on c4 and the knight on e4.
White's 13.Ne6?? was a blunder, and you found 13...dxe6! and 14...Bxe6!. After 15.Nd6+ Nxd6 White resigned.

review.turning_point: 13.Ne6?? gave you the chance, and 13...dxe6! with 14...Bxe6! won a lot of material, moving the game to +7.
review.focus: At 4...Qxe4+ you gave up your queen for a pawn. Count captures before grabbing, and look at 4...Bxc3.

review.headline: A chaotic Beyer Gambit that you won by mate despite a stream of errors

sections.text: After 1.e4 e5 2.d4 d5? 3.exd5? Nc6?? the game was chaotic. 4.dxe5?? missed 4.dxc6, and 5.Qe2 f6? got you a better position.
6.Bf4?? was a mistake, when 6.f4 was better. After 8.Bxh6 gxh6 9.Nd4? Bg4? 10.f3! you kept the advantage.
12.Ne6 attacked the queen, but 12...Qxe6? 13.Qb5+?? was a big error, because 13.dxe6 took the queen. 13...Nc6+ was a discovered check, and you were suddenly worse.
Black returned the favour with 14...O-O-O? and 15...Rhg8??, and you finished with 16.Qxb7#.

review.turning_point: 15...Rhg8?? allowed 16.Qxb7#, a mate.
review.focus: At 13.Qb5+ you gave a check instead of taking the queen with 13.dxe6. Always check whether you can capture a piece first.

review.headline: A clean Vienna win after White's queen walked into a knight

sections.text: You met 2.Nc3 with 2...Nf6 and answered 3.d4 with 3...exd4, a calm line that kept things level. 4...Nc6 and 5...Bb4 developed with threats against the knight on c3.
6.Bg5 h6 asked the bishop a question. White's 7.Qxb4?? was a blunder, because 7...Nxb4! took the queen with the knight, and you were up a lot.
After 8.Bxf6 Qxf6 you kept the extra material. 9.Nd5 attacked your queen, but 9...Nxc2+ 10.Kd1 Qxb2 kept the initiative.
11.Nf6+ gxf6 finished things off, and White resigned.

review.turning_point: 7.Qxb4?? let 7...Nxb4! take the queen, moving the game from about +0.4 to +5.3.
review.focus: You played cleanly, so the habit to keep is checking every capture: 7...Nxb4 won because you saw it was safe.

review.headline: A four-move Bishop's Opening win on the f7 weakness

sections.text: You opened with 1.e4 e5 2.Bc4, aiming the bishop at f7, and Black replied 2...Nc6.
3.Qf3?! was slightly inaccurate, when 3.Nf3 was more solid. But it added pressure to f7 together with the bishop on c4.
Black's 3...Bb4?? ignored the threat. You took the chance with 4.Qxf7#, mate.

review.turning_point: 3...Bb4?? ignored the threat on f7, and 4.Qxf7# ended the game.
review.focus: At 3.Qf3 you brought the queen out early. It worked here, but 3.Nf3 develops a piece and keeps the same idea against f7.

review.headline: A gambit pawn-grab that unravelled after one queen move

sections.text: You opened with a gambit idea: 2.d4 d6 3.dxe5 and 4.exd6 won a clean extra pawn, and you developed sensibly with 5.Nf3, 6.Bd3 and 7.O-O. That is a good way to handle the Nimzowitsch-style setup.

Your opponent then played 8...g6, a real slip that took the evaluation to +2.0 for you. The most accurate reply was 9.Bg5, which would have pinned the knight on f6 to the queen. Instead 9.Bb5? let the edge shrink to +0.6, and 12.Bh6?! after the bishop trade on c6 was another small step away from your best plan.

The game turned at 13.Qd4??. That queen move allowed 13...Nxf3+, a fork of your queen, rook and king, and the evaluation dropped from +1.5 to -2.6. Your opponent missed it with 13...c5, which gave you a second chance, but 15.Kh1?? threw it away again.
After 16.Bg5? and 17.Qd4? you walked into a queen trade that left you worse, and 18...Bxe1 picked up your rook. From there the extra pressure on f2 was decisive.

review.turning_point: 13.Qd4 was the decisive error: it put the queen on a square where 13...Nxf3+ forked three of your pieces, turning a +1.5 position into a losing one.
review.focus: Before every queen move, list the opponent's checks and captures. At move 13, a quick look at 13...Nxf3+ would have steered you to 13.Nbd2 and kept your advantage.

review.headline: A short, sharp win against an early queen sortie

sections.text: Your opponent answered 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 with 2...Qf6?, bringing the queen out early. You did exactly what a coach likes to see and developed with tempo by playing 3.Nc3!, which already put you at +1.5.
Black followed with 3...g5?, trying to defend by pushing pawns, and you punished it with 4.Nd5!, hitting the queen and forcing it to retreat. The knight on d5 became a monster in the centre.
Then came 5.Nxg5?!. It won a pawn, but the engine preferred 5.d4, which kept more control. It hardly mattered, because Black played 5...f6??, opening the king.
From here you finished cleanly. 6.Qh5+! forced the king to move, 7.Nf7+ attacked the queen, and 8.Nxd6+ won it outright. 9.Qe8# ended the game.

review.turning_point: 5...f6 gave you a forced win: 6.Qh5+ drove the king up the board and 7.Nf7+ set up 8.Nxd6+, winning the queen.
review.focus: The only small point is 5.Nxg5?!, which gave up part of your edge. When you are already well ahead after 4.Nd5, prefer solid development such as 5.d4 and keep every piece working.

review.headline: A slow squeeze where small slips handed White the centre

sections.text: You met 1.d4 with a solid 1...d5 2.e3 e6 3.c4 Nf6, and for the first several moves the game was balanced. The first imprecision was 4...g6?!, followed by 7...Bf8 and the trade on f8 with 8.Bxf8 Rxf8?!. After that White was a little more comfortable.

You traded knights with 9.Ne5 Nxe5 10.dxe5 and 10...Nd7, but 11...b6? was the key error here. The engine wanted 11...f6 to challenge the pawn on e5 at once. After 12.b4 c5 13.bxc5, 13...Nxc5? recaptured with the wrong piece, where 13...bxc5 was better.

Credit where due: White's 15.O-O-O? was a mistake and you got back into the game with 15...fxe5. But 16...Nd7?? was the blunder. 16...Kf7 was the safe move, whereas 16...Nd7 allowed 17.Qxe6+ and took a pawn with check.
After that your pieces were tied up. 18...Ba6?? left a piece to be won, and 19.Nc7+ ended it. The engine suggested 18...Rb8 as the better defence.

review.turning_point: 16...Nd7?? was the decisive error: the position was holdable after 15...fxe5, but this move allowed 17.Qxe6+ and a collapse.
review.focus: Before you play a quiet developing move like 16...Nd7, check which checks and captures it allows. 16...Kf7 would have dealt with the threats on e6 and kept you in the game.

review.headline: A wild tactical game you had won, lost on the clock

sections.text: You went for a quick d5 French-style structure, but 7.Ne5 gave White the initiative and then 8.Qf3?? and 9.Bf4?? were both blunders by your opponent. You did not punish 8.Qf3?? with 8...c5, and 8...Bd6?? let the advantage slip back to White. Missing chances early was a theme.

The middlegame was chaotic. 10...h6?? gave White a free chance, but White returned the favour with 13.Be2?? and 14.Bxh5?, and you were alert with 14...Nxh5!. Then 15.Qg4?? allowed 15...Bxe5!, another good shot, which won material back and put you ahead.

You stayed ahead through 17...Qxb2 and 20...Qxe1, but 22...Nd7?? left a piece to be won. Even so, 25...Ree1! set up a decisive threat, and 26...Rf2# was available. In time trouble you played 26...Rh1+?? instead, and 27...Reg1+?? let White's king out.
You finally lost on time on move 34 in a position where you had once had a forced win. This one is about clock management more than chess knowledge.

review.turning_point: 26...Rh1+?? was the moment: 26...Rf2# won on the spot, and after the wrong check the win slipped away.
review.focus: At move 26, with a forced mate on the board, spend your last seconds checking every check. Practise playing the first twenty moves faster so you have time for moments like 26...Rf2#.

review.headline: An Italian that turned on a tactical swindle

sections.text: This was a Bishop's Opening game that went into an open Italian-style centre. After 4.d3 Nd4 5.Nxd4 exd4 you tried 6.c3?! and 7.Nxc3, a sensible gambit-style structure, but 8.Bd2? was a small slip when 8.Bxf7+ was the more accurate shot.
You stayed active with 9.O-O, 10.Re1 and then 11.d4 and 12.e5, opening the centre while Black was still behind in development. By 13.dxe5 Nd7 you were up to +3.6.
Then 14.Qb3?? threw most of that away, since 14.Qf3 was stronger. Your opponent answered with 14...Bxc3??, grabbing a knight but running into 15.Bxf7+!, a fork of the king and the rook on e8.

16.Bxe8?? was a slip too, since 16.Qxc3 simply took the bishop. But Black did not take advantage with 16...Bxd2 and played 16...Qxe8??, and 17.Qxc3! picked up the loose bishop and left you well ahead.

review.turning_point: 15.Bxf7+! was the key shot, because it forked king and rook after Black's 14...Bxc3. That swing turned an equal position into a winning one.
review.focus: Take the free piece first. At move 16, 16.Qxc3 kept everything protected, while 16.Bxe8?? let +4.8 shrink to +2.0.

review.headline: A dominant position thrown away by one greedy capture

sections.text: You played the Italian and got a comfortable game against an opponent rated higher than you. Black's 3...h6 and 4...a6? were slow, and 4.d4 followed by 5.dxe5?! won a pawn.
You then lost some of the edge. 6.Nc3?!, 7.Nd5? and 8.a3? all let Black back in, and 10.Qe2? gave up another half-pawn. But 9.b4! was a good response to 8...Nge7?, pushing the bishop away.
After the trades on e3, Black blundered with 12...Nxd5??, and you played 13.exd5!, a pawn fork of the knight on c6 and the bishop on e6. From there you won material steadily with 14.Bxd5 and 16.Bxc6.

By move 24 you were far ahead. Then 25.Qxh6?? undid everything, because it left your own king short of air and allowed 25...Rxe1#. The engine's 25.Rxe8+ was the winning move, a back rank blow that worked in your favour.

review.turning_point: 25.Qxh6?? turned a totally winning position into a loss by mate; 25.Rxe8+ was a back rank shot that kept everything under control.
review.focus: Before any capture in a won position, check your opponent's forcing replies. At move 25, 25...Rxe1# was the only thing that mattered, and 25.Rxe8+ ended the game on your terms.

review.headline: An early queen trade and a late rook slip

sections.text: Your opponent played the Three Knights with 4.Nd5??, which the engine saw as a real error since 4.d4 was better. You answered with 4...Be7?!, and the game quickly reached a queenless position after 9.Qxd8 Rxd8.

After the queen trade the game was close to level. You developed with 10...Nc6 and then pushed ahead with 13...c5 and 14...b6, which gave you a flexible structure. 11...Nd4?! allowed the bishop trade, but nothing big changed.
White advanced 15.f4 and 16.e5, gaining space, and you stayed solid with 16...Rdc8 and 17...Rc6. The position was still fine at around -0.5.

Then came 18...Rh6??. The rook left c6, which opened the bishop on e4 onto your bishop on b7, a discovered attack. After 19.Bxb7 you were down material. The engine suggested 18...Rc7, keeping the b7 bishop covered.

review.turning_point: 18...Rh6?? moved the rook that had been protecting b7, allowing 19.Bxb7 and ending the game.
review.focus: Before you move a rook or another defender, ask what it is guarding. At move 18, 18...Rc7 would have kept the b7 bishop protected.

review.headline: A long, stubborn win after surviving a shaky middlegame

sections.text: You met 1.e4 with the Petrov and traded queens quickly with 5.Qe2 Qe7 7.Qxe7+ Bxe7. That left a calm position where development mattered. White's 8.Bg5 and 10.Bh4 came with some pressure, and you castled and brought the rook to e8.

11...d5?? was an error that let White settle things, but White's 12.d4? gave it right back, and 12...c6! was a good reply. You then traded your bishop for a knight with 14...Bxf3 and built a queenside pawn storm with 18...b5, 20...a5 and 21...a4.
24...Ne2?? put your knight in danger, but 25.Re1?? gave you an escape, and 25...Nb6! was a precise answer. After 26.Bg4??, you picked up a pawn with 27...Nxa3 and stayed ahead.

The endgame was nearly decided, but 39...c5? and 40...b4?? let the evaluation drop from +5.2 to +0.8. White returned the favour with 41.cxb4?, and 41...cxb4! put you back on top. You converted over the next ten moves and White resigned.

review.turning_point: 25...Nb6! after 24...Ne2?? was the moment you saved the game. Later 40...b4?? nearly lost the whole advantage.
review.focus: In the endgame, play 39...Ne3 rather than 39...c5?. Keep your knight active and don't create new pawn structure issues when you are already winning.

review.headline: A Scotch where White threw away a piece and the queen

sections.text: This was a Scotch Game where you took the pawns correctly and traded on d4 with 4...Nxd4. White then blundered with 5.Be3??, which left you a knight ahead after the exchange. The engine wanted 5.Qxd4 instead.
You responded well with 5...Nc6!, moving the knight to safety while keeping the extra piece. You developed sensibly with 6...Nf6, which kept you around +3 for most of the game.

7...Ne5? was your only real slip, because 7...Bb4 would have kept the pin on the c3 knight and left White with a harder game. You stayed ahead and 9...h6! was a strong response to 9.Bg5?, asking the bishop where it wanted to go.
Then 11.Qg4?? hung the queen to 11...Nxg4!, and you ended up far ahead. The record lists this game as a loss, which does not match the board, so it is worth checking how it ended.

review.turning_point: 11.Qg4?? hung White's queen to 11...Nxg4!, and the position was completely winning for you by move 11.
review.focus: Your only real error was 7...Ne5?. 7...Bb4 would have kept the pin on the knight on c3. When you are ahead, trade pieces and keep your opponent's play restricted.

review.headline: A clean refutation of a speculative knight sacrifice

sections.text: You played the Philidor with 2...d6, 3...Nf6, 4...Nbd7 and 5...Be7, a very solid setup. The engine liked every one of your moves, and your accuracy was 95.9 for this very short game.
White then tried 6.Nxe5??, hoping you would take with the knight. The engine wanted 6.Bc4. This was just a pawn grab that would not work against sensible play.
You found the best reply, 6...dxe5!, which won a knight for a pawn and kept the evaluation at +3.1 for you. If White tried 7.dxe5 Nxe5, you would simply be a piece ahead.

review.turning_point: 6.Nxe5?? was the decisive mistake, and 6...dxe5! was the right capture, winning a piece for a pawn.
review.focus: You made no errors here. The one thing to check is how the game ended, because the record shows a loss from a position with +3.1 for you after 6...dxe5. Make sure you keep playing when winning.

review.headline: A French where a wrong capture was punished with a mating finish

sections.text: You met 1.e4 with 1...Nc6 and the French structure after 2...e6, 3...d5. 4...Bb4 pinned the c3 knight against the king on e1. Following 5.exd5 exd5 6.a3 Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 you doubled White's pawns.
9...a6?! was slightly loose, and 10.Ne5?? was a blunder in reply. You took with 10...Nxe5??, which was your own mistake: 10...axb5 would have won a piece. Fortunately the damage was small.
After 11...Bxb5 12.exf6 Bxf1 you were ahead again, and 13.Qxf1?? let you play 13...Qxf6!. White tried 14.Be3, but 14...Qxc3 and 15...O-O kept your queen dominating.
16.Qxb7? grabbed a pawn but walked into the finish. 16...Qxa1+! used the back rank and 17...Qxc1# was mate.

review.turning_point: 16...Qxa1+! was the decisive blow, using the weak back rank to force 17.Bc1 Qxc1#.
review.focus: At move 10, 10...Nxe5 let the engine score drop from +4.0 to +1.4. Check intermediate moves like 10...axb5 before recapturing, since the bishop on b5 was also under attack.

review.headline: A Bishop's Opening where your tactics rescued your slips

sections.text: You played the Bishop's Opening and 3.Qf3?! was ambitious. Black reacted with 3...d5?, and you took advantage with 4.Bxd5!, winning a pawn.
Several moves wasted some of the advantage. 5.Nc3? allowed 5...Be6?, and 7.Nd5? let Black trade bishops on d5. 5.Bxc6+ and 7.Bxe6+ were the cleaner choices.
9.Qc3? invited 9...Nxc2+??, a fork of your king and rook. But it was a blunder, because 10.Qxc2! simply took the knight and left you up a piece.

After 11.Nf3? and 12.exd5 Rxd5 you built a big lead, and 17.Bxe5 Qxe5 18.Nxe5 Rxe5 19.Qxe5 won more material. The record shows a draw even though the final position was strongly winning for you, so check how it ended.

review.turning_point: 9...Nxc2+?? let you capture the knight with 10.Qxc2!, turning a poor-looking position into a +4.1 advantage.
review.focus: At move 9, 9.Qd3 was the safe move. Avoid putting your queen on a square where a check can fork your king and rook.

review.headline: A solid game wrecked by two tactical oversights

sections.text: This was a Bishop's Opening where you got a decent position. 4.Bxe6 fxe6 traded bishops and gave you a half-open f-file at the cost of doubled pawns. 6...Nbd7?! and 8...Qe7?! were slightly passive, while 8.b4? was a mistake by White.
The pawn exchanges 10.bxc6 bxc6 and 13.dxe5 Nxe5 left the position about level. You had a playable middlegame with 11...Bh6 and 12...O-O.

14...Rac8?? was the real error. The d6 pawn was shielding your queen on e7 from the bishop on a3, so any capture by that pawn would open the diagonal. 14...c5 was the safe move. White missed 15.Qxe5 and played 15.h3??.
You then played 15...Nxe4??, when 15...c5 still fixed things. After 16.Qxe5 dxe5 17.Bxe7 the queens came off, but you were left behind in material and White won easily.

review.turning_point: 14...Rac8?? and 15...Nxe4?? both missed that the d6 pawn was shielding your queen from the bishop on a3.
review.focus: Before capturing or moving, ask which of your pieces is only defended by a pawn on the same line. At move 15, 15...c5 would have kept the position equal.

review.headline: An Italian where the opponent blundered a piece away

sections.text: You answered 3...h6 with 4.d4 and took the centre with 5.dxe5 dxe5 6.Qxd8+ Nxd8. The queens came off, but you won a pawn with 7.Nxe5, which kept you at +2.
8.O-O was sensible, but 9.Be2? was a small slip. 9.Bb5+ was more accurate. Black replied 9...Bb4?, a mistake that let you keep the edge.
10.Bd2? let the bishop trade, but 10...Bxd2?? was Black's mistake because 11.Nxd2! recaptured with the knight, a nice reply that kept your knights active.
12.f4 attacked the centre, and 12...Ng4?? let you win a piece with 13.Bxg4. You finished the game well ahead.

review.turning_point: 12...Ng4?? blundered a knight to 13.Bxg4, giving you a decisive material lead.
review.focus: At move 9 and 10, you chose quiet moves where 9.Bb5+ and 10.Bb5+ kept more pressure. Look for checks before settling on a calm developing move.

review.headline: A short Center Game win when Black won on time

sections.text: Your opponent played the Center Game with 2.d4 and you accepted with 2...exd4, taking a pawn. White then tried 3.f4?, which was a weak move since 3.Nf3 was better.
You hit back with 3...d5 and after 4.exd5 Qxd5 you were a pawn up with an active queen.
5.Nc3? hit your queen but cost White more than it gained, since your queen could simply stay in the centre. You retreated with 5...Qd8?!, which was a small slip; the engine liked 5...Qe6+ better.
The game ended on time after only five moves, with you comfortably ahead.

review.turning_point: 3.f4? was the key mistake by White, because it gave you the pawn and the initiative.
review.focus: At move 5, 5...Qe6+ would have kept the queen active with check. Choose checks that keep your queen in the game over passive retreats like 5...Qd8.

review.headline: An Elephant Gambit where you refuted a queen trap

sections.text: Black went for the Elephant Gambit with 2...d5, and you responded with the natural 3.exd5 and 4.d4. 5.dxe5 won a pawn.
6...Nf4?? was a blunder, because moving the knight from d5 was a discovered attack that put the queens face to face. The engine preferred 6...Nb4.
You found 7.Qxd8+!, the best move. After 7...Kxd8 8.Bxf4 you were a whole piece up, and Black had no compensation.
You then kept things simple with 9.Nc3 Bxc3+ 10.bxc3, 11.O-O-O+ and 13.Nxf7+. The evaluation was +7.1 at the end, but the record lists a loss, so it is worth checking how the game ended.

review.turning_point: 6...Nf4?? left Black's queen exposed, and 7.Qxd8+! won a piece by force.
review.focus: You played this game almost perfectly (accuracy 96.1). The thing to work on is simply finishing: at +7, keep converting rather than relaxing, and check how the result ended up as a loss.

review.headline: A Göring Gambit where you punished a loosening move and mated

sections.text: You met the Göring Gambit sensibly: 2...exd4 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.c3 dxc3 5.Nxc3 Nf6, and you got your pieces out with 6...Bb4 and 7...O-O. That gave you two pawns, while White had a lead in development.
White's 8.a3? was a mistake because 8.Nd5 was better. You hit back with 8...Bxc3!, which pinned the b2 pawn to the rook on a1, so after 9.bxc3 Nxe4 and 10...Nxc3 you were well ahead.
11...d5 gave you central control, and 12.Bxd5?? was a blunder as 12.Qxc3 was better. You took with 12...Nxd5 and kept developing with 13...Be6.
You then traded pieces with 14...Qf6, 15...fxe6 and 16...Nd4, and finished with 19...Qd2 and 20...Qxc1#. A very clean attacking game with 95.3 accuracy.

review.turning_point: 8.a3? let you play 8...Bxc3!, which opened the position and put you well ahead in material and development.
review.focus: You made no errors. To keep sharpening, practise keeping pressure after the first tactic, as you did with 10...Nxc3 and 12...Nxd5.

review.headline: A very short Kennedy Variation game that ended too soon

sections.text: You answered 1.e4 with 1...e5 and White played 2.d4, the Center-style break. 2...Nc6?! was an inaccuracy that let White gain space. The engine preferred 2...exd4, trading in the centre.
3...d6?! was another small inaccuracy. 3...exd4 would have been best, as after 4.cxd4 d5 you would have had a good fight for the centre.
After 4.d5 the evaluation was only -0.5, so you were slightly worse and still had plenty of play. The game ended after just four moves, which looks like a premature resignation.

review.turning_point: Neither 2...Nc6?! nor 3...d6?! was a disaster, but together they let White play 4.d5 and gain space for free.
review.focus: At move 2, 2...exd4 would have resolved the centre. When a pawn is attacked in the centre, trade it before developing the knight.

review.headline: A Scandinavian where you punished one error, then missed the winning check at move 15

sections.text: This was a Scandinavian where Black's queen came out early after 2.exd5. After 3...Qe6+ you chose 4.Qe2?!, which allowed the queen trade and took your small edge down to +0.3. You then developed sensibly with 5.Ngxe2, 6.g3 and 7.Bg2, and the position stayed level.

10.d3?? was your first real slip and put you at -1.9, but 10...Nd4?? gave it straight back. You found the right reply with 11.Nxd4!, a clean way to punish the error, and the evaluation returned to about +0.9.

The game turned at move 14. After 14...Ne7?? you were at +4.9. The move was 15.Nxe7+, which uncovers the bishop on g2 against c6 as a discovered attack, and the engine line 15.Nxe7+ Bxe7 16.Bxc6 bxc6 17.Rxe7 shows you coming out ahead. Instead 15.c4?? allowed 15...Nxd5, and with material at -3 the advantage was gone.

After that you were defending. 18.Ba5? slipped further, and 21.Bh6?? left you facing 21...Rxe1+ with material down to -6. 21.Be3 was the safer move there. A fair fight in the opening and a won position in the middle that slipped away in one move.

review.turning_point: After 14...Ne7?? you stood at +4.9, but 15.c4?? missed 15.Nxe7+ with its discovered attack from g2, and after 15...Nxd5 the evaluation was -0.2.
review.focus: Before every quiet move, list your checks and captures first. At move 15 the check 15.Nxe7+ was the whole game.

review.headline: You built a big advantage against the Hungarian, then let it leak away until 29...Bxc3

sections.text: As Black against 1.g3 you set up in the centre with 1...e5, 2...d5 and 3...Nf6. When White traded with 5.Bxf6?? you recaptured with 5...Qxf6!, the best reply, and from there you were comfortably better. Giving up the bishop pair with 7.Bh3 Bxh3 was fine for you, and you built a kingside pawn storm with 10...h5, 11...g5 and 12...h4.

The engine rated you around +4 by move 13, so this was a position to convert calmly. 13...h3?? let a lot of that go (+4.8 to +2.0); 13...d4 14.cxd4 hxg3 was the stronger break. You did get a nice moment later with 16...Nxe5!, picking the best reply to 16.Ne5?.
The next drift came at 21...f3??, which took the evaluation from +2.5 to level. White returned the favour with 22.e3?? and 24.Qb5+??, but 26...Qa3? and 27...Rd6? kept you from regaining control.
Then 29...Bxc3?? put you at -5.2. After 30.Qxc3 the queen hit both your queen on b2 and the rook on h8, a fork that cost material (-3). 29...Rhd8 was the calm alternative.

review.turning_point: 13...h3?? was the first big letdown at +4.8, but the game was decided at 29...Bxc3??, which allowed 30.Qxc3 to attack your queen and rook at once.
review.focus: At move 29, before taking 29...Bxc3, check which of your pieces the recapture would attack. Looking for opponent forks on every capture saves games like this.

review.headline: A wild Pirc where both sides threw away material and the final blunders at 27.Ne4 and 28.Kg2 decided it

sections.text: You met the Pirc with a big centre, then went for a kingside space grab with 6.h3 and 7.g4. It didn't work: 8.Bg2?! allowed 8...Bxe4??, but 9.O-O?? missed 9.g5, and after 9...Bxd5 you were behind (-2.5 after 10.b3?).
11.Bb2? and 12.Qe2?! kept falling behind, and 11...hxg4 took the pawn structure apart. Credit to Black though: 12...e4?? gave back a lot (from -5.8 to -1.7), and you were back in the game.

Your best chess came at 17.fxe5!, which opened the f-file and uncovered the rook on f1, a discovered attack. After 18.Nxf7? you forked queen and rook, but 18...Qd3?? and 19.Qxd3! let you take the queen. Good punishing move.
Then it went wrong again. 20.Nxe5?? threw away a huge edge, 24.Rxf6! was good, but 27.Ne4?? missed 27.Rxd6+, and 28.Kg2?? left you at -5.8. 28.Rxd6+ was the move both times.

review.turning_point: At move 27 you had +4.0 available and Black had walked into 27...Re3+, but 27.Ne4?? missed 27.Rxd6+, and 28.Kg2?? finished it.
review.focus: At 27.Ne4 and 28.Kg2, you were responding to checks without checking captures. When you have a rook-for-bishop capture with check like 28.Rxd6+, calculate it first.

review.headline: A well-played Philidor where you were close to winning, then the clock took over

sections.text: You played the Italian-style setup with 3.Bc4 and 4.d4 against the Philidor. 7.O-O? was a small slip, since 7.Qd5 was a sharper way to pressure b7, but you recovered quickly. 9.Bd2 and 10.b3 were solid and kept the structure sound.

The middlegame belonged to you. Black's 18...Qxc3? allowed 19.Nxc3!, a clean recapture, and the evaluation jumped to about +1.6, growing steadily as you bought pressure with 20.Bg2 and 23.e5. By move 33 you were at +3.4 with your king marching into the centre.

That's what makes the finish painful. From +3.2 at move 41 you were low on time, and 42.g4?? dropped the evaluation to -0.1, with 44.g5?? and 46.Kh7?? repeating the pattern. Black's 42...Ne3?? and 44...hxg5?? gave you chances, and 43.Bd3! was a good reply, but the clock ran out at move 47.
Overall, a quality performance until the very end: 79% accuracy with a structured plan.

review.turning_point: You were +3.2 at move 41, but 42.g4?? was played in time trouble and the advantage was gone; the flag fell later.
review.focus: In the endgame, 42.g4 was a hurried pawn push. When the clock is low, make the safest move (42.Bd3) and keep the king and bishop together.

review.headline: Black's queen raid worked because 8.Kd2 gave away an advantage that was already yours

sections.text: This was an Exchange French where you opened with 3.d4?! after 2...e6 and Black's queen recaptured on d5. The queen came to f5 and then g4 while you developed with 4.Nc3, 5.Nf3, and 6.Bd3.
7.h3 chased the queen, but it also left g2 undefended, and 7...Qxg2 took a pawn and attacked your rook on h1. The engine actually had you at +4.1 here, because the queen is in danger on g2.

The right reply was 8.Rh2, trapping the queen: 8.Rh2 Qxh2 9.Nxh2 Bd7 10.a3 keeps you comfortably ahead. Instead 8.Kd2?? let the queen escape with 8...Qxf2+, and your king was exposed in the middle of the board. The game was over soon after.

review.turning_point: 8.Kd2?? turned a +4.1 position into -2.5, because 8.Rh2 was the move that made the queen's raid fail.
review.focus: After 7...Qxg2, stop and ask what the greedy queen has left behind. The plan was to attack it with 8.Rh2, not to move the king.

review.headline: You were under pressure in a Colle, a good tactic at 18.Qxf4 went unnoticed and time ran out

sections.text: White's Colle setup with 4.Bd3, 5.O-O and 7.c3 was solid, and by 10.e4 and 11.e5 White had the space. You were already at around -1.2. 12...g6?! and 14...f5 were reasonable, but 15...Bxg5?! opened lines for White's bishop.

You were worse, and 16...f4?! (-3.3) hurt, but then White gave you a chance. 18.Qxf4?? took your pawn and put the evaluation at +0.5 for White. The move was 18...Nfxd4, which unmasks your rook on f8 against the queen on f4 as a discovered attack. After 18...Nd6?? you were back at -5.9.

You did find 24...Nxh6!, the best reply to 24.Bxh6?, and 25.Rxf8+? was a chance, but 25...Rxf8? should have been 25...Kxf8. With the clock low, 26.Bxg6?? and 26...Nxg6?? ended the game: 26...Nxg4 was the move, and after 27.Qxg6+ and 28.Qxh6+ you were material down (-3). You flagged shortly after.

review.turning_point: 18.Qxf4?? gave you a real chance, but 18...Nd6?? missed 18...Nfxd4 and the discovered attack on the queen.
review.focus: At move 18, loose-queen tactics: when the opponent's queen lands on f4 in front of your rook, look for a knight move that uncovers the rook. 18...Nfxd4 was the move.

review.headline: An Italian where early mistakes by both sides led to a messy win on time

sections.text: You opened with the main line: 3.Bc4, 4.c3 and 5.d4. Black's 6...Bb6? and 7...d5? gave you the initiative, but 8.e5?? gave it back and 9.Nc3?? put you at -3.5. 9.Bb3 was the right move there.
Credit to you for 10.Nxd5!, a strong reply after 9...f5??, and 11.Nxb6 won a piece. From there you were at +5, with 12.d5 gaining space and the bishop on c4 still strong.

The middlegame got messy. 13.Qd4?! and 15.e6?! were not the cleanest, and 16...Bxf1 took the exchange. 18.Ne5? let Black off: 18.Kxf1 was better. 19...Nf6?? gave it back, and 20.Bg5? missed 20.Kxf1 again.
With little time left, 22.d6?? was a risk, and 22...Qxd6?? left Black worse. 23.Qxf6! finished with a strong position, and Black ran out of time.

review.turning_point: 10.Nxd5! punished 9...f5?? and 11.Nxb6 put you clearly ahead. That's the move to learn from.
review.focus: Look at 9.Nc3: your knight step walked into trouble. 9.Bb3 was simple. Check what the opponent's last move attacks before developing.

review.headline: A Philidor where you missed a fork at move 6 and the clock ended a recovering game

sections.text: You played the Hanham setup with 3...Nd7 and recaptured on e5 after 4.dxe5 Nxe5. 5...Bd7?! was a little slow, and White made a serious mistake with 6.Bg5??
That was your moment. 6...Nxf3+ forks the king on e1 and the bishop on g5, with a strong initiative for you in the engine line. Instead 6...Nf6?? let White out, and the evaluation came back to level.

10...O-O-O? was another slip, and then 11.Bxa7? gave you a chance. 11...b6?? was the wrong answer; 11...Nxf3+ 12.gxf3 was better. White replied with 12.Bxb6?? and you found 12...Qxb6!, the best reply, and you were up material. 14...dxe5! was another accurate recapture after 14.Nxe5?.
You played well from move 12, and 17...Bxe2 gave you real material (+4). But 19...Nxe4?? left you with a piece to be won, and you timed out at move 20. 19...Rd4 was the right idea.

review.turning_point: 6.Bg5?? gave you a clear chance with 6...Nxf3+ and a fork on the king and bishop. 6...Nf6?? let it slip away.
review.focus: At move 6, when the opponent leaves a piece loose, look for checks first. 6...Nxf3+ forked king and bishop.

review.headline: A calm Queen's Gambit setup spoiled by 18...g5??

sections.text: This was a Queen's Pawn game where you played a Queen's Gambit Declined setup: 3...Nf6, 4...Be7, 5...O-O and 6...Nbd7. That was fine, and the evaluation stayed within a few tenths of level the whole way.

11...exd5?! was a slight inaccuracy, but the structure was still healthy. 13.Nb5 and 15.Ba3 kept White active, and 16.Bxe7 Qxe7 traded the bishops. 17...Qb4?! was playable but made your queen slightly exposed.

The decisive error was 18...g5??. It opened your king and dropped the evaluation from +0.1 to -2.2; 18...Qd6 was the calm move. After 19.Nxg5 you tried 19...Ne4??, aiming at the queen on d2 and knight on g5 with a fork, but 20.Ngxe4 simply took it and 20...Rxe4?! couldn't repair it.
You played 77% accuracy, so most of the game was good. It's the kind of loss where one impatient pawn move undid ten good ones.

review.turning_point: 18...g5?? loosened the king, and 19.Nxg5 made things worse; 19...Ne4?? lost a piece for nothing.
review.focus: At move 18, you were fine. When there's no clear plan, play a waiting move like 18...Qd6 rather than a pawn push in front of your king.

review.headline: A Queen's Pawn game where you were doing fine until the Ng5 and Qh5 attack on f7 arrived

sections.text: As Black against 1.d4 you played the Stonewall-like setup of 2...e6, 3...Nf6, 4...Be7 and 5...O-O against White's early 4.f4. 6...Re8?! was a bit odd, but 8...b6 and the position was fine.

9.e4 dxe4 and 10.Nxe4 gave you a decision. 10...Nxe4? let White recapture, and 10...Bb7 was the strongest. 11...Rb8?! then dropped you to -2.2. White returned the favour with 12.Bb1??, and you found 12...Bb7!, the best reply.

Then the attack started. 13.Ng5 aims at f7, and 13...h6?? was the wrong answer; 13...Nf6 held. After 14.Qh5, 14...Nf6?? was a blunder (-5.2): 14...Rf8 defended. 15.Qxf7+ took a pawn with check, 15...Kh8 16.Qg6 and you ran out of time shortly after.

review.turning_point: 13...h6?? and 14...Nf6?? let the queen and knight combine against f7, and the evaluation went from -0.6 to -5.2.
review.focus: At 14...Nf6, count attackers on f7: queen on h5 and knight on g5 against a single defender. 14...Rf8 added defence.

review.headline: A Two Knights where you were comfortably ahead but the clock and 32.Kf1 cost you

sections.text: In the Two Knights Defense you played the aggressive 4.Ng5, and after 5.exd5 Na5 6.Bb5+ Bd7 you tried 7.a4?!. Black took with 7...Bxb5??, and you recaptured with 8.axb5!, a good reply that opened the a-file for your rook (+1.0).

9.Nf3?? gave away much of the advantage, as 9.O-O was cleaner. But 10...Qxe2+? and your recapture 11.Kxe2! was the right way to take back. After 11...e4? you were around +2, with Black's knight stuck on a5, and 14.Rxa5 picked it up.
You played well in the technical middlegame, building from +2 to +4.5 by move 29. 21.d5? and 23.c3? loosened things a little, and 30.Nc6? was a mistake (4.8 to 2.7).
Then time pressure hit. 32.Kf1?? was a blunder that left you at -3.3, but Black replied 32...h5?? and you recovered with 33.Kg2!. The position stayed at +4 or more but you flagged on move 41.

review.turning_point: 32.Kf1?? briefly flipped the evaluation, but even after you recovered at 33.Kg2! the clock decided the game.
review.focus: From move 30 on you were low on time with a winning position. Use simple, safe moves such as 32.Nd4 and keep the king active rather than long knight maneuvers.

review.headline: A short Winawer where a queen raid with 10...Qg2! won on the clock

sections.text: As Black against 1.d4 you chose 2...e6 and 3...Bb4 against 3.e4, a Winawer-style setup. White pushed with 4.e5 and you challenged it with 4...f6, which is a principled reply. 6...fxe5 took the pawn and 7.Nxe5 recaptured.

7...Nxd4?! grabbed a pawn and was a little risky, but 8.Bd3?? was White's blunder; 8.Qh5+ was the stronger move. You answered with 8...Qh4?, which was a mistake (+0.8 to -0.5). 8...Nf6 was the calmer alternative.

White then went wrong again: 9.g3 Qh3 and 10.Nf3?? let you play 10...Qg2!, the best reply, attacking the rook on h1 and giving you a clear advantage at +2.9. 10.Nb5 was the better try. White ran out of time soon after.

review.turning_point: 10...Qg2! punished 10.Nf3?? and left White with a bad position; the clock decided the game.
review.focus: At 8...Qh4, you went queen-first before developing. 8...Nf6 would have been a more solid developing move.

review.headline: A fast Italian attack that ended with 17.Qxg7#

sections.text: You played the main line of the Italian with 3.Bc4, 4.c3, 5.d4 and 6.cxd4, and after 6...Bb4+ 7.Nc3 Bxc3+ 8.bxc3 you had a healthy centre. Black's 8...d6? lost a bit of ground (+2.6).
You didn't play the most precise moves. 9.Ba3? and 10.O-O?? were slightly inaccurate, since 9.Ng5 and 10.Ng5 were more testing, hitting f7 right away. But the position was still better for you.
You kept control with 12.Qd2, 13.c4 and 14.d5, gaining space and driving Black's pieces back with 14...Na7. 15.Bb2 and 16.Qd4 aimed everything at the kingside.
Black's 16...c5?? was the final mistake, and you found 17.Qxg7# immediately, checkmate on g7. A tidy finish and a good example of lining up queen and bishop on the long diagonal.

review.turning_point: 16...c5?? allowed 17.Qxg7# along the long diagonal, and you spotted it at once.
review.focus: At 10.O-O, compare with 10.Ng5. When Black's king is not yet safe, pressure f7 before you finish development.

review.headline: A Petrov Three Knights where 15...Nb6?? and 16...e4?? undid a good opening

sections.text: You played the Petrov with 3...d6 and 4...Be6. After 5.Bb5+ c6 6.Ba4 b5 7.Bb3 a5 8.a4 b4 you gained queenside space, and 9...Bxb3 traded off White's bishop (10.cxb3). The position was balanced.

15.exd5? was a mistake by White (+1.6), but you replied with 15...Nb6??, which turned the position around (-0.9). 15...cxd5 simply took the pawn. Then 16...e4?? dropped to -3.0; 16...Rc8 was the solid move.

After 17...Qxd1+?! the queens came off with check and you were behind. White's 19.Rd6 and 20.Nd2? gave you small chances, but 21...Rac8? and 24...Be5? kept you from regaining control, and White's c-pawn on 22.c7 was a constant threat.
29 moves of fighting chess, but the game was decided by those two moves on 15 and 16.

review.turning_point: 15...Nb6?? turned a fine position into a worse one, and 16...e4?? added to it (-0.9 to -3.0).
review.focus: At 15...Nb6, look for the simple recapture. 15...cxd5 kept everything protected.

review.headline: A good Italian that slipped away with 18.e5??

sections.text: Against 3...h6 you played the principled 4.d4, and after 4...Qf6 5.dxe5?! Nxe5 6.Bb3 Bb4+ 7.Nc3 d6 the game was fine. 8.Bd2 Bxc3 9.Bxc3 was solid, and 9...a6?? gave you a chance.
You found 10.Nxe5!, the best reply, and after 10...dxe5 11.Qd5 you came out clearly ahead. 12.Qxe5 Qxe5 13.Bxe5 and 14.Bxc7 won material (+2), so you were comfortably better at +4.
Then 17.Rac1? gave away some of it (the engine preferred 17.Rad1), and 18.e5?? was the real blunder (+2.5 to -0.8). 18...Ne2+ hit the king and the rook on c1, and 19...Nxc1 left you down material.
21.Bxb7?? made it worse, and 27.g3? sealed the endgame. 28 moves of good play from you, but the mistakes at moves 17 and 18 gave the game away.

review.turning_point: 18.e5?? dropped a +2.5 advantage in one move, because 18...Ne2+ attacked your king and rook.
review.focus: At 18.e5, before pushing a pawn, check whether the opponent's knight has a check that wins something. 18.Rc4 kept things together.

review.headline: A Caro-Kann that went wrong on 4.d5?? and kept getting worse

sections.text: In the Caro-Kann you gave up a pawn with 3.Nc3 dxe4. The right plan was 4.Nxe4, but 4.d5?? lost the thread (+0.3 to -1.5). 4...Nf6 5.Bc4 e6 followed.

6.Bg5?? pinned the knight on f6 against the queen on d8, but it ignored 6.dxe6. Black's 6...Bb4?? was a mistake, though (-3.7 to -0.6), and 6...cxd5 was the correct reply. Then 7.Bxf6?? gave up your bishop; 7.dxe6 was the move.
From there the game ran away. 8.dxc6?! allowed 8...Bxc3+, 9.Kf1 Bxb2 (-4), and 11.c7 Bxa1 left you down nine. 12.cxb8=Q was a consolation, but resigning was right.

review.turning_point: 4.d5?? gave up your central pawn structure and the opening edge; 6.Bg5?? and 7.Bxf6?? finished it.
review.focus: At move 4, take the pawn back with 4.Nxe4. In gambit-like positions, recapturing material first beats pushing the pawn.

review.headline: A Danish Gambit where you took everything offered, then 15...Qc5?? gave it back

sections.text: You accepted the Danish Gambit with 2...exd4 and 3...dxc3, then 4...cxb2, taking three pawns. 5.Bxb2 recaptured one, but you were up material (+2). 6...Be7? was a slight slip; 6...Bb4+ 7.Nc3 was stronger.

9...b6? gave White more play, and 10.Ng5 Bxg5 11.Qxh5 traded pieces. But after 12.Qh3? you found 12...d5!, with the bishop on c8 attacking the queen as a discovered attack. 13.Qg3?? then 13...dxc4! won a piece for you.

You were comfortably ahead. 14...Qe7?! was a slight inaccuracy, and then 15.Nd5 hit your queen. 15...Qc5?? left the bishop on g5 hanging, and the evaluation went from +0.3 to -4.6; 15...Qd8 was the way.
16.Qxg5 won the bishop back, and 17.Ne7+ Kh8 18.e6+ finished the job. Mate came at move 20, with 20.Qxf6#.

review.turning_point: 15...Qc5?? moved the queen but left the bishop on g5 undefended, and the sequence from 16.Qxg5 was winning for White.
review.focus: At 15...Qc5, see which of your pieces the queen was defending. 15...Qd8 kept g5 covered.

review.headline: A level Bishop's Opening where a free piece went untouched at 11...g5 and the attack followed

sections.text: This was a normal Bishop's Opening and you handled it well. The engine had it dead level for the first ten moves. You developed with 3...Nf6 and 4...d6, got your king safe, and after 9...Nd4 10.Nxd4 Bxd4 you had traded into a comfortable position.

Then your opponent gave you a gift. 11.Kb1 swung the evaluation to +1.8 for you, because the bishop on c4 was left without protection. The engine wanted 11...Bxc4, and after 12.Bxf6 Bxa2+ 13.Kxa2 Qxf6 you would have been clearly better. Instead 11...g5 pushed a pawn in front of your own king and gave the whole advantage back (-0.9).

From there White's h-pawn did the work. 13.h4 and 14.hxg5 opened lines against you, and 14...Nxg5 was a mistake; 14...Qxg5 was the better recapture. After 15.Bh4 pinned the knight on g5 against your queen, you still had 15...Bxc4 available, but 15...f6 let it all fall apart (-5.1).
The rest was a technical finish for White: 16.Bxe6+, 17.Qxh6, then 18.Nd5 and 19.Nxf6+ tore open your king. You resigned after 24.Qh6+.

review.turning_point: 11...g5 passed up 11...Bxc4, which would have punished 11.Kb1 and kept you clearly better.
review.focus: When your opponent blunders, as with 11.Kb1, look at every capture and check before you make a quiet pawn move. 11...Bxc4 was the move, and 11...g5 only weakened your own king.

review.headline: A short game where your knight walked into trouble and a missed capture at 6.Ng3 decided it

sections.text: You opened with 1.d4 and 2.Nc3 and followed with 3.d5, gaining space against 2...Nc6. Black's knight went to a5 at move 3 and the engine already liked your side at +1.8 there.

The first slip was 4.Bd2, which let some of that advantage go. The engine suggested 4.b4 to chase the knight, with the idea 4...Nc4 5.e4 Nb6 6.e5 Ng8. After 4...e6 you then played 5.Ne4, and that move opened the d2 bishop's line onto the knight on a5, a discovered attack. It looks good, but 5.e4 was the safe move and 5.Ne4 dropped you to -2.7.

Black answered 5...Nc4, which was a blunder in turn and brought the position back to level. You then needed 6.Nxf6+ Qxf6 7.Bc3, but 6.Ng3 retreated and let the knight run free. 6...Nxb2 picked up a pawn and the knight on b2 stayed annoying for the rest of the game.
The last two moves, 8.Bc3 and 9.e3, left more material hanging. 8.dxe6 was the engine move, and 9.e3 left a piece to be won. You finished four points down in material.

review.turning_point: 6.Ng3 gave up the chance for 6.Nxf6+, which would have kept the position balanced.
review.focus: At 6.Ng3 you retreated when a capture was available. Before you retreat, list every capture and check for both sides; 6.Nxf6+ was there.

review.headline: A calm Petrov game thrown away by one tempting knight capture at 9...Nxf2

sections.text: This was a Three Knights Petrov and you played it sensibly. You met 4.d4 with 4...exd4, developed with 5...Nc6, 6...Be7 and 7...O-O, and the engine had it around -0.4, a normal small edge for White.

White's 8.O-O-O put the king on the queenside and 8...Ng4 was a fine active move. After 9.Bxe7, though, you had to take back. The engine wanted 9...Qxe7, simply winning the bishop back with a level game.

Instead 9...Nxf2 went for a fork (d1, d3, f2, h1), hitting the queen on d3 and the rooks. But it ignored the bishop sitting on e7 attacking your queen. 10.Bxd8 took your queen first, and after the trades on d3 and d8 you were left down a lot of material.
The evaluation went from -0.7 to -5.2 in one move and White just had to finish: 12.Nd5 and 13.h3 were enough. You resigned in a lost position.

review.turning_point: 9...Nxf2 went after a fork but allowed 10.Bxd8, losing your queen.
review.focus: At 9...Nxf2 you looked for a fork before checking what was attacking you. Always ask what your opponent's last capture threatens first; 9...Qxe7 was calm and good.

review.headline: A clean, patient win where you punished a loose knight move with a mating shot

sections.text: This was your best-played game of the batch at 93.6 accuracy. You met 2.Nc3 and 3.Nf3 with the solid 3...d6, 4...Be7 and 7...O-O. Against 5.Bg5 you played 5...h6 and recaptured calmly after 6.Bxf6 Bxf6, keeping the game equal.

You also handled the central tension well. 16...d5 was the right break at the right time. After 17.exd5 cxd5 18.cxd5 Nxd5 you were back to equal material with active pieces, and 19...Nb4 kept White's bishop and queen busy.

White went wrong with 20.Nh2?, which took the knight off f3 and opened the long diagonal toward g2. The engine wanted 20.Re3. You played 20...Qc6 at once, putting the queen and the bishop on b7 on that diagonal, and the evaluation moved to +1.4.
21.Rac1 ignored the threat, and 21...Qxg2# ended the game with mate on the diagonal you had prepared.

review.turning_point: 20.Nh2 removed the knight from f3 and left g2 exposed; 20...Qc6 aimed everything at it.
review.focus: Keep doing what you did here. Your 20...Qc6 shows the habit to keep: after the opponent's move, ask which defender just left. Nothing from this game needs fixing.

review.headline: A strong opening ruined by 13.Na5, then a tough comeback through tactics at moves 18 to 23

sections.text: You started well. Your Italian setup with 4.d4 and 5.h3 gave you a space edge, and after 5...Bxf3 6.Qxf3 the engine liked you at +1.5 once 7.d5 gained more space and kicked a knight around.

Then the middlegame slipped. 12.Nb3 was a mistake (+1.5 to +0.1); 12.a4 was better. Black replied 12...c5, but the engine's 12...Nxe4 was stronger. You then played 13.Na5??, which left a piece to be taken, and 13...Qxa5 swung the game to -3.5 for you.

You kept fighting, and your opponent gave it back. 17...f5?? was a blunder, and you answered with 18.Qxh5!. Then 21.Bh6! put a bishop en prise on purpose and 22...Qf7?? walked into 23.Qxf5!, which won material and put you at +4.4.
After that you simply converted. Trading queens with 26.Qxf7 Rxf7 left a winning endgame, and the d-pawn marched home: 39.d6 and 42.d8=Q ended the game. Your opponent resigned after 44 moves.

review.turning_point: 13.Na5 left a piece to be won; the recovery came when 17...f5 and 22...Qf7 gave you the chances back.
review.focus: At 13.Na5 you went for the knight jump without checking whether the knight could be taken. 13.a4 Nc7 kept the advantage; check each piece's safety before moving.

review.headline: A wild tactical win where both sides missed strong moves, ending in 19.Bd6#

sections.text: You took the e5 pawn early with 3.Nxe5 and played 4.Nf3. Black's 4...Bg4 and 5...Nc6 were both mistakes and you were at +2.1 after 6.h3. You played 5.Be2 and 6.h3 to challenge the bishop.

Then you gave a lot back. 7.e5?? went for a pawn push when 7.hxg4 was best, and Black missed 7...Bxf3, playing 7...Bc5 instead. After 8.exf6 and 9.fxg7 Kxg7 you were up material again, but 10.Nd4?? allowed a discovered attack and 11.Qxe2?? left a piece to be won.

Black returned the favour with 12...Qg5?? and you answered 13.d3, which opened the c1 bishop onto the queen on g5. 13.Qxg5+ was best, but it was enough: 13...Kf6 missed the threat and 14.Bxg5+ won the queen.
The finish was clean. 15.O-O, 16.Re1+, 17.Bf4+ and 18.d4+ drove the king up the board, and 19.Bd6# ended it.

review.turning_point: 13...Kf6 missed the threat created by 13.d3, and 14.Bxg5+ won the queen.
review.focus: 7.e5, 10.Nd4 and 11.Qxe2 each let the opponent back in. In a good position, take the simple capture first: 7.hxg4 and 11.Nxe2 were the engine's choices.

review.headline: A chaotic Petrov Modern Attack where an early gift made up for several of your own slips

sections.text: White's 4.Nc3?? was an early blunder and you found the right reply, 4...dxc3!, taking a knight. You were at +3.3 and the pawn on c3 stayed a thorn in White's side for several moves.
You then let it slip. 6...Nd4?? gave away the advantage (from +5.0 to +0.6); the engine wanted 6...cxb2. After 7.Nxd4? you found 7...cxb2!, which brought the pawn to b2 and kept you up.

8...b1=Q?? was a blunder, though: 8...bxa1=B was stronger, and 9.Qxb1 followed. Then 9...c6?? was another slip (-4.2), and 10.Bxf6 Qxf6 evened things out again. Both sides kept missing strong moves, and the game stayed messy until the end.
