The end came after 13...Qxa1 14.Qxb7 Bxb7 15.Bxb7 Qxf1+. You were far ahead in material and White resigned.

review.turning_point: 4...dxc3! punished 4.Nc3 and gave you a large early edge that you kept even through the later errors.
review.focus: Your 6...Nd4 gave back a large edge; 6...cxb2 was there. When you are winning, prefer the move that keeps your pawn and tempo over the one that offers trades.

review.headline: A Pirc where pressure and a passed b-pawn carried you, until the clock ended it

sections.text: You met the Pirc with 2.d4 and 3.Nf3 and the standard setup 4.Be2, 5.Nbd2 and 6.O-O. Against 7...b5 you played 8.e5, a good central push, and after 8...dxe5 9.dxe5 Nd5 the engine had you at +1.7.
Black's 11...Bg4 was a mistake and you kept the edge. 12.g3 was not the engine's choice (12.h3 was), but 13.cxb5 and 14.bxa6 won pawns and 16.Nxf3! was the right recapture after 15...Bxf3.

18.Nd4?? was the big error. It left a piece to be won and dropped you from +2.9 to -4.2; 18.Bc4 was better. But Black replied 18...Nxd4 19.Qxc5 and then 19...Ne6?, missing 19...Nf3+, which would have forked your king and rook.
From there you rebuilt: 23...Rxc1 24.Raxc1 and queen trades with 26.gxh4 left a far better endgame. The b-pawn advanced from 32.b4 to 39.b7, and despite 40.Rd8?? you won, with Black out of time.

review.turning_point: 18.Nd4 gave up a piece, but Black missed 19...Nf3+ and handed the game back.
review.focus: 18.Nd4 was a lapse of piece safety. Check whether every piece you move leaves something undefended; 18.Bc4 was safe and kept you better.

review.headline: A Petrov Modern Attack where an early queen trade and a king move at 9...Kd8 sealed it

sections.text: This was a standard Petrov Modern Attack. You took the pawn with 3...exd4 and after 4.e5 played 4...Nd5?!, which the engine marked as slightly inaccurate at -1.0. 5.Qxd4 c6 was a sensible follow up.

6...Qb6 was the first real mistake. 6...Nxc3 was best, and after 6.Nc3 the queen move led into trades on d5 and d4: 7.Nxd5 Qxd4 8.Nxd4 cxd5. Material stayed even but White had the better structure and development (-2.4).

Then came 9.Nb5, heading for c7, and 9...Kd8? was a mistake (-4.6). 9...Na6 10.a3 b6 11.b4 Bb7 12.Bg5 was the engine line, which covers the c7 square without moving the king. After 9...Kd8 10.Bg5+ you had to move the king again and lost the right to castle.
You resigned after 10 moves, which was quick; the position was bad but not yet decided.

review.turning_point: 9...Kd8 gave up castling and left the king exposed to 10.Bg5+.
review.focus: At 9...Kd8 you moved the king instead of defending the c7 square. 9...Na6 was the engine's choice, and 6...Nxc3 earlier would have avoided the whole line.

review.headline: A Smith-Morra Gambit where 7.Bxe4 opened the d-file and left your king stuck in the middle

sections.text: You played the Smith-Morra with 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4, a common way to take the pawn back. The first moves were fine (+0.1 after 3.Qxd4) and the position was close to level. 5.Nd2 and 6.Bd3 followed, which the engine rated about equal.

The real problem was 7.Bxe4. After 6...dxe4 you could simply recapture with 7.Nxe4, which was the engine move. 7.Bxe4 allowed 7...Nxe4 8.Nxe4 and then 8...Qxd1+, since the knight had left the d-file. After 9.Kxd1 your king was stuck in the centre with no castling.

From there Black built up: 9...e5, 10...f5 and 11...e4 gave Black a strong centre, and the evaluation grew to -4.8 after 13.Ngxe4 fxe4 14.Nxe4. The moves 12.Ng5?! and 13.Ngxe4?! only made things worse.
Black's king went long with 15...O-O-O and 17...Bc2+ and 19...Bd3+ drove your king further. You resigned after 19 moves.

review.turning_point: 7.Bxe4 let the queens trade with check on d1 and lost the right to castle.
review.focus: At 7.Bxe4, recapture with the piece that keeps your structure: 7.Nxe4 was the engine move. Watch for open files with queens facing each other.

review.headline: A reversed Sicilian where an early queen sortie and a greedy c5 pawn grab ended in mate

sections.text: You met 1.c4 with 1...e5 and 2...d6, a flexible setup, and the engine had it level through move 2. Then 3.d4 hit your centre and 3...Qh4? was a mistake (-1.4). 3...exd4 was the move, and the queen on h4 was soon chased: 4.Nf3 Qe7.
You fought back. After 5...Bg4 6.dxe5 dxe5 7.Qb3 Bxf3?! you won a knight, though the evaluation stayed negative (-2.1). The engine did not like giving up the bishop so early.
8.Nd5 hit your queen on e7. After 8...Qd6?! 9.c5 hit it again, and 9...Qxc5?! took a pawn but left your king stuck in the middle. 10.Qxb7 went after your pieces, and 10...Qc6? allowed the mate.
10...Ne7 was the engine move, with 11.Be3 Qa5+ 12.b4 Nxd5 13.bxa5 following. 11.Qc8# ended the game.

review.turning_point: 10...Qc6 allowed 11.Qc8#; 10...Ne7 was the only way to stay in the game.
review.focus: 3...Qh4 brought the queen out early and lost time. Develop with 3...exd4 first and keep the queen home until it has a job.

review.headline: A Queen's Gambit Declined where 8...Nd7 cost a pawn and the clock finished the job

sections.text: You played the QGD Three Knights with 1...d5, 2...e6, 3...Nf6 and 4...Be7 and it was near level. After 5.Bg5 you got your king safe with 5...O-O and met 6.e3 with 6...h6, then traded with 7.Bxf6 Bxf6 for an equal position.
8...Nd7? was the mistake (-0.3 to -1.6). The engine preferred 8...g6, with 9.h4 Bg7 10.Bd3 dxc4 11.Bxc4. After 9.cxd5 Nb6 10.dxe6 Bxe6 you were a pawn down with little to show for it.
11...Bg4?! pinned the knight on f3 to the queen, but White simply played 12.O-O and the evaluation went to -2.7 after 12...Qd7 13.h3.
You lost on time at move 13, still in a playable but worse position.

review.turning_point: 8...Nd7 let White win a pawn with 9.cxd5 and 10.dxe6.
review.focus: At 8...Nd7 you gave up the pawn structure. Before moving a piece off its defensive square, check that the d5 pawn stays protected; 8...g6 was the engine choice.

review.headline: An Italian where 11.Bb5 and 12.Qc2 let Black's knight run wild

sections.text: You played the Classical Italian with 4.c3 and 5.d4, the main line. After 5...exd4 6.cxd4 Bb4+ 7.Nc3 Nxe4 the position was sharp and close to level. 8.O-O Bxc3 9.bxc3 d5 and 10.Re1 O-O followed, and the engine had you around -0.5.
11.Bb5? was the first real mistake (-1.8). 11.Bd3 was the engine choice. After 11...Nxc3 the black knight attacked your queen and your bishop at once.

12.Qc2?? was the blunder: the knight on c3 attacked both queen and bishop, and moving the queen sideways let 12...Nxb5 take the bishop. 12.Qb3 Nxb5 13.Qxb5 was the engine line, which kept you in the game.
After that Black's extra material was too much, and 17.Re3 gxh6 18.Rg3+ Kh8 19.Qxh6 Ne2+ ended the game. You resigned after 19 moves.

review.turning_point: 12.Qc2 moved the queen out of the attack but left the bishop on b5 to be taken.
review.focus: At 11.Bb5 and 12.Qc2 you did not see the knight on c3 hitting two pieces. 11.Bd3 would have prevented it; when a piece lands next to your pieces, check what it attacks.

review.headline: An English Defense where an early h5 and a weakened king ended in a queen mate at f7

sections.text: You played the English Defense with 1...b6 and 2...Bb7, a flexible setup that the engine rated slightly worse (-0.9 after 1...b6). 3.g3 e6 4.Bg2 Nf6 and 5.O-O were fine.

5...h5?! was the start of the trouble. It was a loosening move and White's 6.c4 c5 7.d5 opened the centre while your king was still in the middle. 7...exd5 took a pawn but the evaluation was already -1.7.

8.Nh4 hit your pieces, and 8...Ng4 uncovered an attack from your queen on the h4 knight, a discovered attack. Then 9...g5 and 10.Bxd5 Bxd5 11.Qxd5 left your king's side wide open. By 12.Bxg5 Be7 13.Nf5 you were at -4.5.
13...Bxg5? allowed a forced mate: 14.Nd6+ Kf8 15.Qxf7#. 13...O-O was the engine move, with 14.Nh6+ Nxh6 15.Bxh6 Re8 16.Qxh5.

review.turning_point: 13...Bxg5 took a pawn but walked into 14.Nd6+ and 15.Qxf7#.
review.focus: Your king was still in the centre at 13...Bxg5. 13...O-O was the engine move; get the king safe before you take material when the other side has checks.

review.headline: A Scandinavian that turned into a sharp attack, finished by 17.Rxe6! and 19.Qxg7#

sections.text: You met the Scandinavian with 2.exd5 and after 3.Nc3?! e5 took the pawn with 5.Nxe5. 6.Be2 Bxc3 7.bxc3?! Nxd5 and 8.O-O brought you to a good position at about +1.0, with Black's 8...Qf6 pressuring c3.

9.d4?? was the blunder (+1.7 to -0.1). The engine preferred 9.Ng4. After 9...Nxc3 10.Qd3 Nxe2+ 11.Qxe2 Nc6 the position was level. Black then gave you a chance with 12...b5??, which the engine said was a blunder (+1.4).
13.Rfe1? let some of that go again (13.Qe4 was better), but 14.Qxb5 Nxe5 15.dxe5 Qg5 16.e6 fxe6 kept it complicated. Then you found the key shot, 17.Rxe6!, offering a rook.
17...Bxe6?? took it and uncovered your queen's attack on g5 on its own (a discovered attack). 18.Qxg5! won the queen, pinning the g7 pawn against the king, and 19.Qxg7# finished it.

review.turning_point: 17.Rxe6! offered a rook and 17...Bxe6 opened the line for 18.Qxg5, winning the queen.
review.focus: 9.d4 gave up a good position for no reason. Check what your move allows before you play it; 9.Ng4 was the engine choice.

review.headline: A Smith-Morra Gambit where 15.Nxd6 threw away a good position and the clock did the rest

sections.text: You played the Smith-Morra with 2.d4 cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qd1, and Black replied 4...e5 and 5...Bc5. After 6.Be3 Bxe3 7.fxe3 the game was close to even, and 8.Nbd2?! and 9.Be2 let Black get a small edge.

11.Nc4?! allowed 11...Nxe4, and Black had a small advantage (-1.6). You kept calm with 12.Qd3 and 13.Rad1, and Black blundered with 13...Bxf3??, which swung the evaluation to +1.5 for you. 14.Bxf3! was the best reply.
14...Qh4 left you at +2.5, but 15.Nxd6?? gave back most of it. The engine wanted 15.Qd5+ Kh8 16.Bxe4 Qxe4 17.Qxe4 fxe4. After 15...Nxd6 16.Qxd6 e4 you were only at +0.4.
17.Qe6+?! and 18.g3? let Black take over (-1.3), and you lost on time after 18 moves.

review.turning_point: 15.Nxd6 turned +2.5 into +0.5; 15.Qd5+ was the better move.
review.focus: At 15.Nxd6 you grabbed a pawn with a knight that was doing a job. Check your checks first: 15.Qd5+ kept you clearly better.

review.headline: A King's Gambit win that you took over with 12...Bxd4 and 15...Ne3+ and finished with 40...Qe1#

sections.text: This was a King's Gambit Accepted and you took the pawn with 2...exf4. After 3.Nf3 d5 4.e5 you had a good position (+1.9 for you). 4...f6 was the weaker answer, since 4...g5 was best, and 5...c5?? was a blunder when 5...fxe5 was available.
You recovered well with 6...Bg4, 7...Qb6 and 8...Bxc5, and after 9.Be2 Bf2+ 10.Kf1 you had your pieces working. 10...fxe5? gave a little back, since 10...Nc6 was best.

12.Bd4?? looked like a fork of your queen and bishop, but 12...Bxd4! simply took it, and 13.cxd4 Qxb2 left you a pawn up with White's king stuck in the middle. Then 15.Ne5?? gave you 15...Ne3+!, forking the king and queen. After 16.Kf2 Nxd1+ you were up about ten.
From there you converted cleanly: 17...Qxd4+, 18...Bxe2, 22.Rxd5 and a long chase of the king ended with 40...Qe1#.

review.turning_point: 15...Ne3+ forked the king and queen and won the white queen.
review.focus: 5...c5 gave up your advantage in the opening. Before a pawn push, check the pawn you can take: 5...fxe5 6.dxe5 kept control.

review.headline: A London System where you were better in the middle, then let a mate slip away

sections.text: You met the London with 1...d5 and 2...e6 and had no trouble. You traded bishops with 3...Bd6 4.Bxd6 4...cxd6, answered 6.Nc3 with 6...Ne4, and after 7.Nxe4 7...dxe4 8.Nd2 8...d5 the position was level. White's queen sortie with 9.Qg4 and 11.Qh5 plus 10.O-O-O looked threatening but was slow, and after 12.exd4 you stood clearly better (+1.4).

The first slip was 13...Qc7, which dropped you to -1.2. The engine preferred 13...f5, keeping e4 solid. White immediately gave it back with 14.f3, missing the strong 14.Qxd5. After 14...Nxd4 you were fine again, but 16...g6 was the real damage (+0.9 to -4.1). 16...Qf4+ would have forked the king on c1 and the knight on e4.
You deserve credit for 17...Kg7, the only good answer to 17.Nf6+. Even so, 18.Qxh7+ and 20.Qxd4+ left White with the initiative, and you were worse for the rest of the game.

The saddest moment came at 23.Qf6, when White overreached. 23...Qf4+ 24.Rd2 would have led to a forced mate, but 23...Bxg4 let the chance go. 24.Rxd8 was a mistake and you found 24...Rxd8, yet 25.Rf1 was met by 25...Qe7, which walked into a skewer on the e7 queen and d8 rook. 25...Bh5 was the way out.

review.turning_point: 23.Qf6 gave you a forced mate with 23...Qf4+ 24.Rd2, but 23...Bxg4 grabbed a pawn instead and swung the game from winning to losing.
review.focus: At 23...Bxg4 you reached for a capture when a check was available. Before every move in a sharp position, list all your checks first; 23...Qf4+ was one of them.

review.headline: A Petrov where the opponent drifted and you collected material with your queen

sections.text: This was a quiet Petrov with a kingside fianchetto for White. Both sides developed naturally with 4.g3 4...Bg4 5.Bg2 5...Be7 and castled, and the evaluation hovered around zero until 9...Qc7 gave you a small edge. White's 10.Nb3 was careful and the position stayed balanced.

10...d5 was the one inaccurate move of the opening, dropping you to -1.4. The engine liked 10...a5 first. White did not punish it: 11.Bd2 threw away the advantage and 11.cxd5 was the move. After 12.cxd5 12...cxd5 you were back to equality.

Then White went wrong in a big way. 13.Qd1 was a blunder, and your 13...Qc2 gave some of it back; the engine wanted 13...dxe4 first. But 14.Qe1 was worse still, missing 14.Qxc2, and from here you were up in material and in control.

You took it from there confidently. 14...dxe4 and 15...Qxb2 opened the queenside, 17...Qxa2 grabbed more, and 18...Bxf3 followed by 19...Rxd2 kept the pressure on. By 25...Qxb1+ and 26...Rxf2+ White's position was collapsing, and 31...Qxe4 ended it.

review.turning_point: 14.Qe1 missed the simple 14.Qxc2, and from then on you were winning material with every move.
review.focus: 13...Qc2 jumped into the opponent's camp when 13...dxe4 first kept everything safe. Before sending the queen deep, check whether you can win the same thing with a simple pawn capture.

review.headline: A Petrov where a queenside pawn move and the clock cost you a good position

sections.text: You played the main Petrov line with 3.Nxe5, 4.Nf3 and 6.c4, building a small space edge with 7.d5 before Black castled with 7...O-O. The opening was fine at about +0.4.

8.Bg5 was a little loose, and 9.Be3 was the real mistake (-2.0); 9.Be2 was cleaner. Your opponent's 9...Bg4 pinned your knight on f3 to the queen, and it was an error as well: 9...Ng4 was the strong move. After 10.Be2 and 11.O-O you were back to normal.

From there you played well. 13.h3 13...Bh5 14.Nc3 and 15.Qb3 built up your queenside play, and 17.Rfe1 put a rook on the e-file. 18.Bb5 pinned the d7 knight against the rook on e8, though the engine felt it was a touch loose. 18...Bxf3 19.gxf3 damaged your structure, and 20.Rad1 was a touch passive.
21.f4 was the final slip (+0.4 to -0.9). 21.Be2 kept things safe, whereas 21.f4 opened the position for 21...Nf3+. You then lost on time, so a roughly equal middlegame went unplayed.

review.turning_point: 9.Be3 cost you nearly two pawns of evaluation before the opponent returned it with 9...Bg4, and the later 21.f4 loosened your king.
review.focus: 21.f4 pushed a pawn in front of your king when 21.Be2 was calm. Keep pawn moves near your own king to a minimum, and play faster in quiet positions so you have time later.

review.headline: A clean queenless Petrov where the engine liked your side the whole way

sections.text: You played the Petrov and met 3.d3 with 3...d5 and 4.Bg5 with 4...dxe4. After 5.Bxf6 5...gxf6 6.dxe4 you traded queens with 6...Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1, which cost White the right to castle. That is a good practical decision: White's king ends up stuck in the centre.

You developed with 7...Bg4, 8...Bh6 and 9...Bd7, then castled long with 11...O-O-O. White's 12.Ke1 tidied the king, and you used the f-pawn with 12...f5 to challenge the centre. Accuracy 95 percent shows how few real mistakes there were.

White went wrong with 13.exf5, which let you recapture with 13...Bxf5 and put an active bishop on the c2 pawn. 14.Rd1 was another inaccuracy, since 14.Bd3 was the engine's line, and you found 14...Bxc2, grabbing a pawn.

After 15.Rxd8+ 15...Rxd8 you were a clean pawn up and the engine rated you at +3.5. The record shows the game ended as a loss by resignation, so check carefully that you were not too hasty at the end.

review.turning_point: 13.exf5 and 14.Rd1 were White's errors, and you punished the second with 14...Bxc2.
review.focus: There was little to fix in your play. After 15...Rxd8 you were better, so make a habit of checking the evaluation and the material count before ever resigning.

review.headline: A Caro-Kann Exchange where you punished 7...h6 and converted a huge edge

sections.text: You played the Exchange Variation, taking with 3.exd5 and developing 4.Nc3 and 5.Bg5. Black's 5...Bg4 6.Nf3 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 left you with an active queen on f3 eyeing the d5 pawn.

Black's 7...h6 was the big mistake (+0.2 to +3.0), and you found the best reply with 8.Bxf6. After 8...exf6 you played 9.Qxd5 and Black's queen trade 9...Qxd5 10.Nxd5 left a huge position for you. 10...Nc6 was another error.
11.Nc7+ was the tactic that decided the game: it forked the king on e8 and the rook on a8. After 11...Kd7 12.Nxa8 you were far ahead in material. You then took some care with 13.Nb6+ and 14.O-O-O.

When Black grabbed with 19...Bxh2, you trapped it with 20.g3, 21.Rh1 and 22.Rxh2, which restored your lead. The rest was technique: 26.Rxd8, 31.Bxe4+ and 35.R8xe4+ kept simplifying, and the win came after 47 moves. A 97 percent accuracy says it all.

review.turning_point: 7...h6 gave you 8.Bxf6, and 11.Nc7+ then forked the king and the rook on a8.
review.focus: You played almost flawlessly. Keep the habit of looking for the forcing capture first, as with 8.Bxf6 and 11.Nc7+, in every position where the opponent has just weakened something.

review.headline: A Van't Kruijs where you were winning and then lost on the clock

sections.text: White opened with 1.e3, and after 1...e5 2.c3 2...d5 3.Bb5+ 3...c6 you were comfortable. White spent moves on 5.f3, 6.a3 and 7.b4, and the engine rated you better from the start. You grew the centre with 5...Bc5, 7...Bb6 and 12...d4.

13...dxe3 was reasonable, but 14...c4 was a slip (+5.0 to +2.7): the bishop on a7 got uncovered against the e3 knight, but 14...cxb4 was cleaner. After 15.Qd2 15...cxd3 16.Bxd3 came 16...Nd5, a real blunder, because 16...e4 was safer.

White could have punished it with 17.Nxd5, but 17.O-O-O was an error and you replied with 17...Nxe3, a discovered attack on the d3 bishop. After 18.Re1 18...Nxg2 and 19.Rxe5 you were a long way ahead.
You kept the advantage with 20...Be3 21.Rxe3 21...Nxe3. By 30.Bxh7+ and 32...Nxd1 you were still better, but the game was lost on time at move 33. A won position slipped away on the clock.

review.turning_point: 17.O-O-O ignored the safe 17.Nxd5 and let you take over with 17...Nxe3.
review.focus: 16...Nd5 put a knight where it could be hit. Before playing it, ask what the e3 knight can capture. Also manage your clock: by 22...Nf6 you needed to be faster in a winning position.

review.headline: A Caro-Kann Exchange where an early queen raid collapsed

sections.text: You played the Exchange Variation with 1.e4, 2.d4 and 3.exd5, then developed 4.Nc3 and 5.Bg5. Black's 4...a6 and 5...h6 were odd, so you were fine at move 5, with the opening at about equal.
6.Qh5 was slightly loose (-0.9) because the queen came out early. 6...Bf5 was a good reply and you had to be careful. A quieter move like 7.Bh4 kept things safe.

Instead 7.Bxh6 was a blunder (-0.5 to -5.1). Black's 7...Bxc2 was a mistake in turn, because 7...Nxh6 was the correct answer. After 7...Bxc2 you were only slightly worse, but then 8.Qf5 left a piece to be won, and 8.Qe2 was the only calm move.
After 8.Qf5 you were lost, and the game ended soon after. A hurried queen and bishop raid on the h-file is risky when Black has developed pieces nearby.

review.turning_point: 7.Bxh6 grabbed a pawn but gave Black strong play, and 8.Qf5 then left a piece to be won.
review.focus: 7.Bxh6 took a pawn while your queen was already far from home. Before grabbing material, ask what the opponent can do in reply; 7.Bh4 kept the position safe.

review.headline: A Three Knights Petrov where you built a winning position and ran out of time

sections.text: You played the Three Knights with 3...d6, 4...Be6 and 5...Be7, castling with 6...O-O. 7...Nbd7 was a little passive, but 8.d4 was a small mistake by White. After 8...exd4 9.Nxd4 9...Bxc4 10.bxc4 the structure was fine for you.

10...c5 was the first mistake (-1.6): 10...Re8 was safer. After 11.Nf5 11...Re8 12.Nd5 White was hitting back, and 12...g6 was a blunder, since 12...Nxd5 won a piece outright. 13.Nxf6+ forked your king and rook, but 13...Bxf6 simply took the knight.
Then White blundered with 14.Nxd6, missing 14.Nh6+. You found 14...Bxa1, which put you well ahead in material. You were clearly winning after 15.Qf3 15...Re7 16.Bg5.

16...Bf6 was a mistake (+4.3 to +2.5); 16...Be5 was better. Still, after 18.Qxf6 18...Rd7 19.Qxd8+ 19...Raxd8 you were ahead, around +3 to +4. You then lost on time at move 21, with a winning position.

review.turning_point: 14.Nxd6 gave away the game, and your 14...Bxa1 turned a roughly equal position into a winning one.
review.focus: 12...g6 missed 12...Nxd5, which won a piece. When a knight lands on d5 next to your pieces, check if you can simply capture it. Also watch the clock in winning positions.

review.headline: A wild Two Knights game decided by opponent mistakes and a decisive passed pawn

sections.text: You opened with the Italian and 3.Bc4 3...Nf6, then played 4.Nxe5, a blunder that left a piece to be won (4.Ng5 was the safer try). After 4...Nxe5 5.Bb3 Black missed the best reply, and 5...Bc5 allowed 6.d4!, which forked the bishop on c5 and the knight on e5.

6...Nf3+ was another error, and 7.Qxf3 7...Bxd4 8.Bg5 left you under pressure; 8.Qd1 was better. Black returned the favour with 8...O-O, missing 8...Bxb2. You castled long with 10.O-O-O and brought a knight to 11.Nd5.

11...Bg4 was a mistake that let you win the queen with 12.Qxg4 12...Nxg4 13.Bxd8, but 13...Nxf2 forked your two rooks on d1 and h1. 14.Nxc7 was a blunder (14.Bxc7 was better), and 16.Ne6 missed 16.Rxh1. Still, 17.Nxf8 was the best reply, and 18.Rxh1 restored the balance.

The endgame was where you won it. 28...a5 gave you chances, 29.cxb5! and 32.b6! created a dangerous passed pawn, and 40.b8=Q ended the fight. 31.Kf3 was a slip but did not matter; 47.Qf7# finished the game with mate.

review.turning_point: 28...a5 allowed 29.cxb5!, and 32.b6! then created a passed pawn that decided the game.
review.focus: 4.Nxe5 grabbed a pawn and left a piece to be won. In the Italian, remember the knight on e5 can be recaptured by 4...Nxe5, so 4.Ng5 or a quiet developing move kept the position safe.

review.headline: A Zukertort where White's queen grab lost it and your attack finished with mate

sections.text: You answered 1.d4 with 1...d5 and 2.Nf3 with 2...f6, which the engine found a little loose (-1.2). After 3.e3 3...Nc6 4.a3 4...e5 5.dxe5 5...fxe5 the centre was open, but White's 6.Bb5 gave you few problems.

6...Bd6 was a small mistake (+0.5 to -0.6); 6...a6 was stronger. But White's 7.Qxd5 was the real blunder, and you found 7...Bb4+, a discovered attack that uncovered your queen against the d5 queen. After 8.axb4 8...Qxd5 you won the queen for a bishop.

From there you had a comfortable game. 10...e4 and 12...Nge7 added pressure, and 13...Qg4 aimed at the king. 15...Nxb4 kept the material coming, then 16...Nexd5 and 17...Nxd5 simplified into a great position.
21...Qf2+ opened the final attack, and 23...Rxd5 and 24...Rxd2 tied up the loose ends. White's 25.Rf1 allowed 25...Qxg2#, a nice checkmate to finish.

review.turning_point: 7.Qxd5 walked into 7...Bb4+, winning White's queen for a bishop.
review.focus: 6...Bd6 was less accurate than 6...a6, and 2...f6 earlier weakened your king. Prefer simple developing moves in the opening.

review.headline: A Modern Defense where your opponent's pawn pushes let you win the queen

sections.text: You played the Modern with 1.e4 1...g6 and set up 2.d4, 3.Nf3 and 4.Bc4. Black's 3...f6 was loose, and 5.O-O kept things flexible. 6.d5 was a space-gaining idea, though the engine thought it only slightly inaccurate.
6...Nce7 was Black's mistake (+1.1 to +2.9). Then 7.Nc3 was your first error, because 7.d6 kept the initiative. After 7...d6 you got back into the game with 8.Be3 and 9.Be2.

Black pushed too far with 9...f5 and 10...Bh6. 10.Bg5 pinned the e7 knight against the queen, which looked good, but 10.Ng5 was stronger. After 11.Bh4 you again missed the best move; 11.Bxh6 won a piece outright. Black's 11...fxe4 was another slip.
You found 12.Nxe4 and then the decisive 13.Bxd8, winning the queen after 12...Nf5. By 14.h3, 17.Qxf3 and 20.Qxh7 you were far ahead, and 21.Qxg6 closed the game.

review.turning_point: 12...Nf5 was met by 13.Bxd8, which took Black's queen and gave you a winning position.
review.focus: 11.Bh4 missed 11.Bxh6, which won a piece. When your opponent has moved a bishop to h6 near your own, check first if you can simply capture it.

review.headline: A back-and-forth Colle where you finished with a decisive passed pawn

sections.text: You answered the Colle with a Queen's Gambit-style setup: 1...d5, 2...e6, 4...c5 and 5...Nc6. 7...g6 and 9...Qc7 were slightly loose, and 10...O-O-O cost you (-1.8). White did not capitalise, and 12.e4 was a blunder that let 12...dxe4 start a series of trades.

After 14.Bxe4 14...cxd4 and 16.Qxd4 you were nearly level, but 16...Bd6 was a blunder (-2.4) and after White's 17.g3, which missed 17.Be3, 17...Bc6 repeated it. Your 18...Be5 and 19.Qa7+ 19...Kc8 kept you in the game.

20.Rad1 was White's big error: after 20...Rxd1 21.Rxd1 the e4 bishop was loose and 21...Bxe4 won it. 22...Qb8 was a slip, 24...Bf5 gave back ground, and 26...Rd8 left a piece to be won. Fortunately 25.g4 25...Bxg4 and 27.Rxd8+ 27...Kxd8 saved you. 28.Qf8+ was met by 28...Kd7.
After 30.Bxc7 30...Qxc7 31.Qxc7+ 31...Kxc7 you were winning the endgame. 33...Bxb3, 34...Bxa4 and 36...Kxc5 won pawns, and 42...b1=Q+ ended it.

review.turning_point: 20.Rad1 let you play 20...Rxd1 and 21...Bxe4, which turned a worse game into a winning one.
review.focus: 26...Rd8 left a piece to be won; 26...Bf3 was better. After White's rook reached d4, 26...Rd8 left a piece loose. Check what each of your pieces is defending before moving a rook.

review.headline: A short Caro-Kann Main Line where Black's 10...Bb4 lost almost everything

sections.text: You played the Main Line with 3.Nc3 3...dxe4 4.Nxe4 and went for 5.Nxf6+ 5...exf6, giving Black doubled pawns. 6.Qe2+ was a little less than the best (+0.5 to +0.0), but your structure was sound.
You developed with 7.Be3 and 8.O-O-O, with 9.a3 stopping any pin ideas. 8...Qa5 is a typical Caro-Kann plan, and 10.Bd2 kept things safe.
Black then blundered with 10...Bb4, missing 10...Qa4. You found 11.Bxb4!, which forked the queen on a5 and the rook on f8. After 11...Qd5 12.Bxf8 you had picked up a bishop and a rook.
13.Qe8 kept the attack going. 13...Qa1+ 14.Kd2 left Black with no compensation, and Black resigned.

review.turning_point: 10...Bb4 was a blunder, and 11.Bxb4! forked the queen and rook.
review.focus: Very little to fix. The one small dip was 6.Qe2+, which gave away some edge; check whether a quiet developing move keeps more tension.

review.headline: A Mengarini where you were crushing and then grabbed a rook into a mating net

sections.text: White opened with 2.a3 and 3.g3, so you picked up a pawn with 3...Nxe4 and played 4...d5 and 5...exd4. 6.Qxd4 6...Nc6 7.Qe3 was a mistake by White, and you found 7...Bc5!, hitting the queen.
You kept up the pressure with 8...Nd4 and 9...Bf5, and 10...Nxf2 11.Qd2 11...Nxc2+ cleaned up. By 12.Kxf2 you were completely winning, at +7.4.
12...Nxa1 was the blunder (+7.4 to -0.5). It grabbed a rook but left a piece to be won, and 12...Nxe3 was a safe way to keep everything. 13.Bxc5 13...Bxb1 was a slight inaccuracy as well.
14.Qe1+ was a strong follow-up, and 14...Qe7 was a final blunder that allowed a forced mate. 14...Be4 was the only move.

review.turning_point: 12...Nxa1 was a greedy capture that threw away a winning position.
review.focus: 12...Nxa1 won a rook but ignored your own loose pieces. When you are winning, take the safe path first; 12...Nxe3 kept it all.

review.headline: A Ruy Lopez where your opponent's errors let you attack with e5-e6

sections.text: You played 3.Bb5 and after 3...Nd4 4.Nxd4 4...exd4 5.d3 you developed with 6.Bc4 and 7.Bb3. 7...Bb4+ 8.c3 8...dxc3 was a fun line, but 9.Nxc3 was a blunder, and 9.bxc3 was the cleaner way (+0.3 to -1.7).
Black replied with 9...Bxc3+, and you found 10.bxc3!, taking the bishop back. After that you were better: 11.e5 and 12.O-O developed fast, and 13.Re1 added pressure.
13...f6 was a blunder, and you replied 14.e6!. After 14...Ne5 15.f4 15...Bxe6 16.fxe5 16...fxe5 17.Rxe5 you were well ahead.

19.Bf4 was a blunder (+4.2 to +1.1) that left a piece to be won, and 19...Rxf4 took it. 19.d4 was safe. But 20...Rf5 gave it all back, and 21.Rxf5! 21...Bxf5 22.Qxe8+ finished the game, with Black resigning.

review.turning_point: 20...Rf5 was Black's blunder, and 21.Rxf5! uncovered the queen to win the e8 rook.
review.focus: 19.Bf4 left a piece to be won. When you are winning, quiet moves like 19.d4 are best; avoid moves that put your bishop where a rook can capture it.

review.headline: A French Exchange where you hunted Black's king and finished with mate

sections.text: You played the French Exchange with 3.exd5, 4.Nf3 and 5.Bb5, and after 5...Bd7 6.Nc3 6...Nf6 7.Bg5 you built a solid position. 8.O-O and 9.Re1 were slightly slow, but 10.Bxc6 and 11.Ne5 kept the initiative.

13.Bxe7 was a good capture, and Black replied 13...Qxe7, a blunder (+0.4 to +5.7); 13...Nxc3 was the right move. You then played 14.Nxe4, a blunder that gave up much of the lead (+5.7 to +1.8); 14.Nxd5 was the best.
Even so, 15.Qxe4 15...Bb5 16.Qxb7! kept the initiative. 17.Qxc7 17...Rfe8 was another Black error, and you found 18.Qxf7+!, a strong shot that opened the king.
Then you handled a long attack. 23.Qh3 kept pressure on h7, and 24...Qc3 was an error and you found 25.Qxc3!. 27.Nf7+, 28.Rf5 and 30.Nh6+ carried the attack, and 43.Qf7# ended the game with mate.

review.turning_point: 13...Qxe7 was a blunder, and your 16.Qxb7! and 18.Qxf7+! kept the attack going.
review.focus: 14.Nxe4 swapped off a strong knight when 14.Nxd5 kept the advantage. In a won position, look for the strongest capture instead of the first natural trade.

review.headline: A short Petrov where White's 5.Bxd5 lost a queen

sections.text: You played the Petrov and answered 3.Bc4 with 3...Nxe4 4.Nxe5 4...d5, a common line. White then took 5.Bxd5, a blunder (+0.8 to +4.2), when 5.d3 was the right move.
You found 5...Qxd5!, and White continued with 6.Nxf7 6...Qxf7, which cost a knight. The position was now clearly in your favour.
7.Qf3 7...Qe7 was slightly inaccurate (+6.7 to +4.7), because 7...Qxf3 was the cleaner way to trade queens. Even so you remained well ahead.
White then blundered completely with 8.Qxe4, walking into a pin against the king on e1. 8...Qxe4+ won the queen, and White resigned.

review.turning_point: 5.Bxd5 was met by 5...Qxd5!, and 8.Qxe4 8...Qxe4+ finished it.
review.focus: 7...Qe7 let White off slightly. When you are well ahead, trade queens when you can, as 7...Qxf3 would have done.

review.headline: A Queen's Gambit Declined where one rook move cost you a piece

sections.text: You met the Harrwitz Attack with 1...d5, 2...e6 and 3...Nf6. After 4.Bf4 4...Bd6 5.Bxd6 5...cxd6, you traded off the dark-squared bishops, and 6...O-O was a bit passive (-1.2).
7.cxd5 7...exd5 gave you a standard structure, and 8...Re8, 9...Nc6 and 10...Bg4 developed quickly. 11...Qb6 was a sensible attacking move, and the game stayed close.

12...Re7 was slightly loose, and 13...Rae8 was the blunder (-0.4 to -4.8). 13...Bxe2 would have traded bishops with a fork on the queen and rook. After 14.Bxg4 14...Nxb4 you lost the bishop for a pawn.
You kept fighting with 17...Ne4 and 18...dxe4, but White's 24.Nxb7 and 25.Bxc6 consolidated the lead. You lost on time after move 27.

review.turning_point: 13...Rae8 left the g4 bishop to be taken after 14.Bxg4, and you never recovered.
review.focus: 13...Rae8 ignored the attacked bishop. Before developing a rook, check each of your pieces is protected; 13...Bxe2 would have kept the game even.

review.headline: An Italian where an early bishop loss and a later hung piece decided it

sections.text: You played the Italian with 3.Bc4, and Black answered with the early 3...Qf6. After 4.Nc3 4...Nge7 5.d4 5...exd4 you were fine.
6.Bg5 hit the knight with the queen behind it, but 6.Nb5 was stronger. After 6...Qd6 7.Nb5 7...Qb4+ came 8.c3, a blunder that left a piece to be won; 8.Nd2 was the move. 8...Qxc4 took the bishop.
You fought back with 9.Nxc7+ 9...Kd8 10.Nxa8. Black's 11...f6 was a mistake, because 11...Qxe4+ was stronger, and your 12.Rxc3! skewered the queen on c4 and the knight on c6.
14.Nd2 was the final blunder, leaving a piece to be won; 14.Rc3 was the way. After 14...fxg5 15.Qh5 15...Qxb2 you were lost.

review.turning_point: 8.c3 allowed 8...Qxc4, and the lost bishop left you a piece down.
review.focus: 8.c3 blocked a defender and left the c4 bishop loose. When a queen checks on b4, look at which pieces it can take next, and 8.Nd2 kept the position safe.

review.headline: A Petrov where you were winning for most of the game, then lost on time

sections.text: You met 3.d4 with 3...exd4 4.Nxd4 4...Nxe4, a standard Petrov line. 5.Bd3 5...d5 6.Bxe4 6...dxe4 7.O-O 7...Bc5 8.c3 kept the position balanced, and 9...f5 expanded in the centre.

10.Ne6 was a blunder, since 10...Bxe6 simply won a piece. 10...Qh4 missed it, and 11.Nxf8 followed. You found 11...Bxf2+ and 12.Kf1 12...Bxe1, then 13...Qxe1+ 14.Kxe1 14...Kxf8, leaving you well ahead.

You kept the pressure up. 17...b5 was a small mistake, but 23.Nxb5 allowed 23...Bc4+, which forked the king on e2 and the knight on b5. 24...Bxf1 then picked up the rook, and by 29...Nxh3 you were around +6.
The endgame was won, but 51...Rxf2 allowed 52.a8=Q (+5.3 to -2.5); 51...Bc8 would have kept everything under control. 52...Rf1+ made it worse, and you lost on time at move 54.

review.turning_point: 51...Rxf2 let White's a-pawn promote with 52.a8=Q, swinging a won ending.
review.focus: 51...Rxf2 took a bishop and ignored the a7 pawn. In a won endgame, count the opponent's passed pawns first; 51...Bc8 kept it safe. Also watch the clock.

review.headline: A Philidor where you got a big edge, converted it into a huge material lead, and then lost to a mate in the final moves

sections.text: You met the Philidor with a classical setup: bishop to c4, d4 and the queen to e2. Your opponent answered with 3...h6 and 6...c5, and then went wrong at once with 7...Bd7??, which jumped the evaluation to +3.4 in your favor.

You did not get the most out of that gift. 8.Bf4 was fine looking but gave back a lot; the sharper 8.e5 was the way to punish the bishop on d7. Even so, you stayed clearly better and kept the pressure with 9.Bxb5 and 10.Qxb5+.

The decisive moment came when your opponent played 16...Qe7??. You spotted the shot immediately with 17.Bxc7!, and after 18.Qxe7+ you were far ahead in material. That was real tactical alertness, and the rest of the middlegame was a matter of keeping control.

You pushed on, picked up the a-pawn with 31.Rxa7 and stood close to +5. Then 33.Ree7?? doubled rooks on the seventh but allowed 33...Rd1+, a forced mate. A quiet move like 33.Ra3 would have kept everything under control.

review.turning_point: 17.Bxc7! after 16...Qe7?? turned a small edge into a crushing material lead, and 33.Ree7?? then threw it all away by walking into a forced mate.
review.focus: Before every move in a winning position, check the opponent's checks and forcing replies. On move 33 a single look at 33...Rd1+ would have shown the mate and kept you at +4.8.

review.headline: An even Vienna where you won a piece and attacked, then dropped the queen and ran short of time

sections.text: You answered the Vienna with a classical setup, and after 3.Bc4 you traded your light-squared bishop for White's with 3...Be6 and 4...Bxc4. That kept things calm and left you equal, around -0.5 for Black.

The first big moment came at 6.Nd5??, where White put the knight on d5 and walked into trouble. Taking with 6...Nxd5 was natural but not best; 6...Nxe4 was stronger. The recapture 7.cxd5 let White off the hook and the evaluation drifted back near equal.

You still played active chess, and 11...Nxe4 followed by 13...Qxb2 grabbed pawns and put you ahead on material. By then you were around +2 and had real winning chances, although your queen was far from home.

Then came 14...Qa3??. The queen walked into 15.Qb5+ and the position collapsed to -5.8. Instead, 14...Nc3 would have forked the queen on e2 and rook on b1 and kept you in the game. You then lost on time in a position that was already difficult.

review.turning_point: 14...Qa3?? took the queen out of play and let 15.Qb5+ in, while 14...Nc3 forking the queen and rook was the way to keep your edge.
review.focus: On move 14, before moving the queen again, look at what a knight jump like 14...Nc3 attacks. Candidate moves that hit two pieces at once deserve a look before a queen raid.

review.headline: A Stafford Gambit where you took advantage of an early error, then gave back the advantage with two blunders

sections.text: Your opponent chose the Stafford Gambit and played 3...Nc6?, which you answered perfectly. After 4.Nxc6! dxc6 5.d3 you were already around +1.8 and had a healthy extra pawn.
6.Be3? was the first slip, and the stronger move was 6.Be2. After that, 6...Bb6 gave you a second chance, and you built up with 7.Nc3, 8.Be2 and 9.Qd2, still holding about +2.5.

The decisive blunder was 10.h3??. It lost the advantage because the better move, 10.Bxg4, simply took the knight. After 10...Nxe3 11.fxe3! you recovered well, and when 13...Bxh3 came you played the clean 14.gxh3, which kept you clearly better.

With a big lead you went wrong again at move 18. 18.Ne2?? moved the knight off c3 and uncovered the bishop on a5 against your queen on d2, so 18...Bxd2 won your queen and decided the game. 18.Qf2 would have kept you in control.

review.turning_point: 10.h3?? let the knight on g4 off the hook and 18.Ne2?? later opened the bishop on a5 onto your queen, which finished the game.
review.focus: Before moving a knight that is guarding something, look at what it blocks. On move 18 the knight on c3 stood between a bishop and your queen.

review.headline: A fast Italian win: your opponent grabbed pawns and then hung the queen

sections.text: You played the Italian with 3.Bc4 and your opponent replied with 3...d5, a sharp central break. You took it with 4.exd5, and the evaluation moved to +1.4 for you.
Black then played 4...Nb4, attacking c2, but you calmly developed with 5.Nc3. That solid move kept everything covered, and it was the right way to respond to a loose-looking attack.
Your opponent went on with 5...Nxd5?, which let you play 6.Nxd5 and win a knight for a pawn. The better try was 5...c6, but after the exchange you were up around three points of material.
Black then lost the thread completely with 6...Qg5? and you finished with 7.Nxg5!, taking the queen. You answered both opponent errors accurately and the game ended almost at once.

review.turning_point: 6.Nxd5 won a piece, and 7.Nxg5! after 6...Qg5? won the queen and finished the game.
review.focus: You played this cleanly. A good habit to keep is the one you showed at move 5, calmly developing with 5.Nc3 instead of reacting to the knight on b4.

review.headline: A Philidor where you took over after a sharp tactic, then lost on time while winning

sections.text: You played a flexible setup with a bishop on g4 and a fianchetto. By 9...Be6?! and 10...d5?! you were already slightly loose, and 11...dxe4?? let White play 12.gxf6, swinging the evaluation to -3.6. The better answer was 11...d4.

Even so, you fought. White's 15.Bxe5?? was a serious mistake, and you found 15...Nxe5!, a discovered attack because moving the d7 knight uncovered your queen on the d8 square against the knight on d6. That swung things back in your favor.
You went on to win material with 18.O-O-O Qxb7. The position stayed good for you, but 23...Bf8? was a slip and 24...Kc8?? left a piece to be won; 24...Kc7 was safer.

Later White blundered with 27.Qe7??, and 27...Bxe7 was the move to play. Instead 27...Rd8?? let White back in. By the end you were in time trouble and lost on the clock after 31.Kd2, in a game that you were winning by a lot.

review.turning_point: 15...Nxe5! turned the game around after 11...dxe4?? had put you in trouble, and 27...Rd8?? threw away a clearly winning chance.
review.focus: When the clock gets low, look for the one forcing move. On move 27, 27...Bxe7 simply took the queen, but it was missed under time pressure.

review.headline: A Philidor where you traded off the queens' pieces and won material with a sharp queen sortie

sections.text: You played a classical line with 3.Bc4 and 4.Bb3, which met 3...Be6 by trading bishops. After 5.axb3 the open a-file gave you something to aim at, and you were comfortably around +0.3.
You kept developing smoothly with 6.d4, 8.Qxd4, 9.Bg5 and 11.Qd3, a sensible plan. 10.O-O?! was a small inaccuracy, because 10.Rxa7 was available, but your position remained fine.
Black went wrong with 15...Nd7?, and you reacted immediately with 16.Qxd5!. That queen move pinned the knight on d7 to the queen on d8 and won a pawn, taking the evaluation to nearly +2.

17.Qxb7?! was a little greedy, since 17.Qf3 was cleaner, but your opponent then blundered with 17...Bg5??. You answered 18.Bxg5! hxg5, a trade that left you well ahead. From there you doubled with 19.Rad1, built pressure and won with 22.Nxc5.

review.turning_point: 16.Qxd5! punished 15...Nd7 by taking a pawn with tempo, and 18.Bxg5! after 17...Bg5?? kept you clearly ahead.
review.focus: On move 17, 17.Qxb7 grabbed a second pawn but left the queen far from the king. Compare it with 17.Qf3, which kept more control.

review.headline: A quiet Giuoco Pianissimo that was decided by a single tactic on the f-file

sections.text: You played a calm Italian with 4.d3 and 5.Be3, offering a trade of bishops. After 5...Bxe3 6.fxe3 you got the semi-open f-file, a useful feature for the rest of the game.
You developed with 7.O-O and 8.Nc3, then posted the knight on d5 with 9.Nd5. 10.Qe2?! was a small inaccuracy; 10.h3 was cleaner. Even so the position stayed balanced.
12.Nxf6+ Qxf6 13.Nd4 set a trap that your opponent fell into. 13...Bxc4?? took a bishop but left the queen on f6 facing your rook on f1 along the open f-file.
14.Rxf6! won the queen for a bishop, and your opponent resigned. Great use of the open file you made on move 6, and good calm play before the tactic.

review.turning_point: 13...Bxc4?? took a bishop but 14.Rxf6! won the queen on the open f-file.
review.focus: Your only inaccuracy was 10.Qe2?!, where 10.h3 kept the knight on g4 at bay. Look at whether a quiet pawn move can solve the problem before you move the queen.

review.headline: A six-move Petrov miniature: one blunder, one check, one queen

sections.text: You went into the Petrov Damiano line with 3.Nxe5. Your opponent replied with 3...Nxe4 and you brought out the queen with 4.Qe2, a well-known idea that puts the queen on the e-file opposite the king.
Black went wrong at once with 4...Nf6??, retreating the knight off the e-file. The correct answer was 4...Qe7, which would have kept the balance.

You found the shot with 5.Nc6+!. That is a discovered check, because the knight leaves e5 and uncovers your queen on e2 against the king on e8. Black has to deal with check and cannot save the queen on d8, which the knight on c6 also attacks.
After 5...Be7 you simply took with 6.Nxd8 and were up the queen, around nine points of material. This was a model finish and a great reminder of the 4.Qe2 trap.

review.turning_point: 5.Nc6+! was a discovered check that won the queen after 4...Nf6??.
review.focus: Nothing to fix here. Keep the habit of looking for checks when the queen faces the king along a file, as you did on move 5.

review.headline: A Vienna Gambit where you survived a worse position, missed a forced mate, and then lost on time while winning

sections.text: White chose the Vienna Gambit with 3.f4 and you met it with 3...d6 and 4...dxe5. After 5.Nf3 Nbd7?! and 6.Bc4 Bb4 White had a small lead in development, and 7...Bxc3?! 8.bxc3 Nxe4 won a pawn but left you a little worse.
9.Qe2? was a mistake, but your reply 9...f5?? was a blunder, because 9...Nd6 was the safe move. White did not take full advantage, but 10.Ba3 b6? left you around -4, and you needed White to err.
The game turned on the kingside. After 13.gxf5 gxf5! and 14.Nxe5?? you played 14...Qg5+? when 14...Rg8+ was better. After 15.Kh1?? the quiet 15...Nf2# was a forced mate, but you played 15...O-O-O?.

You still had a winning position. 17...Ng3+! was a fork of the queen on e2, the rook on f1 and the king on h1, and after 18.Kg2 Nxe2 you were up a queen. You went on to lose on time in a position that was totally winning.

review.turning_point: 15.Kh1?? allowed 15...Nf2#, a forced mate. You played 15...O-O-O? instead, though you still got a winning attack with 17...Ng3+!.
review.focus: After 14.Nxe5 the checks 14...Rg8+ and, a move later, 15...Nf2# were the key. Start every attacking move by listing all the checks, then manage the clock.

review.headline: A slow Giuoco Pianissimo where you converted a queenside attack and won on time

sections.text: You played a classical Italian with 4.d3, 5.Be3 and 6.Nbd2. After 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 you had the bishop pair, a good start, and you pressed on with 9.Bg5 and 11.Bh4.
15.Nf3?! was a small slip, and 15...O-O-O? from Black missed 15...Qg7. Then 16.Bd5?? gave back the edge, since 16.Qxf7 was stronger. Black replied 16...Na5??, which was another error.
You rebuilt with 17.b4 and 18.Bxc6?!, then played the pawn break 20.a4 and the strong 22.a5!. Black's king on the c8 square had no good cover.
24.Rfb1? was a small mistake, where 24.Nd2 was better, but Black replied 24...Ka8??. You found 25.b6! and 27.Ra7+, and won on time with a strong position.

review.turning_point: 22.a5! and 25.b6! broke open the king's position on the queenside.
review.focus: At move 16, 16.Bd5 threw away a clear chance. 16.Qxf7 took a pawn with the queen already on h5. Check every capture before choosing a quieter move.

review.headline: A Petrov where you outplayed your opponent after a knight misstep and converted with pressure on the a-file

sections.text: You played the Petrov and accepted a queen trade early, with 7...Qe7?! 8.Qxe7+ Bxe7. The position stayed level, and you developed with 9...O-O and 10...Re8.
You captured with 12...cxd4 and then 13...Nbd7?!, and 14...Rd8?? weakened the position, where 14...Bd8 was safer. But your opponent replied with 15.Nd6??, which is a blunder.
You found 15...Bxd6!, winning a knight, and from there it was a clear plus. White's 22.Be3? let you play 22...Ra5!, and 23...Rxa7 won the pawn on a7 with an edge.
You closed the game with 25...Bxb4! and 26...Bxc3, then 27...Bxa1, picking up pawns and the rook on a1 with your bishop. A pleasant, technical win.

review.turning_point: 15...Bxd6! punished 15.Nd6?? by taking a knight outright and set up the whole conversion.
review.focus: Look at 14...Rd8?? again: 14...Bd8 was the safe move and avoided any risk. Check your pieces' defenders before choosing a rook move.

review.headline: A wild Petrov Three Knights game with plenty of errors on both sides, decided on the clock

sections.text: You played the Three Knights Petrov and put the bishop on e6 with 4...Be6?! after 4.g3. After 7...c6? and 8.Ne2? both sides had made inaccuracies, but 10.c3?? from White really helped you, because 10.Nxe6 would have forked the queen and the rook.
You chose 9...Nbd7??, which allowed that line, but White did not take it. After 10...Bc4 and 11...Ne5 you were comfortable.
The middlegame turned on 15.Nxe7+? Qxe7!, which was the right recapture, and after 19.Qxd2 Rxd2 you had a nice endgame with the rook on the seventh. Then 23...g4! was a strong reply to 23.a4?.

You got a little loose with 28...Nxe4? and 29...Nxc3?, and 40.Bc6+?? was a discovered check from White that gave you a chance. After 40...Kd6?, 42...Ke6?? and 43...Nc6??, the position was bad for you, but you won on time after 43 moves.

review.turning_point: 15...Qxe7! equalised after 15.Nxe7+?, and the endgame later turned wild with mistakes on both sides.
review.focus: In the endgame 40...Kd6? and 42...Ke6?? gave up the edge. Try to calculate king moves carefully when checks are around.

review.headline: A Petrov that stayed level until one pawn move cost a piece

sections.text: You went into the Petrov and traded queens early with 5...Qe7 and 7.Qxe7+ Bxe7. That is a very safe line, and you reached a balanced endgame with equal chances.
You developed with 8...c6 and 9...Bg4, and 10...Bxf3 11.gxf3 wrecked White's pawns. Then 11...Nbd7 and 12...O-O were a sensible plan.
13.Bh6 Nh5 14.Be2 Rfe8?! was a slightly loose move, and then White played 15.f4, attacking the knight on h5. You replied with 15...g6??, which dropped it.
After 16.Bxh5 you were down material and resigned. 15...Ndf6 was the right way to keep the knight protected.

review.turning_point: 15...g6?? left the knight on h5 loose, and 16.Bxh5 won it.
review.focus: Before pushing a pawn like 15...g6, ask which piece it leaves undefended. The knight on h5 had no support after that move.

review.headline: A Scotch Gambit that went wrong when you lost your queen on move 13

sections.text: You played the Scotch Gambit with 3.Bc4 and 4.d4. After 5.Nxd4?! Nxd4 6.Qxd4 you had a safe, equal position, and Black replied with 6...c6?, which was inaccurate because 6...Bd6 was better.
7.O-O?! was fine, and 7...d5 attacked the centre. Then 8.Be2?? was the first blunder, because 8.exd5 would have kept you ahead. After 8...dxe4 you were behind.
10.f3?? was a second mistake: the best move was 10.Bf4. After 10...exf3 11.Bxf3 Bd6, White was under pressure and the queen was exposed.
Finally, 13.Qg3?? walked into 13...Bxg3, winning your queen. 13.Nc3 was the move that kept you in the game.

review.turning_point: 13.Qg3?? put the queen where the bishop on d6 could capture it.
review.focus: On move 8, 8.Be2 missed 8.exd5. When your opponent challenges the centre, take the pawn first and ask if the opponent has a recapture.

review.headline: An Alekhine Defense where you built a strong advantage and then gave it away with a series of blunders

sections.text: You played the Two Pawns Attack with 3.c4 and 4.d4, and set up a classical space advantage. By 7.O-O you were comfortably over +1, and Black's 7...Nc6? only worsened it.
8.d5! was a good reply, driving the knight away. Then 11.Qg4?? was an error, where 11.Bd3 would have kept the pressure. After 12...dxe5 13.Bxh6!, you recovered with a clever bishop grab.
The game was decided in the middlegame. 17.Ne4?? left a piece to be won, since 17.Nf3 was safer. Black answered 17...g6??, missing 17...Bxe4, and you replied with 18.Bh5??, where 18.Nf5 was better.
After 18...Bxh4 you took with 19.Qxh4?, losing the queen to 19...Qxh4. You would have been better off with 19.Qg4.

review.turning_point: 17.Ne4?? left a piece loose, and 18.Bh5?? and 19.Qxh4? turned a decent position into a lost one.
review.focus: On move 17, 17.Ne4?? left a piece loose. Before every move, check whether the piece you move was protecting something else.

review.headline: A messy Philidor against a lower-rated opponent that you won by mate after taking a long lead

sections.text: Your opponent opened with 3.d3 and 4.h4, and you replied with 3...h5?! and 4...Ne7?!. After 5.Bg5? f6! you kicked the bishop and then followed with 6...Nd7??, where 6...d5 was better.
You kept building with 7...c6 and 8...d5, but 9...b5? and 10...Bb7? loosened your queenside. White's 12.Ng5?? gave you a chance, and you played 12...Be7??, where 12...fxg5 won the knight outright.
After 15.bxc5?? you found 15...Qxe6!, a strong reply, and later 18...Qxg2! after 18.c4??. Those two moves were the key tactics and put you far ahead.
You finished the game with 21...Bxa1 and 24...Nxh4, and the attack with 33...Rh2# was a nice mate. One slip was 17...Qxd5??, where 17...Bxd5 was safer.

review.turning_point: 15...Qxe6! and 18...Qxg2! punished two White errors and gave you a winning material lead.
review.focus: On move 12, 12...Be7?? let the knight on g5 escape. Check whether a capture like 12...fxg5 wins a piece before you move a different piece.

review.headline: A Bishop's Opening that stayed equal until a queen move walked into a knight attack

sections.text: You answered the Bishop's Opening with a solid setup and 3...Be6. After 4.Bb3 Nf6 5.h3 Be7 you were solid, and 6.a3 Bxb3 7.cxb3 gave White doubled pawns, a nice result for you.
You developed with 8...O-O, 9...c6 and 10...Qc7. After 12.Bxf6 Nxf6 13.O-O d5 you had a healthy position. 14...cxd5?! opened the c-file against your own queen, which was a small risk.
15...Bd6? was the mistake, because 15...e4 was stronger. Your opponent then blundered with 16.Qe2??, but 17.Nb5 attacked your queen and bishop at once.
17...e4?? ignored the threat. 17...Qd7 was the right move, and after 18.Nxc7 you were down a queen. You resigned after 19.Qxf3.

review.turning_point: 17...e4?? ignored the attack from the knight on b5 and lost the queen to 18.Nxc7.
review.focus: When an enemy knight lands on b5, check what it attacks before you move. 17.Nb5 hit both Qc7 and Bd6, and 17...Qd7 would have saved you.

review.headline: An Italian Game where you had a big edge and then lost the queen on move 16

sections.text: Your opponent played the offbeat 3...h6 and 4...g5. You responded with 4.O-O and 5.d4, opening the center, and after 6.Nxd4 you were already around +1.9.
You continued with 8.Nc3, 9.Bb3 and 10.f3, keeping Black cramped. 11.Nf5?! was slightly loose, but 12.Nd5 and 13.Nxf6+ kept things under control.
15.Qd5? was a mistake, since 15.f4 was stronger. But Black replied with 15...Nc6??, a blunder that left the queens facing each other. 15...O-O-O was the right move.
16.Qxf5 was the move, and it would have won the queen. Instead 16.Ba4?? pins the knight on c6 to the king on e8, but Black took with 16...Qxd5 and you were down a queen.

review.turning_point: 16.Ba4?? missed the simple 16.Qxf5, which won the queen after 15...Nc6??.
review.focus: On move 16 you had a capture available that won the queen. When your opponent blunders, check every capture before looking for something clever.

review.headline: A Cochrane Gambit where you won the piece and gave it back with one knight capture

sections.text: Your opponent chose the Cochrane Gambit with 3.Nxe5 and 4.Nxf7?, a fork of your queen and the rook on h8. You found the right answer with 4...Kxf7!.
After 5.Bc4+ d5 6.exd5 you were doing fine at around +2. The best move was 6...Bd6, which would have kept a comfortable position.
Instead 6...Nxd5?? walked into trouble. 7.Qf3+ hit both the king and the knight on d5, and after 7...Qf6 8.Bxd5+ you were down material.
You resigned after eight moves. It was a shame, because 4...Kxf7! gave you an excellent position.

review.turning_point: 6...Nxd5?? put the knight on a square where 7.Qf3+ attacked the king and the knight at once.
review.focus: On move 6, 6...Bd6 was safe. When you are a piece up, look first for moves that develop and protect before you capture.

review.headline: An Italian Game that was balanced until a blocking bishop move lost material

sections.text: You played the Paris Defense line with 3.Bc4 and 4.d4, and Black replied with 4...Bg4. After 5.dxe5?! dxe5 6.Qxd8+ Rxd8 the queens came off, and you were fine.
7...Nd4 8.Nxd4 Rxd4 9.b3?! was a bit slow, and 9...Bb4 put pressure on your knight. 10.a3?? was the first blunder: 10.f3 was the right move.
Black replied with 10...Bxd2+?, a mistake, and you took with 11.Bxd2!. That was the right recapture.
After 11...Rxe4+ you needed a good reply. 12.Be2?? blocked the check, but the bishop on e2 was pinned to your king on e1, so 12...Rxe2+ won it. 12.Be3 was the move to play.

review.turning_point: 12.Be2?? blocked the check with a pinned bishop, and 12...Rxe2+ won it.
review.focus: When you are in check, list every legal reply and ask what happens to the piece you interpose. On move 12, 12.Be3 kept everything protected.

review.headline: A speculative bishop grab that your opponent never punished, finished by a mating queen

sections.text: You were Black in a Petrov Italian, and everything was normal until 5...Bxh3. After 5.h3 your bishop had a safe retreat in 5...Bh5, but taking the pawn left it with no way out. After 6.gxh3 you were a bishop down for a pawn (-3.8), with nothing concrete to follow up.

To your credit, you kept developing sensibly: 7...Nf6, 8...Be7, 10...Nbd7 and 11...d5, then 13...Ng6 to bring the knight toward the kingside. White's moves like 7.d3, 9.Nbd2 and 12.Ba2 were slow, and the pawn structure after 6.gxh3 left White's king without its usual cover. The engine still preferred White, but the position was playable.

15...Qxh3 put your queen right in front of that exposed king, and 16...Nh5 and 17...Nhf4 added attackers. When White played 18.cxb7?? grabbing a pawn, it ignored the threat on g2. 18...Qg2# was mate, with the knight on f4 covering the square. 18.Qf3 was the way to defend.

review.turning_point: 18.cxb7 grabbed a pawn and ignored the mating threat on g2; 18.Qf3 was needed, and your 18...Qg2# finished it.
review.focus: 5...Bxh3: before taking a pawn with a bishop, ask whether it can get out again. The engine's 5...Bh5 kept your piece safe and your position healthy.

review.headline: A well-earned advantage that slipped away, and then the clock ran out

sections.text: Your opponent's 4...Bg4?? against your Bc4 setup was an early error (+2.7 for you). You answered with 5.h3?, and the engine preferred 5.Bxf7+. After 5...Bxf3 6.gxf3 your structure was a little ugly, but you were still fine (about +0.1), and your pieces came out naturally: 7.Be3, 8.Nc3, 9.Qd2 and 10.O-O-O.

11.Bh6 was a slip (the engine liked 11.f4), but your opponent answered 11...Nxd4??, and you found the right reply. 12.Bxg7! forked the knight on d4 and the rook on f8, and after 13.Qe2 Kxg7 14.Qxf3 you were comfortably ahead (+3.5).

You traded queens with 17.Qe3 and 18.Qxe5+, and 19.Rd7 put a rook on the seventh. Then 20.a3?? dropped the advantage from +3.0 to +0.5; 20.Bxe6 was the strong continuation. Later 29.Ke2? and 30.Nc5?? turned the game around (-1.4), and 31.Kf1?! went further wrong.
You also lost on time at move 31, which suggests a lot of this was played with a rushed clock.

review.turning_point: 20.a3?? threw away a +3.0 position when 20.Bxe6 was available, and the advantage never came back.
review.focus: 20.a3: when you are clearly better, look for the forcing option first (20.Bxe6) and spend your thinking time there, since the clock decided this game.

review.headline: A solid Petrov that drifted slightly worse, then lost on time

sections.text: You played the main line of the Petrov, 3.Nxe5 3...d6 4.Nf3 4...Nxe4, and you were fully equal. White played 5.Bc4 and 6.Bb3, and you developed with 5...d5, 6...c6, 7...Nf6 and 8...Be7, which is all sound.

The first inaccuracy was 10...Nbd7?. After 10.Nd4 the engine recommended 10...Bg4, which would have stepped the bishop away from the knight and hit the queen on e2. Instead 11.Nxe6 11...fxe6 12.Qxe6 left you a pawn down with a displaced structure.
You fought back with 12...Nc5 and 13...Nxb3?!, but after 14.axb3 you remained slightly worse (-0.7). You then ran out of time at move 14, so the game was decided by the clock rather than the board.

review.turning_point: 10...Nbd7 let White take on e6 with 11.Nxe6 and then win a pawn with 12.Qxe6; 10...Bg4 would have kept the balance.
review.focus: 10...Nbd7: when a piece is attacked, such as your bishop on e6 after 10.Nd4, check whether a move can both save it and make a threat (10...Bg4).

review.headline: You found the knight win with 11...gxf5, but twice missed it earlier

sections.text: You were Black in a Petrov Three Knights. After the early bishop trade on e6, White's 8.Nf5 put a knight where a pawn could attack it, and 8...g6 was a good start, hitting it right away.

White then blundered with 9.Bg5?? (+2.4 for you), and the piece was simply available with 9...gxf5. You played 9...Be7?? instead, and the engine swung to -3.6 for you. White returned the favor with 10.f4??, and again 10...gxf5 was the move. 10...Nbd7?? missed it a second time.

On the third try you found it: 11.Nd5?? gxf5! and you were a knight up. The trades 12.Bxf6 12...Nxf6 13.Nxf6+ 13...Bxf6 kept your edge, and the engine still had you ahead (+3.4) at the end after 21...Qxg2 and 22.Rf7. Your king walked to the queenside, which was risky, but the record shows a resignation in a position the engine still liked for you.

review.turning_point: 9...Be7?? passed up the free knight on f5 (9...gxf5), and 10...Nbd7?? did it again.
review.focus: 9...Be7 and 10...Nbd7: after every opponent move, ask first what is attacked and what is undefended. The knight on f5 was attacked by the g6 pawn, and capturing it was right both times.

review.headline: A big attack built and then spoiled by a string of oversights

sections.text: You met the Hyperaccelerated Dragon with a sound Bc4 and c3 setup. 5...Nf6? was a mistake, and your 6.e5! was the right punishment, hitting the knight at once. But 7.Nbd2?? let the knight trade off and cost you the edge (+2.2 to -0.1); 7.d5 was better.

9.Qb3? and 10.O-O-O?? put your king on a risky side, and the engine preferred 10.O-O. But you stayed active with 11.h4 and 12.h5, and your opponent's 13...Nxc4?? and 14...Bh8?? were big errors. 14.Qxc4! and 15.hxg6! were the right strikes, and after 15...d5 you were at +7.3.

Here the game turned. 16.Qe2?? missed 16.gxh7+, which kept the attack going. 18.Ne6 forked the queen and rook and looked strong, but 18.Rxh7 was far better (+4.0 to -0.3). Black's 18...Qc6?? was another error, but 20.Qg4?? and 23.Qxe7?? finished you off, and you lost material at the end.

review.turning_point: 16.Qe2?? from +7.3: 16.gxh7+ would have kept the king hunt going.
review.focus: 16.Qe2: when you are winning, check every forcing move first (checks and captures). 16.gxh7+ was the move that kept the attack.

review.headline: An Italian where the opponent's bad knight move was not punished, and the clock ran out

sections.text: You played the Classical Italian with 4.c3 and 5.d4 and a normal fight developed. 8.e5 was a good idea, and your opponent's 8...Ng4?? gave you +2.5. The engine's choice was 9.O-O, but you chose 9.Ng5??, a discovered attack from your queen on the g4 knight that did not hold up, and the advantage dropped to +0.7.

Your opponent erred again with 9...d6?, but you did not take advantage: 10.Be2?? was the problem, and the engine wanted 10.e6. After 10...Nh6 and 11.Ne4?! the position was slightly worse for you (-0.6), with your bishop on c1 aiming at the h6 knight.

12.g4?? was the final slip, going after the f5 knight but leaving the d4 pawn to be taken with 12...Nfxd4. 12.Bg5 was better. You then lost on time at move 12, which suggests you were short of time early.

review.turning_point: 9.Ng5?? gave away a +2.5 advantage when 9.O-O was stronger, and 10.Be2?? missed 10.e6.
review.focus: 9.Ng5: after an opponent's mistake like 8...Ng4, calm development with 9.O-O keeps the pressure. Don't go for a clever move when a solid one works.

review.headline: A Petrov where the early queen trade left your king in the middle

sections.text: You played the Petrov with 3...d6 and 4...Nxe4, and the opening was fine and equal. 5...Qe7 and 7...Bf5 were natural, and you kept your development up while White played 8.g4 and 9.h4 on the kingside.
9...h5? was the first mistake (-1.3). The engine liked 9...Nc6 instead, getting a piece into play. After 10.g5 Nfd7 11.Nd5, you traded queens with 11...Qxe2+, but that left your king in the centre.

12...Na6? made it worse (-3.1); 12...Kd8 was the engine's choice. After 13.N3f4 13...c6 14.Bxa6 you lost material, and 14...cxd5 15.Bxb7 and 16.Bxd5 left you down material. 16...Ne5?! and 17...Nc4?! gave the evaluation another push (-6.5) before you resigned.

review.turning_point: 12...Na6? let White win material with 14.Bxa6; 12...Kd8 was the safer move.
review.focus: 9...h5: develop your queenside pieces first (9...Nc6) before starting pawn moves, since a loosened kingside left you exposed after 11.Nd5.

review.headline: A comfortable win after an early open game, with two clean tactics

sections.text: You opened with 1.e4 and 2.d4 against 2...Nc6, and after 3.dxe5 3...Nxe5 4.Nf3 4...Nxf3+ 5.Qxf3 you had the better structure. 9.e5 9...d5 10.exf6 won a piece and 11.fxg7 won a pawn. 12.Qe4+? was a small slip, as 12.O-O was cleaner.

After 13.Qxe7+ 13...Kxe7 14.Bh6 the queens were off and you kept the initiative. Black went wrong with 16...c5??, and after 17.Rfe1?! 17...cxb4 18.Nxc4 18...Kf6?? you found 19.Nxb6!, winning a bishop (+5.1).

23.Nc8?? gave away most of your edge (+5.5 to +0.2), since 23.Be3 was the move. Black's 23...Rc6?? gave it right back, and 24.Ne7+! forked the king and rook. After 25.Nxc6 25...bxc6 26.Bc3+ it was over.

review.turning_point: 19.Nxb6! won a bishop after 18...Kf6??, and 24.Ne7+! won the game after a second Black error.
review.focus: 23.Nc8: when you are up a lot, check what your last move leaves hanging. 23.Be3 kept everything protected.

review.headline: A wild King's Gambit full of swings, with a winning position at the end

sections.text: As Black in the King's Gambit you played 2...d6, 3...Nc6 and 4...Be6, which was fine. White's 6.O-O? and 8.Nb5?? gave you chances, but 8...a6?? missed 8...Bxc4, which won material (the evaluation went from +2.3 to +0.2).

10.f5 10...Bxc4 11.Nxc4 and 12.Bg5 12...g6? led to complications. 13.a4?? let you play 13...gxf5!, and 14...Qxf5?? then threw the edge away (14...Rdg8 was better). 15...Qg6! recovered well, and 18...Qg5! after 18.Nh4? was a strong move (+4.0).

19...Nxe3 and 20.Rxf7 left you well ahead, but 20...N7f5?? and 21...Rdf8?? gave it back (-4.1). White then played 22.Rxc7+?? and 22...Kxc7! reversed things again. 33.Rf1? 33...Rxf2! finished the work, leaving you at +5.0 at the end of the record. That is still well ahead, so this loss is worth reviewing.

review.turning_point: 21...Rdf8?? gave up a big edge; 21...Rd7 was the move, and 22.Rxc7+?? by White swung it right back.
review.focus: 21...Rdf8: in sharp positions, check the opponent's checks and captures after your move. 21...Rd7 would have kept everything protected.

review.headline: A winning Smith-Morra position thrown away in two moves

sections.text: You played the Morra-style 2.d4 2...cxd4 3.Qxd4, and the opening was balanced, with 6.Nbd2, 7.Bd3, 8.O-O, 9.b3 and 10.Bb2 all sensible. Your opponent erred with 11...Bc5??, and the engine preferred 11...dxc3.
12.cxd4?! and 13.Nxe5 gave you the upper hand (+2.4), and 14.Ndc4 14...Bxc4 15.Nxc4 followed by 16.e5 kept the pressure on. 18.Bxd4 18...Bxd4 put you at +4.7.

19.Qc2?? swung the evaluation to -3.5 for you; the engine wanted 19.Nd6+. The f2 pawn was under attack from the bishop on d4 and the knight on g4. 20.Rd1? made it worse (-7.1), and 20.h3 was needed. 20...Bxf2+ 21.Kh1 21...Qxd1+ ended it.

review.turning_point: 19.Qc2?? turned +4.7 into -3.5; 19.Nd6+ was the strong move instead.
review.focus: 19.Qc2: before a quiet move, ask what the opponent is threatening. Black's bishop on d4 and knight on g4 both aimed at f2.

review.headline: A quick win after your opponent took the bait on d5

sections.text: You played the Petrov Italian with 3...d5?!, an unusual move, and after 4.exd5 you took back with 4...Nxd5?. The engine preferred 4...e4. 5.Nxe5 put you under pressure (-1.4).
5...Qg5? went for the knight but was risky (-3.4); 5...Be6 was safer. White's 6.Bxd5? did not take the best route (6.O-O was better), and the capture ended your trouble.
6...Qxe5+! was the key shot: the queen forked the king on e1 and the bishop on d5. White tried 7.Qe2, but 7...Qxe2+ won the queen, and White resigned.

review.turning_point: 6.Bxd5? by White allowed 6...Qxe5+!, forking the king and bishop and winning the queen.
review.focus: 5...Qg5: before an early queen move, check what happens if the opponent captures the piece you are bypassing. 5...Be6 was the safer option.

review.headline: A strong h-file attack undone by a hanging rook at the end

sections.text: You played a quiet Giuoco Pianissimo, and 5.Be3 5...Bxe3 6.fxe3 opened the f-file. You pushed on the kingside with 7.h3, 8.g4, 10.h5, 13.g5 and 15.O-O-O, a plan that worked well.

Your opponent erred with 15...Rxh5?, and the engine preferred 15...Qd7. 16.Rxh5 16...Nxh5 17.Rg1 and 19.Qh8 kept the pressure going, and 20.Qxg7 won a pawn back. 21.Bxf7?! was a risk, but 22.Nxf7 was fine.

22...Re8?? was another mistake (+3.3). 23.Nh6? let some of it go (23.Rf1 was better), and after 23...Qxg7 24.Rxg7 you were still ahead. Then 24...Nh5? attacked your rook on g7, and 25.Nd5?? ignored it. 25.Rf7 was the right move. 25...Nxg7 cost you the rook.

review.turning_point: 25.Nd5?? left the rook on g7 attacked by the knight on h5; 25.Rf7 kept everything safe.
review.focus: 25.Nd5: after every opponent move, check which of your pieces it attacks. The knight on h5 hit your rook on g7.

review.headline: A clean, accurate win after punishing an over-ambitious pawn push

sections.text: You were Black against the Van't Kruijs (1.e3), and you set up smoothly: 2...d5, 3...Nf6, 4...Bc5, 5...Nbd7, 6...O-O, 7...b6 and 8...Ba6. You also had a clear plan of pressure on the e-file with 9...Re8, 10...Qe7 and 11...Rad8.

White's pawn storm with 10.h4, 11.g4 and 12.g5 looked threatening, but you replied calmly with 12...Nh5. 13.f4?? was the mistake, and 13...exf4! was the right punishment (+4.7). After 14.exf4 14...Be3 15.Qd1 15...Bxf4 you were already winning.

17...Nxh1 collected material, and you kept control through 19...Nxe4, 21...fxe4 and 24...Qxd5. The only small inaccuracy was 18...Ng3?!, where 18...Qc5 had a discovered attack. You finished with 32...Ree2 and 35...Rc2#.

review.turning_point: 13.f4?? weakened White's king, and 13...exf4! opened lines for your bishop and knight.
review.focus: 18...Ng3: when you are far ahead, look for the cleanest strong move such as 18...Qc5, which created a discovered attack, before choosing a more forcing one.

review.headline: A good opening, then a rook given away on e4

sections.text: In this Scotch Gambit you went 4.d4 4...exd4 5.Nxd4?!. Black's 5...Qe7? was a mistake (the engine preferred 5...Nxe4), and your 6.O-O! was the right reply, with 7.Re1 adding to the pressure.
8.f4?! was a bit loose, and your opponent's 8...Nxe4?? returned the favor, giving you +3.1. 9.Nd2 9...f5 10.Nxe4 10...fxe4 left the engine rating you clearly better (+3.2) despite the pawn deficit.
11.Rxe4?? took the pawn, but it was defended by the queen on e7, and 11...Qxe4 won your rook. 11.Bd5 would have kept your edge. You resigned right after.

review.turning_point: 11.Rxe4?? captured a pawn that the queen was defending, and 11...Qxe4 won a rook.
review.focus: 11.Rxe4: before capturing, count how many pieces defend the target. The queen on e7 covered e4.

review.headline: A solid London defence that went wrong on a single knight move

sections.text: You set up solidly against the London with 1...d5, 2...e6, 3...Bd6, 4...Nf6 and 5...Nbd7. Your fianchetto with 6...b6 and 7...Bb7 was fine. 9.Bb5 caused some annoyance, but 9...Qe7 was fine.

10...Bc8? was the first slip (-1.1); 10...a6 was better. 11...a6?! came a move late. Your opponent's 12.Bxf6? was an error, and you found the right reply with 12...Nxf6!, which kept you close to equal.

14...Bxe5 and 16...Nc5 kept things balanced. But 17...Nd3+?? moved a knight that was blocking the queen on a3 from your queen on e7, a discovered attack against you, and 18.Qxd3 cost you the knight. 17...dxc4 was the move that kept the position close.

review.turning_point: 17...Nd3+?? opened the a3 queen onto your queen and lost the knight; 17...dxc4 was fine.
review.focus: 17...Nd3+: before moving a piece, ask what it was blocking. The knight on c5 was shielding your queen on e7.

review.headline: Opponent's early pawn moves around the king gave you an h-file mating attack

sections.text: In a Queen's Pawn game, your opponent's 2.h3 and 3.f3?? weakened the king. You kept your structure with 3...e6, 4...Nbd7 and 5...c5, then traded with 7...Bxd7 and 8...Bxc5.

11...O-O-O? was a small slip (11...Bb5 was better), but you recovered with 12...e5. 14.g4? was an overreach, and 14...Nf6! was the right reply. 16.Ng3? allowed 16...hxg4!, opening the h-file against the king.

17.Nf5 17...Bxf5 18.fxg4 18...e4 left White in trouble, and 19.Rxf5 19...Qg3+ 20.Kf1 20...Rxh3 started the final attack. 21...Rh2+, 22...Rh1+ and 23...Qxg4+ kept the king on the run, and 24...Qxd1# was mate.

review.turning_point: 16.Ng3? allowed 16...hxg4!, opening the h-file for your rook and queen.
review.focus: 11...O-O-O: pick a safe king placement before the position opens. 11...Bb5 was the engine's choice.

review.headline: A crushing endgame win that ended as a draw on time

sections.text: You played the Queen's Gambit Declined with 2...e6, 3...Nf6 and 4...Bb4+. 5...Nc6?! and 6...Nxd5?! were a bit loose, but after 8.Bxc6 8...Bxc6 9.Bxb4 9...Nxb4 you were fine. 12...Bxf3 13.Qxf3 13...Qxf3 14.gxf3 simplified the game, and 15...exd5 left an equal endgame.

White erred with 19.exd5? and you replied well with 19...Rxd5!. After 20.Rc5 20...Rd7 21.d5? you chose 21...Re2??, and the engine preferred 21...Re5. But White answered 22.dxc6??, and 22...Rxd1+! delivered check on the back rank and won a rook. 23.Kg2 23...bxc6 left you far ahead.

You then picked up pawns with 25...Rxb2, 31...Rxa3 and 32...Rxf3, and the a-pawn promoted with 36...a1=Q. You were at +9 and then had a second queen with 70...h1=Q+, but the game ended as a draw on time at move 71.

review.turning_point: 22.dxc6?? allowed 22...Rxd1+!, which won a rook and decided the game.
review.focus: 21...Re2: check what your opponent's reply can do before moving (21...Re5 was the engine's choice). Also watch the clock: a totally winning position ended as a draw.

review.headline: A flawless Scandinavian where your bishop took the queen

sections.text: You met the Scandinavian with 2.exd5 2...Qxd5 3.Nc3, and after 3...Qd6 you built a natural position with 4.d4, 5.Nf3, 6.Be2, 7.O-O and 8.g3. Every move was accurate (96.9).
9.Bf4 was the key move, putting the bishop on the diagonal that faced Black's queen on d6. Black played 9...a6??, which ignored the threat, and you found 10.Bxd6!, winning the queen.
Black resigned right away. The engine's alternative for Black, 9...Qd8, was needed to avoid it.

review.turning_point: 9...a6?? left the queen on d6 to your 10.Bxd6! (+6.1).
review.focus: 9.Bf4: you made no real mistakes, so keep doing the same thing. Put your pieces on squares that create a threat and check which squares the opposing queen can reach.

review.headline: A messy Philidor where both sides kept slipping, until White put the queen on a square your knight could take

sections.text: You answered 1.e4 with the Philidor and developed the bishop early with 3...Be6. White castled and left the e4 pawn loose, so you grabbed it with 5...Nxe4 and went a pawn up. After 7.Bxe6 Nxe6 the bishops were gone and you were comfortably ahead.

The first real chance came after 8...f6?! and 9.dxe5, which handed you +1.4. Recapturing 9...fxe5 gave it all back. Taking with 9...dxe5 opens the d-file and produces a discovered attack, queen against queen, and keeps your edge.

From there both sides kept missing things. 10.Nc3 and your 10...Be7 (10...Nc6 was better), then 11.Qd5 and 11...Nc5 (11...Qc8 was the engine choice), and 12.Be3 missed 12.Nxe5. The evaluation hovered near zero. Credit to you for 12...c6!, a calm, accurate reply that kept everything protected.
White then went wrong for good with 13.Qe4, putting the queen on a square attacked by your knight on c5. You simply took it.

review.turning_point: 13.Qe4 stepped onto a square your c5 knight attacked, and 13...Nxe4 won the queen outright (+5.8).
review.focus: On 9...fxe5 you gave back a clear edge. When you recapture in the centre, compare the options: 9...dxe5 opened the d-file with a discovered attack and kept you ahead.

review.headline: A slow-opening game that you built into a strong centre, let slip in a tactical scramble, and then finished with a queen mate

sections.text: White's quiet setup of 1.h3, 2.e3 and 3.a3 gave you time to build a classical centre with ...e5, ...d5, ...Nf6, ...Be7 and castling. You stretched the position with 10...e4 and then 12...c5, which opened lines while you were ahead in development (+1.7 to +1.9).
The best moment was 21...Ne5!. The knight stepped away from d7, uncovering the rook on d8 against the queen on d5. That discovered attack lifted you to +4.1.

After that the conversion went wrong. 22...Ned3?? let White back in (22...Rg6 was the engine move), 23...Na4? gave up more, and 24...Naxb2?? grabbed a bishop when 24...Rg6 was stronger. By 26.a4 the position was close to level again.
27...Qxc5 recaptured with the queen when 27...bxc5 was correct, and 30...Qg5, with low time, lined the queen up against g2 and the king. White also slipped. 32.Ra2?? allowed the finish, 32...Qxg2#.

review.turning_point: 21...Ne5 gave you a big edge, but you let it go with 22...Ned3, and the game was only decided when 32.Ra2?? allowed 32...Qxg2#.
review.focus: On 27...Qxc5 you recaptured with the queen when the pawn recapture 27...bxc5 was available. When you are comfortable, prefer the recapture that keeps your queen safe from tricks.

review.headline: A Two Knights scramble where a sloppy 10.Nf3 almost cost you, but your opponent's 13...Nxg4 gave it all back

sections.text: You went for the sharp 4.Ng5 against the Two Knights and won a pawn with 5.exd5. After 6.d3?! Nxc4 7.dxc4 the bishops were traded and the game stayed roughly level (+0.1).
8.Be3? was the first slip. 8.Nc3 was simpler. After 8...Bxe3 9.fxe3 you were a little worse (-1.3), and Black's 9...Bg4?? then handed the advantage back to you (+0.8).

You couldn't hold it. 10.Nf3?? blocked the bishop's attack on your queen but walked into 10...e4. 10.Qd3 was the move. After 11.h3 exf3 12.hxg4 fxg2 13.Rg1 you were still worse (-0.7), though White's pieces were tangled up too.
Black's 13...Nxg4?? took a pawn on g4 but left the knight loose. 14.Qxg4! won it cleanly, finishing a piece up (+3.9) and Black resigned.

review.turning_point: 13...Nxg4?? let your queen take the knight with 14.Qxg4!, turning a worse position into a piece-up win.
