review.focus: On 10.Nf3?? you blocked a threat with a move that lost ground. Against 9...Bg4 the engine liked 10.Qd3, keeping the queen safe without allowing 10...e4.

review.headline: A short opening skirmish that ended when White's clock ran out after four moves

sections.text: White opened 1.d4 and went for the Jobava-style 2.Bf4 and 3.Nc3. You responded sensibly with 1...d5 and 2...e6, a sturdy setup that keeps the centre solid and the bishop on c8 for later.

3...Bd6 challenged the bishop on f4 straight away, and when White moved it to e5 you hit it again with 4...f6. The bishop on e5 was attacked by both the bishop and the pawn, so White had to decide what to do with it (-0.3, equal.)
The game ended there, as White ran out of time. There was not much to analyse on the board. Your play was accurate throughout (91.4).

review.turning_point: There was no tactical moment. 4...f6 put the question to the bishop on e5, and White's clock expired.
review.focus: No errors to fix. Just note that 4...f6 loosens your e6 pawn and the king's diagonal, so be ready for that if the game had continued.

review.headline: A French Exchange where an unsound knight sacrifice left you down material, until your opponent's clock ran out

sections.text: You played the Exchange French with the usual 4.Nc3 and 5.Bg5. 6.Bh4 pinned the knight on f6 to the queen, but 6...g5 broke it and cost you your edge. 6.Bxf6 was the better route. After 7.Bg3 and 8.Nf3 things were still level.
The real damage came with 12.Nxg5??. After 12...hxg5 13.Qxg5 Bxc2 you had given a knight for two pawns and then lost the c2 pawn too (-3.1). 12.Ne5 was the calmer plan.

Things got worse with 16.h5?! Nxh5 and 17.Qxd5?!, and you were close to -6. Credit for fighting on. Black's 22...Qh8? let you off (22...Rxh3+ was stronger), and after 23.Ng5?! Rxh3+ 24.gxh3 and 25.Qxb7 the material was level again.

26.Ne6+ forked the king on g7 and the rook on f8, and you kept making threats. The engine still had you around -3.5 when your opponent's time ran out at 29.Qf3. This was a win on the clock more than on the board.

review.turning_point: 12.Nxg5?? gave up a knight for two pawns and swung the game to -3.3; only the clock rescued you later.
review.focus: Before a sacrifice like 12.Nxg5, count what you get back. Here it was only pawns, while 12.Ne5 kept the position equal.

review.headline: A Bishop's Opening where a queen hit two pawns at once, and the game ended on the clock after eight moves

sections.text: After 1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 d6 3.c3 you developed with 3...Be6?!. The engine preferred 3...Nf6. White simply took the bishop with 4.Bxe6 and after 4...fxe6 the pawns on e6 and e5 were a target.
5.Qb3 was the strong follow-up. The queen hit both b7 and e6. 5...Nc6?! only defended one idea, and 5...Qc8 would have covered both.
6.Qxb7 won a pawn, and after 6...Nge7 7.Qb3 Rb8?! (7...d5 was better) 8.Qxe6 won a second pawn. At this point the engine had you at -2.4.
The game ended on time after only eight moves. Whatever the reason, the clock decided it and your accuracy (78.3) was not the issue.

review.turning_point: 5.Qb3 attacked two pawns at once, and 5...Nc6?! let 6.Qxb7 win material.
review.focus: On 5...Nc6, when a queen hits two pawns, look for one move that guards both (5...Qc8). Also watch the clock, since this game was lost on time.

review.headline: A clean Scandinavian win where Black's greedy knight capture cost the queen

sections.text: Against the Scandinavian you took the main line with 3.Nc3, 4.d4, 5.Bd2 and 6.Nge2, and added 7.g3 and 8.Bg2. Sound development and a quick 9.O-O (+2.1) were all you needed while Black pushed pawns with 7...g5? and 9...h5.

10.Ne4 was the key idea. Moving the knight off c3 opened the diagonal from your bishop on d2 to the queen on a5. Black's 10...Nxe4? took the knight and missed it, so you replied 11.Bxa5! and won the queen.
You kept it simple after that. 13.Qd2 Nxc3 14.Nxc3 Bb4 and 15.Qxg5 won a pawn, and your queen and pieces kept running Black's king around.
The finish was routine: 22.Nxf6, 24.Qc5+, 28.Qxf7, and 31.Qxg8 ended the game with a huge material edge (+13).

review.turning_point: 11.Bxa5! won the queen right after Black's 10...Nxe4?, and the game was decided there.
review.focus: A clean game (94.5), so the habit to keep is 10.Ne4: before you move a piece, ask what it uncovers behind it.

review.headline: A Petrov where White's greedy queen check lost the queen, and you converted without trouble

sections.text: In the Petrov you regained the pawn quickly after 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4, then built up with 5...Qe7, 6...Nf6 and 7...Be6. The trade 9.Nxe6 fxe6 was equal.

10.Qh5+?? was a blunder. You answered 10...Nxh5!, and the knight's capture opened the line from your queen on e7 to the bishop on g5, a discovered attack. After 11.Bxe7 Bxe7 the queens were off and you were up a piece.
You won another pawn with 13...Nxg2+ and kept your pieces active with 14...Nf4. The only slip was 19...Bh4?, which dropped some of your edge (+5.7 to +3.5) when 19...Rxf5 was stronger.
White replied with 20.Bf3??, and later 23...Rxf3 won a bishop (+7.0). Black resigned a few moves later.

review.turning_point: 10...Nxh5! punished 10.Qh5+?? by taking the queen with a discovered attack.
review.focus: 19...Bh4? gave back some advantage. With a big lead, first check which enemy pieces are loose: 19...Rxf5 was stronger.

review.headline: A French Exchange where you let a queen pin slip twice, but converted a messy middlegame into a mating attack

sections.text: Black's 5...Qc6?? (+5.3) walked into trouble. 6.Bb5 would have pinned the queen against the king. You missed it with 6.Nf3?? and again with 7.Bg2??, so a huge lead fell to +0.9.

8.Bd2? Nxc3 9.Bxc3 was fine, and after 10.d5 exd5? you found 11.Bxg7!, winning a pawn back. 12.Bf6?? (12.Bc3 was better) and 13.Bh4 Ne5? kept the game turbulent, and 14.Qe2? passed up the strong 14.Nxe5.
Black's 14...Be6?? let you in with 15.Nxe5!. After 15...Bxe5 16.Qxe5 Qxc2 you were up a piece for a pawn. Then 17.O-O Rg6 18.Qh8+ Kd7 19.Qxa8 won a rook.
20.Qd8+ forked the king on d7 and the rook on f6, and after 20...Kc6 21.Bxf6! you were far ahead. The king hunt ended with 28.Qh4#.

review.turning_point: 15.Nxe5! won a piece for a pawn and opened the way for the queen to reach the rooks.
review.focus: 6.Nf3 and 7.Bg2 both missed 6.Bb5, a bishop pin on the queen against the king. When the opponent's queen steps into your bishop's line, check whether it is pinned.

review.headline: A Petrov where two slips let a lower-rated opponent's knight take over

sections.text: You met the Three Knights with a solid 3...d6 and 4...Be6, and the 5.Bxe6 fxe6 trade was fine. 6...Nbd7? (6...c5 was better) let White play 7.d4, and after 7...exd4 8.Nxd4 the knight on d4 was well placed.

8...c6?? was the first blunder (-1.2 to -3.6). It gave the knight a route to e6, hitting your queen and bishop. 8...Qe7 was the engine move. White missed 9.Nxe6 with 9.Re1??, and you got a break (-0.7). 9...e5?! then gave up some of it.
10.Ne6 hit the queen again. 10...Qe7?? walked into 11.Nc7+, which checked the king and attacked the rook on a8. After 11...Kd8 12.Nxa8 you were down a rook.
From there it was a losing grind with 13.Bg5 h6?!, 14.Bxf6, 15.exd5 and 17.Qxd5+. Your opponent was rated 1115, so these were avoidable errors rather than a strong opponent.

review.turning_point: 10...Qe7?? allowed 11.Nc7+ and 12.Nxa8, losing a rook (-4.1).
review.focus: 8...c6 left the d4 knight free to jump to e6. Before a quiet pawn move, check what your opponent's most active piece can reach.

review.headline: A Philidor that swung back and forth, and a time scramble that cost you a roughly level game

sections.text: You went for the Philidor with 3...Be6, and after 4.Bxe6 fxe6 5.d3 Nd7?! 6.Bg5 Be7 7.Bxe7 Nxe7 the position was balanced. 8...c6?! and 9...d5?? were the first slips (9...Ng6 was the engine choice, -2.1).
Credit to you for coming back. White's 10.c3?? undid their advantage, and after 11.b4 a5?! 12.a3 c5?! 13.Ng5 h6? you found 14...O-O! (+0.1) after 14.Ngf3?? had missed 14.Qh5+.

15.h3 cxb4 16.axb4 axb4 17.cxb4 Qxb4 won a pawn, and after 18.Rxa8 Rxa8 your rook reached the second rank. 21...Nc5? (21...b5 was better) kept things unclear, but you were still holding with 23...Kh7.

The end was a time scramble. 24...Nf4?? (24...Qc5 was stronger), 26...d4??, and then 27...Kh8??, which left a piece to be won. White did not find the right captures, but your flag fell at 30.Kh2, with the evaluation around -0.8.

review.turning_point: 26...d4?? and 27...Kh8?? threw away a balanced game while you were low on time.
review.focus: 27...Kh8?? was played short of time, when 27...Ng6 was fine. In blitz, take a few seconds on checks and keep your knights protected.

review.headline: An Open Sicilian where Black stumbled with 12...Ne8, allowing a queen win

sections.text: You played the Open Sicilian with 3.d4 and 4.Nxd4, then went for Bg5 and Bc4 against the ...g6 setup. The opening stayed balanced (+0.3 to +1.2) while Black developed with 5...a6 and 7...Bg7.
8.O-O?! was a small slip. The engine preferred 8.Nxc6 bxc6, which keeps more pressure on. After 9.Re1 Ne5 10.Bb3 b5 you played 11.f4, pushing the knight back to c6.

12.e5 attacked the knight on f6, and Black played 12...Ne8??. You spotted the shot: 13.Nxc6! dxc6 14.Qxd8 won the queen. The d-pawn recaptured away from the d-file, so your queen met their queen with nothing in the way.
Black resigned straight away, with a huge material lead (+9) and a position that couldn't be held.

review.turning_point: 13.Nxc6! deflected the pawn off the d-file and let you take the queen with 14.Qxd8.
review.focus: 8.O-O?! allowed Black to hold the position together. Where the engine liked 8.Nxc6 bxc6, look for pawn-structure-damaging trades like that.

review.headline: A calm Colle setup that ended on the clock after three moves

sections.text: Your opponent chose the Colle System with 1.d4, 2.Nf3 and 3.e3. You mirrored it with 1...d5, 2...e6 and 3...Nf6, a flexible and solid setup.
All three of your moves matched the engine's top choices (99.4), and the evaluation stayed near zero (-0.1 after 3...Nf6).
The game ended when your opponent's time ran out, so nothing was settled on the board.

review.turning_point: No turning point: the game was decided on the clock after three moves.
review.focus: Nothing to fix. 3...Nf6 is solid development, so keep following the same principles of developing pieces and castling.

review.headline: A short Open Sicilian where Black grabbed a pawn and lost the queen

sections.text: You played the Open Sicilian and traded early with 4.Nxd4 Nxd4 5.Qxd4. The queen on d4 was centralised and covered key squares (+0.9).
After 5...e6 6.Be2 Qb6, Black offered a queen trade. 7.Be3?! was a small inaccuracy, because the simple 7.Qxb6 axb6 kept a bigger edge (+1.6 to +0.7).
Black then grabbed the pawn with 7...Qxb2??. The pawn was poisoned, because your queen on d4 still covered b2 along the diagonal. 8.Qxb2! won the queen (+6.8).
Black resigned, down a queen for a pawn.

review.turning_point: 8.Qxb2! took the greedy queen, leaving you with a decisive material lead.
review.focus: 7.Be3?! allowed a queen-grab trick that happened to fail. Where possible, make the cleaner move: 7.Qxb6 axb6.

review.headline: A Van't Kruijs where your queenside pawn storm won space, and two knight forks turned a messy middlegame into a win

sections.text: White opened with 1.e3, 2.Nc3, 3.h3 and 4.Bb5+, and you built a flexible centre with ...e5, ...d5, ...Nf6 and ...c6. 5...b5, 6...a5 and 7...b4 pushed White's pieces back, and 8.Na2 left the knight stranded. You were already around +3.
11...e4 and 12...c5 kept the initiative, and 15...d4 won a pawn after 16.d3 exd3. White's play looked passive, with the engine at +4.4 for you after 17.Bxd3.

17...Bf8?? (17...b3 was better) and 18...Ne4? gave a lot back, but White's 19.exd4? let you in. 19...Ng3! forked the queen on e2 and the rook on f1. 21...Bxb5? (21...Nxd4 was stronger) allowed White to hang on.
23.Bd2?? was the decisive blunder. 23...Nxb3! forked the rook on a1 and the bishop on d2. From there you converted cleanly with 25.Bxh7+ Kxh7 and 28...Qxd6.
29.Rxf7 allowed 29...Ne2+ 30.Kf2 Qxd1, finishing with a big material edge (+8).

review.turning_point: 23.Bd2?? allowed 23...Nxb3!, a knight fork that won material and took control.
review.focus: 17...Bf8?? gave back much of your lead. After a pawn win, look for the move that keeps your pieces working: 17...b3 was stronger.

review.headline: An Italian where you reached a winning edge in the opening, then lost the thread on the 11th move

sections.text: You took the classical route with 4.c3 and 5.d4. After 5...exd4 6.cxd4 Bb4+ 7.Nc3 Nxe4, the sharp Moller-style position was fine. 8.O-O Nxc3 9.bxc3 Bxc3 and 10.Ba3 kept the pressure on.

Black's 10...d6? (10...d5 was stronger) handed you a big edge (+2.8). 11.Rc1 would have kept it. You tried 11.Qb3?? and the bishop on c3 took the rook, 11...Bxa1, so you were down a rook (-7 in material).
Black's 12...Kd7?? let you back in with a chance to win. 13.Be6+ and 14.Bxc8+ was the engine path, but 13.Bxf7?? dropped back to -2.3.
14.Ng5?! Nxd4 and 15.Be6+?! tried a skewer on the king and the bishop on c8, but 15...Nxe6 simply captured the bishop. You resigned at -10 in material.

review.turning_point: 11.Qb3?? left the rook on a1 hanging to 11...Bxa1 and turned a +2.8 position into a lost one.
review.focus: Before 11.Qb3 you needed to check what the bishop on c3 attacked. The rook on a1 was loose, so 11.Rc1 or a safe move was needed.

review.headline: An Amazon Attack where you won the queen and led for most of the game, then lost the queen and the game on time

sections.text: White opened with 1.d4 and an early queen (2.Qd3, 3.Qf3). You played soundly with 2...e6, 3...Nf6, 4...Nbd7 and 5...b6, putting a bishop on b7 pointing at the queen on f3. After 11...c5 White's 12.dxc5?? was a mistake (+4.9).
12...d4? threw away most of your edge. 12...Ne5 would have forked the bishop on d3 and the queen on f3. After 13.Qxb7 dxc3 14.bxc3 Bxc5 you were close to level (-0.7).
Then White blundered with 15.Qf3??. 15...Ne5! forked the bishop on d3 and the queen on f3, and you were winning (+4.5). After 17.Qxf6 Qxf6 you had won White's queen for a knight.
You kept the lead with 20...Rxd3, 21...Bxe3 and 22...Rdxe3, up a lot of material (+7). But 23.c4 opened the long diagonal against your queen. 23...Rxe2?? took a knight and left the queen hanging.
After 24.Bxf6 you were down material (-3.4), and your time ran out at 25.Re1.

review.turning_point: 23...Rxe2?? ignored the attack on your queen, and 24.Bxf6 turned +5.8 into -3.4.
review.focus: On 23...Rxe2 you captured without checking what White's last move had opened. After 23.c4, ask what the bishop on b2 now attacks.

review.headline: An Italian that went wrong on the sixth move, when a pin idea ignored a loose bishop

sections.text: You played the standard Italian with 3.Bc4 and 4.O-O, and the position was level (+0.2 after 4...Nf6). 5.d4 then offered a pawn in a line where Black could take with the bishop.
Black took with 5...Bxd4, winning a pawn (-1 in material). The simple answer was 6.Nxd4, capturing the bishop that had just captured and keeping the game level (-0.1).
Instead you played 6.Bg5??, pinning the knight on f6 to the queen. The idea was reasonable, but it left the bishop on d4 alone and active. The engine put you at -3.6, and the game ended there.

review.turning_point: 6.Bg5?? tried a pin when 6.Nxd4 could simply have removed the bishop that had taken your pawn.
review.focus: On 6.Bg5 you made a threat without capturing. When an enemy piece sits next to yours and you can take it, check first whether 6.Nxd4 wins material.

review.headline: A clean opening, lost only on the clock

sections.text: You met 1.g3 with the classical 1...e5 and followed up with 2...d5, taking space in the centre straight away. Both moves were sound, and the engine rated all five of your moves as accurate.

Your development was natural: 3...Nf6 and 4...Bc5 put two pieces on active squares, aiming at the centre and the f2 square. White chose a quiet fianchetto set-up with 2.Bg2 and 3.d3, then 4.h3 and 5.Nf3, and nothing sharp happened.
After 5.Nf3 the evaluation was +0.5 in your favour, a comfortable position. The game ended there because your clock ran out, not because of anything on the board.

review.turning_point: There was no turning point on the board. The game was decided by the clock after 5.Nf3, in a position that was fine for you.
review.focus: There are no errors to fix, so the work is time management: after sensible moves like 4...Bc5, decide how much time you can afford per move so a sound position is never lost on the clock.

review.headline: A big opening edge, thrown away by one slip and then lost on time

sections.text: You played a standard Italian with 3.Bc4 and 4.O-O. Black chose the unusual 3...a6 and then 4...Qf6, bringing the queen out early, and after 5.Nc3 Nd4 you stood at about +2.8, with the queen on f6 and the knight on d4 both looking loose.

Then came 6.Nd5, which cut the evaluation to +0.6. The engine preferred 6.Nxd4 exd4 7.Nd5, which keeps the same ideas while Black's pieces stay awkward. Your opponent immediately handed it back with 6...Qc6??, missing 6...Nxf3+, and you were up to +4.8.

You followed with 7.Nxd4, a knight trade that cut your edge to +2.8. The engine liked 7.Nxe5 Qd6 8.c3 Qxe5 9.cxd4 instead, keeping more pressure. Later 10.Ba4?! and 11.Nxf6+?! were small concessions, though 12.Bb3 O-O still left you at +1.3.
The game ended on the clock after 12...O-O, with you still better.

review.turning_point: 6.Nd5 gave away most of a +2.8 edge, and although 6...Qc6?? briefly gave it back, 7.Nxd4 let a lot of it slip again.
review.focus: Before a knight jump like 6.Nd5, check what your opponent's last move allows: 6.Nxd4 exd4 7.Nd5 kept the advantage. Also keep an eye on the clock, since you lost on time while still better after 12...O-O.

review.headline: A dominant win that ended in a stalemate

sections.text: This was an Italian with 3.Bc4 d6, and you built it sensibly with 4.Nc3, 6.Re1 and the central break 7.d4. After 8.Nxd4 Nxd4 9.Qxd4 the position was equal, and 9...c5 pushed your queen back to 10.Qd1.

Trades followed with 14.e5 dxe5 15.Bxe5 Qxd1 16.Raxd1 Bxf3 17.gxf3. Then Black played 17...Nh5?, where 17...Rad8 was better. You punished it with 18.Bxg7!: moving the bishop off e5 let your rook on e1 attack the bishop on e7, a discovered attack, and 19.Rxe7 left you a pawn up with the stronger pieces.

Black kept helping you. 20...a5? allowed 21.Nf6+!, and after 22.Nd7?! Nf5 23.Re5 Rg8+ 24.Kh1 Nh4 25.Rh5, Black played 25...Kh7??. Your 26.Rxh4! won the knight on h4 and pinned the h6 pawn against the king, taking the evaluation to +5.1. You then collected pawns with 32.Rxc5, 33.Rxa5 and 35.Rxh6+, and finished with 41.axb3 and 42.Rxf6.
The ending was completely won, but 51.Nf6?? left Black's king on f8 with no legal move while the black b4 pawn was blocked. That was stalemate. The engine's 51.h7 Ke8 52.h8=Q# was mate.

review.turning_point: 51.Nf6?? turned a completely winning endgame into a draw by leaving Black with no legal move.
review.focus: In a won endgame, count your opponent's legal moves before every move. At 51.Nf6 the king had none, whereas 51.h7 Ke8 52.h8=Q# was mate.

review.headline: A Petrov that swung back and forth until your rook and bishop took over

sections.text: You answered 1.e4 with the Petrov. After 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.Qe2 Qe7 6.d3 Nf6 7.Qxe7+ Bxe7 the queens came off and the game was level, with 8.Bg5 and 9.Bxf6 Bxf6 simplifying further.

Your opponent erred first. After 20.Rad1 Bf7 it was only +0.3, but 21.c5?? jumped to +2.8 for you. You kept it growing with 21...Nd5 and 22...Nc3 (+3.3), but then 23...Nxa2?? threw it away and left you at -2.1. The engine preferred 23...dxc5, simply taking the pawn.

You kept fighting, and 29...a4! and 31...Rc3! were precise answers to White's errors. But 33...a2?? was another slip: 33...Bxd2 34.Rxd2 was the engine's idea. White returned the favour with 34.Rxa2??, when 34.Bxa2 was needed, and 34...Bxa2! won a rook.
From there it was a matter of technique: 38...Bxd2, 41...Rxf1, and the rook and bishop hunted down White's pawns until 66...bxc1=Q and 70...Qg7# ended it.

review.turning_point: 34.Rxa2?? gave back everything you had thrown away with 33...a2, and 34...Bxa2! won the rook.
review.focus: Look at 23...Nxa2 and 33...a2. In both cases a simple, solid move (23...dxc5, 33...Bxd2) kept your edge, while the pawn grab or pawn push gave it away.

review.headline: A level London game decided by a pawn grab and an a-file trick

sections.text: White played the London with 2.Bf4, and you reacted with 2...Nc6 and 4...Bd6. After 5.Bxd6 cxd6 and a few trades (9.Nxe4 dxe4, 12.Bxc6 Bxc6) the game was about equal.
Your 15...Qb4+ was active, and after 16.Qd2 the queen needed to stay safe. Instead, 16...Bxa4?? grabbed a pawn, and 17.Qxb4 axb4 traded queens. The engine's 16...Qb6 17.O-O O-O kept things balanced.

Then 18.Nc5 attacked your bishop on a4, which was standing on the same file as White's rook on a1 and your own rook on a8. After 18...Bxc2?? the bishop left a4, which was a discovered attack from the rook on a1 onto your rook. 19.Rxa8+ Ke7 20.Rxh8 cost you both rooks.
The engine's 18...Ke7 19.Rxa4 Rxa4 20.Nxa4 would have kept the game alive. Instead you resigned soon after.

review.turning_point: 18...Bxc2?? moved the bishop away from a4 and opened the a-file, so 19.Rxa8+ and 20.Rxh8 cost you both rooks.
review.focus: Before moving a piece, ask what it is currently shielding. At 18...Bxc2 the bishop on a4 was blocking the a-file for your rook on a8, so the engine's 18...Ke7 was needed.

review.headline: A Scandinavian where one check led to a lost knight

sections.text: You met the Scandinavian well: 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qa5 4.d4 Nf6 and 5.Bd2 e5 is the Mieses line, and the position stayed level through 6.Nf3 exd4 7.Nxd4.
Black then played 7...Qe5+, checking your king and attacking the knight on d4 at the same time. Your bishop on d2 blocked the d-file, so the knight was not protected by your queen.

You answered with 8.Be2??, which blocks the check but leaves the bishop pinned against the king by the queen on e5. After 8...Qxd4 you had lost a knight, and the evaluation dropped to -3.8. The engine's 8.Qe2 would have offered a queen trade that kept everything protected.

review.turning_point: 8.Be2?? blocked the check but left the knight on d4 undefended, and 8...Qxd4 won it.
review.focus: When you are in check, look at what the checking piece also attacks. At 8.Be2 the queen on e5 hit both your king and the knight on d4, and 8.Qe2 handled both.

review.headline: A queen trade that went well, then two slips against a patient opponent

sections.text: You played the Philidor line with 3.Bc4 and 4.d4. After 4...Nc6 5.dxe5 dxe5 6.Qxd8+ Nxd8 the queens were off and you stood at +2.1, a nice start with Black's king stuck in the middle.
Here 7.O-O?? let most of that go. The e5 pawn was loose, and the engine wanted 7.Nxe5 Nf6 8.f3, keeping the initiative. After 7...Bd6 8.Rd1 Nf6 9.Nc3 a6 10.Be3 b5, the evaluation was level.

You then lost the thread. 11.Bb3 Bg4 12.Bd5?! Rb8 left your bishop on an exposed square, and 13.Bc6+?? lost it: the check looked forcing, but 13...Nxc6 simply took the bishop. The engine suggested 13.Ba7 Rc8 14.Bb3.

review.turning_point: 13.Bc6+?? gave away a bishop for nothing, since 13...Nxc6 took it.
review.focus: Before playing a check like 13.Bc6+, see whether the checking piece can just be captured. Also revisit 7.O-O, where 7.Nxe5 kept an edge.

review.headline: A sharp finish after White ran the h-pawn too far

sections.text: White played a Colle-style setup: 3.Nf3, 4.Ne5 and 5.c3. You answered solidly with 3...Nf6, 4...Bd6 and 5...O-O, then traded off with 7.Nxd7 Bxd7. The position stayed balanced.
White then pushed 8.h4 and 9.h5. Your 9...Qc7?! was a small inaccuracy, since 9...h6 was the engine's choice to shut the h-pawn down, but 10.g3 Ne4 put your knight on a strong central post.

Then White blundered with 11.h6??. Your 11...Bxg3! pinned the f2 pawn against the king and hit the g3 pawn with a clear threat. After 12.fxg3?? the queen on c7 looked down the diagonal at g3: 12...Qxg3+! 13.Kf1 Qf2# was mate, with your knight on e4 supporting the queen on f2.
You found both strong moves in a row and finished with accurate tactics.

review.turning_point: 11.h6?? let you play 11...Bxg3!, and 12.fxg3?? lost at once to 12...Qxg3+ and mate.
review.focus: Look at 9...Qc7?!. When the opponent starts pushing the h-pawn, 9...h6 stops it before it reaches 11.h6 and keeps your position simpler.

review.headline: A winning attack thrown away in time trouble

sections.text: Black played the early 2...Bc5, which the engine called a mistake, but your reply 3.d3? let it off. The engine wanted 3.Nxe5. After 4.Be3? you also missed 4.Nxe5, but 5.c3! was a good answer to 4...Bb4+. By 10.d4 exd4 11.cxd4 you were about +2.

You built up pressure with 12.Qc2 and 13.Rad1, and 14.e5? was a slight slip, but the real chance came with Black's 25...Nc6??. You played 26.Rxc5!, which was a discovered attack on the c6 knight by your bishop on f3, and the rook also pinned it against the queen on c7. After 27.Rxc6 you were far ahead, about +5.0.

You kept control with 29.e6 and 30.Rxg5?!. Then, with the clock low, 31.Qe5?! Qf7? gave you a chance, but 32.Qf4?? allowed 32...Rxf4 33.exf4 and the advantage disappeared. The engine's 32.Qb8+ Qf8 33.Qxf8+ Rxf8 34.Rc5 was safe.
You still pushed with 35.Rb8+ and 36.Ne3, but 39.Ng4?? was another time-pressure error and you lost on time.

review.turning_point: 32.Qf4?? turned a winning position (+5.0) into a losing one (-1.4) in a single move.
review.focus: Time management: both big errors, 32.Qf4 and 39.Ng4, came when you were low on time. Spend less on the early moves like 3.d3 and 4.Be3 so you have time for the critical ones.

review.headline: A wild win from a huge opening gift

sections.text: White began 2.f3 and 3.g4??, which was a serious blunder against 3...Nxe4!. After 4.fxe4 Qh4+ you had a big edge, with the white king in trouble after 5.Ke2.

Your 5...Qxg4+?? was the one slip: the check hit the king on e2 with the queen on d1 behind it (a skewer), but the engine's 5...d5 kept more. White needed 6.Nf3 but replied 6.Ke1??, which uncovered the queen on d1 against your queen on g4, though it wasn't enough. After 6...Qxe4+ the queen forked the king on e1 and the rook on h1, so 7.Ne2 Qxh1 won the rook.
You kept collecting material with 8...Qxh2, 11...Qxd5 and later 14...exf4, 17...Nxd4+ and 21...Nxb5. You promoted with 36...h1=Q and your opponent was out of time after 43...Ba6+.

review.turning_point: 3.g4?? was answered by 3...Nxe4!, and 6.Ke1?? followed by 6...Qxe4+ let you win the rook on h1.
review.focus: At 5...Qxg4+ you gave a check that looked strong but was not necessary. The calmer 5...d5 kept more. Before checking, ask what happens when the king steps away.

review.headline: A Petrov that turned into a quick mating attack

sections.text: You answered the Petrov with 3.Nxe5 and 4.d4, steering into a solid line. After 5.Nf3 Nxe4 6.Be2 d5 7.O-O Be6 8.Re1 Nc6, you were comfortable at about +1.5.

Then you drifted: 9.c3?!, 10.Nbd2?! and 11.Nb3?, which uncovered your bishop on c1 against the knight on g5 (a discovered attack), but 11...Nxf3+ simply traded. The engine liked 11.Bb5 Qd6. Black's 12...O-O-O? helped, but 13.Bf4?? gave the edge back.

Black blundered right away with 13...f5??, and you returned with 14.Qe2??, where 14.Nc5 was stronger. Your opponent then played 14...Bd7?, and you found the strong 15.Qb5!, a discovered attack because the queen leaving e2 opened the rook on e1 against the queen on e7. After 16.Bxd5 Bd6 17.Nc5 b6??, Black was lost.
The finish was 18.Qa6+! Kb8 19.Qb7#, with the knight on c5 covering b7.

review.turning_point: 17...b6?? allowed 18.Qa6+! Kb8 19.Qb7#, a mate supported by the knight on c5.
review.focus: Look at 13.Bf4 and 14.Qe2, where 13.Nc5 and 14.Nc5 kept you in control. Use the knight on c5 earlier to target b7 before hurrying the bishop.

review.headline: A calm London defence that won a pawn and then a rook ending

sections.text: You met the London with 2...e6 and 3...Bd6, and 4...Nf6 and 5...Ne4 made it clear that White's bishop would have to trade. After 6...Nxg3 7.hxg3 you had traded off White's London bishop, and 7...Nd7, 8...b6 and 9...c5 built a solid centre.
White went wrong with 13.Ne5?, which the engine called a mistake, and you found 13...Nxe5!. After 14.dxe5 Bxe5 you had won a pawn, and 15.Bb5+ Bc6 16.c4 Bxb5 17.cxb5 kept things simple.

Your queen and rooks took over: 19.f4 Qa7 20.fxe5 Rxa2 gave you strong play against the king, and 21.Qc3 Qa3+ 22.Kb1 forced White back. 22...Ke7?! was slightly loose, where castling with 22...O-O was better.
You closed it out with 24.Ra4 Rxa4 25.bxa4 Qxc3, winning the queen, and White resigned.

review.turning_point: 13.Ne5? Nxe5! and the follow-up 14...Bxe5 won a pawn and gave you a lasting edge.
review.focus: At 22...Ke7?! you left your king in the centre while ahead. Castling with 22...O-O would have kept it safe and kept your lead.

review.headline: A messy Petrov saved by a queen check

sections.text: You played a Three Knights Petrov and reached an equal position after 4.Bc4 Be6 5.Bxe6 fxe6. 6...Nbd7?! and 8...Nxf6?! were slightly passive, but 10...Qb6 got you active.

Then 11...Ng4? was a mistake. White's 12.d4 O-O-O 13.h3 exd4 gave you a chance, and after 14.Nxd4?, moving the knight uncovered the queen on d1 against your knight on g4 (a discovered attack). You played 14...Nf6??, but the engine's 14...Nxf2 15.Kxf2 was better. 15.Nxe6 and 18.Nxf8 cost you material.
White's 19.Qxd6? gave you a chance: 19...Qxf2+ was the engine's move. You played 19...Nh5??, and White's 20.Qxh6?? gave you another chance.
This time you found 20...Qxf2+!, and after 21.Kh1 Ng3+ 22.Kh2 Qf4 23.Kg1 Qf2+ 24.Kh2 Qf4 the game ended as a draw by repetition.

review.turning_point: 20.Qxh6?? allowed 20...Qxf2+!, which turned a lost position into a draw by repetition.
review.focus: Look at 19...Nh5, where 19...Qxf2+ was available immediately. When your opponent's king has weaknesses on f2, check that first.

review.headline: A fast Italian win that went wrong only in the details

sections.text: You played the Italian with 3.Bc4 and 4.c3, and Black's 4...a5? let you strike with 5.d4!. After 5...exd4 6.cxd4 Ba7 7.O-O Nh6 8.Bxh6 gxh6 your bishop traded for a knight and wrecked Black's pawns.

9.g3? was a slip, since 9.d5 Ne7 kept more. But Black answered 9...Qf6?, and you found 10.e5! to force the queen back with 10...Qg7. After 11.Nc3 d6 12.Nd5 Bb6?, Black let you play 13.Nxb6?! cxb6 14.exd6 and you were far ahead.

After 14...Bg4 15.Re1+ Kd7 16.d5 Nd4, your 17.Ne5+?! was a discovered attack: the knight moved with check and uncovered your queen on the bishop on g4. Black's 17...Kxd6? lost the bishop to 18.Nxg4. After 19.Re4 Nf5 20.Qf3, you swept in with 21.Qf4+ Kc5 22.Qc7+ Kb4 23.Be2+.

review.turning_point: 17...Kxd6? ignored the loose bishop on g4, and 18.Nxg4 won it.
review.focus: Look at 9.g3?, where 9.d5 Ne7 kept your centre pressure. A quiet move like g3 gave Black time to get organised.

review.headline: A messy middlegame won by a b-file attack and a mating net

sections.text: You played the Two Knights with 3.Bc4 and 4.d3, castling by 5.O-O. After 5...Bc5 6.Be3 d6?, 7.Nbd2? was a miss, since 7.Bxc5 dxc5 8.Bb5 was stronger. Black's 7...Bg4? let it go.

You built with 10.Qb3 O-O-O 11.a4?! g5? 12.a5?!, and Black's 12...a6?? gave you a great chance, but 13.Qa4?? let it slip: 13.d4 was the engine's choice. After 14.hxg4 Bxg4? you again slipped with 15.b4??, where 15.Bxa6 was best.

You kept finding good ideas: 17.b5! opened the b-file, 19.bxa6 Nxa6 20.Bxa6 won a knight, and 21.Bxb7+ Kxb7 exposed the king. 22.Qb5+?? was a slip, where 22.Rb1+ was better, but 22...Kc8?? and 23.a6! put Black in a mating net.
24.Qb7# finished it.

review.turning_point: 17.b5! opened the b-file against Black's king, and the attack never stopped until 24.Qb7#.
review.focus: Look at 13.Qa4 and 15.b4. In both cases a straightforward alternative (13.d4, 15.Bxa6) kept the edge, and the queen sortie only worked because Black erred.

review.headline: A pawn-losing sequence started by an early queen exposure

sections.text: You played an Italian with 3.Bc4 and opened the centre with 4.d4. After 4...exd4 5.Nxd4 Nxd4 6.Qxd4 c5, your queen was pushed back by 7.Qd1 and you stood at +1.9.

Then 8.Nd2? cut the edge to +0.6, since 8.Nc3 Nf6 was the engine's choice. After 8...Nf6 9.b3 a6 10.Bb2 b5, you traded with 11.Bd5 Nxd5 12.exd5 Bb7, and 13.Nf3? let Black in again, where 13.Ne4 was better.

After 13...Qe7+, your 14.Qe2?? was the decisive error. With Black's queen on e7 and your king on e1, the queen on e2 was pinned and had to trade. 14...Qxe2+ 15.Kxe2 Bxd5 won a pawn, and 17.Nd2?! Bxg2 won another. The engine's 14.Kf1 Qe4 would have kept you in the game.

review.turning_point: 14.Qe2?? stepped the queen in front of Black's queen on the e-file and cost you the d5 pawn.
review.focus: At 14.Qe2, look at checks on the e-file before you move. 14.Kf1 Qe4 was the safe way to meet 13...Qe7+.

review.headline: A fine opening, then a premature resignation

sections.text: You played the Queen's Pawn Game with 1...d5 and 2...e6, developing well with 3...Nf6, 4...Be7 and 6...O-O. After 5.Bxf6 Bxf6 the game was equal.

White pushed the kingside pawns with 7.h4, 8.g4 and 9.g5. You answered with 7...Re8 and 8...e5, which hit the centre. But 9...Be7?! was slightly passive, and the engine's 9...exd4 10.gxf6 was the idea.
After 10.dxe5 the evaluation was only -0.4, a small edge for White. You resigned there, but the position was still very playable.

review.turning_point: 10.dxe5 was nothing decisive, and the game was still close when you resigned.
review.focus: Look at 9...Be7?! and the decision to resign after 10.dxe5. At -0.4 there was a lot of game left, so keep playing and make your opponent find the win.

review.headline: A good opening ruined by one hanging bishop

sections.text: You played the Ruy Lopez with 3.Bb5, and after 4...Nf6 5.d3 Black made a mistake with 5...Ng4?. You found the strong reply 6.h3!, and after 6...Nf6 you stood at +1.6.
7.Bg5?! pinned the knight on f6 to the queen but was not best, and after 7...O-O 8.Nbd2 Nd4 Black hit your bishop on b5 and your knight on f3 at the same time. That left you at +0.7.
Then 9.Nc4?? ignored the attack on your bishop. After 9...Nxb5 you had lost a piece and were at -3.4. The engine's 9.Bc4 h6 would have kept the game balanced.

review.turning_point: 9.Nc4?? left the bishop on b5 attacked, and 9...Nxb5 won it.
review.focus: At 9.Nc4, check what your opponent's last move attacks. Black's 8...Nd4 hit the bishop on b5, so 9.Bc4 had to be played.

review.headline: Two opening slips against a Petrov that turned out playable

sections.text: You played the Petrov with 2...Nf6 and 3...d6. White's 3.Nxe5 was a pawn grab, and 4.Nc4 was the main line. Here 4...Nbd7?? was a slip, since 4...Nxe4 5.Qe2 was stronger.
White replied 5.Bd3?, a mistake, and you reached equality with 5...c6 and 6.O-O. But 6...d5?? was another slip, where 6...Nc5 was the engine's choice. After 7.exd5 cxd5 you were down material.

8.Ne3? and 8...d4?! created complications, and 9.Nf5 Bc5 10.Re1+ Kf8 11.Qf3 g6 kept you active. 12.Nh6? was a discovered attack on your knight on f6, but 12...Kg7! covered it, and 13.Ng4 Nxg4 14.Qxg4 Ne5 left you with +1.7.
You resigned there, even though the engine had you better.

review.turning_point: 12.Nh6? was met by 12...Kg7!, which swung the game back in your favour.
review.focus: Look at 4...Nbd7 and 6...d5. Both gave away ground in the opening, so 4...Nxe4 and 6...Nc5 are worth knowing. Also, check the evaluation before resigning, since 14...Ne5 left you at +1.7.

review.headline: A fast win against the Norwegian Defence

sections.text: Black played the Norwegian with 1...g6 and 2...Nf6. You played the usual 2.d4 and 4.e5, which kicked the knight to 4...Ng4. 3.Nd2?! was a bit slow, since 3.e5 was the engine's choice, but 5.h3 Nh6 6.Ngf3 e6 kept the centre safe.
You developed with 7.Bb5+ Bd7 8.a4 a6 9.Be2, and 11.O-O?! was a slight inaccuracy, since 11.dxc5 was stronger. After 11...cxd4 12.cxd4 Qc7 13.exf6 you won a pawn.
Black erred with 13...Qf4?, and your 14.Qb3?! was slightly passive but put the queen on the b-file against the pawn on b7. After 15.Ne5 Qxf6 16.Nxc6 bxc6 17.Qb7 Bd6 18.Qxa8, you won a rook.
Black tried 19...Ng4, but 20.Bxg4 won a knight and 21.Nf3 closed it out.

review.turning_point: 18.Qxa8 won a rook and left Black with no way back.
review.focus: Look at 3.Nd2?! and 11.O-O?!. In both, the engine preferred a more direct central move (3.e5, 11.dxc5), so be ready to open the position when you have the space.

review.headline: A wild Goldsmith Defense where both sides swapped the advantage, ending in a queen mate on g6

sections.text: Your opponent's 1...h5 gave you a comfortable start, and by 4...d5 you stood at +2.2. 5.Bg5?? threw it away: 5...dxe4 hit your bishop on d3 and the evaluation swung to -1.9. 5.exd5 Nxd5 6.O-O was the clean way to keep your edge.
You hit back with 6.Bxf6, and 6...exd3? gave some of it back, since 6...exf3 was stronger. After 7.Be5 dxc2 8.Qxc2 things had settled into a fair position (-0.6) with your bishop strong on e5.

Then 11...f6?? loosened Black's king and the e6 pawn, putting you at +4.7. 12.Bg3?? let it slip: 12.Qg6+ Ke7 13.Ne4 was the punch. Black returned the favour with 12...Qb6??, and 13.Rhe1 set up a pin on the e-file against e6, but 13.Qg6+ was still the stronger idea.
Even after 15.Nxd5? the queen check on g6 was in the air, and 15...Qd8?? let you finish the job with 16.Qg6#. Well spotted at the end.

review.turning_point: 11...f6 handed you a big edge, but you did not take it at once with 12.Qg6+; the queen finally landed on g6 with mate on move 16.
review.focus: Look at checks first. At 12.Bg3 and again at 13.Rhe1 the queen check 12.Qg6+ (or 13.Qg6+) was the strongest move on the board.

review.headline: A winning position built on a neat discovered check, thrown away with one queen capture and a mate on e8

sections.text: This Petrov Three Knights went sharp quickly. After 5.Nxe5 Re8 6.Ng4 your knight on f6 was attacked, and 6...Nxg4 was the best answer. 6...Bxc3? was a mistake that cost you your edge (+1.4 down to -0.3), though the position stayed playable.

Credit where it is due: after 7...Nxe4 your opponent played 8.Bf4??, and you found the best answer, 8...Nxc3+, a discovered check from the knight that uncovers your rook on e8 against the king on e1. It also brought a discovered attack on the queen's side. The evaluation jumped to +5.4.
You then simplified well with 11...Rxe2 and 12...Bxg4, and 13...Rxe1 kept trading down while up a lot. You were at +7.6 when White played 15.Bxc7.

15...Qxc7?? was the one mistake that mattered. It lined the queen up on the c-file and took away its defense of the back area, and 16.Re8# was mate. 15...Qf8 would have kept everything covered and the win intact.

review.turning_point: At 15.Bxc7 you were far ahead, and 15...Qxc7?? allowed 16.Re8# instead of the safe 15...Qf8.
review.focus: Before capturing, ask what the capture stops defending. At 15...Qxc7 your queen left the defense of e8, so check the opponent's checks and mates first.

review.headline: A topsy-turvy London game, level on the board, that you lost on the clock

sections.text: Against the Accelerated London you played a sound setup with 3...Bd6, 5...Ne4 and 6...Nxg3, and the position was balanced for ten moves. Then 11.Ne5?? from White gave you a chance (+1.6), and 11...Bxe5 12.dxe5 O-O-O was the way to cash it in.

Instead 11...f6?? dropped you to -4.0. You were rescued because 12.Nc6? missed 12.Ng6, which would have forked your queen and the rook on h8. You then found 12...Qf7!, the best move, to stay in the game.

More swings followed. 13.Nf3? and 14.c5?? let you back in, and 14...bxc5! was another accurate answer. 16.Rc1? gave you a chance, but 16...Nb6?? threw it away (16...c4 was right). 17.Qa3 created a pin against your c5 pawn and bishop on d6, and 17...Nc4?? was another miss; 17...c4 was the better move.
By 19.Bd3 the position was level, but you lost on time. After a tangled middlegame like this, the clock became the opponent.

review.turning_point: 11...f6?? turned a good position (+1.6) into -4.0; 11...Bxe5 would have kept the initiative.
review.focus: Time management: you lost on time in an even position after 19.Bd3. Also, at 16...Nb6 the simple 16...c4 was better than sending the knight away; keep your pawn breaks in mind.

review.headline: A pawn won with a nice 3.Nxe5, a long edge, then a knight lunge that cost a rook

sections.text: Black's 2...c5? was a mistake, and you found the best answer, 3.Nxe5!, picking up a pawn. After 5.Qxd4 d6 you stood at +3.4, which is a big edge for a blitz opening.

The edge started to leak, though. 6.Nf3?! and 7.Qd3?! were slow, and 9.Bh4?? pinned the f6 pawn against the queen on e7 but let Black organize; 9.Be3 was the engine's choice. 10.h3?? was another careless move when 10.Nc3 Nb4 was the cleaner plan.

Black returned the favor with 7...Bd7? and 12...Be6?, which put you at +3.8 again. Then came the decisive error: 13.Nb5?? opened a discovered attack from your queen on d2, but 13...Nxc2+ 14.Kd1 Nxa1 left you down about a rook. 13.Nd4 Nc6 14.Nxe6 was the safe move.
16.b3? added to the damage (16.Nxa7 was better), and after 16...Bxb3+ the game was over.

review.turning_point: 13.Nb5?? went from +3.8 to -2.5, because 13...Nxc2+ and 14...Nxa1 won your rook.
review.focus: Before a knight jump like 13.Nb5, check what the enemy knight on b4 can capture: the checks on c2 and the rook on a1 were the whole story.

review.headline: An even, well-played game against Stockfish until a single knight move cost a piece

sections.text: You handled the Zukertort with confidence. 4...Qxe7 recaptured neatly, 6...Ne4 and 9...f5 gave you a Stonewall-type setup, and for twenty moves the engine had you at -0.3 to -0.8, close to equal. With 81.8 accuracy, that was solid.
There were small slips: 14...Qg5?!, 17...Nc6?! and 19...Qg6?! each lost a little, but nothing serious, and 15...Ne7 and 18...Qf6 kept your position together.
Then 20...Ne5?? decided it. The knight just hung to the pawn, 21.dxe5 won a piece for White, and the evaluation fell from -0.4 to -6.3. 20...e5 21.Qb3 would have kept the game balanced.
After that you fought on with active tries: 23...Bxg2, 24...f4 and a cute 29...Qe4+, which forked the king and the knight on b7. Stockfish had an answer in 30.Bxe4 Rxd2+, so the loss stayed.

review.turning_point: 20...Ne5?? let the d4 pawn capture a knight for free, swinging the game from near equal to -6.3.
review.focus: Run a blunder check on every knight jump: 20...Ne5 stepped onto a square attacked by the d4 pawn. 20...e5 was the safer way to keep the balance.

review.headline: An opening pawn push cost a pawn, and a bishop jump at move 16 threw away your best moment

sections.text: Against the Modern Defense, 3.Ne2?! was a bit passive, and 4.e5?? gave Black the chance to grab material: 4...cxd4 5.Nxd4 Bxe5 left you a pawn down. 4.dxc5 Na6 was the sounder way to meet 3...c5.

8.Re1? was another small inaccuracy that left you down (-1.6), when 8.Nb5 d5 would have kept pressure. Black missed some chances, such as 7...Bg7? instead of 7...Nc6, and you stayed in it through 10.Qd2 and 13.Bb3.
Then Black blundered with 14...e5??, and you found the best answer, 15.Nf5!, a discovered attack from your knight on d4 that opened the e3 bishop onto the queen on b6. You were at +2.3.
But 16.Bb6?? undid it all. The bishop was just taken by 16...Qxb6, and you were suddenly down material. 16.Nxg7 Rd8 kept a strong attack. After that, 17.Ne7+ and 20.Bxd5?! could only slow the loss.

review.turning_point: At 16.Bb6?? you went from +2.6 to -4.3 by putting a bishop where the queen could take it, when 16.Nxg7 would have kept your edge.
review.focus: When you are ahead, check that every piece you move is protected. 16.Bb6 stood on a square covered by the queen on b6; 16.Nxg7 was the safe, strong move.

review.headline: A quiet Saragossa that turned on a greedy bishop capture and a second slip

sections.text: Against the Saragossa (1.c3) you built a normal setup with 1...d5, 2...e5, 3...Nc6 and 4...Bg4. 5...Qf6?! was a little loose, and after 6.h3 Bh5 7.b4 a6 the board was equal.
8...Bxb4?? was the first big mistake (+0.4 down to -2.9). 8...Bxf3 9.Nxf3 d4 was the better way to use the pin on g2 and h1. After 9.cxb4 Nxb4 you were already behind.

10.Qxc7 hit your queen and the b4 knight, and 10...Qc6?? was a second blunder (-4.9); 10...Ne7 was the move. Then 11.Qxe5+ forked your king on e8 and the bishop on h5, although 11.Qxc6+ would have been even stronger.

review.turning_point: 8...Bxb4?? was the moment; it gave away a bishop for pawns, where 8...Bxf3 would have kept things level.
review.focus: After 8.a4, check forcing captures before grabbing material. The pawn on b4 looked loose, but 8...Bxb4 was a blunder that cost the game.

review.headline: A long, careful grind against the Larsen Opening that finished with a rook mate on h4

sections.text: You met 1.b3 with 1...e5 and then got a lot of help: 2...d5?! allowed 3.Bxe5, but 3...Bg4 and 4...Qe7 gave you good play and after 8...O-O-O you were at -1.7 for White, meaning +1.7 for you.

Credit for 10...Kb7!, the best answer after 10.Nxa7+?? That stepped out of the check with a tidy king walk. 11...Bd7? was your one mistake (11...Bf5 was best), and 12.e3?? gave White a chance to correct, since 12.Bxd4 was needed.
From there the pieces came alive: 17...Nd5, 18...Nxc3, 19...Bxf1, 20...Qb4 and 22...Bxd4+ kept winning material while you stayed accurate. 16.d4?? from White was another gift.
The endgame was a clean conversion, with your rooks doubling and the king hunt finishing with 46...Rh4#. At 88.2 accuracy, this was strong, patient play.

review.turning_point: 10.Nxa7+?? went wrong for White, and your answer 10...Kb7! changed the game, since the knight on a7 had nowhere to go.
review.focus: Your one real mistake was 11...Bd7?, which gave away part of your edge. 11...Bf5 kept both bishops active, so look at the safest developing move first.

review.headline: A queen's gambit scramble where one hanging rook and a knight fork turned the game, and you won on time

sections.text: In the Queen's Gambit Declined you played 5...h6 and 7...O-O quietly. 8...Nd7? cost you some ground (8...c5 was better), but White returned the favor with 9.Bc2?? and the game was balanced again.

15...Bxf1 grabbed the exchange, and 17...Bxd4 and 18...Qxd4 kept you active. Then 19...Reb8?? was a blunder (+2.6 to -4.8); 19...Qc5 was the move. White missed it with 20.Qf3?? instead of 20.Qxb8+, which would have exploited your back rank.
22...Nd7?? was another error (22...Qg7 was right), and by 23.Nxf7 you were at -2.5. But 24.h3?? let you back in, and you found 24...Ne5!.
25.Re1?? walked into 25...Nxf3+!, a knight fork of the rook on e1 and the king on g1. After 26.Kh1 Rxf7 and 27...Qxf2 you were completely winning, and you finished on time.

review.turning_point: 24.h3?? gave you a second chance, and 24...Ne5! followed by the 25...Nxf3+ fork turned -3.0 into a winning game.
review.focus: At 19...Reb8 and 22...Nd7 you moved a piece away from the key square. Before leaving a defender, check what it was guarding, because 19...Qc5 was the safe move.

review.headline: An Italian where your opponent went wrong in the middle and a bishop sacrifice finished it

sections.text: Against 3...Qf6 you played the normal 4.c3 and 5.d4. 6.Bg5? aimed at a skewer on the queen on f6 and bishop on e7, but 6...Qg6 gave Black counterplay against e4 and g2, and 7.Qd2?? made it worse (-3.1). 7.Be3 was the safer move.

You came out well after 8.Bxe7, because Black's 8...Ngxe7?? was a blunder. 8...Qxg2 would have forked your rook on h1 and bishop on f3. You were back to roughly equal, then 9...h5? gave you an edge again.
10...Qh6?? was the blunder, and you found the best answer, 11.Bxf7+!. The king had to walk with 11...Kd7, and 12.Be6+ Kd8 kept it exposed. A neat tactical finish.
13.Nf7+ finished the game with Black's king stuck in the middle.

review.turning_point: 10...Qh6?? let you play 11.Bxf7+!, which broke open the king and decided the game.
review.focus: The slip was 7.Qd2??: you left your bishop on g5 and your e4 pawn hanging. 7.Be3 Qxe4 8.Bd3 would have kept things safe.

review.headline: A Philidor where you survived some wobbles and then converted a king hunt into a clean win

sections.text: You played the Philidor pleasantly with 3.Bc4, 4.Nc3 and 5.Nd5. 11.Qd2?! and 12.Bxh6?! were a bit greedy, but 12...Re8?? gave you +2.2, since 12...gxh6 was needed.
14.Bxg7?? went wrong (14.Nh4 was the move) and 15.h4?? was a second slip. You were behind at -2.3, but Black's 18...Ke7?? gave it back.
You found the best answer, 19.Nf5+!, a fork of the king on e7 and the bishop on h6. After 20.Nxh6 and 21.Nxf7+ you were completely winning, and 23.Nxd6+ kept the attack going.

24.Qxe8?? was a blunder, since 24.Nxe8+ Rxe8 25.Qf7 was cleaner, and Black returned the favour with 24...Qxe8??. You then found 25.Nxe8+!, which restored the winning edge, and converted with 26.f4 and the rook invasion until Black resigned.

review.turning_point: 18...Ke7?? gave you 19.Nf5+!, a fork that turned a -1.3 position into +4.3.
review.focus: Calculate captures to the end. 24.Qxe8 nearly threw the win away, while 24.Nxe8+ was a clean tactical finish.

review.headline: A Cochrane Gambit that went through plenty of swings before a queen trade and rook mate

sections.text: Against the Cochrane Gambit, 4.Nxf7? forked your queen and the rook on h8, but you replied 4...Kxf7!, the best move. 5...Ke8? was a small slip (5...d5 was better), and 8.Bxf6 Qxf6 kept you roughly level.

11...Qf7?? was the first big mistake (+2.8 to -0.2), when 11...dxe5 was right. 12.Re1?? let you back in, and 12...Bxc4 was a reasonable grab even if 13...Kd8?? and 15...Qc5?? kept giving chances away.
Then 16.h3?? went wrong for White, but you answered 16...Bxd6?? instead of 16...Qxd6, and 17.Qh5?? followed. You found the best answer: 17...Qxh5!, picking up the queen.
From +6.8 you went on to win with 20.Rxb4 and 24...Nf3+, and finally 32...Re1#.

review.turning_point: 17.Qh5?? let you play 17...Qxh5!, a clean queen win that turned a roughly level game into a big advantage.
review.focus: You made a few errors (11...Qf7, 13...Kd8, 15...Qc5, 16...Bxd6). Slow down at 11...Qf7 and consider 11...dxe5 first.

review.headline: A smooth Petrov win, built on patience and finished by a queen fork

sections.text: You played the Petrov correctly: 3...d6, 4...Nxe4 and 5...Qe7 kept everything balanced (-0.1 to -0.5). 9...Nbd7?! was the one slight inaccuracy (9...g5 was a shade better), but 10.Nxe6 fxe6 gave you an open f-file.

Your plan was clear: 11...g5, 12...Bg7 and 13...e5 grabbed space, then 14...O-O-O and 15...Kb8 tucked the king away. You followed with 16...Nb6, 17...Qd7 and 19...Nfd5, building a harmonious position at 96.4 accuracy.
White went wrong with 23.dxe5?, a discovered attack by the rook on d1 on your knight. You replied 23...Nb4!, the best move.
24.Bc4?? blundered, and you found 24...Qxc2+!, a queen fork of the king on b1 and the bishop on c4. After 25.Ka1 Qxc4 you were clearly winning.

review.turning_point: 24...Qxc2+! after 24.Bc4?? forked the king and bishop and won material.
review.focus: A fine game. Small thing: 9...Nbd7?! allowed Bh4 to cause some pressure, while 9...g5 would have settled the pin sooner.

review.headline: A Caro-Kann Advance won by a kingside pawn storm, then nearly thrown away before a late mating attack

sections.text: You played the Advance Variation solidly with 3.e5, 4.d4 and 5.Bd3, and after 9.O-O-O 10.h4 and 11.g4 you started a kingside attack. 12.g5?? was a mistake, though: 12.Ng5 Ng6 would have kept up the pressure.
Black went wrong with 13...b5??, and 14.Ng3? missed 14.g6. Still, 17.Nf4! was a nice answer to 16...a4?, and 20.Ngxh5 broke the kingside open.
21...c5?? was a blunder, and you found 22.Nf6+!, giving a crushing attack (+7.2). 23.gxf6 Nf5 24.Rdg1+ Kh8 left the king exposed.
25.Qd2?? missed a forced mate with 25.Qe2 Nh6 26.Qh5. Black returned the favour with 25...cxd4??, and you found 26.Qg5!, which pinned the f6 pawn to the queen. Black resigned after 27.Qh5+.

review.turning_point: 22.Nf6+! after 21...c5?? blew open Black's king and gave you a winning attack.
review.focus: At 25.Qd2 you had a forced mate with 25.Qe2. When the king is exposed, check every forcing queen move before a quiet one.

review.headline: A Philidor where you missed free rook captures again and again

sections.text: In the Philidor, 4.dxe5 Nxe4 5.exd6 Nxd6 was fine, but 8...c6?? left you behind at -2.5; 8...Nc6 was the move. 10...Nd7?! and 12...Qb6? kept you under pressure.
White got a chance with 11.Qd2? (11.Bxd6 was better), and 16.Be2?? gave you one more, which you took with 16...Qc8!. That kept you in the game.
17...Nde4? tried a discovered attack by uncovering the d8 rook on d1, but 19...Bf5?? was a clear miss (19...Rxd1 was the move). 21.Rxe7 Nxd1 22.Qxd1 and 22...Bxh3? led to a lost position at -4.8.

White blundered several times: 27.Qh3??, 28.a4?? and 29.Nf3?? each left the rook on e7 hanging. But 27...g6??, 28...h5?? and 29...Qc1+?? all missed it. 27...Rxd3 and 28...Qxe7 would have turned the game.

review.turning_point: From move 27, White left a rook on e7 hanging three times, and 27...g6, 28...h5 and 29...Qc1+ each missed 28...Qxe7.
review.focus: Before every move, ask what is hanging. At 28...h5 and 29...Qc1+ the rook on e7 could be captured by 28...Qxe7.

review.headline: A rook grab on h8 that nearly won, thrown away by a bishop check and a weakened kingside

sections.text: You played the King's Knight solidly with 3.d3, 4.Be2 and 6.O-O. 9.Bb2?! was a bit soft, but after 10.d4 exd4 11.Nxd4 Nxd4 12.Bxd4 you were fine.
12...b6?? from Black was a blunder, and you took 13.Bxh8, picking up a rook on h8 and moving to +3.5. After 13...Nf4 14.Bb2 Qg5 you were still clearly better.
15.Bf3? gave some of it back, and 15.Bg4 Bh6 was stronger. After 15...Bxh3 you were still at +2.9.
16.Bg4+?? was the decisive mistake, since 16.g3 was right. 17.g3?? lost on the spot at -5.4; 17.Bf6 would have forked the rook on d8 and the queen on g5.

review.turning_point: 16.Bg4+?? gave away the bishop and your lead; 16.g3 would have kept you clearly ahead.
review.focus: When ahead, look at the safest move first: 16.g3 was calm, while 16.Bg4+ was a check that just lost a piece.

review.headline: A Kan Sicilian where a queen misstep and a hasty bishop jump wasted an equal middlegame

sections.text: Against the Kan you played 6.Be2, 7.Be3?! and 8.a3?!, a little slow, and Black took the lead with 9...d6 and 10...Nbd7. After 11.Ndxb5?! axb5 12.Nxb5 you got two pawns for a piece, which was a speculative sacrifice.
13.Nxd6+ Bxd6 14.Qxd6 got you in the game, and 14...Qe7? let you back to +0.9. 14...Nxe4 would have been Black's best.
15.Qc7?? pinned the knight on d7 against the queen but let Black off the hook: 15.Qxe7+ was the better move and kept your edge. After 15...Bxe4 you were already worse.
17.Bc5?? looked like a skewer on the queen and the rook on f8, but 17...Qxc5 just took the bishop. 17.c4 was the move, and after 18.Rxd7 Nxd7 19.Qxd7 Qxc2 you resigned.

review.turning_point: 15.Qc7?? passed up 15.Qxe7+, which would have kept the game balanced; after that Black took over.
review.focus: At 17.Bc5 you moved a bishop to a square the enemy queen could capture. Check whether the piece is protected before attacking with it.

review.headline: A won Caro-Kann Exchange that slipped away through a few loosening moves and a queen sacrifice

sections.text: You won the game early. Black's 6...Bf3?? was a blunder, and you found the best answer, 7.gxf3!, going to +4.8. Your opponent had no real compensation.
You played purposefully with 9.Qd2, 11.O-O-O, 13.Kb1 and the h4-h5 pawn push, staying at about +4. 18.Bf4 Bxf4 19.Qxf4 simplified comfortably.
The first loosening was 21.Ng3?!, which dropped you to +2.9. Then 24.Qg3?? was the real blunder (+3.3 to -0.5); 24.Qe5 g5 25.f4 was much stronger.
26.Rg2? and 28.Rdg1?? followed (28.hxg6 fxg6 was needed). The last gasp 29.Qxg5+ hxg5 30.Rxg5+ gave up the queen and the game.

review.turning_point: 24.Qg3?? swung the evaluation from +3.3 to -0.5; the position was still winning with 24.Qe5.
review.focus: When you are far ahead, keep it simple. At 24.Qg3 you went for an attack, but 24.Qe5 would have kept the control.

review.headline: An Alekhine's Defense where an early slip, a greedy queen and a rushed pawn push all cost you

sections.text: Against the Alekhine you played the Two Pawns Attack with 3.c4 and 4.d4, and 5.Nf3 dxe5 6.Nxe5 was normal. 7.Qf3? was a small mistake (+1.1 to -0.1) when 7.Nc3 Nc6 was the safe move.
7...Bg6?? gave you a big edge (+2.3), but 8.h4?? let it go. 8.Be3 e6 9.Nc3 would have kept it. 8...Qxd4 9.Nxg6 hxg6 10.Qxb7 e6 made it messy.
11.Qxc7?! was greedy, and 12.Be3?? looked like a skewer on the queen and the knight on b6 but 12...Qxb2 escaped and hit your rook on a1 (12.Nc3 Bb4 was needed).
13.Bxb6?! won a knight, but 14.c5? lost to 14...Re5+. 14.Be3 Bb4+ was better. Your last move 15.Qxe5 was the best of a bad set, and Black just took the queen.

review.turning_point: 12.Be3?? let the queen go to b2 with tempo, swinging the evaluation to -3.8.
review.focus: At 8.h4 you reached for a quick pawn move in a tense position. 8.Be3 would have finished your development and kept the +2.3 you had.

review.headline: A patient defense against an early queen sortie, undone by one queen trade

sections.text: Your opponent tried the Wayward Queen idea, and you handled it calmly. After 2.Qh5 you played 2...d6, then 3...g6 to push the queen back, and you developed with 4...Nf6 and 5...Bg7 before castling with 6...O-O. The engine had you roughly level for the whole opening, which is a good result against a line designed to rush you.

The first real damage was 13...Ne6, a blunder that took you from +0.9 to -0.8. With 13.d4 hitting your e5 pawn, the engine wanted 13...exd4 14.Nxd4. Instead, after 14.dxe5 14...dxe5 15.Bxe6 15...fxe6 you traded your knight for the bishop and ended up with doubled e-pawns, which White could aim at for a long time.

To your credit you defended well from there. You traded a pair of rooks with 19...Rxd1+ 20.Nxd1, kept your pieces compact, and the evaluation stayed in the -1 to -2 range for twenty moves, which is very playable at your level.

Then came 34...Qd2, the decisive mistake (-1.5 to -3.7). It invited 35.Qxd2+ 35...Rxd2, but that recapture pulled your rook away from d8, where it had been guarding the bishop on a8, and 36.Rxa8 took the bishop. The engine's 34...Bc6 kept the bishop covered.

review.turning_point: 34...Qd2 offered a queen trade that dragged your rook off d8, so the bishop on a8 fell to 36.Rxa8 and the evaluation dropped from -1.5 to -3.7.
review.focus: Before offering a trade, ask what the recapture removes from your position. After 34...Qd2 35.Qxd2+ 35...Rxd2 your rook no longer guarded the bishop on a8; 34...Bc6 was the engine's safer choice.

review.headline: A Petrov where early slips let White's center roll, and a rook move ended it

sections.text: You chose the Petrov and, after 3.Nxe5 3...d6 4.Nc4, were fine. 4...Be7? is where it started to slip (-0.1 to -1.4). The engine wanted 4...Nxe4 5.Qe2, taking the central pawn right away.

White returned the favor with 5.d4?, a real mistake, but you missed 5...Nxe4 and played 5...d5? instead. 6.e5 kicked your knight back and gave White plenty of space. 6...Nfd7?! and 8...f6?! kept you on the back foot (-2.5), and after 9...fxe5 10.dxe5 you were a pawn down again.

You fought back well, though. 13...Rxf4 took a pawn back and 14.g3?? gave you a gift (-2.0 to 0.0), as the pawn attacked your rook. But 14...Rf7? was a mistake, since the engine liked 14...Rf8, and 15.e6 then attacked the rook on f7 again.
15...Rf3?? was the final blunder: 16.Qxf3 simply took the rook. The engine suggested 15...Rf8 to keep things together.

review.turning_point: 14.g3 brought the game back to equal, but 14...Rf7? and then 15...Rf3?? gave the advantage away and cost a whole rook.
review.focus: On 15...Rf3 the rook stepped onto a square covered by White's queen on d1; always check which squares an attacked piece can safely reach. 15...Rf8 was the engine's answer.

review.headline: Exchange Caro-Kann where a bishop retreat dropped the c2 pawn and the queen never found safety

sections.text: You played the Exchange Variation with 3.exd5 3...cxd5 4.Nc3 and 5.Bg5, and when Black went 6...a6 you kept the bishop active with 7.Ba4 and 9.Bb3. Castling with 10.O-O was sensible and the position was only slightly worse for you at -0.6.

11.Bd2?! (-1.4) gave up the pressure from the bishop on g5, and after 12.Re1 12...O-O 13.a4 13...b4 14.Ne2 14...Na5, your bishop on b3 was under attack. That brings us to 15.Ba2??, the blunder (-1.4 to -3.8).

The bishop on b3 had been one of the guards of c2, which was attacked by the bishop on f5 and the rook on c8. Moving it to a2 abandoned the pawn, and 15...Bxc2 took it. The engine's 15.Rc1 kept the pawn protected.

After that your queen shuffled between c1 and d1 while 18...Bxa4 took a second pawn. 19.Bxd5?! did uncover your rook on a1 against the bishop on a4, a discovered attack, but your queen on c1 was already facing the rook on c8, so 19...Rxc1 took it.

review.turning_point: 15.Ba2 gave up the guard of c2 and let 15...Bxc2 in, and the queen was driven around the c1 and d1 squares afterward.
review.focus: Before retreating a piece (15.Ba2), ask what it was defending. The bishop on b3 was covering c2; 15.Rc1 was the engine's way to keep that pawn.

review.headline: A good opening edge that slipped away, then a knight move allowed a decisive tactic

sections.text: You began well in the Petrov: 3.Nxe5 3...d6 4.Nf3 4...Nxe4 5.d3 5...Nf6 6.d4 and the sharp 9.Bb5+ followed by 10.Bxd7+ gave you a clear plan. After 11.O-O 11...c4 12.Re1 and 13.Ne5 the engine had you at +1.3, a real advantage.

It faded with 14.Bd2? (+1.1 to 0.0); 14.Bh4 was the engine's choice and kept the bishop active. Black then made the mistake 15...Ba5?, but 16.b4? did not take advantage. 16.Nxd5 was the move, because the knight leaving c3 would uncover your bishop on d2 against the bishop on a5, a discovered attack.

From there Black took over: 17...a5 and 19.Nb5 19...Nxe5 20.dxe5 kept you busy, and 21.Re2? (-1.9) allowed 21...axb4 22.axb4 22...Bxf2+ 23.Rxf2. When Black played 23...Rxa1?? you were back in the game, and 24.Qxa1 put you at about -0.2.

Then 24...Qb6 and your 25.Nd6?? (-5.1). The queen on b6 was eyeing the rook on f2, and 25.Nd4 would have blocked that diagonal. Instead 25...Qxf2+ took the rook and 26...Nxd6 took the knight, leaving a forced loss.

review.turning_point: 25.Nd6 ignored the threat against your rook on f2 and cost a rook and a knight after 25...Qxf2+ and 26...Nxd6.
review.focus: On 25.Nd6, check what the opponent's last move (24...Qb6) is aiming at before making your own threat. 25.Nd4 would have blocked the diagonal to f2.

review.headline: A quick Philidor where a queen on b3 hit two targets and you could only defend one

sections.text: You went for the Philidor with 2...d6 and answered 3.Bc4 with 3...Be6. White took it with 4.Bxe6 4...fxe6, which gave you doubled e-pawns but a half-open f-file. The engine had you at only -0.7, so that was fine.
You developed with 5...Nf6 and 6...Be7, but 7.Qb3 created two threats at once: the queen eyed both the b7 pawn and the pawn on e6.
7...b6?? (-0.2 to -2.1) protected b7 but left e6 hanging, and 8.Qxe6 took a pawn with the queen centralized. The engine's 7...Qc8 covered both pawns at once, since the queen on c8 guards b7 and e6.
A -1.6 evaluation is uncomfortable, but the game was still long, and you resigned very early.

review.turning_point: 7...b6 defended only one of the two targets of 7.Qb3, so the e6 pawn fell to 8.Qxe6.
review.focus: When a queen attacks two things, look for one move that covers both. On 7...b6 the engine's choice 7...Qc8 would have defended b7 and e6 at once.

review.headline: A solid reply to the Vienna Gambit, with no errors and an early resignation

sections.text: You answered 1.e4 with 1...e5 and 2.Nc3 with 2...d6. When White played 3.f4 you replied with 3...Nf6, and 4.Nf3 4...Be7 developed another piece. All of your first four moves were accurate.
5.fxe5 5...dxe5 6.Nxe5 left you a pawn down, but the engine rated the position at only -0.3, which is a small price in a gambit line like this one.
No errors were flagged in your game, and the accuracy was 92.2. The game ended after 6.Nxe5 with you resigning at an evaluation that was not close to decisive.

review.turning_point: There was no real turning point: after 6.Nxe5 the evaluation was only -0.3 and the game was still wide open.
review.focus: A pawn down at -0.3 after 6.Nxe5 is not a reason to resign. Play on, because your development was sound and the game was still early.

review.headline: An early skirmish that left you worse after one inaccurate knight move, 4...Nd5

sections.text: White opened with 2.d4, and you took the pawn with 2...exd4 and developed with 3...Nf6. After 3.Nf3 and 4.e5 your knight was attacked, so the position was already getting sharp.
4...Nd5?! (-0.6 to -1.3) was your only real inaccuracy. The engine liked 4...Ne4 5.Qxd4, which kept your knight on the outside and avoided the pressure that came later.

After 5.Qxd4 5...c6 6.Bc4 6...Qa5+ 7.Bd2 7...Qb6 8.Bxd5 8...cxd5 9.Qxb6 9...axb6 the queens came off and material was level. But the engine still rated it clearly better for White (-3.3), because you now had doubled pawns on the b- and d-files and White's pieces were more active.

review.turning_point: 4...Nd5 let White's queen into the center with 5.Qxd4 and set up the exchanges that ruined your pawn structure.
review.focus: At 4...Nd5, think about where the opponent's queen will land. 4...Ne4 was the engine's choice and kept the knight outside the line of fire.

review.headline: A comfortable Queen's Gambit Declined that unraveled in two moves, 10...b6?! and 11...Qe7??

sections.text: You met 1.d4 with the Queen's Gambit Declined: 2.c4 2...e6 3.Nc3 3...Nf6 4.Bf4 4...Bd6 5.Bg3 5...O-O 6.e3. 6...Nbd7?! was a small inaccuracy (-0.9), but the position was fine.

After 7.Bxd6 7...cxd6 8.cxd5 8...Nxd5 9.Nxd5 9...exd5 the trades left you with doubled d-pawns, and 10.Qb3 hit the pawn on d5 and the one on b7. 10...b6?! protected b7 but not d5, and 11.Qxd5 took the pawn.

11...Qe7?? (-1.6 to -4.6) was the decisive blunder. The queen on d5 now eyed your rook on a8 along the long diagonal, since b6 had opened it, and 12.Qxa8 took the rook. The engine's 11...Qc7 avoided that.

review.turning_point: 10...b6 opened the long diagonal, and 11...Qe7 ignored the threat on a8 so 12.Qxa8 took the rook.
review.focus: On 11...Qe7, first ask what the opponent's last move attacks. 11.Qxd5 looked down the diagonal at a8, and 11...Qc7 was the engine's answer.

review.headline: A Philidor that swung wildly, and you reached a winning position before overreaching

sections.text: You set up a Philidor with 3...d6, 4...Nbd7 and 5...Be7, castled with 6...O-O and played 7...Re8. You held a modest edge through 11.Rae1 (+0.8), but 12...d5?? (+1.0 to -1.7) was your first blunder. The engine preferred 12...a5.

13...cxd5? did not help (-2.5): 13...exd4 would have been a pawn fork on the knight on c3 and bishop on e3. After 14.dxe5 14...Ng4?! you were struggling, and 16.Qe2? gave you a chance, but 16...Bf6?? (-4.4) threw it away. The engine's 16...h5 was safer.
White's 18.Qd1?? gave you a lifeline, and you found 18...Nxf3+!, a fork of the king on g1 and the rook on e1, which brought the evaluation back to level. By 22.Rxe8+ 22...Qxe8 you were fine.

25.Qe2?? was White's blunder (-0.5 to +2.2), but 26...Qxh3?? (+2.1 to -1.8) took a pawn and left a piece hanging. Then 27.Qc4? pinned the f7 pawn against your king on g8, and 27...dxc3?? allowed a forced mate with 28.Qxf7+. The engine's 26...Qd6 27.Nb5 was safer.

review.turning_point: 26...Qxh3 grabbed a pawn from a clearly better position and left a piece loose, and 27...dxc3 then allowed a forced mate.
review.focus: When you are better, as at 26...Qxh3, check what the opponent's last move threatens. 26...Qd6 27.Nb5 kept you in control.

review.headline: A comfortable edge thrown away by one greedy capture, then a mating blunder

sections.text: This was an Open Sicilian that got simplified quickly. After 6.Nf5 d5 7.exd5 Bxf5 8.dxc6 Qxd1+ 9.Kxd1 the queens were off and the position was roughly level, with your king a bit exposed on d1 but nothing urgent.

Then Black slipped. After 13.Nxd5+ the reply 13...Kb8 was a big mistake, and you answered it perfectly with 14.Ne3, keeping the extra material. From there you improved steadily: 16.Ba5, 17.Nc4, 19.Rad1 and finally 20.Nxd6 left you well ahead, with evaluations around +5.

The game turned at 22.Nxf7. It looks like a free pawn, but the bishop on c4 was left hanging to 22...Bxc4+, and a winning position became a losing one. Simple 22.Bxe6 fxe6 23.Nc4 would have kept everything under control.
By move 28 you were already worse, and 28.Rdd7 walked into a forced mate after 28...Ra1+. Quiet 28.h4 was the safer try.

review.turning_point: 22.Nxf7 grabbed a pawn but dropped the bishop on c4 to 22...Bxc4+, swinging the game from about +5.5 to -4.0.
review.focus: Before a capture like 22.Nxf7, check what it stops defending. When you are far ahead, ask what your opponent's checks and captures do after your move, and prefer the safe consolidating move such as 22.Bxe6.

review.headline: A King's Gambit where you drifted out of the centre and ended a pawn down

sections.text: White opened with the King's Gambit, and 2...d6 declined the pawn. That is playable, but the engine preferred taking it with 2...exf4 3.Nf3, which keeps the centre pawn fight simple and gives you a clear plan.

After 3...Nd7 White got a strong centre with 4.d4, and 5.Nc3 put the pressure on e5. By 5...Be7 the evaluation had slipped to about -1.8 for you. The engine's idea was 5...exd4, relieving the tension rather than waiting.
You were rescued by 6.Bd3, which was a slip by White; 6.fxe5 was stronger. But you did not cash in. After 6...O-O 7.h3 b6 8.dxe5 dxe5 9.fxe5, you were a pawn down and the game ended there.

review.turning_point: The opening choices of 3...Nd7 and 5...Be7 let White build a big centre; the chance to hit back with 5...exd4 was missed.
review.focus: Release the central tension with ...exd4 when White has built d4 and e4, as at 5...exd4. Waiting with 5...Be7 let White choose the moment to capture on e5.

review.headline: A Vienna Game where a loose f7 and a lost tempo cost you the game

sections.text: White chose a Vienna with an early bishop on c4, and your 3...c6 and 4...d5 hit the centre in the right spirit. After 5.Bb3 dxe4 6.Nxe5 the position was tense but fine for you, roughly -1.0.

The problem was 6...Bd6. It left f7 unprotected by anything useful and the knight on e5 now attacked it. The engine wanted 6...Be6 to challenge the bishop on b3. White then missed 7.Nxf7, which would have been a fork of the queen and rook, and you found the best reply to 7.d4 with 7...O-O!.
Then you gave it back. 8...Re8 and 9...Nbd7 both let White go after f7. 8...Nbd7 and 9...Be6 were the safer moves, because the e8 rook and the d7 knight left f7 with too few defenders.
After 10.Bxf7+ Kf8 11.Bxe8 the material was clearly against you, and 11...Nxe5 12.dxe5 Qxe8 did not change that.

review.turning_point: 6...Bd6 left f7 under attack and missed the idea of challenging with 6...Be6; later 8...Re8 and 9...Nbd7 made it worse.
review.focus: After a knight lands on e5, count the attackers on f7 before developing. At 6...Bd6 and 9...Nbd7 you should have asked what protects f7.

review.headline: One premature pawn push in a Sicilian cost a pawn and the game

sections.text: You played the standard Open Sicilian: 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3, and Black went for a Najdorf-style setup with 5...a6. Everything was normal, with a small edge for White.

Then came 6.e5. Pushing the e-pawn to attack the knight is thematic in other lines, but here Black simply captures it with 6...dxe5. With the d-pawn gone from d6 you had no tactic ready, and you were a pawn down at about -1.5.

The engine's choice was calm: 6.Be3, developing and keeping the tension. The game ended at this point, but a pawn down with the position still open you had plenty of play left, so it is worth playing on in such positions.

review.turning_point: 6.e5 gave away a pawn for nothing; 6.Be3 was the developing move.
review.focus: Before pushing a pawn like 6.e5, check that the capture 6...dxe5 does not simply win it. If the push does not create a threat you can name, develop instead.

review.headline: A messy game where you were winning at the end and let it slip

sections.text: In a King's Indian Attack structure you broke in the centre too soon. 6...e5 was a blunder: after 7.dxe5 Bxe5 8.Nxe5 Qxe5 9.Bf4 White had a clear lead, and the engine preferred the quiet 6...Nbd7.
It got worse. 11...Bh3 let White win material with 12.Bxb7 and later 14.Bxa8, and you were at about -6 by move 14.

Then White blundered back. 17.f4 gave you a chance, and the engine move was 17...Qd4+, which would have been a fork of the king and the bishop on d5. After 20.Rd1 you took with 20...Qxd1, but 20...Ne3+ was a fork of king, queen and rook.
After 23...Nxd5! you were clearly ahead, around +4, and 25...Qxa2+ kept it going. But 27...f6 gave it away (27...Qe6 was the pinning move), and 28...Rc8 allowed a forced mate.

review.turning_point: 27...f6 let a winning position slip away; 27...Qe6 would have pinned the white queen against the king.
review.focus: At 27...f6 you were far ahead, and any pawn move that opens a line near your own king is risky. Look at checks and pins first, as with 27...Qe6.

review.headline: A Scandinavian where your opponent gave up the queen and you converted calmly

sections.text: You met the Scandinavian with the usual 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qa5 4.d4 Bf5 5.Bd2, a sound setup with a small edge. After 5...Nc6 you played 6.d5, attacking the knight.
Black replied 6...Qxd5, which stepped into a queen capture. You found 7.Nxd5!, and the material jumped to +8. Everything after that was a matter of technique.
You cleaned up with 11.Nge2 Nxe2 12.Qxe2, then 15.Bg5 and 16.Bxf6 won more material, and 19.Qxd8+ traded the queens into a won ending, still around +5.
The one slip in a long ending was 34.Re1; the engine preferred the check 34.Rc1+. Black did not make the most of it (34...Re8), and you finished by pushing the f-pawn, ending with 48.Rf5 and 49.Rf1#.

review.turning_point: 6...Qxd5 allowed 7.Nxd5!, giving you a huge material edge.
review.focus: In won endgames like 34.Re1, look at checks first: 34.Rc1+ was the engine move and kept everything tidy.

review.headline: A London System game where you punished two loose moves and took the exchange

sections.text: Both sides played a quiet London. The first real moment came at 9...c5, which was a mistake; the engine wanted 9...dxc4, which would have been a discovered attack by the bishop on b7 against the knight on f3.
But White answered with 10.cxd5, and the engine move was 10.Bxd6. You found the best reply with 10...Bxg3!, since after 11.fxg3 exd5 the pawns were level.
White then went wrong again with 12.dxc5, and after 12...bxc5 you had the better structure. You gave back some of it with 14...Ne4 (14...Rxe3 was the engine move), but the position stayed manageable.
The finish was neat. White played 20.Rxc5, and you replied 20...Rxc5!, with the material swinging heavily your way. After 22.Bd3 Rxe3 White resigned.

review.turning_point: 20.Rxc5 was a blunder and 20...Rxc5! took advantage, swinging the material to your side.
review.focus: The opening mistake was 9...c5, which cost a lot of the position. When White's pieces are aimed at your centre, check 9...dxc4 first, as the engine did.

review.headline: A roughly balanced Scandinavian where a late slip failed to cost you the game

sections.text: A normal Scandinavian: 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qa5 4.d4 Bf5 5.Bd2 e6. After 6.Nf3 Bb4 7.a3 Bxc3 8.Bxc3, the queens came off with 10.Qe5 Qxe5+ 11.dxe5 and the position was about level.
The inaccuracies started with 12.Bd3, where the engine liked 12.Bd4. After 12...Nxc3 13.Bxf5 you stayed in the game, but 15.Bb5+ was another mistake: 15.Be2 was calmer.
You fought on with 17.Rxb2 and 18.Rxb5, getting your pieces active. Then 22.Rd6 was a blunder; the engine move was 22.Rbd3.
Luckily Black replied 22...Na5, missing 22...Nxe5. After 23.Rbd3 the position was fine, and White resigned.

review.turning_point: 22.Rd6 was the move that could have lost the game, and 22...Na5 missed the chance to punish it with 22...Nxe5.
review.focus: Before a rook lunge like 22.Rd6, check what captures it allows, such as 22...Nxe5. 22.Rbd3 was the safe move.

review.headline: You built a winning position in the Urusov Gambit and then missed the finishing line

sections.text: You took the gambit pawn with 2...exd4, then 4...Be7 was a small slip: 4...Nxe4 was the engine move. White responded 5.Nxd4, and you got through with 5...O-O.
The turning of the game was 7.Bd3 and your reply 7...dxe4!, found with care. The follow-up 11.Bg5 pinned your knight, but 11...Bxd4! was a sharp answer and took you to +4.9.
You kept the pressure up with 14...e3 and 15...Bxb2, and the engine was clear that you were winning for a long time.
Then the end: after 23.Rxe3 you took 23...bxa6, but 23...Bd4 was the engine move and kept the advantage. 24.Re8# ended it. A fine game to come back to, because the play before it was strong.

review.turning_point: 23...bxa6 was a blunder that allowed 24.Re8# in a position where 23...Bd4 kept the win.
review.focus: At 23...bxa6 you were winning, so before any capture look at every check and mating threat. Your own king's safety needed a check, not a pawn capture.

review.headline: A wild King's Knight game where you attacked well and finished with a mate

sections.text: Black went for 3...f5 and you took the pawn back with 5.dxe4. Then 6.Be2?! was a little passive, and 6...d5 was a mistake by Black. 7.Bg5 was not best (7.exd5 was), but 8.exd5! put you back in control.
After 9.Nxd5 Bxg5 10.Nxg5 Qxg5 11.Nxc7+ Kf7 you were attacking. 12.Bc4+ and 13.Qf3+ forced Black's king around, and at 13...Bf5 you were at +7.7.
Then 14.Qd5 and 15.Qd6+ were both mistakes. 14.Ne6+ was a fork of the king and queen, and the same fork was there at move 15. 17.Ng5+ was a discovered check, but 17.Nc7+ was stronger.
You stayed calm with 19.O-O-O!, and later 25.Bd3! and 26.Rxd3! kept control. The finish was 28.Rd6#.

review.turning_point: Moves 14 and 15 threw away a +8 edge because the forking 14.Ne6+ was missed.
review.focus: When you are winning, as at 14.Qd5, look for the check that wins material, 14.Ne6+, before reaching for the queen move.

review.headline: A queen's pawn game where White blundered early and you converted in a tactical melee

sections.text: After 6.Ne5 Nbd7 7.Nc3 Nxe5 8.dxe5 Nd7, White played 9.Nb5, which was a mistake, and you found the best reply, 9...Nxe5!. That won a pawn and set the tone.
The biggest moment was 16.Bd3, which looked natural but dropped material to 16...Nxd3+, a fork of the bishop on b2 and the king on e1.
