You then had a few wobbles. 20...Be4 was a blunder, and 24...b5 too, when 24...Bc5+ was the engine move. 25...Qb6+ was another mistake.
White's 26.Kxd3 was a blunder, and your 26...Rad8+ was a skewer on the king and queen on the d-file. After 27.Bd4 Rxd4+ 28.Ke3 Rxd1+ you were clearly winning.

review.turning_point: 16.Bd3 allowed 16...Nxd3+, a knight fork that won material for you.
review.focus: At 24...b5 you had a big lead; checking with 24...Bc5+ first would have kept your king safe and avoided the late wobbles.

review.headline: A Petrov where you won the center, pushed a passed pawn and promoted with mate

sections.text: A standard Petrov line, simplified with the early queen trade 7.Qxe7+ Bxe7. White then pushed 14.d4?, and you grabbed the pawn with 14...Bxd4!, which gave you a lasting edge.
The pawn you pushed to d4 became a powerful asset after 17.c4 d4. White drifted with 19.Nc2 and 20.b4, both mistakes.
One slip of your own: 19...Nc6 was a mistake. 19...Rxe2 was stronger, winning more at once. Even so, 20.b4 gave you the chance to break through with 20...Nxb4.
Finally 23...d3 and 24...Rxe2 25.Rxe2 dxe2 left a pawn on e2 that cannot be stopped. The ending was 28.Bxf4 e1=Q#.

review.turning_point: 14...Bxd4! punished 14.d4, and later the passed pawn on d3 and e2 decided the game.
review.focus: At 19...Nc6 you had 19...Rxe2 and it was the more forcing move. When your opponent leaves a piece loose, take the forcing line first.

review.headline: A Danish Gambit where you took the pawns, then loose moves threw away the edge

sections.text: You accepted the Danish Gambit all the way: 2...exd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Bc4 cxb2 5.Bxb2 d6. That left you a pawn or two up, with a normal defensive plan of getting the king safe.

Then the mistakes started. 7...g5 was a mistake, and 8...Be7 was a blunder, since the engine wanted 8...g4. White replied with 9.Nxg5, a blunder, but 9...Bxg5 was a blunder too; 9...d5 was the engine move.
You found 10...Qxg5! after 10.Bxg5, which put you in a strong position at +3.5.
11...Bh3 was the final error; 11...Qg7 was the engine move. The game ended here, with your position no longer as good as it had been.

review.turning_point: 11...Bh3 threw away a strong position at +3.7; 11...Qg7 was the safer move.
review.focus: At 8...Be7 and 11...Bh3, stop and check what White's last move attacks before you move. 8...g4 and 11...Qg7 were the engine moves.

review.headline: A Stafford Gambit refuted by 4.Nxc6, followed by drifting after 6.Be3

sections.text: Black played the Stafford Gambit and you took the pawn with 3.Nxe5. After the mistake 3...Nc6 you found the best reply, 4.Nxc6!, and dxc6 left you well ahead at +1.9.
Then 6.Be3 was a mistake. After 6...Bxe3 7.fxe3 Ng4 your pawn structure was broken and the king was exposed; 6.Be2 was the engine move.
The slide continued with 10.Bg2 and 11.Nc3, both mistakes, and after 12.Qf2 Black was at about +3 in the engine's view.
You did fight back: 18.Qxa7 and 19.Qxb7 picked off pawns, but 21.d4 was the final blunder, allowing a forced mate after 21...Qxf1+.

review.turning_point: 6.Be3 let Black wreck your pawn structure with 6...Bxe3 and 7...Ng4, ending your opening edge.
review.focus: At 6.Be3 you allowed 6...Bxe3 and 7.fxe3, wrecking your pawn structure. 6.Be2 kept things simple and kept the extra pawn.

review.headline: A Petrov with an early punish of 3...Bc5, then a king-side attack finished with 32.Qg7#

sections.text: Black played 3...Bc5? in the Petrov, and you found the best reply, 4.d4!. After 4...Bb4+ 5.c3 Ba5 you were at +4.2.
6.b4 was a slight misstep (6.Nc4 was the engine move), but you kept a healthy edge through 10.Nc4 and 11.Bg5.
13.Nxd6 was a blunder, dropping you to +1.1. Black missed their chances though, with 16...Ned7 and 17...Bb7 mistakes. After 17...Bb7 you were at +4 again.
From there you kept control, with 22.axb5, 24.Rxa7 and 25.Bxd7 pulling everything together. After 26.Bxe6 the material was +8, and the finish was 32.Qg7#.

review.turning_point: 17...Bb7 let you back to around +4 after 13.Nxd6 had thrown the advantage away.
review.focus: At 13.Nxd6 you gave back a lot of advantage; 13.axb5 was the safer way to keep the pressure.

review.headline: A well-played game where one retreat, 21...Bc8, let a winning edge slip

sections.text: You answered a quiet 2.d3 with solid development. 11...O-O-O?! was a little loose, but the plan of 12...h5 and 13...h4 was good, and after 14.gxh4 Bxh4 you opened lines against the white king.
You took a pawn with 18...Rxh2, and White's 20.f3 was a mistake that put you at about +4.7.
But 21...Bc8 was a blunder, dropping to +1.3; 21...Ne6 was the engine move. 22...Rxh1 was another small mistake, where again 22...Ne6 was best.
Later 28.Qg7 was an error by White, but you didn't find the best reply, 28...Qd6. After 28...c5, 29.exd5 turned things around, and the game ended with 36.Qg8+.

review.turning_point: 21...Bc8 gave away most of a winning advantage; 21...Ne6 kept it.
review.focus: At 21...Bc8 you retreated when 21...Ne6 kept the pressure on. With an advantage, look for the move that keeps pieces active.

review.headline: A Caro-Kann where 11.h5 wasted a good position

sections.text: You played the main-line Caro-Kann by the book: 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5.Nxf6+ exf6 6.Qe2+, and it was balanced.
9.h4?! was a little ambitious, but Black's 10...f5 was a mistake and 10.Be3 had set up a chance. The engine move was 11.Ng5, keeping control.
Instead 11.h5 was a blunder. After 11...f4 your bishop was attacked, and 12.Qd3 fxe3 13.fxe3 Bg3+ left you down material with the king stuck in the centre.

review.turning_point: 11.h5 allowed 11...f4, hitting the bishop on e3, and the position collapsed.
review.focus: Before pushing a pawn like 11.h5, ask what the opponent's reply attacks. 11.Ng5 was the safer move.

review.headline: A Philidor where you punished an early slip and drove the king into the open

sections.text: Black played 3...a5 and 4...c6?, and you found the best reply, 5.dxe5!. After 6.Be2 dxe5 7.Qxd8+ Kxd8 8.Nxe5 you had a pawn extra and Black's king could no longer castle.
You developed with 9.O-O and 11.Re1, and then 12.e5 opened the position while Black's king was still on f7.
13.exf6?! was a small inaccuracy (13.a4 was the engine move), but Black replied 13...Kxf6, an even bigger mistake, and the king became a target.
You kept up the checks with 16.Bg4+ and 17.Nf7+, at +6.3, and Black resigned.

review.turning_point: 13...Kxf6 walked the king into the open, and your checks on 14.Bg5+ and 15.Ne5+ drove it forward.
review.focus: Small point: 13.exf6 gave up some of your pawn pressure, so 13.a4 was cleaner. Otherwise a model game.

review.headline: A Petrov where you punished loose play and converted with an extra pawn

sections.text: A normal Petrov until 8...Ne4, which was a mistake because 9.Bxe7 took your bishop; the engine move was 8...O-O. After 9...Qxe7 you were slightly worse, around -2.
White then blundered with 10.Nxe4, and you found 10...dxe4!, bringing the position back to level.
11...e3 and 12.fxe3 Qxe3+ opened the e-file, and 13.Be2 stepped into a pin on the e-file against the king. You found 13...Qxd4!, and you were ahead.
After that you kept your advantage, finishing with 27...Rxc3+, and White resigned soon after.

review.turning_point: 10.Nxe4 and 13.Be2 were both mistakes, and 10...dxe4 and 13...Qxd4 were the best replies.
review.focus: 8...Ne4 was the one real mistake. In the Petrov with a bishop on g5, castle with 8...O-O before the knight jumps.

review.headline: A Petrov where White's pawn storm got going and you let the counterchances slip

sections.text: You answered 1.e4 with the Petrov, and White went for a sharp setup with 4.a3, 5.h3 and 6.g4 to chase your bishop. You were only slightly worse, but 7...h5?! (-1.4) invited 8.g5, and 8...Ng4 left your knight on the edge of the board.
White's 9.Bh3? was a chance for you. 9...d5 was the engine's choice, while 9...Qd7? (-2.2) let the advantage drift away. 10.Rg1? gave you a second chance and 10...Nc6! was exactly the right answer.
The costly moment was 12...O-O-O?? after 12.f3. Your king walked toward the open side, and 13.fxg4 just took the knight. 12...f5 would have kept the position under control.

Later White handed you chances with 20.b4?? and 21.a4??, but 20...Qf7?? and 21...Bg4?? gave them straight back. At the end 23...Rh1+ set up a skewer of king and queen, but 24.Rg1 answered it, and 23...Rxg4 was the engine's preferred move.

review.turning_point: 12...O-O-O?? took a position near level (+0.5 before it) down to -2.2, because 13.fxg4 took your knight.
review.focus: Before committing the king as in 12...O-O-O??, check every loose piece you own. Your knight on g4 was hanging to 13.fxg4, and one scan of the opponent's captures would have caught it.

review.headline: A level Sicilian game ruined by one hasty knight move

sections.text: You steered into a Smith-Morra with 2.d4 cxd4, but 3.Qxd4 took the pawn straight back, and after 3...Nc6 4.Qd1 the game was level. 5.Nf3 and 6.Nbd2 were sensible development.

7.e5?! (-0.8) pushed the pawn to kick the f6 knight, and 7...Ng4 sent it to an active square. You kept things going with 8.Nc4 and the knight check 9.Nd6+, and by 9...Kf8 the position was roughly equal again.

Then came 10.Ng5?? (-4.3). It uncovered your queen's attack on the g4 knight, a discovered attack that looks attractive. But 10...Bxf2+ came with check first, and after 11.Ke2 Nd4+ 12.Kd3 Nxe5+ your king was dragged into the open. The engine wanted 10.Ne4, holding the position together.

review.turning_point: 10.Ng5?? turned an equal position into -4.3, because 10...Bxf2+ was a check you had not accounted for.
review.focus: On 10.Ng5, list the opponent's checks and captures before you make a threat of your own. 10...Bxf2+ was there on the board the whole time.

review.headline: A solid Slav-style setup undone by one oversight on move 11

sections.text: You set up a sound structure with 1...d5, 2...e6 and 3...Nf6, then 5...O-O and 6...c6 against White's fianchetto. By 7...Nbd7 the evaluation was about -0.5, which is perfectly playable.
8...Nb6?! (-0.8) cost time, because 9.c5 kicked the knight and 9...Nbd7 just went back. After 10.Bf4 b6 White played 11.Ne5?, which the engine considered a mistake in favour of 11.b4.
That was your chance. 11...Nxe5 12.Bxe5 Nd7 would have kept the position healthy. Instead 11...Ne8?? (-6.5) left the c6 pawn hanging, and 12.Nxc6 took it, and the evaluation became decisive.

review.turning_point: 11...Ne8?? turned a position that was +0.7 for you into -6.5, as 12.Nxc6 took the pawn.
review.focus: When an enemy knight lands on e5 as with 11.Ne5, ask first whether you can capture it. 11...Nxe5 was available, and retreating with 11...Ne8 left c6 loose.

review.headline: A clean win: you punished a castling slip and ground down the attack to mate

sections.text: Against the Owen Defense you took the centre with 2.d4 and built calmly with 4.Bd2, 5.Nf3 and 6.g3. Then 7.e5 kicked the knight, and Black answered with 7...O-O??, which the engine called a blunder.

You found the right answer, 8.exf6!, taking the knight, and after 8...Bxf6 you had won a knight for a pawn. 9.Bh6 and 10.Bxg7 swapped off Black's best defender, and from there every evaluation was above +4.

You improved your position without hurry: 12.O-O, 13.Ne5, 14.Re1, 15.h4 and 16.Qg4. Then 22.g4 got the pawns moving and 25.gxh5 gxh5 26.Qxh5 opened the king up. 28.Qxh6+ Kg8 29.Nf6+ Qxf6 30.Qxf6 won Black's queen outright.
The finish was calm: 31.Raxc1 dealt with the promotion, then 35.Rxc6, 38.Bxe6 and 39.Rcxe6 cleared the way, and 41.Qg6+ Kf8 42.Re8# was checkmate.

review.turning_point: 8.exf6! was the key capture. Black's 7...O-O?? allowed it, and it took the knight with an advantage you never gave back.
review.focus: When you were far ahead you repeated the queen with 18.Qf4, 19.Qf3, 20.Qf4 and 21.Qf3. Next time start the concrete plan, like 22.g4, a few moves earlier.

review.headline: A brilliant refutation of the English, followed by a series of slips that ended in mate

sections.text: You met 1.c4 with 1...d5?! and White answered 2.Nc3??. You found 2...d4! and after 3.e3?? the strong 3...dxc3! picked up a knight for a pawn. This was well calculated, and the engine liked it.
You kept your edge through 7...Ne5?! 8.dxe5 Qxd3 and 11...Qxc4, but several inexact moves followed, including 10...Bh6?, 12...Qxa2? and 14...Qa4?. Still, the evaluation stayed above +1.

Then came 15...e5?? (-2.1). White's 15.e4 had uncovered the bishop on d2 onto your h6 bishop, a discovered attack, and 15...Bxd2 was the answer. White's 16.Nb5?? gave it back and 16...Qxb5! was good, but 21...Bxg2?? (-2.3) and 26...Rd3?? let White back in.
27...Qa3?? (-6.9) hurt, and 28.Bh6+ Ke7 was already difficult. White's 29.Bg7?? gave you a chance, but 29...Rxf3?? allowed 30.Bxf6+ Kf8 31.Qa8#. 29...Qd6 was the move.

review.turning_point: 15...e5?? gave up a +1.9 advantage, because 15...Bxd2 was needed to deal with the threat on h6.
review.focus: On 29...Rxf3??, you were still fighting but your king was exposed. When the king is open, list the opponent's checks first: 30.Bxf6+ and 31.Qa8# were all forced.

review.headline: A short Italian game: a free advantage gone after you forgot the c4 bishop

sections.text: You played the Italian with 3.Bc4, and Black's 3...Nd4 invited 4.Nxd4 exd4, a knight exchange. 5.d3 was fine, and Black's 5...Bc5?? gave you a chance (+3.2).
6.c3?? (+0.6) let that go. 6.Bxf7+ Kf8 7.Bb3 was the engine's idea. After 6...Qe7 7.Nd2 Nf6 the position was roughly level.

8.Nb3?! and 9.Nxc5?! were not what the engine wanted, and Black's 8...b5? (+1.6) was a mistake, with 8...d5 stronger. But the b5 pawn now attacked your bishop on c4, and 10.O-O?? ignored that. 10...bxc4 took the bishop and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 10.O-O?? ignored the b5 pawn's attack, and 10...bxc4 took the bishop, going from +0.8 to -3.1.
review.focus: On 10.O-O?? ask what the last opponent move threatens. 8...b5 had been aiming at your c4 bishop for two moves, and 10.Bb3 would have saved it.

review.headline: A topsy-turvy King's Gambit that ended with the clock

sections.text: After 2.f4 your 2...d6?! and 3...Nd7?! were passive. After 5.fxe5, 5...Nxe4?? (-2.1) was the wrong recapture; 5...Nxe5 6.Bb3 was better. White's 6.O-O? gave you a chance, but 6...Be7? missed 6...dxe5.
You hung on, and 8...Ne6! was a good answer to 8.b4??, giving back the pawn after 9.Bxe6 fxe6. The game was almost level by 10...cxd6.
17...Bb5?? (-1.1) pinned the d3 pawn against the rook on f1 but allowed White back in; 17...Bd6 was better. After 18.Ne5?? you got your chance back, but 20...Bxd3?? (-2.6) left a piece to be won.
You fought on well with 24...Bf6! and 28...Qxa7!, but 29...Nd3?? uncovered your e8 rook on e1 as a discovered attack, and 30.Rxe8 Rxe8 31.Rxf6 took your bishop. The clock then ran out on move 38.

review.turning_point: 20...Bxd3?? turned a roughly level game (+0.5) into -2.6, and you never fully recovered.
review.focus: Before 20...Bxd3??, check whether your capture is defended. 20...Ba4 kept the balance, but taking the pawn left a piece hanging.

review.headline: A Colle that went wrong in the middle, then a sharp queen finish

sections.text: You played the Colle with 1.d4, 2.e3 and 3.Nf3, and 4...Bxf3 5.Bxf3 gave you the bishop pair. 6.c4 and 7.Nc3 built a good centre, and 8.cxd5 exd5 left you with an edge.
9.O-O?! was a little slow, and 9...Be7? missed 9...cxd4. But 10.Re1? let it slip, since 10.dxc5 was better. 11.Qb3? c4 chased your queen away, and the position was about equal.

12.Qxb7 took a pawn, and 12...Na5?? was a blunder. Your 13.Qb5! was the best answer, hitting the a5 knight, and 14.Qa4 Nc6? let you play 15.Qxc6!, taking the knight. 16.Nxd5 then took another pawn and 16...Ra6 ended the game.

review.turning_point: 14...Nc6? left the knight loose, and 15.Qxc6! took it, taking the evaluation from +2.0 to +4.3.
review.focus: 10.Re1? and 11.Qb3? let a good position go equal. At 10.Re1 the engine wanted 10.dxc5, so exchange in the centre before spending time on other moves.

review.headline: A Petrov where the opponent hung a piece and then walked into a forced loss

sections.text: You won a pawn early with 3...Nxe4 and followed with 4...d5. After 5.Bb3 Be7?! 6.Re1 O-O 7.Nxe5 you were fine.
7...Re8?? (-3.6) was a mistake that left a piece to be won. 7...Nc6 was the engine's choice. But 8.Nf3?? gave it all back (+0.5), since 8.Rxe4 was needed.
You played 8...Bc5?! 9.d4 Bf8 10.c4 c6, then 12...Nxc3 13.bxc3 bxc5 took a pawn. White tried 14.Ne5 c4 15.Ba4 and your 15...Bb7? (-0.9) was a bit loose.
16.Qf3?? was the real blunder, and 16...f6! was a strong answer. 17.Ng4?? then allowed a forced win for you. White resigned soon after.

review.turning_point: 16.Qf3?? and your 16...f6! answer, then 17.Ng4??, moved the game from -0.9 to a forced win.
review.focus: 7...Re8?? left a piece to be won. When the opponent captures on e5 with 7.Nxe5, protect your e4 knight first; 7...Nc6 was the safe move.

review.headline: A winning rook ending thrown away by the clock

sections.text: Against the Bird you played 1...d5, 2...e6 and 3...Nf6, and 6.Ba4? b5! hit White's bishop and drove it back, 7.Bb3 a5 8.a3 a4 9.Ba2. Your queenside pawns gained space and the bishop ended up buried.
14.Ng5 Nxg5 15.fxg5 Ne4 16.Nxe4 dxe4 17.Bxe4 Bxg5 simplified, and the position was roughly level. 20...Qf6? (-0.0) was inexact, and 21...f4?? (-2.1) missed 21...Bxc1.

23...Rac8? and 24...g5?? (-6.5) made it worse, and it looked lost. But 28.Bxh7+?? gave you a chance and 28...Qxh7! was the right answer. From there you collected material with 29...Bxe6 and 30...Kxh7.
By 42...Rxb2 you were over +7, but the clock ran out on move 44 in a winning position.

review.turning_point: 28.Bxh7+?? by White and 28...Qxh7! flipped the game from -5.1 to +3.5.
review.focus: After 24...g5??, you needed all your clock to survive. Practise faster, simpler moves in winning positions, like 32...cxd4 and 33...Rc2, so the flag does not decide it.

review.headline: A French Exchange where you got outplayed at first, then punished a blunder with 23.Nxd8!

sections.text: You took the pawn with 3.exd5 and played 4.Nc3, 5.Nf3 and 6.Be2. Black's 6...f6? was a mistake, and your 7.O-O! was the strong answer. 9.Nxd5 cxd5 traded knights.
14.Rad1?? (-1.0) was a blunder, since 14...Bb4 15.Qc2 Bxe1 16.Rxe1 left you giving up the exchange. 14.a3 was the engine's choice.

18.g4?? loosened your king, but Black's 18...g6?? failed to use it (18...dxc4 was stronger), and 19.Ng5?? kept letting it slip (19.Bg5 was better). Then 21.Nxe6 took a pawn, and Black went wrong with 21...Nb4?? and 22...Rfd8?? after 22.Bxb4?!.
23.Nxd8! was the shot, and 24.Nxb7 Qxb7 25.Bxf5 gxf5 26.Qxf5 piled it on. 35.d8=Q finished it.

review.turning_point: 22...Rfd8?? let you play 23.Nxd8!, taking the evaluation from +1.0 to +5.2.
review.focus: 14.Rad1?? left the e1 rook undefended against 14...Bb4. Before a rook move, check whether the other rook still has protection.

review.headline: A Reversed King's Gambit where you did not take the free pawn and paid for it

sections.text: After 1.e4 f5? you were better, but 2.d3? passed up 2.exf5. 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 pinned the knight against the queen, but the engine preferred 4.exf5.
6.Qd2 O-O 7.O-O-O? (-1.5) put the king on an open file, and 7.exf5 Bxf5 8.d4 was the engine's idea. After 7...Bxc3 8.Qxc3, Black's 8...Nc6? was a mistake, since 8...c5 was better.
9.h4?! and 10.Bd2?? were slow, and 10...fxe4 11.dxe4 Nxe4 took a pawn. 13.Bd3? Nxf2 14.Bxh6 gxh6 15.g4?! Nxd1 16.Kxd1 Rxf3 17.Be2 Rxb3 captured your queen and finished the game.

review.turning_point: 10.Bd2?? let Black play 10...fxe4, taking the evaluation from +0.3 to -1.4.
review.focus: 2.d3? passed up the free pawn on f5. Take material when the opponent's move weakens the position: 2.exf5 was good.

review.headline: A long Petrov battle where White's pawn storm was handled well until a blunder

sections.text: White played the g4 and h4 pawn storm against your Petrov, 6.g4 Bg6 7.d3 h5 8.g5. You were around -2.0 at one point, but White's 9.h4? helped you, and 11.Nd5?? was a blunder that 11...Nxd5! punished by trading knight for bishop.
From there the game was balanced. You played 14...Nc5, 15...Qc7 and 17...O-O-O?!, and White's 21.b5? gave you a chance, but 21...c5? (-0.2) was not best. 21...Nc5 was.
25.Qa4?? was another opportunity, and 25...Qa7? lined up a skewer on the a-file against queen and bishop but 25...f5 was stronger. You traded queens with 29...Qxb3 and reached a level endgame.
37.d4?? gave you a chance, but 37...Ra4?? ran into 38.Bxa4. 37...Bxe4 was the engine's choice. The ending was difficult, and 50...Kxb5? did not help; 50...Kb4 was better.

review.turning_point: 37...Ra4?? turned a position near level into -5.3, because 38.Bxa4 took the rook.
review.focus: On 37...Ra4?? your rook walked into a bishop's capture. Before moving a rook, check every enemy piece that attacks the target square.

review.headline: A Philidor where you had chances early, then a knight move dropped a piece

sections.text: You played the Philidor, and 3...Be6 4.Bxe6 fxe6 5.Nc3 gave you a decent position. 6.d4 exd4 7.Nxd4 e5 8.Ne6 was awkward to meet, and 8...Qe7?? was a mistake; 8...Qd7 was best.
White's 9.Nxf8?? gave it all back, and after 9...Rxf8 you were close to level. 11.f4 O-O-O 12.Nd5 Nxd5 13.exd5 and then 13...e4?? (-0.8) missed 13...Qh4.
14.Qg4? was inaccurate, but 15...Rde8?! let White pick up e3. 19...Ng4?? (-4.6) was the real error, as 20.Qxg4 took the knight. 19...Re4 was the right move.
You kept finding ideas, like 25...h3!, but 28...Qb2?! allowed 29.Rxe8+ Rxe8 30.Qxe8+, which ended the game.

review.turning_point: 19...Ng4?? turned -0.3 into -4.6, as 20.Qxg4 took the knight.
review.focus: 19...Ng4?? left a piece to be taken by 20.Qxg4. Before a knight move, check that its landing square is protected.

review.headline: A game that swung wildly: you were +5.5 and gave it all back

sections.text: You met 1.d4 with 1...d5 and 3...Nf6, and 4.c5 b6 5.b4 Bb7? was a bit loose. White's 6.f4?? was a mistake, but 6...Na6?? (-3.9) wasted it; 6...a5 was better.
7.Bd2?? by White gave you a second chance, and 7...bxc5? 8.bxc5 Nxc5 9.dxc5 Bxc5 left you a bit ahead. 10.a3? O-O! was good. Then 11.g3??, 12.Nc3?? and 13.a4?? each helped you, and you reached +5.5.

But 11...a5??, 12...Re8?? and 13...Ne4?? (+5.5 to -1.9) threw it away. 13...d4 was the move, and 11...d4 would have opened the long diagonal for your b7 bishop with a discovered attack. 14.Nxe4 dxe4 left you down material.
From there you fought on, but 35...Qh3?? with little time left lost on the spot to 36.Qxh3.

review.turning_point: 13...Ne4?? gave up a +5.5 advantage, because 14.Nxe4 took the knight.
review.focus: In a winning position as at 13...Ne4??, look for the simple, strong move. 13...d4 kept the advantage and kept pieces defended.

review.headline: A Scandinavian win: you punished an early blunder and finished with a knight check and mate

sections.text: You met the Scandinavian with 2.exd5, 3.d4 and 4.Nf3. Black's 4...Nxd4?? gave you a big edge, and 5.Nxd4 e5 6.Nf3 Qe4+ 7.Qe2 left you comfortably ahead.
8.c4 Bb4+ 9.Bd2 Bxd2+ 10.Nbxd2 Qc2 11.Qxe5+ Kf8 12.Qxc7 collected pawns. But 15.Qd8+?? (+4.8 to +2.3) was a slip; 15.Qd6+ was better.
17.Rae1?! and 18.Ne4?? were inexact, and Black's 17...Qxa2? and 18...Bxe4?? helped. Then 19.Rxe4! pinned the e7 knight against the rook on e8 and you were winning again.
21.Rxe7 Rxe7 22.Qxe7+ Kg7 23.Ng5 set up 24.Ne6+!, a fork of king and rook, and 25.Qxf8# was checkmate.

review.turning_point: 19.Rxe4! took the evaluation from +4.0 to +6.1 after Black's 18...Bxe4??.
review.focus: 15.Qd8+?? was an unnecessary check that cost about 2.5 pawns. Before giving a check, ask what it forces; 15.Qd6+ was the cleaner move.

review.headline: A Danish Gambit that turned into a long, lucky escape and then a drawn rook ending you should have won

sections.text: You accepted the Danish Gambit with 2...exd4, 3...dxc3 and 4...cxb2, then hit back in the center with 5...d5. After 6.Bxd5 Nf6 7.Bxf7+ Kxf7 8.Qxd8 you found the in-between check 8...Bb4+, which forced 9.Qd2 and let you trade queens on your terms. That left a level, comfortable position.

The trouble began with 11...Nc5?! and especially 12...Nfxe4??, which the engine put at -2.1. The calmer 12...Rd8 kept things even. After 13.Ne5+ you walked the king forward with 13...Ke6?, when 13...Kg8 was the safer route, and the position slid to about -4.

Your opponent helped you back. 18.Nd3+ and 19.Bc1+ both let the advantage shrink, since 18.f3 and 19.f3 were stronger. Then 32...Rb1? gave them a chance, but 33.Kg3 was a real blunder and 33...Rxb2 was exactly the right punishment, swinging the game to +4.9. From there you picked up pawns steadily and reached a rook against a bare king.

The ending is the frustrating part. With a forced win available you played 55...Rf6??, then 57...Kd5??, and 58.Kxf6 left only kings. A king and rook against a lone king is a technique drill: bring the king close and keep the rook a safe distance, like the 55...Rd5 and 57...Rd6 ideas the engine showed.

review.turning_point: 33...Rxb2 punished 33.Kg3 and gave you a winning position, but it was thrown away at 55...Rf6 when the rook was left hanging to the king.
review.focus: Practice the king-and-rook technique so that 55...Rf6 never happens: check where the enemy king can reach before putting the rook anywhere near it.

review.headline: A clean Italian where one center pawn grab collapsed your opponent's position in a few moves

sections.text: You played a classical Italian with 3.Bc4, 4.c3 and 5.d4, a sound way to claim the center. After 7.O-O Qf6 your opponent was already pressing, and 8.e5 dxe5 9.dxe5?! was a small slip: 9.Bg5 was the more accurate way to keep your edge. Even so, the position stayed fine.

Then came the key moment. Your opponent grabbed on e5 with 9...Nxe5??, a blunder worth about +4 to you. You responded perfectly with 10.Nxe5!, removing the knight and leaving the queen on e5 exposed to attack.

11.Re1 hit the queen straight away. Black tried 11...Bxf2+ 12.Kxf2 Qxe1+ 13.Qxe1+ and you came out with a big material lead, about +5 after taking the queen back. It is worth noticing that you did not panic about the check on f2. Recapturing with the king was safe because the queens were about to come off.
The finish was tidy. 14.Bxe6 fxe6 15.Qxe6+ took more material, and 16.Bg5 brought your last piece into the game. Black resigned at +9.6, facing a hopeless position.

review.turning_point: 10.Nxe5 answered the blunder 9...Nxe5 and turned a roughly equal game into a winning one.
review.focus: At 9.dxe5 you recaptured automatically; look for the developing move such as 9.Bg5 first, so you keep more control when the center opens.

review.headline: A slow French Exchange against a 2380 where slips on the queenside and then missed shots let the stronger player take over

sections.text: Against a 2380 you handled the opening well. The Exchange French is quiet, and after 6.Nf3 and 7.Be2 everything was equal. 8.Bh4 kept your bishop active, and 10.Qd2 with 11.Rfe1 were sensible. Nothing wrong yet.

The problems began with 12.Rad1?!, then 13.a4? and 15.b3??. The engine preferred 13.Bd3 and 15.Bd3, developing instead of pushing pawns. After 13...b4 your knight had to retreat to a2, and the loosened queenside gave Black targets and time for 15...Ne4.

Credit for 17.Bxe7, simplifying a tricky position, and Black's 14...a5? and 19...Qd6?? gave you chances. In particular 19.Qc7?? was a real missed opportunity: 19.Qxf6 was much stronger, and then 20.Qb7?? repeated the error when 20.Qxd6 was there. Your queen went on a raid on the queenside that cost time and tempo.
After 21.Qxb8+ Rxb8 22.Ne5 Nxe5 23.dxe5 Qxe5, you were a lot of material down at about -5.6. 25.g3?! weakened the king, and 25...Qxf2+ 26.Kh1 Qf3+ 27.Kg1 Nf2 finished with 28.Rd2 Nh3#.

review.turning_point: 19.Qc7 and 20.Qb7 sent the queen away from the defence of the position, passing up 19.Qxf6 and 20.Qxd6.
review.focus: Before a queen raid like 19.Qc7, check what your opponent's best reply does to your king; the safer 19.Qxf6 was there.

review.headline: A wild win as Black where both sides handed material back and forth until your tactics came through

sections.text: You met the Mason Attack with a solid set-up with 1...d5, 2...e6 and 3...Nf6 and 4...Bd6 and 5...O-O. 6...Re8?! was a little loose, but 8.Ne5 Ne4 was fine. After 9.Nd2?, the engine suggested the strong 9...Qh4+, a good idea to remember against a weakened kingside. You played 9...Ndf6?? instead, and the edge was gone.

12.cxd5 was the moment: 12...exd5 was correct, and 12...Nxd5?? lost material (-5.3). But 13.Bxe4? gave it back, since 13.Nxe4 was better. Then your reply 13...Nxe3! was great: the knight on e3 forked the queen on d1 and the rook on f1.

15.Bxb7?? from your opponent was an error, but 15...Nxf1?? missed the stronger 15...gxh5, and after 16.Qf3 Nxd2 17.Bxd2 Rb8 you were still worse (-3.5). Then 18.f5?? gave it all back: 18...Bxe5! 19.dxe5 Qxd2 and the position was clearly winning for you (+4.5).

You kept finding good moves: 20...Qxb2, 22...Rxd1+, and 24...Qxe5 simplified. 26...Qf5?! was slightly off, since 26...Qa1+ was a back rank idea, but 27.a4 Qf1# ended the game anyway. Nice conversion once the position opened up.

review.turning_point: 13...Nxe3 forked the queen and rook and rescued you after 12...Nxd5, and 18...Bxe5 later decided the game.
review.focus: At 12...Nxd5 you recaptured with the wrong piece; before taking, check what the other recapture, 12...exd5, keeps defended.

review.headline: A quick Italian win: your opponent's queen walked into the bishop's line

sections.text: A short and instructive game. You played the Italian with 3.Bc4 and 4.d4, building the center while eyeing f7. Black's 4...Qe7 was a bit careless, as the queen was blocking its own bishop and exposed to ideas of 5.Ng5.

5.Ng5 was the right idea, putting a second attacker on the weak f7 point. Black replied 5...Qf6??, and the engine saw that 5...Nd8 was needed instead. After 6.Nxf7 you were a pawn up, with the knight attacking the rook on h8 and the pawn on d6.

Black's last move 6...Qe6?? stepped into the bishop's diagonal. Your bishop on c4 was already pointing at e6, so 7.Bxe6! simply took the queen, and your material advantage jumped to about ten points. Black resigned at once.

Credit to you for not rushing in earlier. Your development and your calm 4.d4 made f7 weak, and the opponent did the rest. Keep an eye out for this pattern: when the queen sits near the c4 bishop's diagonal, look at the squares it can go to.

review.turning_point: 6...Qe6 put the queen where 7.Bxe6 could take it, ending the game.
review.focus: Good game with no errors; keep checking forcing moves such as 5.Ng5 for what your opponent's most natural reply does.

review.headline: A messy Queen's Pawn game where both sides blundered, and you won by keeping calm after a big swing

sections.text: You set up in a London-style way against 1.d4 and met the early 5.Ne5 with 5...Nbd7. After 8.Bh2 the engine flagged 8...b6?? as a blunder, and 8...Ne4 was the right move. Luckily 9.c3?? missed 9.Nc6, a strong move that opens the bishop on h2 against your bishop on d6 and wins time.

More chances came your way. 10...c5?? and 11.b3?? were poor, because 11.Nxf7 was a strong tactic there. You then played 11...Qc7? and 13...Nh7??, and 14.Bc2?? again passed up a good move: 14.Bxh7+ was the engine's pick.

15...fxe5?? was the big mistake, leaving the knight on h7 to be taken, and after 16.Qxh7+ Kf8 17.Nh4 you were under pressure at -3.3. 17...e4?! at least opened your bishop on d6 against the bishop on h2 with a discovered attack, but 18.Bxd6+ Qxd6 19.Ng6+ Kf7 kept White comfortably ahead.

The turning point was 20.Ne5+?? and your reply 20...Nxe5!, which swung the evaluation by almost seven pawns. From there 23.Bh5+ Qxh5 and 25.fxe4 left you far ahead, and you finished with 32...Kg8!, the best answer to 32.Rf1+. A resignation at move 38 was a good result.

review.turning_point: 20.Ne5+ was a blunder and 20...Nxe5 took advantage, changing the game from losing to winning.
review.focus: Look again at 15...fxe5: before capturing, ask what your opponent's queen move 16.Qxh7+ attacks, and consider 15...Ndf8 instead.

review.headline: A sharp Knight Attack where you won material early, then let a misjudged queen grab and a king walk unravel everything

sections.text: You went for the aggressive Two Knights line with 4.Ng5, and your opponent's 5...Nxd5? let you play 6.Nxf7!, hitting the queen and rook. After 6...Kxf7 7.Qf3+ Ke6 8.Nc3 you were happily on top, and 8...Nd4? let you finish with 9.Bxd5+!, a fine move.

The trouble started with 10.Bxb7??, which threw away the lead, since 10.Qd1 was the safe move. Fortunately Black replied 10...Bxb7??, and 11.Qxb7! got you back to +2.9, with the queen hitting the rook on a8 and the pawn on a7.

Then you took a pawn with 12.Qxa7?? when 12.Qd5+ was a skewer of king and queen. 12...Nxc2+ attacked your rook, and 13.Ke2? made it worse, since 13.Kd1 was better. After 13...Nxa1 you were behind material.
14.Nb5+?? was the decisive mistake. It left a piece to be won, and 14...Rxb5 left you at about -4.5. From there the game ran away: 16.Be3?! Rxb2+, and in the end 22.Kd1 Rxd2# finished it.

review.turning_point: 10.Bxb7 and then 12.Qxa7 grabbed pawns when 10.Qd1 and 12.Qd5+ kept a winning advantage.
review.focus: When you are ahead, as at 10.Bxb7, take a quiet move first like 10.Qd1 instead of grabbing a pawn; check your own king and undefended pieces before every capture.

review.headline: A Hungarian where you went wrong early and then missed the one move that would have saved the queen

sections.text: Against 1.g3 you played the sensible 1...e5, 2...d5 and 3...Nf6. After 5.Nh3 you grabbed with 5...Bxh3?, and the engine preferred 5...Nc6. 6.Bxh3 recaptured and your small edge shrank from +1.3 to about +0.1.

You developed with 6...O-O, 7...Nbd7 and 8...c6, and 9...Qe7 and 10...Rfe8 were normal. 11...e4?! was a little hasty, as it traded off your central pawn after 12.dxe4 Nxe4 13.Nxe4 dxe4. Still the position was balanced.

14.Qd4?? from your opponent was a real mistake, since 14.Bxe4 was the correct reply. Your answer was the big miss: 14...Be5 would have skewered the queen and the bishop behind it, with 15.Qxe4 Bxb2 following. Instead 14...Rad8?? allowed 15.Qxg7#.
That is the lesson here: when a queen appears on a central square, look for attacks with a bishop first. The game ended in 15 moves, with an accuracy of 31.

review.turning_point: 14...Rad8 passed up 14...Be5 and let White play 15.Qxg7#.
review.focus: At 14...Rad8, run a checklist of checks, captures and threats against your king first; the weak g7 point needed defending.

review.headline: A Petrov where you took on e5, the king was pulled out, and you still found the final shot

sections.text: You went for the sharp 3.Nxe5 line against the Petrov. After 4.Qe2 d5 5.d3 Qe7 you chose 6.Nxf7?!, a speculative sacrifice, and after 7.dxe4 dxe4 8.Nc3 Qb4 9.Qxe4?! Qxe4+ 10.Nxe4 you still had an edge of about +2 in the ending.

You developed with 11.Bd3, 12.Bf4?! and 13.f3. Black replied 13...Nd4?, and 14.O-O-O! was an excellent answer. After 15.fxe4 Bd6? you landed the key move, 16.Bc4+!, a discovered attack by the rook on d1 on the knight on d4 while checking the king.
17.Rxd4?? was the mistake, throwing away the edge; the engine wanted 17.Bxd6+ first, and then 18.Rxd4 kept everything. Instead 17...Bxf4+ left you at about +0.5 with the evaluation down from +5.8.

Both players then wobbled. 20...Kd6?? gave you a chance, but 21.Rhe1?? let it slip, since 21.Rd1+ was stronger. Black returned the favour with 21...Re6??, and 22.Bxe6! won decisive material (+5), finishing the game.

review.turning_point: 16.Bc4+ should have won more, but 17.Rxd4 let it slip, and 22.Bxe6 regained the lead.
review.focus: At 17.Rxd4, check what a recapture does to your bishop on f4; 17.Bxd6+ first kept everything protected.

review.headline: A Petrov where an early knight sortie and a run of loose moves handed your opponent a pawn and the initiative

sections.text: You played a sensible Petrov setup with 3...d6, 4...Bg4 and 5...Be7. The first real error was 9...Nh5??, which allowed 10.Bxe7 and the evaluation dropped from +0.3 to -1.6. The calmer 9...c6 kept things equal.

Your opponent gave you chances. 11.d4?? returned some of it, and 12.dxe5 dxe5 13.Nd5 Nxd5 14.exd5 was the main line. But 14...Rad8?? was a blunder, and 14...Nf4 was the right plan, with the knight jumping into the center.

Your opponent offered chances: 11.d4?? and 15.c4? both gave ground. But 15...Qb4?? (the engine liked 15...Nf4) and 16...c6?? let White play 17.Nxe5 Bxe2 18.Qxe2 Nf4, when 15.Nxe5 and 16.Nxe5 had been strong ideas all along.

Then 19...Nxd5? was the mistake that finished it, since 19...Ng6 was the stronger choice. After 20.cxd5 cxd5 you were two pawns down, and 21...Rd7? lost outright to 22.Nxd7. The common thread was moving pieces away from where they were needed.

review.turning_point: 9...Nh5 led to 10.Bxe7, and after that your pieces never got coordinated.
review.focus: At 9...Nh5, check what your knight leaving f6 uncovers; a quiet move such as 9...c6 would have kept your structure intact.

review.headline: A short Sicilian where the clock ended the game, not the board

sections.text: You answered 1...c5 with 2.d4, and after 2...cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qd1 you were ready to develop. 4...Nf6 5.Nc3 g6 6.Nf3 Bg7 followed, and everything was equal. A fair start.

7.Bb5? was the one mistake in the game, with the evaluation falling from +0.1 to -1.6. The engine suggested 7.Bc4, which keeps the bishop safe from tricks. After 7.Bb5 the e4 pawn is loose, because 7...Nxe4 would use the discovered attack by the bishop on g7 against your knight on c3.

Your opponent missed it. 7...a6?? was a blunder, and the position went back to about equal (+0.2). At that point 8.Bxc6 was the engine's choice, but you played 8.Ba4?!, and 8...b5 gave Black space and tempo on the queenside.
The game ended on time after only eight moves, so the position was still balanced. The lesson is practical: when the clock is short in the opening, stick with simple developing moves like 7.Bc4.

review.turning_point: 7.Bb5 left e4 loose, but 7...a6 gave you the chance back, which 8.Ba4 did not use.
review.focus: At 7.Bb5, check every loose pawn before moving a piece; 7.Bc4 kept e4 and the knight safe.

review.headline: A Philidor where you were doing well in the middlegame and then lost the thread with two moves

sections.text: You played the Philidor setup with 2...d6, 3...Nf6 and 4...Be7, and 6.Bxf6 Bxf6 simplified. You handled 7...c6 and 8...Nd7 well, and 9...Nb6?! was only a small inaccuracy, with 10.Nc4 Be6 11.Nxb6 Qxb6 the natural result.

12.Bg4? gave you a chance. The engine saw 12.Rb1 as better. You grabbed with 12...Qxb2, a sensible move, and 13.Na4?? was a further error by White, since 13.Bxe6 was needed. You were at +4.0 for a moment.

13...Qd4?? was the first real slip. 13...Qa3 kept the advantage, while the queen move to d4 allowed 14.Bxe6. Then 14...fxe6?? was a blunder, and 14...Qxa4 was the right move, taking the knight with the queen. After 15.c3 Qxa4 16.Qxa4 you were about five pawns down.
From there 16...b5 and 17...d5 gave some activity, but White's queen on b3 and b4 kept control, and you lost on time at around -5.6. Time trouble hurt here, so a simple plan matters.

review.turning_point: 13...Qd4 and 14...fxe6 turned a +4 position into a lost one when 14...Qxa4 was available.
review.focus: At 14...fxe6, look for the capture that wins material, 14...Qxa4, before recapturing automatically.

review.headline: A chaotic King's Pawn game against an 1817 where early opening choices cost you, and then a good defence collapsed in the endgame

sections.text: 2.b3? is an unusual way to respond to 1...e5, and the follow-ups 4.d3 and 5.Nf3? let Black take on e4. You were around -2.4. Your opponent then went wrong with 6...exd3??, so after 7.Bxd3?! the position was nearly level again.
Black kept drifting: 7...Qe7?, 8...Bg4? and 9...Bh5?? each gave you a chance. But 10.O-O?? was a mistake, and 10.Bb5 was best. After 11.Nxc6 Qxe2 12.Nxa7+ Kb8 13.Nc6+ bxc6 14.Bxe2, queens were off.

You fought well in the middlegame. 17.Ne4! forked the bishop on c5 and the rook on d6, a good tactic after 16...g5?. 17...Nxe4 18.fxe4?? was a slip that undid some of it, but 19.Bxh8 kept you in the game.

The end was a series of blunders. 21.Rxf7?? allowed a forced mate, and 21.g4 was the move that gave your king room. Each time afterwards, with 22.Rxh7??, 23.e5?? and 24.Bf6??, 22.g4, 23.g4 and 24.g4 were still the answer. The engine's 21...Rd1+ shows the back rank problem, and 24...Re1# ended the game.

review.turning_point: 21.Rxf7 gave up the key defensive move 21.g4 and left the king on h1 with no escape square.
review.focus: Before grabbing with 21.Rxf7, spend the move on 21.g4 so your king has an escape square.

review.headline: A messy Old Indian Attack where you reached a winning position, then let a long king hunt go wrong

sections.text: You played a solid Queen's Pawn setup against the Old Indian Attack. 11...Bd6?! and 12...Rfe8?! were a little passive, and 13...e5? was too early. After 14.cxd5 Bxd5?! 15.dxe5 Nxe5?! the game was roughly level, and White's 16.Nxe5? and 17.Kxg2 started to help you.

Then 18.f4?? was a big blunder, and 18...Bxa1! was exactly right. You collected a rook and went to +6. The g-pawn march with 21.g4, 22.g5 and 23.g6 opened your king, and 24.gxf7+ Kxf7?! and 25...g6? gave away some of the advantage.
26...Ke8?? was a serious error, and 26...Kf8 was needed. After 27.Qxg6+ Rf7 White erred with 28.Qe4+??, and 28...Qe7! was the best reply. 29.Qc6+ Kf8 30.Qh6+ were just checks.

31.Qh8+?? was a blunder, and 31...Bxh8 simply took the queen. You played 31...Rf8?? instead and the evaluation swung from +6.7 to -4. Later 33...Ke8?? and 34...Kf7?? finished with 35.Qg6#. The lesson is to calculate every check from the queen before moving your king.

review.turning_point: 31...Rf8 missed 31...Bxh8, which would have taken the queen and kept a winning game.
review.focus: At 31.Qh8+, look at which piece can capture the checking piece first: the bishop on c3 could take it with 31...Bxh8.

review.headline: A winning game against the Damiano Defense that slipped away when your king went for a walk

sections.text: Black opened badly with 2...f6?, and you punished it with 3.Nxe5 fxe5 4.Qh5+ g6 5.Qxe5+. After 5...Qe7 6.Qxh8 you were up big at +3.4. 6...Qxe4+ forced 7.Kd1, an early sign that your king was exposed.

You offered a queen trade with 8.Qc3 and 9.Qe3 Qxe3 10.dxe3, and the position stayed good (+3.7). 11.Nc3 b5 12.a3 d5 then led to 13.Bxb5??, which dropped the lead to +0.6. The engine preferred 13.Bd3.
Black's 14...Bd7?? gave you a way back, and 15.Nc7+! forked the king on e8 and the rook on a8. 16.Nxa8 won the rook and put you at +7 in material.

Then the king walked. 17.Ke2 Bb5+ 18.Kf3? Ng5+ 19.Kg3 Bd6+ 20.Kg4?? was the decisive error, since 20.f4 was safe. 20...h6?? missed 20...Ne4, but 21.h4?? Bd7# ended the game. A king walk forward should only happen when you are sure about every check.

review.turning_point: 20.Kg4 stepped into the net, when 20.f4 would have kept the king safe.
review.focus: At 18.Kf3, keep the king near the pieces: 18.Ke1 was calmer and avoided the string of checks.

review.headline: A wildly swingy game that you won in the end, with chances on both sides and time trouble in the endgame

sections.text: You played a flexible Queen's Pawn setup. White went for a pawn storm with 5.f3, 6.b4 and 7.g4, and 10...c5? gave White a good chance. But 11.a4?? was a blunder, since 11.bxc6 was the correct move. Your reply 11...c4! was spot on.
You traded off pieces with 16...Bxc3 and 19...Bxa4, but 14...O-O?? had already loosened your position. In the heat of the middlegame 22...c3?? gave White a chance, and 23.Bc1?? missed 23.Bxa6.

24...Nc4?? was a serious blunder, dropping you to -7.9 and leaving a piece to be won. White replied 25.Bb5??, and 25...Rxb5! reversed the evaluation, so you were saved. From there 26...Nd6??, 30...Qe2?? and 31...Nh7?? were more slips, partly from time trouble.

You found 32...Ng5! and 34...Qxf3!, which were strong. 33...Nxf3+?? missed 33...Nxh3+, which forked the king and rook, but you still finished the game with 39...Rxb1! and 42...Qc2#. A win, though a lucky one.

review.turning_point: 25.Bb5 let you play 25...Rxb5, saving a game that 24...Nc4 had nearly lost.
review.focus: At 24...Nc4, check what the knight leaves undefended: 24...Nbd7 kept everything covered, especially when low on time.

review.headline: A textbook punishment of the Damiano Defense, finished in eight moves

sections.text: Black's 2...f6? is the Damiano Defense, and it is bad. You answered exactly as the engine would: 3.Nxe5 fxe5 4.Qh5+. This is the standard sacrifice, and it works because the king has to move. After 4...Ke7 you simply took with 5.Qxe5+.
5...Kf7 6.Bc4+ brought the bishop out with check, and 6...d5 7.Bxd5+ kept the initiative. Every one of your moves was a check or a threat, which kept Black from untangling.
7...Be6?? was the final blunder. The bishop on e6 was pinned to its own king on f7 by your bishop on d5 at 7...Be6, and your queen on e5 simply took it with 8.Qxe6#.
Accuracy of 99.9 says it all. Remember this pattern: when the king has been dragged out into the open by a queen check, bring bishops with check and look for an immediate finish.

review.turning_point: 7...Be6 left the bishop pinned to the king, and 8.Qxe6# ended the game.
review.focus: Nothing to fix here; just remember the pattern of checking forcing moves first, as in 6.Bc4+ and 7.Bxd5+.

review.headline: A long win as Black where your opponent's pawn lunges backfired and you converted with a queen raid

sections.text: Against the f3 setup you played 3...Nf6, 4...Bd6 and 5...O-O?!, a little loose but fine. White then overextended with 7.b4? and 8.b5, and your 9...c5 and 10...c4 gained space while 11...e5 hit the center. 12...Qe7? was the one slip (the engine liked 12...g6).
The key moment was 15.e4??, a blunder, and 15...dxe4! was the right reply. After 16.Nxc4 Qc7 17.fxe4? Qxc4! you were up material. 18.h3 Nxe4 19.Bxe4 Bxe4 20.Rf1 Bxg2 gave you a huge edge.
21...exd4?! was a little greedy, since 21...Qxc3+ would have forked the king and the rook on a1. 22.Bd2? missed 22.Rxg2. You kept finding good moves such as 22...Rfe8+ and 25...Bxe2.

26...Qxa2 and 27...Qxd2+ led to a won endgame, and 31...Nxf3+ forced a trade into a clearly winning ending. You then brought the rook in, took pawns with 36...Rxa4 and 39...Rxb5+, and finished with 46...Rh1#. A strong, patient conversion.

review.turning_point: 15...dxe4 answered 15.e4 and 17...Qxc4 won a lot of material.
review.focus: At 12...Qe7 and 5...O-O, pay attention to what your queen move allows; 12...g6 kept your structure and avoided the trade.

review.headline: A Caro-Kann Exchange where small slips on your side were erased by a sharp knight sortie

sections.text: You played the Exchange Variation with 3.exd5, 4.Nc3, 5.Nf3 and 6.Bd3, and 7.Bxf5 Nxf5 8.O-O brought you into a normal, level position. Black's 10...Qc7?? was a blunder, and 10...Bb4 was the better move.
You passed up 11.Nxd5 and 12.Nxd5, which grabbed the d5 pawn, and played 11.b3?? and 12.Bb2?? instead. Black also missed 11...O-O, so your position stayed fine.

A long maneuvering phase followed with 13.a3, 14.b4 and 15.b5. Then 17.Ne5 set a trap, and Black's 17...f6?? walked into it. 18.Nf7! forked the rooks on d8 and h8. Black took 18...Rdf8 19.Nxh8 Rxh8, and you were ahead.
20.Rxe6 added material, 21.Nxd5?! was fine, and 22.Qxh5 kept control. 23...Re8?? walked into a pin along the e-file, and 24.Qxe8+ was a back rank finish. A good attack.

review.turning_point: 18.Nf7 forked two rooks and decided the game.
review.focus: At 11.b3 and 12.Bb2 you skipped 11.Nxd5; look for captures before quiet moves.

review.headline: A winning attack that swung back and forth, then lost on the clock in a won position

sections.text: This Vienna Game started quietly. You met 4.Bc4 with 4...Be6 and 5...Be7, which is solid, though 7...Nbd7 and 8...a5 gave White time to castle long and build up the center with 10.d4. Nothing was decided yet, and the position was roughly level.

Then White blundered with 12.Bd3, and you found the right answer. 12...e4! is a fork of the bishop on d3 and the knight on f3, and the evaluation jumped past +3. The simplifications that followed kept your edge intact.

You gave some of it back. 15...Qb6 was a mistake (15...Nf6 was the engine's choice), and 16...g6 was a real blunder that threw away almost the whole advantage. White's 16.h4 and 17.Ne5 were both inaccurate, and you punished 17.Ne5 with 17...Nf6!. After 18.Nd7 and 18...Nxe4 you were winning again.

The next big slip came at 31...Bf2, when 31...Rxc3+ was far stronger, and 32...Kg8 and 33...h5 let White back into the game. You still promoted with 40...h1=Q and reached +8, but the game ended when your clock ran out at move 44 in a completely winning position.

review.turning_point: 12...e4! answered the blunder 12.Bd3 with a fork and turned a level game into a clearly better one.
review.focus: Time and consolidation: after 31...Bf2 the win was nearly thrown away, and you later lost on time at move 44. Once you are far ahead, trade pieces quickly and play simple moves to save clock.

review.headline: A Center Game where your opponent's greedy bishop trade handed you a big edge and you finished with a mating attack

sections.text: In this Center Game you took the pawn with 2...exd4 and met 3.Qxd4 Nc6 by developing sensibly. After 7.Nd5 Nxd5 White played 8.Bg5, which let you start winning space and pieces.

The key moment was 9.Bxe7. White grabbed a bishop-for-knight trade but it was a blunder, and you showed good judgment with 9...Ndxe7!, recapturing so that your structure stayed healthy. After 10.Bb5 Bd7 11.Bxc6 Bxc6 12.O-O Bxe4 you had a big lead.

You made some slips on the way. 14...Nd5 allowed 15.Qxd5, and 17...h6 and 19...f5 each gave back a chunk of your advantage. White returned the favor with 17.h3 and especially 20.gxf5, so you were again clearly better.
From there you simplified calmly with 24...Rxd4 and 25...Rxe8, then brought the queen to the king. The finish came with 35.Qxg8+ Kxg8 36.Kg1 Qh2#, a clean mate.

review.turning_point: 9...Ndxe7! punished White's trade on e7 and left you with a large lead that held for the rest of the game.
review.focus: Check what your pieces are protecting before moving them. At 14...Nd5 the engine preferred 14...d5, because the knight move left a piece hanging to 15.Qxd5.

review.headline: A short Exchange French where a greedy pawn grab on move 9 nearly cost you a big edge

sections.text: You went into the Exchange French with 3.exd5 exd5 and developed naturally with 4.Nc3, 5.Nf3, 6.Bd3 and 7.O-O. Your opponent started to drift with 5...f6 and 6...b5, which weakened the kingside and the long diagonal.

You had a strong position by the time you played 8.Re1+, with the evaluation around +3. Then came the one real mistake: 9.Bxb5+. It picked up a pawn but gave back almost all of your advantage, because the bishop could be hit. The engine suggested 9.a4, keeping everything protected and the pressure on.

Luckily your opponent answered with 9...c6 rather than 9...axb5, and you got the chance to repair things with 10.Bd3!. That retreat kept the bishop safe and restored the big advantage. Your opponent resigned a moment later.

review.turning_point: 9.Bxb5+ swung the evaluation toward your opponent, but 9...c6 returned it and 10.Bd3! put you back in charge.
review.focus: Before you grab a pawn, check whether the capturing piece will be attacked. At 9.Bxb5+ the quiet 9.a4 kept a clear plus without any risk.

review.headline: A Scotch queen trade where you built a big edge, gave it away, and won only because your opponent ran out of time

sections.text: After 4.dxe5 Nxe5 5.Nxe5 dxe5 6.Qxd8+ Kxd8 the queens came off early and left your opponent's king stuck in the center. You developed with 7.Bc4, 8.O-O and 9.Rd1+, a very natural way to use that.

Your opponent's 9...Bd7 was a blunder that put the bishop in the line of your rook on d1. The engine wanted 10.Be6, while your 10.Nd2 let it off the hook, and 10...f5 gave you a second chance. You then played 11.Nb3, a discovered attack that opened the d-file, and 11...fxe4 let you take on d7.

Here you were comfortably ahead, but 14.Ne6 was a blunder (14.Be6 was the move). After 14...Kxd7 you were behind, and 16...Be7 and 17.Be3 let the advantage change hands again. Later errors such as 19.Bxd4 and 28.g3 made it worse.
You were still worse when the clock decided it. 29...Kd3 gave you counter-chances, and 30.Bxg6! made use of them. Your opponent ran out of time at move 32.

review.turning_point: 14.Ne6 threw away a won position, and you were the one defending from then on.
review.focus: Look for the move that keeps your advantage safe before going for another capture. At 14.Ne6 the quiet 14.Be6 kept everything protected, and at 10.Nd2 the same went for 10.Be6.

review.headline: A wild London-style game where your opponent's pawn storm backfired and you mated on the kingside

sections.text: Your opponent started 1.d4 d5 2.e3 e6 3.f4 Nf6 4.c3 and then lunged forward with 5.g4, a blunder that weakened the king. You answered 4...Ne4, a good outpost, but 5...Bd6 was not the best reply, since the engine saw 5...Qh4+.

You found good ideas after that. 6...h6! was the right reply to 6.g5, and after 7.h4 hxg5 8.fxg5 you took the g-pawn with 8...Nxg5. That was a slip, as 8...Bg3+ was stronger, and 9...f6 also let a tempo go.
Your best moment was 10...e5!, a discovered attack on the queen on g4 by the bishop on c8. After 11.hxg5 Bxg4 12.Rxh8+ you were far ahead on material.
The rest was mostly technique. 17...b6 and 27...Qc4 gave back some of your advantage. But 29.Na1 cost White the game, and you finished with 29...Qd3+, 30...Qxe3+, 31...Nd3+ and 32...Qf2#.

review.turning_point: 10...e5! opened the bishop on c8 against White's queen and led to a huge material gain.
review.focus: Look at checks and forcing replies first. At 5...Bd6 the engine preferred 5...Qh4+, which would have punished 5.g4 immediately.

review.headline: A smooth Stafford Gambit refutation: you took the pawn, kept your head and mated

sections.text: Your opponent chose the Stafford Gambit, but you took on e5 with 3.Nxe5 and handled the early tricks well. 3...Nc6 was a mistake, and you found the right answer with 4.Nxc6! dxc6, which gave you an edge.
The only real slip was 6.Be3. The engine liked 6.Be2, because the bishop on e3 allowed 6...Ng4. Luckily your opponent played it, a blunder, and you answered with 7.Bxc5!.

After 9.Bb4 Nxf2 10.Kxf2 Qf6+ your king was a little exposed, but you kept it safe with 11.Bf3 and 12.Bc3, and you stayed up a lot of material. 13.d4 and 14.Re1 started to bring the rest of your pieces in.
17.Bg4 was a small inaccuracy that offered a trade you did not need, but the evaluation stayed above +4. You finished cleanly with 18.Qxg4 and 19.Qxg7#.

review.turning_point: 7.Bxc5! took the bishop after the blunder 6...Ng4 and left you with a lasting material lead.
review.focus: Develop the bishop to a square where it can't be attacked. At 6.Be3 the engine preferred 6.Be2, which would have kept everything under control.

review.headline: A quick, sharp win as Black where one greedy capture by your opponent lost everything

sections.text: This was a Bishop's Opening where you played 2...d6 and 3...c6. That was your only inaccuracy, because the engine liked 3...exd4, and after 4.dxe5 Qh4 5.Qf3 d5 you were a bit worse for a moment.
Your opponent then took on d5 with 6.exd5, a blunder, and you saw straight away that the bishop on c4 was loose. 6...Qxc4! won it, and the evaluation went from -1.3 to +2.5.
After that you simply kept making useful moves. 9...Nd4 and 10...Nxc2+ drove the white king out, and 11...Nxe3 took the queen. White's pieces were scattered, and you were up a huge amount.
You kept the initiative with 12...Nxc4+, 14...Bf5+ and 15...Na5+, and your accuracy of 95.9 shows how clean the rest was. White resigned after 18...Nxd2+.

review.turning_point: 6...Qxc4! punished 6.exd5 and turned a slightly worse position into a winning one.
review.focus: Your opening move 3...c6 was the one slip; the engine preferred 3...exd4. Capturing in the center keeps your pieces active.

review.headline: A Pirc where you got a slightly awkward opening and then won with a kingside attack

sections.text: Your opening was a bit imprecise. 4.Be3 and 5.Ne2 both lost a little, and the engine preferred 4.c3 and 5.d5. After 5...exd4 6.Nxd4 Nxd4 7.Bxd4 the position was roughly level, which was fine.

You played sensibly with 8.O-O, 9.Re1 and 10.Nd2, though 11.Be3 was another small inaccuracy. Your reward came when Black played 14...Bh4, a blunder that let you start an attack with 15.Qh5 Bxg3 16.Qxh7+.
Black then went wrong again with 17...Nxe5, and you found 18.Qh8+!, a skewer: the king on f8 has to move and the rook on e8 falls. After 18...Ke7 19.Rxe5+ Kd7 20.Rxe8 you were far ahead.
The rest was clean technique. 21.Qxg7, 25.Bf5 and 26.Qe5+ kept the attack alive, and the game finished with 28.Qxe7+.

review.turning_point: 18.Qh8+! was a skewer that won the rook after 17...Nxe5, and the position was decided.
review.focus: Work on your opening setup. At 4.Be3 the engine liked 4.c3, which supports the center and keeps the bishop safe from being hit.

review.headline: A Damiano Defense where you were winning early, then let the attack slip away

sections.text: Your opponent chose the Damiano with 2...f6, and you punished it right away: 3.Nxe5 fxe5 4.Qh5+ Ke7 5.Qxe5+ Kf7 6.Bc4+ d5 7.Bxd5+ Kg6. The black king was running around in the open, and you were clearly ahead.
Then came 8.d4, a blunder. The engine saw 8.Qg3+ instead, which kept the attack going while the black king had no shelter. After 8...h6 and 9.Qg3+ the advantage had gone from over +3 to just over +1.
10.Bf4 was another mistake, since 10.Be3 was safer. 11.Bxc7 won a pawn but the position was now balanced, and 12.O-O Na6 was fine for Black.
13.Qf4 was the decisive blunder, because 13...Nxc7 took the bishop on c7. 14.e5 then gave away yet another piece. You resigned after 14...Nfxd5.

review.turning_point: 8.d4 allowed Black to defend, when 8.Qg3+ would have kept your attack going.
review.focus: When the king is exposed, keep checking and attacking. At 8.d4 the forcing 8.Qg3+ was better than a quiet developing move.

review.headline: You refuted a bishop sacrifice, then missed a defensive move and ran into a forced mate

sections.text: In this Petrov, 3.Bc4 Nxe4 was fine, and White went for 4.Bxf7+, a blunder. You took with 4...Kxf7!, the right idea, and after 5.O-O you were clearly better.
Your next moves were a little loose. 5...Bd6 was slightly inaccurate, and the king walk after 7.Ng5+ Kg8 8.Qf3 Be7 9.Nc3 g6 let White build threats. 9...g6 was another small slip.
10...Nxd5 was the blunder. The engine preferred 10...Kg7, which would have kept your large advantage. After 11.Qxd5+ Kg7 12.Qf7+ Kh6 White had a forced mating attack, and it was over soon after.

review.turning_point: 10...Nxd5 allowed a forced mate where 10...Kg7 would have kept your lead.
review.focus: After you win material, check every forcing move before capturing. At 10...Nxd5 the knight capture opened the way for 11.Qxd5+, and 10...Kg7 was the safer move.

review.headline: A Wayward Queen game where your pawn storm broke through and you delivered mate

sections.text: White opened with 2.Qh5 and you handled it calmly: 2...d6, 3...g6, 4...Nf6 and 5...Bg7. Your opponent kept moving the queen, while you developed with 6...O-O and 7...h6.
8...Be6 was a mistake, since 8...c6 was better, and 9.Bxe6 fxe6 made your pawns messy. Luckily 10.Na3 was a slip, and you found 10...g5!, an excellent pawn break that began a kingside attack.
You kept pressing with 15.Bh6 Bxh6 16.Qxh6+, and 19.fxg4 Qxg4 put your queen on the open file. Then 23...Nxg3! was a powerful shot that opened things up.
24.Nxe6 was a blunder by White. You had a forced mate with 24...Nxe4+ 25.Kh1 Qg2#, but you chose 24...Ne2+, a discovered check. It still won, because 25.Kh1 allowed 25...Qg2#.

review.turning_point: 10...g5! started a kingside pawn storm that White never managed to stop.
review.focus: Look for the forcing line to the end. At 24...Ne2+ the engine found a mate with 24...Nxe4+ 25.Kh1 Qg2#, and you should always check all checks first.

review.headline: A sharp game where White's bishop sacrifice failed, but a few slips let the attack through

sections.text: You played a standard Queen's Pawn setup with 1...d5, 2...e6, 3...Nf6 and 5...O-O. Then 9...Nxe5 was a small slip, but 10.fxe5 Nd7 was fine and the position stayed balanced.
White went for 11.Bxh7+, a blunder, and you were right to take with 11...Kxh7!. After 12.Qh5+ Kg8 13.Nf3 you were well ahead.
Then the slips started. 13...g6 was a mistake (13...f5 was the idea), and 14...Re8 was a blunder, as 14...Qe8 was necessary. White's 15.h4 was inaccurate, but 15...c5 did not take advantage.
17...Kh7 was the final blunder, since 17...Ba6 was needed. After 18.hxg6+ fxg6 19.Qf7+ you were lost and resigned.

review.turning_point: 13...g6 and 14...Re8 gave away a winning advantage after you had won material.
review.focus: Keep your king covered when you have an advantage. At 14...Re8 the engine wanted 14...Qe8, and at 17...Kh7 it wanted 17...Ba6.

review.headline: A Petrov Italian where an early bishop trade cost you a pawn and White's attack kept growing

sections.text: You started with 1...e5 and 2...Nf6 and then played 3...d6, a slightly odd move. After 4.Ng5 the key mistake was 4...Be6. The engine preferred 4...d5, because 5.Bxe6 fxe6 6.Nxe6 left you a pawn down.

review.turning_point: 4...Be6 gave White an early lead and you were fighting uphill from there.
review.focus: Don't trade your bishop for nothing in the opening. At 4...Be6 the engine preferred 4...d5, which challenges the center and avoids losing a pawn.

review.headline: An Owen Defense where you got a good position, tangled yourself up, and lost a big rook

sections.text: You played the main line with 1.e4 b6 2.d4 Bb7 3.Bd3 and then gained space with 4.d5. After 7.Nxd5 Bxd5 8.exd5 you had a good position with a nice center.

review.focus: When a queen checks you, look at every capture before moving the king. At 20.Kg3 the engine found 20.Qxd4, taking the queen that had just given check.

review.headline: A messy Scandinavian where you won a huge advantage, nearly lost it, and then won on time

sections.text: In this Scandinavian you played 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 and developed solidly with 6.Nf3 and 7.h3. Black lost the thread with 7...Qh5. The engine preferred 7...Bxf3 8.Qxf3, but 8.Be3 let Black get back in with 8...Ne5.

review.focus: Keep your clock in mind in a winning endgame. At 50.d5 you were low on time, and 50.b4 was the safe move.

White's 5.g3? and 7.Nc3? were not accurate either, but 8...h5?! and 9...Ne5?! weakened your king and left you worse (-3.4).
After 10.Nxe5 Qxe5 11.e4 h4 12.Bf4 Qf6?! 13.dxe6 the engine wanted you to play 13...Qxe6, but 13...h3?? allowed a forced mate.
14.Bf3?? missed 14.Qxd7#, the mate on the spot, but 14...g5?? let it come anyway, and 15.Qxd7# ended the game.

review.turning_point: 13...h3?? ignored the threat on d7 after 13.dxe6; the engine's 13...Qxe6 would have kept you in the game.
review.focus: 6...Qc7? and 7...a6? skipped the simple 6...cxd4 and 7...cxd4 exchanges. Take the central trade when you can, and keep the d7 square covered.

review.headline: A wild Goldsmith Defense where you survived the opening and won with a passed a-pawn

sections.text: 1...h5?! 2...h4 and 3...g5?! was a very aggressive start that didn't work; after 5.Bxg5 and 6.Bxh4 you were at -3.2, and 6...Bxd4? made it worse.
Then White blundered with 10.Bxg8??, and 10...Rxe4+! forked the king and the queen on d4. After 11.Qxe4 fxe4 you had traded a rook for a queen, and the evaluation flipped to near equal.

12.Bf7+?? was a mistake by White, but 12...Ke7? gave back part of it. You were then clearly better (+3.2), but 14...Bf5??, 15...Nd7?? and 16...Nf6?? let it slip to about equal; the engine's 15...Kxf7 simply took the loose bishop.
You came back with 21...Qf6! and 22...Qxe7!, then 25...Rb8! and the rook grabbing pawns on b2, a2 and c2. The a-pawn ran home with 34...a1=Q and White resigned.

review.turning_point: 10.Bxg8?? allowed 10...Rxe4+!, which swung the evaluation from -5.7 to about equal.
review.focus: On 15...Nd7?? the engine's 15...Kxf7 simply took a loose bishop. Always check what the opponent's last move left undefended before you develop.

review.headline: An Italian where an unforced error nearly cost you the game before your opponent returned the favor

sections.text: You played the Italian with 3.Bc4 and 4.d4, then 5.O-O. After 5...exd4 6.Nxd4 Nxd4 7.Qxd4 you had a small edge. 8.Qd5 and 9.Qa5 chased the queen around, and 11.Bxe6 was a sensible trade.
12.e5?! was a bit loose, but your opponent replied 12...d5 and 14...d4. Then 15...b6? was a mistake (the engine's 15...Qd8 was better), putting you at +3.4.
16.Nd6+?? was a blunder: the knight just hung to the queen, and the engine's 16.Qa4 was needed. You were saved when your opponent replied 16...Kd8??, not 16...Qxd6.
17...dxe3?? was another mistake by your opponent, and 18.Rad1 and 19.Nf5+ brought a winning attack. Your opponent resigned.

review.turning_point: 16...Kd8?? was a lucky escape for you; the engine's 16...Qxd6 was the stronger reply.
review.focus: On 16.Nd6+?? you gave a check without seeing that the queen could just take the knight; the engine's 16.Qa4 kept your edge. Before any check, look at which pieces can capture it.

review.headline: A chaotic Three Knights Petrov where you won with mate despite two missed mates

sections.text: You developed solidly with 4...Bg4, 5...Bh5, 6...Bg6, 7...Nbd7 and 8...Be7. White castled long and pushed pawns with 10.O-O-O, 11.a3?? and 12.h4?, but your 10...a5? and 11...a4? gave back the edge.
13...Qb6?? was a blunder (the engine's 13...h5 was safer), and 14.h5 b4 15.Nxa4?? let you hit back with 15...Rxa4!, a good reply. But 16...bxa3?? allowed 17.gxf7+ (the engine's 16...fxg6).

21.Kc2?? was a big mistake by White, giving you a forced win, but 21...Nxa4?? missed 21...Qb2#, an immediate mate. Later 29...Nxf2?? also missed the forced mate in the engine's line starting 29...Qb2+.
You stayed accurate when it counted: 25...Rb8!, 26...Qxb3+! and 28...Nxd3+! kept the pressure on, and 30.Qf3?? allowed 30...Qb1+ and 32...Qd3# for the win.

review.turning_point: 21.Kc2?? gave you a forced mate with 21...Qb2#, and you missed it, though 32...Qd3# finally ended it.
review.focus: On 21...Nxa4?? you missed 21...Qb2#, an immediate mate. Before making any capture, scan all the checks first, because forcing moves can finish the game.

review.headline: A Sicilian win where you let an early edge fade, then punished 13...Nh5 and finished with a queen attack

sections.text: You met the open Sicilian in classical fashion with 3.d4, 4.Nxd4, 5.Nc3 and 6.Bc4. After 6...e5 the position was already comfortable for you at +0.9, and you had a stable, active setup.

The first key moment came when your opponent played 7...Nc6, a real blunder that pushed the evaluation to +2.8 in your favour. You didn't take full advantage: 8.O-O brought it back to +0.3, while the engine's 8.Ng5 d5 9.Nxd5 kept the initiative. Taking a moment to look for forcing moves after an opponent's slip is worth the effort.

You stayed calm after that, trading on f3 and re-routing the queen and bishop. Then 13...Nh5 left that knight stranded, and the evaluation jumped from +0.6 to +6.3. You cashed in with 14.Bxd4 exd4 15.Qxd4, and the queen on d4 also hit g7 with the rook on h8 behind it, which is why 15.Qxd4 pins the pawn. 16.Qxd6 then won another pawn.
The finish was efficient. 17.Qe5+ drove the king to f8, 18.Qxh5 picked up the loose knight, and after 18...g5 you ended it with 19.Qxf7#.

review.turning_point: 13...Nh5 by your opponent, which took the evaluation from +0.6 to +6.3 and left a knight to be collected with 18.Qxh5.
review.focus: 8.O-O: right after 7...Nc6 gave you +2.8, the engine wanted the more forcing 8.Ng5 and your edge slipped to +0.3. When an opponent errs, check checks, captures and threats before choosing a quiet developing move.

review.headline: A wild Philidor Exchange where you were pushed back for a long time, then won through a counterattack and your opponent's blunders

sections.text: The opening followed 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5.Nxc6 bxc6, and white's pieces came out smoothly with 7.Bd3, 8.Be3, 9.Qf3 and 10.Bc4. By 11...a5 you were down about 2.3 and under pressure.

White gave some of that back with 12.Nd5? and 13.Nxf6+?, but 13...gxf6 and especially 14...Qc8 (the engine preferred 14...Qe7) put you in real trouble. After 15.Qxf6 and 16.Qxh8 white was winning, and by 17...Ke7 you stood around -7.5.

Credit to you for 18...Bxh6!, the best reply to 18.Rd2?. Moving the bishop off f8 opened the eighth rank so your rook on b8 attacked the queen on h8, which makes 18...Bxh6 a discovered attack. White answered with 19.Qc3??, missing the better 19.Qxb8, and after 19...Bxd2+ 20.Qxd2 you were back in the game.
It stayed messy: 21...d5?? and 22...Kd6?? gave chances back, but white kept going wrong too. 24.Bb5+?? allowed 24...Rxb5!, which won a piece, and 25...Bxg2, 27...Qxf3 and 29...Qxc2# finished the job.

review.turning_point: 18...Bxh6! followed by 19.Qc3?? changed the game from about -4.4 to -0.3, and 24.Bb5+?? later put you clearly ahead.
review.focus: 21...d5: with your king exposed in the centre you needed to be careful about checks. The engine preferred 21...Kd7, and 22...Kd6 was another move that walked into queen checks, where 22...Kf8 was safer. Before each king move, list white's possible checks.

review.headline: A chaotic King's Gambit Declined where both sides kept swapping the lead, and your counterattack won in the end

sections.text: After 2.f4 Nf6?! 3.fxe5 Nxe4, white's 4.d4? gave you an edge, but 4...Qe7?? gave it back; the engine wanted 4...Qh4+. Then 6.Bxe4 dxe4 traded a bishop for your knight, and the position was roughly level.

Your plan with 7...f5, 8...Nc6 and 9...Qb4? was ambitious but loosened things. 10...a5?? was a clear blunder (-3.5), and white followed with 11.Nd5, 13.Nxc7+ and 14.Nxa8, leaving you down six points of material.

You fought back with 14...b4? and white replied poorly: 15.axb4?? and 16.b3?? let you back in. Unfortunately 16...Qa1+?? looked like a skewer of king and rook (the king just stepped away with 17.Kd2), and the engine preferred 16...Na2+. Later 19...Nxe3+ was a good shot, a fork of the king on f1 and the rook on d1.

The real swing came after 20...Ba6+, when white played 21.Ke1?? and your evaluation went from -3.0 to +8.6. You then slipped with 22...Qf1+?? and 24...Bd3+??, and 26...Qxh1?? too, but white still failed to punish you, and 30...Bxe7! finished the game.

review.turning_point: 21.Ke1?? by white, which swung the evaluation from -3.0 to +8.6 in your favour.
review.focus: 22...Qf1+: you were at +6.9 after 21...Qxg2, and this check dropped it to +1.2; the engine preferred 22...Bb4+. When you are winning, compare queen checks with quieter moves that keep your pieces together; 24...Bd3+ and 26...Qxh1 repeated the same pattern.

review.headline: A Queen's Pawn game where you recovered from a bad position with a big queen win, then let a forced mate slip and survived to win on time

sections.text: White chose an unusual setup with 2.f3, 8.f4 and a rook lift via 9.Rf3, 10.Rg3 and 11.Rg5. Your play was reasonable until 11...Ndf6??, where the engine preferred 11...g6. 12.g4 then threw the knight back, and by 14.Rxh5 and 17.Qxg4 you were down five points of material.

You fought on, and white went wrong first with 21.Bxh6??. 21...e4 forked the bishop on d3 and the queen on f3, though the engine liked 21...Rxh6 even more. White answered with 22.Bxe4?? and 23.Qxe4??, and 23...Bxe4! won the queen, swinging material from -5 to +4.

From there you were up around seven points. 24...Rxh6?! 25.Rxh6 Qxh6 and the tidy 27.Ndxe4 kept you in control. 38...Rh8?? let a lot of the advantage go (engine: 38...Rg4+), but 40...Rh4+! was a strong skewer of king and knight, and 41...Qxe4 kept you clearly ahead.

Then came the big miss: 42...Qg4+?? gave up a forced win; the engine had 42...Qf4+ 43.Kg6 Qh6#. After 43.Rxg4 you were down a queen's worth and the position was lost for a long time, but the game ended on time in your favour.

review.turning_point: 23...Bxe4!, which won the queen after 23.Qxe4?? and moved you from lost to completely winning.
review.focus: 42...Qg4+: you had a forced mate with 42...Qf4+ 43.Kg6 Qh6#. When you are far ahead, scan every check and forcing move first; this one lost your queen to 43.Rxg4.

review.headline: A Scandinavian where the early queen trade left your king stuck, and a hopeful knight sacrifice at the end cost the game

sections.text: After 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.d4 e5, 4.dxe5?! looked tempting, since opening the d-file made a discovered attack on the queen. But 4...Qxd1+ 5.Kxd1 simply traded queens and left your king in the middle, which is where the early trouble started.
6.Bc4?! eyed the f7 pawn, but 6...Nxe5 and 7...Bd7 got black comfortable quickly. After 8.Nf3 Nxf3 9.gxf3 your structure was damaged and black castled long at once with 9...O-O-O.

11.Bxf7 won a pawn, but 11...Bc5 and 12.b3?! (-2.9) allowed 12...Bd4 and 13...Bxf2 to win material back. You kept developing sensibly with 14.Bb2, 15.Bc4 and 16.Bd3, and 18.Bxf6 gxf6 made the structure a little worse for black, but it wasn't enough to equalise.
At 21.Nxb5?? you tried to complicate, but 21...Bxb5 just left you a knight for a pawn down. The engine's 21.Nd5 Bh3 22.Nxe3 was the tougher defence.

review.turning_point: 21.Nxb5??, which dropped a knight for a pawn when you were already under pressure at -1.7.
review.focus: 21.Nxb5: when you are a bit worse, resist the desperate sacrifice and keep solid with 21.Nd5. Also revisit 4.dxe5, where trading queens left your king on d1 with no castling.

review.headline: An Owen Defense where 4...f5?! opened your king early and you were always catching up

sections.text: You went for an Owen setup with 1...b6 and 2...Bb7, which is playable though slightly loose at -0.9. White built a calm centre with 2.Nf3, 3.d3 and 4.Nc3.

4...f5?! was the real problem (-1.9). 5.exf5 Nf6 6.fxg6 left you two pawns down, and 7.Ng5 d5?! let white go further. 8.Nf7 attacked your queen and the rook on h8, and 9.Nxh8 won the rook, putting you about seven points behind.

You did fight well to get a knight back with 10...Bxh8, and 11.gxh7 d4 12.Ne4 Nxe4 13.dxe4 Bxe4 won a couple of pawns, so you gave white practical problems. Still, white kept things under control with 14.Bh5+ and 15.Bg4.

The mistake that sealed it was 18...Qf5? (-6.4); the engine preferred 18...Bxc2. After 19.Bg4 you had to trade queens on bad terms with 19...Qxg4, and 20.Qxg4+ left you down a whole queen's worth of material.

review.turning_point: 9.Nxh8, which won a rook for white; combined with the two pawns already gone after 6.fxg6, you were never able to equalise.
review.focus: 4...f5: before opening the position with a pawn push in front of your king, finish developing. Pushing 4...f5 allowed 5.exf5 and 6.fxg6 and gave white tempo-gaining captures.

review.headline: A short game where white played too many flank pawn moves, and you resigned in a position the engine liked for you

sections.text: White opened with 2.h4, 3.Qe2 and 4.f3, which are all loosening moves. You answered sensibly with 2...Nf6 and 3...d6, and by 4.f3 you were comfortably ahead at +1.6.

4...Nbd7?! cost a little (+1.6 to +0.6); the engine preferred 4...Nc6. Then 5.b4?? was a blunder from white, and the engine's 5...d5 6.Nc3 d4 7.Nd1 Bxb4 would have used the opened lines to hit the b4 pawn. 5...b6?! kept the edge at +1.4 but didn't punish it.

You carried on with 7.Nc3 c6 and white's 8.g4 weakened the kingside even further. At that point the engine still had you at +1.3, but the game ended with your resignation after only 8 moves, which was premature.

review.turning_point: 5.b4??, which gave you +2.5 and the chance to take over the centre.
review.focus: 5...b6: when white overextends with 5.b4, fight for the centre with a move like 5...d5 rather than a slower pawn move; and think carefully before resigning, as the engine had you better at the end.

review.headline: A Philidor where an early bishop trade gave you a small edge, but 13.Qb5?? and 20.Rfe1?? decided the game

sections.text: You played the Italian approach with 3.Bc4 and 4.Bb3, then 5.d4 exd4 6.Nxd4 Nxd4 7.Qxd4. After 8.e5?! dxe5 9.Qxe5 Bb4+ 10.c3 Bd6 11.Qe2 O-O the position was balanced.

12.Bxe6 won a bishop for the moment, and the engine's 13.Bxf7+ Kxf7 14.Be3 would have kept you comfortable. Instead 13.Qb5?? left the bishop on e6 hanging, and 13...Rxe6+ took it with check, leaving you at -4.4.
You kept fighting. 15.Qxb7 won a pawn and when your opponent played 17...Rxe3?, you found the best reply with 18.Na3!, which brought you back to about -0.5 and gave real chances.
But 20.Rfe1?? (-0.3 to -4.6) was the decisive error; the engine's 20.Qf3 kept you safe. 20...Qc5+ 21.Kh1 Ng4 22.Rf1 Nf2+ forced the rook for a knight, and 25...Qxe1# ended it.

review.turning_point: 13.Qb5??, which left the bishop to be captured and dropped the evaluation from +0.2 to -4.4.
review.focus: 13.Qb5: after 12.Bxe6 Re8, your bishop was attacked. Always ask what your opponent's last move attacks before playing; 13.Bxf7+ kept everything defended.

review.headline: A four-move knockout where your opponent gave away a pawn and a knight

sections.text: White tried a Tennison Gambit with 2.Nf3?, and the engine rates it a blunder because the expected gambit does not compensate for the pawn. You correctly took it with 2...dxe4!, going a pawn up.
3.Ng5 aimed at the pawn on e4 and made threats, and here you played 3...f5?, which weakened your king and slipped from +0.9 to -0.3. The engine's 3...Bf5 4.Nc3 held the pawn more safely.
White then blundered with 4.Nxe4??, taking the pawn but walking into 4...fxe4!, which won the knight for a pawn, and white resigned.

review.turning_point: 4.Nxe4??, which let you win a knight for a pawn with 4...fxe4!.
review.focus: 3...f5: after the pawn grab, prefer a developing move like 3...Bf5, which keeps your king safe, rather than pushing the f-pawn.

review.headline: An attacking Two Knights game where your sacrifices worked, until 10.Qxc6+?? gave your queen away

sections.text: You went for the sharp line with 4.Ng5 d5 5.exd5, and after 5...Nxd5? you struck at once with 6.Nxf7!, a fork of the queen on d8 and the rook on h8. 6...Kxf7 7.Qf3+ forced the king into the open.
7...Qf6? (the engine preferred 7...Ke6) made it worse for black, and you found 8.Bxd5+!, then 9.Bxc6+, which put you well ahead. After 9...bxc6 you stood at +2.6.
Then came 10.Qxc6+??. It looked forcing, but the queen on f6 simply took it with 10...Qxc6, and your evaluation fell from +2.6 to -7.4. The engine's 10.Qh5+ Kd8 11.Nc3 Bd6 kept you comfortable.
After that you were a queen down. 11.O-O Qxc2 and 12.Re1 Bd6 left you little hope, and 15.dxe5 Qxg2# was the end.

review.turning_point: 10.Qxc6+??, where the queen walked into a capture by the queen on f6.
