review.focus: 10.Qxc6+: before capturing with check, ask which black pieces defend that square. The queen on f6 covered c6, so 10.Qh5+ was needed.

review.headline: A near-perfect Petrov grind where you punished 12.Na3? and converted a long endgame to checkmate

sections.text: A textbook Petrov: 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4, followed by 5.Qe2 Qe7 6.d3 Nf6 and 7.Qxe7+ Bxe7. After 8.Bg5 Be6 9.Bxf6 Bxf6 10.d4 c5 you were solid and equal.

12.Na3? gave you an edge, and you found the best reply with 12...cxd4!. After 13.Nxd4 Nxd4 14.cxd4 Bxd4 you were a pawn up. 15...Bc5?! was slightly inaccurate, but 16...Bxa3 17.bxa3? Bxc4 won a piece and the game was effectively over.

You then went after white's king: 20...Re2, 21...Bxa2+ and 23...Ra2+ kept the pressure on. At 26...Ra1+ you chose a skewer of king and rook that carried back rank ideas, but the engine had a forced mate with 26...Be4 instead. You still won comfortably.

In the endgame you picked up pieces, pushed the f-pawn and promoted with 42...f1=R?!. The engine would have taken a queen with 42...f1=Q, but it made no difference. The long king walk ended with 72...Ra1#.

review.turning_point: 12...cxd4! after 12.Na3? began your edge, and 16...Bxa3 17.bxa3? Bxc4 won the piece that decided it.
review.focus: 26...Ra1+: with a forced mate available, 26...Be4 was the cleaner route. Before playing a forcing check, see if a quieter move wins faster. 15...Bc5 is the same theme; 15...Bxf2 was stronger.

review.headline: A Philidor where early looseness with 3...Bg4 and 10...O-O-O left you a step behind, ending in a tactic on e5

sections.text: After 2...d6 3.Nc3 Bg4?! (a pin on the knight) 4.Be2 Nf6 5.d3 Qd7 6.O-O Nc6, you developed in a normal way. 7.Nd5 Nxd5 8.exd5 Ne7 9.c4 c5 was fine, but you were already a bit worse at -0.8.
10...O-O-O? was the first real mistake (-0.6 to -2.1); the engine preferred 10...Nf5 11.b4. After 11.b4 b6?! 12.bxc5 dxc5 your king and queenside pawns were exposed.

13.Nxe5 attacked the bishop on g4 and the queen on d7. You answered 13...Qf5?, which lost the bishop to 14.Bxg4 and you resigned. The engine's 13...Bxe2 14.Qxe2 Qf5 forks the queen on d1 and the rook on f1 first, and was far better.

review.turning_point: 13...Qf5?, which allowed 14.Bxg4 and lost a bishop.
review.focus: 13...Qf5: with the bishop attacked twice, trade it off with 13...Bxe2 first. Before moving a queen, always check which of your pieces become undefended.

review.headline: A McConnell game where you got an early advantage, gave it up with 6.Nc3??, and eventually lost a bishop

sections.text: Black's 2...Qf6? brought the queen out early, and you found 3.Nc3! to keep the initiative. After 3...Bc5 4.Nd5 Qd8 5.d4 you were already at +2.1, and 5...c6? was another black error (+4.2).

6.Nc3?? was the missed chance. The engine's 6.dxc5 cxd5 7.Qxd5 won a piece and left you far ahead; the retreat brought you back to +1.2. After 6...exd4 7.Nxd4 Qf6 8.Be3 d6 you were fine but no longer winning.

9.Bc4?! Qe5 10.Qf3? (the engine preferred 10.Qd2) and 11.Nf5? uncovered the bishop on c5 against your bishop on e3. After 11...Bxe3? 12.Qxe3?, the engine's 12.Nxe3 was better. 12...Bxf5 13.exf5 Qxe3+ 14.fxe3 left you with doubled pawns.
Then 16.Kd2?? lost a piece: after 15...Ne3, 16...Nxc4+ won the bishop on c4 and the game was over. 16.Bb3 was the engine's choice.

review.turning_point: 6.Nc3??, where retreating the knight gave up the chance to win a piece with 6.dxc5.
review.focus: 6.Nc3: when your opponent attacks a piece, look for a capture or counter-capture that wins material first; 6.dxc5 cxd5 7.Qxd5 was far stronger than retreating.

review.headline: A Petrov where white's kingside rush put you under pressure, until 23.f4?? let your knight take over

sections.text: After 4.Bc4 Bg4 5.d3 Be7 6.h3 Bh5 7.g4 Bg6, white went for a kingside attack with 8.Be3, 9.Qe2 and 10.O-O-O. Your queenside counterplay with 10...Qa5 11.Kb1 b5 12.Bb3 b4 gave you real play.

13...O-O?! (-2.2) castled into the pawn storm, and 14.Nh4 Qb5 15.Nxg6 hxg6 16.h4 c5?! and 17.h5 pushed you back. 17...Nb6? was a mistake (-5.6; the engine liked 17...g5), but white's 18.c4?? gave it back.
21.g5 Nh5?! and 22.Rdf1? continued the pressure. 22...Qd7? left the knight on h5 vulnerable to 23.Rxh5, which the engine preferred over 22...Qd7. White didn't take it.

23.f4?? exf4! changed everything. After 24.Bd2?? Ng3! forked the queen on e2 and the rooks on f1 and h1, 25.Qh2 Nxh1 won a rook, and 26...Ng3! and 27...Nxf1 added more. You finished with 28...bxc5, 29...Bxg5 and 30...Rxf4.

review.turning_point: 23.f4??, answered by 23...exf4! and 24...Ng3!, which turned a bad position into a winning one.
review.focus: 22...Qd7: with your knight hanging on h5 to 23.Rxh5, the engine preferred 22...Kf7. Always look at which of your pieces are loose after your last move.

review.headline: A Petrov where you recovered from 16...Nxg4?? thanks to white's passive 18.Kh2?? and 19.Rh1??, and finished with mate

sections.text: 3.Bd3 d6?! was a slightly unusual choice but you stayed solid. White played 4.O-O, 5.h3 and 6.Re1, and you got the bishop pair out with 5...Bh5 and 6...Be7. After 7...O-O you were comfortable.
On the queenside, 8...c6, 9...b5, 10...a5 and 11...a4 gained space. 13.d4 and 14.Bg5 h6 15.Bxf6 Nxf6 were routine, and 16.g4 was white's idea.
16...Nxg4?? was the mistake (+0.6 to -1.4); the engine preferred 16...Bg6. After 17.hxg4 Bxg4 you were a point down. But white replied with 18.Kh2?? and you found 18...Kh8!, the best reply.
19.Rh1?? was another error, and you played 19...f5!. 20.exf5 Rxf5 21.Kg2 Bxf3+ 22.Qxf3 Rxf3 won the queen, and the rest was smooth, with 25...e4, 28...dxe4, 29...Rxf3+ and 32...Qf3# at the end.

review.turning_point: 19.Rh1?? answered by 19...f5!, which turned a roughly equal position into +4.3.
review.focus: 16...Nxg4: before sacrificing a knight on g4, check white's recapture and whether you get enough. 16...Bg6 kept the bishop and was stronger.

review.headline: An Italian where 4...f6?? gave you a huge edge, and the game was won despite several queen adventures

sections.text: 3...h6 4.d4 f6?? was a serious blunder. You took it with 5.dxe5?! fxe5 6.Nxe5, and after 6...Nxe5 7.Qh5+ g6 8.Qxe5+ Qe7 you won a pawn.
9.Qxh8 won the rook, and although 9...Qxe4+ 10.Be3?! Qxc4 took a bishop back, you remained well ahead at +3. 11.Qe5+ Be7 12.Nc3?! d6 kept things under control.
13.Qh8?? was a blunder (+3.0 to -1.7); your queen in the corner nearly got trapped, and the engine suggested 13.Qd5. Black missed it, though, and your 14.O-O-O?! and 15.Qg7? were again loose.

You finished well: 16.Qxg6! and 17.Qxe8+! (a back rank threat with the king on c8) won a rook, and 20.Qxg8! added more. 19.c3?? had been a slip (the engine preferred 19.Qxe6+), but you were winning by so much that black resigned.

review.turning_point: 4...f6?? gave you a huge edge, and 16.Qxg6! then won more material.
review.focus: 13.Qh8: the corner queen grab nearly got you into trouble. The engine's 13.Qd5 offered a queen trade and kept you winning. Watch for squares where your queen can be trapped.

review.headline: An Italian where 11.Bc5?? nearly cost you the game, but 12.Re1! turned it around and you finished with a queen attack

sections.text: 3...h6 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4 Nxd4 6.Qxd4 Qf6 7.Qd1?! gave white a slightly worse position, and 9.Be3?! allowed 9...Qh4. After 10.g3 Qxe4 you were down a pawn.
11.Bc5?? was a blunder (+2.1 to -1.9); the engine preferred 11.Nd2. Your opponent replied with 11...Bxc5??, the wrong capture, and the engine's 11...Qxc4 would have won a piece.
12.Re1! was a great reply. It put the rook on the e-file, pinning the queen on e4 against the king on e8, and after 12...Qxe1+ 13.Qxe1+ you had traded queens and regained your pieces.
14.Qe5 was strong, and 14...d6?? allowed 15.Qxg7!. You kept going with 16.Qxf7+, 17.Nc3 and 19.Qxf6, and the finish was neat: 20.Qxh8+, 21.Qxa8 and 22.Qe8#.

review.turning_point: 12.Re1!, which pinned the queen on e4 and flipped the game after your opponent's 11...Bxc5??.
review.focus: 11.Bc5: before moving a piece forward, check if it can be captured with tempo. 11.Nd2 kept your bishop on c4 safe; instead 11.Bc5 gave black a free capture.

review.headline: A Philidor-style game against 1.Nf3 where you survived 22...Rxd2?? and 26...Rd4??, thanks to 27.f3??, and won on time

sections.text: After 1.Nf3 e5? (-1.5) your opponent played 2.e4?, and you settled into a Philidor structure with 2...d6, 3...Nf6 and 4...Bg4. 7.b4 Nb6, 8.a4 c6 and 9.a5 Nbd7 were harmless, and the game was balanced.
You opened the centre with 10...d5, 11...dxe4 and 12...b6. 14.Rxa8 Qxa8 15.cxb6 Nxb6 16.Bb2 Qa2 was active, and 17.Bxe5 Bxb4 followed by 18...Bxd2 and 19...Bxe2 won back material cleanly.
22...Rxd2?? was a blunder (-0.4 to -3.6). After 22.Bxf6 the engine liked 22...gxf6. 25.Be7?? helped, but then 26...Rd4?? (engine: 26...Rc2) put you in trouble again.
You were rescued by 27.f3??, because 27...Rxb4! took the bishop for free. After 28.Qh6 Rb2 and 33...Qc5+ you were winning, and 34...Qxg5+ won the queen. The game ended on time in your favour.

review.turning_point: 27.f3??, which lost a bishop to 27...Rxb4! and flipped the evaluation from -3.8 to +4.8 in your favour.
review.focus: 26...Rd4: instead of attacking the bishop, the engine preferred 26...Rc2. Look at whether your opponent has a strong queen check before making an active-looking rook move.

review.headline: A queen trapped by one accurate reply, then a long cleanup

sections.text: You met Black's early queen adventures calmly. After 3...Qxd5 the queen kept hopping (4...Qf5, 5...Qf6) while you simply developed with 4.Nc3, 5.Bd3 and 6.Nf3. That is exactly how to punish a queen that comes out too soon, and you were already comfortably better.

Then Black tried 6...Bb4??, which pinned your knight on c3 to your king. It looks scary, but you found 7.Bg5!, attacking the queen. After the exchanges you won the queen for a bishop and the evaluation jumped to around +6. Spotting that the pin did not actually stop your move is the whole game.

From there you kept making threats. 14.Bxh7+ won a pawn with check, and 16.Nxf7+?! was a little loose, though you were so far ahead that it barely mattered. 22...Rxf2 and 23.Qxg7+ kept your attack rolling and Black's king never found shelter.

The end is where I would look closely. 30.Qg5+ was the one real slip, since 30.Rf1+ was a skewer along the f-file that led to a forced mate. Black resigned anyway, but it is a good habit to run through every check before picking one.

review.turning_point: 6...Bb4?? let you play 7.Bg5!, which attacked the queen and won it for a bishop after the trades.
review.focus: At 30.Qg5+ you had a forced mate starting with 30.Rf1+. When you are winning, list every check and forcing move first; it is the fastest way to finish.

review.headline: A patient Center Game grind, decided by tactics and a lost clock

sections.text: White opened with the Center Game and pulled the queen back with 4.Qd1, so you were comfortable early on. You built a tidy setup with 5...Nf6, 6...Bd7 and 9...O-O, and after 12.Bxd7 Qxd7 the position was equal with a solid structure for you.

With 13...b5?! and 14...b4?! you gained space on the queenside and pushed the knights back. 15.Nd5 a5 kept the grip, and the evaluation moved in your favour to around -1.3 for White. White then drifted: 18.Bd2?? and 19.Ng4?? both made the position worse for them.

Your 19...Nd3?? was the slip, because 19...Nexg4 would have won a piece. Fortunately White replied 20.Nxf6+?, a fork of queen and rook, but you simply recaptured with 20...Bxf6!. After 22...Nf2+ 23.Rxf2 Bxf2 you traded a knight for a rook and were clearly ahead.
White gave up a bishop with 27.Bxg5 fxg5 and your extra material told. You kept the knights away with 28...Bc3 and 30...d5, and White's clock ran out at move 35 with 35...Re1 coming.

review.turning_point: 20...Bxf6! recaptured the knight after 20.Nxf6+, and 22...Nf2+ then won an exchange.
review.focus: At 19...Nd3?? you had 19...Nexg4, which won a piece outright. When the opponent's knight steps up and hangs something, count what each of your captures attacks before choosing a quiet move.

review.headline: A winning gambit position thrown away by a run of blunders

sections.text: Black chose the Blackburne-Kostic gambit with 3...Nd4. After 5.c3?! and 6.Bxd5 you won a pawn, and when Black grabbed with 7...Nxe4? you found 8.Qe2!, which pinned the knight on e4 to the king.
Black's 8...Bf5?? lost a piece to 9.d3!, and after 10.dxe4 and 11.Nxc3 you were a piece up with a big advantage (+5.7). Castling long with 13.O-O-O was natural, and you were close to winning.

Then the slips started. 14.Bg5? gave some of it back, and 16.Na4?? and 17.Rd7?? dropped the evaluation to -3.8. It left your e4 pawn loose, since 17...Qxe4+ would have forked your king and queen. Black missed it, and 18.f3! got you back in the game.

The next moves wasted that rescue. 20.Bc2?? let Black push on. 22.b3?? missed 22.Qxb5, which forks the queen on b4 and the bishop on g5. 23.Nd1?? and finally 29.Rd5?? with a trade that left you down material ended it.
Strong moves like 8.Qe2!, 9.d3! and 24.hxg5! show you can play well. The problem was a lack of care once ahead.

review.turning_point: 22.b3?? ignored 22.Qxb5, which would have forked the queen and bishop and kept your advantage.
review.focus: At 17.Rd7?? you left your e4 pawn loose with the king on b1 and the queen on b4 hitting it. Before every rook raid, check what your opponent can capture with check.

review.headline: A well-judged Petrov that turned into a big attack and a mate

sections.text: You went for 3...d6?! rather than 3...Nxe4, which was a touch passive, but White also drifted with 5.Na3. Your 6...b5 grabbed space and set up the tactic that mattered: White played 7.Bd5??, and you took with 7...Nxd5!, and after 8.exd5 Bxd5 you had won a pawn.

In the middlegame you were a bit hesitant. 10...h6?!, 11...Be6?! and 12...Bd7?! let White regroup, but 13.Nd5? was a mistake and 13...c6! kicked the knight away. After 15.b3 b4 you were gaining space on the queenside with a clear edge.
The decisive moment came with 23.Rf4?. You replied 23...Bxf4!, winning the rook for a bishop after 24.Bxf4 Qxf4. From +3.5 you went to around +6.9, and White had no compensation.
The conversion was clean. 25...e3 cramped White, 29...Nxf3+ shattered the kingside, and the queen and rook finished it with 41...Qg4#.

review.turning_point: 23...Bxf4! answered 23.Rf4 and left you well ahead on material.
review.focus: At 19...O-O?! you had 19...exf3, opening lines when ahead. Castling there let White trade the e-pawn with 20.fxe4. When you are better, open the position.

review.headline: A calm king-side fianchetto, then a clean knight-and-bishop punishment

sections.text: White opened with the Wayward Queen Attack, 2.Qh5, and you answered sensibly with 2...d6 and 3...g6, kicking the queen around. By 7.Bxf6 Qxf6 8.Qxf6 Bxf6 the queens were off and you were comfortable in a structure with a nice bishop pair.

9...Be6?! allowed 10.Bxe6 fxe6 and doubled pawns, but 12...d5 was the right break. White's 13.exd5?? gave you the chance, and 13...e4 was available straight away. You played 13...exd5?!, which was a bit slower.

White then blundered with 14.b5??, and you found 14...e4!, which discovered an attack from the bishop on f6 on the knight on c3. It won big material: after 15.dxe4 Bxc3+ 16.Ke2 Bxa1 you collected a knight and a rook.
You kept the king in the open at the centre under pressure with 18...Re8+, 21...Nxf3+ and 23...Rac8+. White's clock ran out at move 29.

review.turning_point: 14...e4! discovered an attack on the knight on c3 and won a knight and a rook.
review.focus: At 13...exd5?! the stronger 13...e4 immediately was available. Look for the pawn break that uncovers a piece before you recapture.

review.headline: A fine Open Sicilian that ended on the clock

sections.text: You went into the Open Sicilian with 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nxd4 5.Qxd4, and the queen sat well in the centre. Black replied 5...Nf6 and the position was balanced.
The bishop moves were a little slow. 6.Bg5?! h6 7.Bh4? gave Black time, and 6.e5 would have kicked the knight. Even so, Black's 7...b6? was the real mistake, as 7...g5 was needed.
You ended up with a pleasant advantage around +1.4 after 8...Bb7. The game finished when your clock ran out on move 8.
That makes this a time-management game. You were not outplayed on the board. Much earlier you could have saved time by following a simple development plan.

review.turning_point: 7...b6? gave you an edge, but the game was lost on the clock at move 8.
review.focus: Time management: the position after 8.Bc4?! was fine, but a fine position was lost on time. Use a quick developing plan like 8.e5 to keep the initiative and save clock.

review.headline: A London System that backfired on White's queen

sections.text: White chose an accelerated London, and you set up a compact structure with 2...e6, 3...Bd6, 5...O-O and 7...b6 followed by 8...Bb7. It is a very solid way to meet the London, and nothing happened for a long time.

White's first mistake was 10.c4?, which let you hit the centre with 10...Qc7. After 11.Ng4? the knight moved and uncovered an attack from the bishop on g3 on your bishop on d6. You played 11...dxc4?!, which had its own idea but the engine preferred 11...cxd4.
The idea worked, though. 11...dxc4 discovered an attack from your bishop on b7 on the queen on f3. White's 12.Nxc4?? missed it, and you took with 12...Bxf3!, winning the queen.
White resigned shortly after. It was a solid and patient game from you, with a nasty trap set by the quiet bishop on b7.

review.turning_point: 11...dxc4 discovered an attack on the queen, and 12...Bxf3! won it after White missed the threat.
review.focus: At 11...dxc4?! the engine liked 11...cxd4 first. Check which recapture keeps your pieces safe before you go for a trap.

review.headline: A trappy Two Knights win with some wild moments in the middle

sections.text: You played the Two Knights Attack with 4.Ng5 and when Black answered 4...d5 5.exd5 Nxd5?, you found 6.Nxf7!, a fork of the queen on d8 and the rook on h8. Black replied 6...Qf6??, which dropped the knight on d5 to 7.Bxd5!
You kept the pressure with 8.O-O and 9.Bxc6+, then 10.Nxe5 took another pawn. You were now well up in material (+5.2) and Black's king had no safe place.

11.Re1?? was a slip. 11.d4 would have kept things tidy. Black replied with 11...Rxf2??, which should have been 11...Bxf2+, a fork. Then 12.Ng4+?? uncovered a check from the rook but it was a blunder, as 12.Nf3+ was best.
Black missed 12...Re2+, a discovered check that would have won. Instead 12...Kd8?? let you play 13.Nxf2!, and 14.Qe2 Bg4 15.Qe8# finished the game.

review.turning_point: 12.Ng4+?? nearly threw the game away, but 12...Kd8?? missed 12...Re2+ and let you win with 13.Nxf2!
review.focus: At 11.Re1?? and 12.Ng4+?? you were winning but missed forcing replies. Before a check, look at what your opponent's checking replies are.

review.headline: A Philidor queen trade where one pawn and the clock decided it

sections.text: You chose the Philidor and kept things solid with 3...d6 and 4...Nbd7. After 5.dxe5 Nxe5 6.Nxe5 dxe5 7.Qxd8+ Kxd8 the queens were off and the position was roughly equal.
The only real mistake came at 8...Bd6?, which left the f7 pawn without enough protection. 9.Bxf7 won a pawn, and the evaluation dropped to about -1.7.
8...Bb4 was better, as the bishop would have pinned the knight on c3 to the king and kept White busy. You then played 9...Rf8, 10...Bd7, and White regrouped with 10.Bb3 and 11.Bg5.
The game ended on the clock at move 11, so time was the main issue as well as the pawn.

review.turning_point: 8...Bd6? left f7 loose, and 9.Bxf7 won a pawn.
review.focus: At 8...Bd6? check what is attacked on f7 before developing. 8...Bb4 pinned the knight on c3 to the king and was a better way to keep White occupied. Also keep an eye on the clock.

review.headline: A Sicilian where one pawn capture opened the e-file and cost a bishop

sections.text: You met the Paulsen-style Sicilian with an Open setup: 3.Ne2 cxd4 4.Nxd4. After 4...Bc5 5.g3?! the evaluation dropped to about -0.1, and 7.Bg2?! and 8.f4?! kept the game level without developing the queenside pieces.
9.fxe5 Qxe5 10.O-O?! was fine, but 11.c3 d5! was the key move: it hit your pawn on e4, which was the only thing shielding the bishop on e3 from the queen.
12.exd5?? took a pawn but opened the e-file, and 12...Qxe3+ won the bishop with check. 12.Bf4 was the safe move.
You resigned soon after, since you were down a bishop with the king under fire.

review.turning_point: 12.exd5?? opened the e-file and allowed 12...Qxe3+, winning the bishop.
review.focus: Before capturing at 12.exd5, ask what that pawn was protecting. The e4 pawn was blocking the queen from your bishop on e3.

review.headline: A winning position, then the queen was dropped in one move

sections.text: In the Vienna, you answered with 2...d6 and 3...Be6?!, a bit odd but fine. White made a bold try with 6.Nd5??, and you found 6...Nxd5!, a discovered attack that uncovered your bishop on e7 against the bishop on g5.
7...Bxg5?? was a mistake, as 7...Bxd5 was better. Even so, White blundered again with 8.d4??, and you found 8...Bg4!, which pinned the knight on f3 to the queen on d1.
After 9.dxe5 dxe5 10.Nxe5 Bxd1 you won the queen, and by move 17 you were around +11 in material. You collected pawns with 14...Qxb2, 15...Qxc2 and 16...Qxa2.
Then it all went wrong. After 21.Be6 your queen on d5 was attacked, and 21...Qf5?? stepped to a square that the bishop also attacked. 21...Qc5+ was the right move. 22.Bxf5 ended the game.

review.turning_point: 21...Qf5?? moved the queen onto another square attacked by the bishop on e6 and threw away a big advantage.
review.focus: At 21...Qf5?? check every square your queen can go to for attackers, and look for a check like 21...Qc5+ first. Slowing down once you are way ahead is a skill.

review.headline: A shaky Scandinavian that turned around after one opponent slip

sections.text: You played the Scandinavian main line with 4.Nc3, 5.Be3 and 6.Qd2, and had a pleasant, slightly better position. 7.Nge2?! was a little slow, and 11.d5?! gave the advantage away.
12.dxc6?? was the big mistake. Black's 12...Bxh3 won your bishop, and the position turned worse for you (-3.5).
Black did not follow it up. 13...b6?? missed 13...Be7, and you found 14.Qxd6!, a skewer along the d-file. 14...Rb8?? should have been 14...Qxd6, and after 15.Qxd8 Rbxd8 you were clearly better again.
16.Nb5 and 17.Nxa7 picked up another pawn, and 17...Rxc6?? let you finish with 18.Nxc6! Black resigned with a lost position.

review.turning_point: 14.Qxd6! used the skewer on the d-file and flipped the game after 13...b6??
review.focus: At 12.dxc6?? you could have played 12.Bg2 and kept things balanced. Check that your capture does not leave a piece loose, here the bishop on h3.

review.headline: A messy 69-move win that included a missed mate

sections.text: Black's queen moves in the Scandinavian (3...Qe6+, 4...Qd5, 7...Qe6+) cost time, and you were comfortably better early on. 10.Qe2?! and 11.O-O-O?? undid it, and 12.Kb1?? allowed 12...Qxa2+ and a dangerous attack.
Black went wrong too. 11...Nb4? helped, and you hung on with 17.Kf1 and 18.Nxc3. After 22.Qe5?? Nd7?? you found 23.Qxg7!, then 24.Bxe7!, and Black's 23...O-O-O?? lost material.
You then slipped again. 28.Bf6?? left a piece to be won, 29.d5?? and 30.Rhe1?? kept things level, and 33.Rde5?? missed a forced mate: 33.Rc1+ Kb8 34.Rxd8#.
Good moves returned with 35.R6e5!, which pinned the pawn on g5 against the rook on h5, and 38.h4! and 39.Rxh5!. You pushed the g-pawn with 48.g6, made a queen with 54.g8=Q and finished with 69.Qa6#.

review.turning_point: 38.h4! and 39.Rxh5! won the decisive material after a long and level struggle.
review.focus: At 33.Rde5?? you had a forced mate starting with 33.Rc1+. Look at checks around the king first, especially in rook endings.

review.headline: A London where you were worse, and the opponent resigned anyway

sections.text: You met the London with a classical setup: 2...e6, 3...Bd6, 5...Ne4 and 6...cxd6 after 6.Bxd6. You built a solid centre, castled with 7...O-O and gained space with 12...e5 and 13...e4.
15...Ne8?! and 20...d5?! slowed you down, and White's 19.c4 and 24.b5 gradually gave them the better game. By move 23 the engine had White up around +1.8.
27...Ra7?? was the real mistake. It left White's a-pawn free to advance, and the position went to -2.4. 27...Nh4 was the way to keep fighting.
After the exchanges on c1 and c8 the pawn on a7 was a real problem. The engine had you far behind by move 35, but White resigned, which is a gift you did not earn.

review.turning_point: 27...Ra7?? let the a-pawn become a monster, and it was White's resignation that turned the result.
review.focus: At 27...Ra7?? think about passed pawns near the edge. 27...Nh4 kept your pieces active and dealt with the pawn on a6 later.

review.headline: A bad middlegame, a big swing, and a missed defence at the end

sections.text: In the Petrov you allowed 4.Bg5 and 5.Bxf6 Bxf6, and White castled long with 8.O-O-O. 9...Bb7?!, 11...a4?! and 13...Bxe5?! were a bit loose, and after 14...f5?! and 15...Bxc3?! White was clearly better (-2.5).
White then blundered with 20.Ng5??, and you found 20...Qxe2!, a skewer of the queen and rook along the e-file. You came out ahead on material and the evaluation jumped to +4.3.
22...Rxh2?! was greedy. Then 23.Be6+ Kh8?? was a mistake, as 23...Kf8 was the right move. White tried 24.Bxd5??, and 24...Bxd5! won the bishop, so you still had a winning position.
26...Ree2?? was the final slip, allowing a forced mate. 26...Kg8 would have kept your advantage, and White won.

review.turning_point: 20...Qxe2! won a rook, but 26...Ree2?? gave it all back with a forced mate.
review.focus: At 26...Ree2?? you had a won position and walked into a forced mate. Before every move in a won position, check your opponent's checks and threats.

review.headline: A clean Two Knights attack ended in mate

sections.text: You played the Two Knights Attack with 4.Ng5, and Black's 4...Qe7?? was a blunder. You found 5.Bxf7+!, winning a pawn and dragging the king to d8.
6.Bb3 retreated the bishop safely, and 7.Nf7+ then hit the king and rook with check. After 8.Nxh8 you had won the rook, and you were up around +3.7.
Black took a pawn with 8...Nxe4, but you stayed calm with 9.Bf7+, 12.O-O and 13.d3. By 14.dxe4 Bxf2+ 15.Rxf2 Qxf2+ 16.Kxf2 you had traded down while far ahead.
17.Qh5, 19.Nxc8+ and 20.Qxh7 finished the job, and 27.Qxc6# was mate. A very accurate game.

review.turning_point: 4...Qe7?? allowed 5.Bxf7+!, and 8.Nxh8 then won the rook.
review.focus: Nothing wrong here. To keep improving, practise the Two Knights lines where Black plays the better 4...d5, so you are ready if the opponent finds it.

review.headline: A winning Italian game undone by one careless pawn push

sections.text: You played the Italian with 3.Bc4 and 4.d4. Black replied with 4...d5??, and 5.Bxd5 won a pawn. After 6.Bb3 exd4 7.Nxd4?! you were still clearly ahead.
You kept developing sensibly with 8.O-O, 9.Be3, 10.f3 and 12.Nc3, and traded at the right times: 14.Bxd4, 16.axb3 and 17.Bxf6 all helped you hold the advantage at around +4.
20.Nxc7?! took a pawn with the knight, and the knight stayed active with 23.Nd5 and 24.Nxb6. You were up material and heading toward a win.
The mistake came at 30.b5??. After 30...Ra1+ you were facing a forced mate. 30.Ne3 would have kept your advantage.

review.turning_point: 30.b5?? allowed 30...Ra1+ and a forced mate in a position you were winning.
review.focus: At 30.b5?? your king on h1 had no escape square. In a won position, always check your opponent's checks before pushing a pawn.

review.headline: A wild Petrov where both sides blundered and the queen fell last

sections.text: White grabbed a pawn with 3.Nxe5, and the engine then liked White. After 3...d6 White played 4.Bb5+??, and you found 4...c6!, which attacked the bishop and left White in trouble.
5.Nxc6 bxc6 6.e5 cxb5 was messy, and you came out well ahead on material. After 7.Qf3 dxe5 8.Qxa8 White grabbed the rook, so material was level.
8...Nc6?? was your blunder, as it left a piece to be won with 9.Qxc6+. 8...Qc7 was best. You were still in the game, and 10...Bd6, 11...O-O and 12.d4 Nd5 kept it going, though 12...b4 was better.
White then blundered with 13.Qh3??, and 13...Bxh3! won the queen. White resigned.

review.turning_point: 13.Qh3?? allowed 13...Bxh3!, a pin that won White's queen.
review.focus: At 8...Nc6?? you could have played 8...Qc7. Before blocking or developing, check whether the queen on a8 attacks a loose piece.

review.headline: A Stafford-style win where the opponent missed two shots

sections.text: You went into a Petrov with 3.Nxe5, and Black's 3...Nc6? let you play 4.Nxc6! dxc6 and win a pawn. 5.d3 Bc5 was a normal reply, and you were comfortable.
6.Be3? and 12.Rf3? allowed Black back in, and Black's 10...Nd5 and 11...Qg5 built an attack. Then 14.h3?? was a blunder and should have been 14.Na3, as 14...Qxe5 was available.
Black missed it with 14...h4??, and you found 15.Rxg4!, winning the bishop on g4. Black's 15...Qf6? was another slip, as 15...Qxe3+ was stronger.
After 16.e4 Qe6 17.exd5 Qxd5 you were far ahead. You finished with 19.Bg4+, 23.Bxc8 and 25.Qxa7#.

review.turning_point: 15.Rxg4! won a bishop after Black missed 14...Qxe5.
review.focus: At 14.h3?? you allowed 14...Qxe5. Check which of your pieces is loose before playing a pawn move that weakens a square.

review.headline: A quiet Italian game that was fine until one careless bishop move at the end

sections.text: You went for a classical Italian setup with 3.Bc4 and 4.d4, and Black met it with an early ...Bg4. After 5.dxe5 Nxe5 6.Be2 Nxf3+ 7.Bxf3 the center had cleared and you were slightly better, around +0.5.

From there you built a sensible position. The g3 and b3 pawn moves prepared your bishops, and 13.Na4 forced the queen to move with 13...Qa5+ 14.Bc3 Qg5. Then 15.h4 chased it further, and you kept a steady edge near +0.9 after 16.Bh5 Qh6.

The trouble started with 17.Bd2, which took your bishop off the long diagonal. After 17...Qf6 the queen was aiming straight at your rook on a1. The calm answer was 18.Bc3, putting the bishop back in front of the rook and holding your edge.
Instead you played 18.Bg5, hoping to hit the queen, but 18...Qxa1+ simply took the rook with check. You were suddenly down a whole rook and the game was over.

review.turning_point: 18.Bg5 left your rook on a1 hanging to the queen on f6. The evaluation went from +0.9 to -6.0 in one move, when 18.Bc3 would have kept everything protected.
review.focus: Before every move, ask what the opponent's last move is aiming at. After 17...Qf6 the queen eyed your rook on a1, so 18.Bg5 had to be checked against that first.

review.headline: A Petrov where you stayed close, then missed the chance to turn it around at 20.Bf2

sections.text: This was a Petrov, and you handled the opening reasonably, answering 3.Nxe5 d6 and winning your pawn back with 4...Nxe4. After 8.Nd4 Nbd7 9.Nxe6 the recapture 9...fxe6 was a small inaccuracy, and 9...Qxe6 was the more natural way to keep your structure healthy.

Both sides castled long, and your plan with ...h6 and ...g5 gave you some kingside space. The position got harder after 14...Kb8, because White could swap queens with 15.Qxe6 Qxe6 16.Rxe6 and you were left a pawn down at around -1.0. Then 17...Nb6 and 19...Na4 sent your knights toward the edge, where they did very little.

The big moment came with 20.Bf2, a real mistake by White that put you at +0.7. The right reply was 20...Rxe2 21.Bxe2, which would have won a piece and turned the game your way. You played 20...Nf4 instead and fell back to -2.9, and 21.Rxe8 Rxe8 traded off your rooks.

After that you were fighting uphill. 24...b4 opened lines near your own king, when 24...c6 25.Ne4 Kc7 would have been a calmer defense. White finished with 25.Bb5 and 26.Bxe8, and you resigned after 28.Kxd2.

review.turning_point: 20.Bf2 gave you a real chance, and 20...Rxe2 21.Bxe2 was the way to take it. After 20...Nf4 the opportunity was gone and the evaluation fell to -2.9.
review.focus: When your opponent plays a surprising move like 20.Bf2, stop and look for forcing replies across the whole board. Here 20...Rxe2 was available and needed to be seen before 20...Nf4.

review.headline: A Petrov Italian where an early grab on d5 led to a quick loss in 10 moves

sections.text: After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4 you chose 3...d5, a known idea, but it needs care. After 4.exd5 e4 5.Ne5 White had the more comfortable game, though it was still only around even.

The first real error was 5...Nxd5, which dropped you to -2.5. The quieter 5...Qe7 6.d4 exd3 would have kept your position together. After 5...Nxd5 your knight and your e4 pawn were both stuck in the middle of White's pieces.

White then played 6.Qe2, and your 6...f5 weakened your king. The better move was 6...c6 7.Qxe4. After White's inaccurate 7.d4 you had one more chance to hold on with 7...Be6 8.Nc3, but 7...Bd6 allowed 8.Qh5+.

From there it was one-sided. 9.Nxg6 attacked more than you could cover, and 9...Ne7 ran into 10.Nxh8+, which took your rook. 9...Nf6 was the better defense, although you were already in serious trouble.

review.turning_point: 5...Nxd5 started the slide. After it every move had to deal with a weak king and loose pieces, and 7...Bd6 let in 8.Qh5+ with a strong attack.
review.focus: In this opening, when you take on d5 with the knight, check what the knight on e5 and the queen can do against your king first. At 5...Nxd5 the calmer 5...Qe7 kept the position balanced.

review.headline: A Philidor where you punished a bishop blunder and kept the lead until the clock caused trouble

sections.text: You played the classical Italian-style setup against the Philidor with 3.Bc4, 4.d4 and 8.Re1. The push 10.e5 was a little loose, but after 10...Nxe5 11.Nxe5 dxe5 12.Rxe5 the position was still close to level.
Black then blundered with 12...Bd6, which allowed 13.Qxd6! and won a bishop at once. The evaluation jumped from +0.3 to +5.1. Your queen on d6 also hit the bishop on d7, which kept Black tied up.
You kept the lead with 17.Qd5, 18.Qd3 and 20.Rd1. When Black played 22...Qe5 you found 23.Nxa8!, winning the rook. After 24.Rd7 and 25.Qd5 Qxd5 26.Rxd5 you had a huge endgame edge.

In the endgame you were nearly winning on the board, but the clock hurt you. 47.Rc7 threw away most of the edge, and 48.Kc4 made it worse. Luckily Black replied with 47...a5 and 48...Rf4+, giving it back, and you went on to win on time.

review.turning_point: 12...Bd6 13.Qxd6 was the decisive moment. After it you were a bishop up and later cashed in with 23.Nxa8.
review.focus: When you are far ahead and short of time, pick the simplest safe move. At 47.Rc7 the line 47.Bc5 Rg2 48.Bd4 kept everything protected.

review.headline: A Bishop's Opening where the knight dash 11...Ng4 started a bad run

sections.text: You met the Bishop's Opening with a solid setup: ...d6, ...Be6, ...Nf6 and short castling. After 8.f4 Nbd7 9.fxe5 dxe5 10.Ng3 the position was balanced.

10...Qb6+ was not needed, though it was still playable. Then 11.Kh1 Ng4 was the first big error. The simple 11...Nc5 would have kept things level, while 11...Ng4 left the knight offside and dropped you to -4.8.

White missed their chance with 12.Qe2, since 12.Bxe6 fxe6 13.Qxg4 was the strong reply. You then played 12...g6, which weakened the kingside, when 12...Ngf6 was safer. White missed the same idea again with 13.h3, and you got back to about -1.2 after 13...Ngf6 14.Bh6 Rfd8.
After 15.Qf2 you had a real chance: 15...Qxf2 16.Rxf2 Bxb3 17.axb3 would have won a piece. You played 15...Nc5 instead, and 16.Be3 Qc7 17.Bxc5 cost you a knight and the game.

review.turning_point: 15...Nc5 missed the one clear chance in the game. 15...Qxf2 16.Rxf2 Bxb3 would have won a piece, while the knight move lost one soon after.
review.focus: When the opponent offers a queen trade, as with 15.Qf2, check whether it wins something first. Here 15...Qxf2 was the move to calculate before 15...Nc5.

review.headline: A Vienna Gambit where White got careless and your knight jump decided it

sections.text: You defended the Vienna Gambit calmly. After 3.f4 d6 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.fxe5 dxe5 the center was open and the position was balanced. Then 6.d3 Bb4 and 7.Bd2 Bg4 developed your pieces quickly.
8.h3 was a slip by White, and you could have cashed in with 8...Bxf3 9.Qxf3. 8...Bh5 was a bit passive, but White then went wrong with 9.Qe2, which gave you the game.
You found the best reply, 9...Nd4! The knight hit the queen, and 10.Qe3 made things much worse for White. Then 10...Nxc2+ forked the king on e1, the rook on a1 and the queen on e3.
White resigned right there. You were already at +6.8, with the whole attack still to come.

review.turning_point: 9.Qe2 was the error, but the credit goes to 9...Nd4!, which you found immediately. Then 10...Nxc2+ was a knight fork of the king, the rook and the queen.
review.focus: After 8.h3 your bishop on g4 was attacked, and 8...Bh5 was too passive. Look at 8...Bxf3 9.Qxf3 first when your opponent asks the bishop a question.

review.headline: A long, messy Petrov where you were worse for a while, then White cracked and your pawn queened

sections.text: This Petrov started well enough, but 5.Bc4 Be6 was a mistake that left you under pressure. After 6.Bb3 Qe7 7.O-O Nc5 8.Re1 Nxb3 9.axb3 you had traded your knight for the bishop, and you were still a bit worse.

The middlegame was sharp for both of you. White's 11.Nc3 and 14.Qb5 were big errors, but your own 12...b6 and 14...Kb7 gave the chances back. After 15.Nc5+ Kc8 16.Qxc6 bxc5 17.dxc5 Qxc5 you were down a piece in a wild position, near -5.5.
Then White blundered. After 18.Qa8+ you found the best reply, 18...Kd7!, and 19.Qxa5 Qxa5 20.Rxa5 Bb4 21.Bd2 Bxa5 22.Bxa5 left you ahead for the first time in the game, around +1.0.
You then made some small errors, like 25...Bf7 and 26...c6, but White gave far more back with 39.Kf4, 40.Kg5 and 41.Be3. The key idea was 46...d4!, and the d-pawn marched all the way to 53...d1=Q.

review.turning_point: 18...Kd7 and 19...Qxa5 were your best moves of the game. After White overreached with 18.Qa8+ and 19.Qxa5, the position finally turned in your favor.
review.focus: In the rook endgame, 39...Re2 gave away part of a big edge. 39...Re4+ 40.Kg5 Rxd4 was the cleaner way to win a pawn and keep control.

review.headline: A Sicilian where you took the initiative, punished 11...d5, and finished with a rook

sections.text: You played the Open Sicilian with 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 and 6.Bg5. After 6...e5, 7.Nxc6 let Black off easier than 7.Bxf6 gxf6 would have. Even so, 8.Bc4 and 9.O-O kept you active.

10.h4 was a little loose, but Black went wrong first with 11...d5. You replied accurately with 12.exd5! cxd5 13.Bxf6 Bxf6 14.Nxd5 Bxd5, and after the queen exchange on d5 and d8 you were comfortably better.

19.Re2 allowed some counterplay, but Black helped you by playing 22...Bxe3. After 23.Rbe1! h5 24.Rxe3 you had won the bishop back, and the extra piece plus the open lines gave you total control at about +5.
You finished well. 27.hxg5, 28.Rxf7+ and 30.Rb6+! forced the king away, and then 31.Rxb8 picked up the rook. After 33.Rd8+ Ke7 34.Rxd1 Black resigned.

review.turning_point: 22...Bxe3 gave you a big edge, and 23.Rbe1! was the accurate follow-up that kept it. After 24.Rxe3 the bishop was yours and the win was straightforward.
review.focus: At 7.Nxc6 you could first have played 7.Bxf6 gxf6 and kept the pressure on. Look for the exchange that damages your opponent's structure before you release the tension.

review.headline: A short Italian-style attack where Black walked into your knight and resigned on move 8

sections.text: You opened with 1.e4 and 3.Bc4 against the Philidor, then played the quiet 4.d3. After 4...Nc6 5.Ng5 you put a knight on g5 aiming at f7, a sensible way to pressure the weakest square in Black's camp.
Black answered with 5...Nd4??, which dropped the evaluation to +2.8 for you. Safer was 5...d5 6.exd5. You punished it with 6.Bxf7+, winning a pawn with check and dragging the king out with 6...Kd7.
7.Bb3 was a small slip. The cleaner move was 7.c3, which attacked the knight on d4 right away. It cost you under a pawn, so it did not change the result.
Black then played 7...h6, and you found the best reply, 8.Nf7!, which forked the queen on d8 and the rook on h8, and Black resigned with the evaluation at +4.3.

review.turning_point: 7...h6 gave you a chance and 8.Nf7! took it. The knight hit the queen and the rook at the same time, so Black could not hold on to both.
review.focus: At 7.Bb3 you could have played 7.c3 to challenge the knight on d4 right away. In attacking games, look for the move that removes the opponent's best defender before you retreat.

review.headline: A quiet Petrov where you got a pawn and an edge, then dropped it with 23...Rfe8

sections.text: White played a slow setup with 3.d3, 4.h3 and 8.Nh2, and you built your position well with ...g6, ...Bg7, ...b6 and ...Bb7. By 11...d5 you were comfortable, and 12.exd5 Nxd5 13.Nc2 Nxe3 14.Nxe3 left you with the easier game.
14...Bh6 was a small inaccuracy, but you recovered with 15...Bxf3 16.Nxf3 O-O and kept equality. After 17...Nc5 White went wrong with 18.O-O, which was a clear mistake.

You found the best reply: 18...Qxd3! After 19.Qxd3 Nxd3 you were up a clean pawn with the better position, around +2.5. 20.Ng4 Bg7 21.Rab1 e4 22.Nd2 Rad8 23.Nxe4 picked up your e-pawn, but you were still at +4.0.

Then came 23...Rfe8??, the blunder. It let both knights come into the game with 24.Nef6+, and after 24...Bxf6 25.Nxf6+ you were at -3.8. The right move was 23...f5, which forked the knights on e4 and g4 with the pawn.

review.turning_point: 23...Rfe8 turned +4.0 into -2.7 in one move. The pawn push 23...f5 attacked both knights at once and kept your large advantage.
review.focus: Before you make a quiet move in a winning position, look at every check and capture your opponent has. At 23...Rfe8 you missed 24.Nef6+, while 23...f5 would have hit two knights at once.

review.headline: A Petrov that stayed level until the endgame, when both sides missed wins before you took the queen on move 64

sections.text: This was a Petrov. You took the pawn with 3.Nxe5, Black won it back with 4...Nxe4, and after 6...Qxe2+ 7.Bxe2 the queens came off. You then traded pieces calmly with 14.Bxd6 Rxd6 and 16.Nxe4 Bxe4, and everything stayed near equal.

21.Nh4?? was the first big blunder, and it allowed a forced mate. Black missed it with 21...g6?? and your 22.Nf3! came right back in time to hold the position. The stronger line for Black was 21...Rxe1+ 22.Rxe1.
You then drifted. 26.b3?? let the knight run with 26...Nd2, and 27.b4?! made things worse. By 37...fxg4 the evaluation was around -6 against you.

Black blundered with 41...c6+??, and after 42.Ke6?? Kxc5?? the game was nearly level again. You found 43.Kf6! and kept going, and in the queen ending Black played 63...Qd5+??. You finished with 64.Qxd5+, winning the queen.

review.turning_point: 41...c6+?? swung the game from -6.9 to +6.4, but 42.Ke6?? gave it right back. The real finish came at 64.Qxd5+, when Black walked into a queen loss.
review.focus: In the king and pawn ending, 42.Ke6 gave away a winning position. 42.Kd6 Kc4 43.Kxc6 was the right way to use the king, because it kept the pawns protected and attacked c6.

review.headline: A Petrov with a risky ...g5 plan that got messy, until your rook on f2 decided it

sections.text: You played ...d6, ...Be7 and then the bold 5...h6 and 6...g5, after which 7.Bg3 c6 settled into a playable position. 10.Qc2 and 11.Ng1 were slightly strange by White, and you answered 11...Nh5! hitting the bishop on g3.
13...f5 was the first slip, since 13...Nf4 14.Nd2 d5 was cleaner. After 14.exf5 Bxf5 15.g4, White was winning back ground and you were around -2.6 after 15...Rdf8.
You fought back well. 18...d5 and 19...e4! got the pieces moving, and White blundered with 20.Ne5?? You missed 20...Rxf2, playing 20...Nxe5, but 21.dxe5?? gave you another chance.

21...Rxf2! forked the queen on c2 and the bishop on g2, and the evaluation climbed to +4.5. After 22.Rd2 Qe3 and 23.Ne2 Rxg2 you were far ahead, and you finished cleanly with 27...Rxc2+ and 35...Qxe6.

review.turning_point: 21...Rxf2! was the turning point, because the rook forked the queen on c2 and the bishop on g2. After that you were winning for the rest of the game.
review.focus: At 13...f5 you opened lines when your king was still unprotected. The calmer 13...Nf4 14.Nd2 d5 kept your center and avoided the pawn loss.

review.headline: A Dutch-style game where you won a bishop for nothing, then let the edge slip away in the endgame

sections.text: You set up a solid Dutch structure against the Bird, and 7...Bg4 8.Be2 Bg7 developed your pieces. 10...Ne4 11.Nxe4 dxe4 12.Ne5 Nxe5 13.fxe5 was an even trade, and you stayed level with 13...Be6.
17...Qg5?! and 18...Bf8?! were a little loose, but White blundered with 19.Qf2??, which lost a bishop. You took it at once with 19...Qxg4, and the evaluation rose to +3.7.
After that you were fully in charge. 20.e6 f5 21.h3 Qg5 22.Bf4 Qe7 and 23...Qxe6 won back the pawn and kept the extra piece. You were still around +4.5.
The edge slipped with 26...Bxb3? and 27...Qxb3?, both a bit greedy. After 28.Raf1?? a5?? 29.Rxf5 Rf8 30.Qc7+ you needed 30...Kg8. 30...Kh6?? lost at once to 31.Rxf8.

review.turning_point: 19.Qf2?? gave you a bishop, and you took it with 19...Qxg4. Later 30...Kh6?? gave it all back and turned +0.2 into -6.6.
review.focus: When you are winning, trade down and stay safe. At 26...Bxb3 the quieter 26...Rf8 kept your edge, because you did not need the pawn.

review.headline: A Two Knights Knight Attack where you punished 5...Nxd5 and finished with mate on move 9

sections.text: You went for the sharp 4.Ng5 against the Two Knights Defense, and after 4...d5 5.exd5 Black grabbed with 5...Nxd5?, a mistake that raised your score to +1.4. The best defense was 5...Na5 6.Bb5+ c6.

You found 6.Nxf7!, the knight sacrifice that forked the queen on d8 and the rook on h8. After 6...Kxf7 7.Qf3+ the king was pulled out into the open, and the queen hit both the king and the knight on d5.
Black replied 7...Ke8?, but 7...Ke6 was the better try. You found 8.Bxd5! and kept the initiative, and 8...Bd7?? lost at once.
You finished with 9.Qf7#, a clean mate. It was an accurate game, with nothing to criticize in your moves.

review.turning_point: 6.Nxf7! was the decision. It broke up the king's cover and every move after that was forcing, with the mate on f7 as the payoff.
review.focus: Your play was clean, so study the idea behind it. After 5...Nxd5, 6.Nxf7 only works because 7.Qf3+ comes with check right after, so always look for that follow-up before sacrificing.

review.headline: An Italian where 3...f6 gave you a big opening edge, and you converted all the way to mate on move 65

sections.text: Black played the weak 3...f6?, and you found the best reply, 4.d4!, opening the center before Black could develop. After 4...Qe7 5.dxe5 Nxe5 6.Nxe5 Qxe5 7.Nc3 Bb4 8.O-O you were clearly better, around +1.5.

The advantage grew after 9.Bd2 Bxc3 10.Bxc3 Qc5 11.Qe2, and Black's 12...Qd6? pushed it to +5.2. Your queen then went on a long hunt with 13.Qh5+ g6 14.Qh6 and 15.Qg7, a little greedy but safe enough for now.

The big moment was 21.Qh8+??, which let Black off the hook. The strong move was 21.Qxf7+ Kd7 22.Be6+. Luckily Black repeated with 22...Rf7?? again, and this time you took with 23.Bxf7+, winning the rook.
After 24.Qxf6 Qxf6 25.Bxf6 you were far ahead and converted well. Low on time, 38.Rdd6?? allowed a mating attack, but Black missed it with 38...Rc4??. You won with 49.h8=Q and 65.Qfc2#.

review.turning_point: 23.Bxf7+ won the rook and ended any real resistance. After that, only your time trouble at 38.Rdd6?? gave Black any chance.
review.focus: With the clock running low, choose the safe move. At 38.Rdd6 the line 38.f3 Rb2 kept everything protected and avoided the mating threat.

review.headline: A French Exchange where an early slip left you worse, and 14.Qf4 cost a piece

sections.text: You played the Exchange French with 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 Qd8, and 5.Bb5+ c6 6.Ba4 a5 was fine for you. The mistake was 7.Nf3?, which dropped you to -1.5. The quieter 7.Bb3 kept a small edge.
You tried to complicate with 7...b5 8.Nxb5!, a sharp piece sacrifice. After 8...cxb5 9.Bxb5+ you got two pawns back for the piece, though Black stayed comfortably ahead at around -2.
You developed with 10.Be2, 11.Bg5 and 12.O-O, but Black kept improving. 13.Qd2 Ne4 attacked your queen, and the position was already difficult.
14.Qf4?? lost a piece. The best choice was 14.Bxe7, which broke up the bishops. After 14...Nxg5 15.Nxg5 Bxg5 you were down a piece, and Black converted with 16.Qe4 Nc6 and 18...Nxd4.

review.turning_point: 14.Qf4?? stepped into 14...Nxg5 15.Nxg5 Bxg5, and the game was over from there. 14.Bxe7 would have kept the position difficult but playable.
review.focus: Before moving the queen, count the captures around her. After 13...Ne4, 14.Qf4 let 14...Nxg5 15.Nxg5 Bxg5 hit your queen, while 14.Bxe7 solved the problem first.

review.headline: A Philidor where 4...Nxe4 cost you a knight early and you never quite recovered

sections.text: White played the quiet 3.h3 and 4.Nc3, and the position was equal until you grabbed with 4...Nxe4. After 5.Nxe4 you had a pawn for a knight, and the evaluation fell to -2.9. The calm 4...c5 5.Bc4 was the way to keep the balance.

You tried to fight back with 5...d5 and 6...e4, but 7.Nh2 d4 8.Nxe4 simply won the pawn too, and the position went to -3.6. After 8...Bf5?! 9.Ng3 Qe7+ the checks gave you some activity, but White had no trouble with 10.Be2.
To your credit, you kept making threats. 10...d3 11.cxd3 Bxd3 12.O-O Bxe2 13.Nxe2 Nc6 14.Re1 O-O-O brought your pieces out, and after 15.Nd4 you had a real chance to complicate.
That chance was 15...Qxe1+ 16.Qxe1, which would have won back some of the loss. You played 15...Qb4? instead, and after 16.Nxc6 bxc6 17.a3 Qd4 18.Qg4+ you were down too much to continue.

review.turning_point: 4...Nxe4 gave up a knight for a pawn, because 5.Nxe4 just won the piece. The position was equal before it and -2.9 right after.
review.focus: Before taking a pawn in the opening, check if the piece that takes can be captured back for free. At 4...Nxe4 the answer was yes, and 4...c5 5.Bc4 was the solid choice.

review.headline: A wild Scandinavian where 10.Qd3 hung your queen, and you missed two chances to win a rook

sections.text: You met the Scandinavian with 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qd8 and 4.d4, and then played an aggressive pawn storm with 5.h3, 6.g4, 7.h4 and 8.h5. The position was fine around +0.9 early, but the pawn storm left your king without much protection.

The first big error was 10.Qd3??, which stepped into the bishop on h7 and dropped you to -5.3. Black missed 10...Bxd3 and played 10...Nc6, and you got away with it. After 11.Qb5 Rb8 12.Ne2?? you were still worse, but Black then slipped back with 13...Qd6??.

Then 15.dxc6?? picked up a knight but allowed 15...axb5, which took your queen, and although 16.Rxd6 cxd6 won Black's queen back you were behind. 15.Qc4 was safer. You still fought on well with 20.Nxb4! and 23.Kd2!, and got back into the game.

The big chance came with 24...Ra8??, which left a rook hanging. 25.Bxa8 would have won it, and you were at +5.6. Instead 25.Bf3?? gave it all back, and after 25...Bxd3 26.cxd3?? the chance was gone. You lost with 31.Kb3?? Nxd3.

review.turning_point: 25.Bf3?? threw away a won game. 25.Bxa8 would have won a rook, and the evaluation dropped from +5.6 to +0.2.
review.focus: When your opponent blunders, make a habit of looking at every capture first. At 25.Bf3 and again at 26.cxd3, 26.Bxa8 was on the board and you did not play it.

review.headline: A Giuoco Piano where 15.Bxg7+ gave away a bishop, and a late swing was not enough

sections.text: This was a slow Italian. You played 4.O-O, 5.d3, 6.Bb3 and 7.Nc3, and the position stayed level until 11.d4?!, which opened the center too early. After 11...exd4 12.Nxd4 Bxd4? 13.Bxd4! you came out all right, and Black's mistake gave you back an even game.
You then played 14.Bxe6 fxe6 15.Bxg7+??, and this was the decisive error. After 15...Kxg7 16.Qg4+ you were down a bishop for a pawn, and the evaluation sat near -4.

The calm 15.Be3 Qh4 would have kept things level. After the mistake you kept fighting with 17.Qh5+ Kg7 and 20.Nd5 Nf3+. Black went wrong with 23...Nf6?? and you found 24.Rg3!, which swung the game to +2.4.
But 26.Qf5?? gave it all back, since 26.Ne7 kept the lead. After 27.Qf3?! Nxd5 and 31.Qxb7? Rxg3 you were lost, and you were mated on 35...Rf1#.

review.turning_point: 15.Bxg7+ was the move that decided the game, because it gave up a bishop for a pawn. 26.Qf5 later gave away your best chance to come back.
review.focus: Before sacrificing, count what you get back. At 15.Bxg7+ you gained only a pawn, and the quiet 15.Be3 kept everything protected.

review.headline: A London System where you were winning big, but 56...Qg5 let the game end in stalemate

sections.text: You met the London System with 2...Nc6 and 3...f6, a slightly unusual setup. White played 5.Nbd2?, and you found the strong reply 5...e5!. After 6.dxe5 fxe5 7.Bg5 Be7 8.Bxe7 Qxe7 you had a comfortable game.

White pushed the kingside pawns with 10.g4, 11.h4 and 13.h5, and you went a bit wrong with 14...h6? (14...Be8 was better). After 15.Nxf7 Qxf7 16.Qc2 Nxg4 you took a pawn and were still comfortable at +1.4.
18...Qg3? was another small slip, but White then blundered with 20.Bxg4?? and 21.Nf1??. You replied perfectly with 20...Rhf8! and 21...Qg2!, and the evaluation climbed to +6.

You then converted with the rooks and the c-pawn, queening with 45...c1=Q+. The only problem came at 56...Qg5??, when 56...Qg1 57.axb6 would have led to a forced mate. After 57.a6+ Kxa6 White had no legal move and the game ended in stalemate.

review.turning_point: 56...Qg5?? turned a forced win into a draw. White had only the king left, and 57.a6+ Kxa6 left no legal move.
review.focus: In a won position, check whether your move leaves the opponent a legal move. At 56...Qg5 the line 56...Qg1 57.axb6 kept the attack alive, while the game move led straight to stalemate.

review.headline: A Pirc where 9.Bh6 dropped a piece, and 24.Ka1 ended the game in mate

sections.text: You met the Pirc with the Bd2 setup, then pushed 5.e5. After 5...dxe5 6.dxe5 Ng4? Black made the first mistake, but 7.Qe2?? gave it back at once. The right plan was 7.f4 Nh6 8.Nf3, which kept control of the center.
9.Bh6?? was the first big blunder. Black simply took the bishop with 9...Bxh6+, and you lost a piece. The quiet 9.Be3 would have kept the position about equal.

You fought back well and tried to build an attack with 11.Qb5, 12.Qxb7 and 15.Nd5. Black stayed ahead until 18...c6?, which gave you 19.Qxh6!. After 19...Be6?? you were suddenly at +1.7, and 20.Nf6+ was the move to find.

20.Ne3?? was a mistake, and after 20...Rb8?? 21.Nf3?? you gave the advantage away. Black blundered with 23...Nd2+, giving you one last chance, but 24.Ka1?? lost to 24...Qb2#, when 24.Kc1 was the move.

review.turning_point: 9.Bh6?? lost a piece for nothing. You recovered and reached +4.5 after 20...Rb8, but 24.Ka1?? finished the game with mate.
review.focus: In the final position, check every king move before you play it. At 24.Ka1 the king walked into 24...Qb2#, while 24.Kc1 Qd4 25.Qxh7+ kept your attack going.

review.headline: A Philidor where Black's 7...b5 let you in, and you finished with mate on move 30

sections.text: You played the Philidor with 3.Bc4 Bg4 4.Nc3 and 5.h3, and after 5...Bxf3 6.Qxf3 Qf6 7.Qd3 you were comfortable at around +1. Black then played the weak 7...b5??, and you got a big opening edge.

8.Nd5?? was not the best, and 8.Bxb5 was the safer move. But Black replied 8...cxd5?? and 9.Bxd5! was strong, hitting the rook on a8 and the f7 pawn. After 9...a6 you took 10.Bxa8, capturing the rook.

You kept the initiative with 11.Bc6, 12.b3 and 13.Bxd7+, trading into a strong attack. 14.Ba3 and 16.Qb7+ drove the king around, and 17.O-O-O brought the rook in. 19.g3? was an inaccuracy, since 19.Qc8+ was stronger, but you were still winning.
The ending was clean. After 25...Qf2+ 26.Kb1 Qxg3 27.Qd5+ Kf6 28.Qf5+ Ke7 you found 29.Bxd6+, and 29...Ke8?? allowed 30.Qc8# with mate.

review.turning_point: 8...cxd5?? opened the way for 9.Bxd5!, and after 10.Bxa8 you had captured the rook. Everything after that was conversion.
review.focus: At 8.Nd5 you sacrificed a knight when 8.Bxb5 was simpler and kept everything protected. Always check the quiet capture before going for a sacrifice.

review.headline: A Modern Defense where you kept a small edge until 18.Nxc5 hung your queen

sections.text: You played a sensible setup against the Modern Defense, with 4.Bc4 and 5.O-O. After 6.Nbd2 c6 the position was fine for you, although 7.b3?! was a little slow. Black took the pawn with 8...dxe4, and 9.Nxe4 won it back.
You were doing well through the middlegame, at around +1.5. 10.c4 a6 11.Bb2 Nf5 12.Qc2 Nxd4 13.Nxd4 Bxd4 14.Rfd1 e5 gave you the better pieces.
15.Kh1? was the first slip, since 15.Bxd4 exd4 16.Qb2 would have kept the edge. After 15...Bf5 16.f4?! c5 17.fxe5 Nc6 Black was suddenly fine.
Then came 18.Nxc5??. The knight on e4 had been shielding your queen from the bishop on f5, and moving it let 18...Bxc2 take the queen. 18.cxb5 was the safe move, and after 19.Rxd4 Nxd4 you resigned.

review.turning_point: 18.Nxc5?? moved the knight that was protecting your queen from the bishop on f5, and 18...Bxc2 won the queen.
review.focus: Before moving a piece, ask what it was blocking or protecting. At 18.Nxc5 the knight was shielding the queen on c2, and 18.cxb5 kept everything safe.

review.headline: An opening where Black's 4...Nd4 gave you a big edge, which slipped away from 9.Bg5 on

sections.text: Against the unusual St. George setup you reacted well with 3.d4 and 4.d5. Black replied 4...Nd4?, a mistake, and after 5.Nxd4 exd4 6.Qxd4 you had won a pawn and stood at about +2, which is a very good start.

You kept things under control with 7.Qc3 and 8.Bd3, and the evaluation stayed comfortably above +2. The problem started with 9.Bg5??, which let the evaluation drop from +2.0 to -0.1. The simple 9.O-O Be7 kept your edge.
Black missed the strong 9...Nxe4, but 10.Bh4?? did not take advantage; 10.Bxf6 gxf6 was best. After 10...g5 11.Bg3 Bg7, 12.h4?? loosened your kingside and the evaluation turned to -2.1.
From there Black took over. 13.Qd2 Nxg3 14.fxg3 Bxb2 15.Rf1 Bxa1 cost you the rook on a1, and you were left chasing a lost game. You were mated on 31...Qd3#.

review.turning_point: 9.Bg5?? was the move that threw away a good position. The calm 9.O-O kept the edge, and after 9...h6 10.Bh4?? you gave Black an extra tempo.
review.focus: Once you have won a pawn and are comfortable, choose development over adventures. At 9.Bg5 9.O-O Be7 kept everything safe and your advantage stayed intact.

review.headline: A Center Game where you stayed active, took the initiative, and finished with mate on move 26

sections.text: The game started with 1.e4 e5 2.d4 Nc6 3.dxe5 Nxe5 4.Nf3 Nc6, and you took a small edge. After 5.e5?! d6 6.Bb5 Be7 7.O-O a6 8.Bxc6+ bxc6 you had a comfortable game.
9.Re1 Nh6 10.Bxh6 gxh6 11.Qe2 doubled Black's pawns on the h-file and kept up the pressure. Black's 12...f5 was a bit loose, and you were up to around +2.6.
13.e6? was a small slip, since 13.Nd4 was better, but Black returned the favor with 13...d5?. You found the best reply, 14.Ne5!, and after 15.Nf7 Qc5? the evaluation climbed to +4.0.

The crushing sequence came after 19.Nxg5?? (19.Nxh6+ was stronger) 19...Kh8??. You then played 20.Nxe6!, which forked the queen on d4 and the rook on f8. After 21.Nxf8 Rxf8 you were far ahead, and you finished with 26.Qg7#.

review.turning_point: 19...Kh8?? gave you the chance, and 20.Nxe6! forked the queen on d4 and the rook on f8, so Black could not hold both.
review.focus: At 19.Nxg5 you took the wrong piece. The check 19.Nxh6+ Kh8 20.Rxg5 kept more control, so before capturing, compare the checks with the other captures.

review.headline: A Queen's Pawn game where you had a big chance with 7.Qxb7 on the board, and the clock ran out

sections.text: This was a Queen's Pawn game where White played an early queen excursion with 3.Qa4+ and 6.Qb3. You answered with 3...c6, 5...c5 and 6...c4, which made some sense, although 6...c4?! was a little loose.

Then White blundered with 7.Qxb7??, taking a pawn deep in your camp. The evaluation went up to +4.6 for you. The correct reply was 7...Bc6, which attacks the queen and leaves it with nowhere safe to go: 8.Qxa8 would be the best White had.
You played 7...Nc6?? instead, which let the queen out, and 8.Ne5 put pressure on your position. After 8...Rb8?? you were at -1.9. The right answer was 8...Nxe5 9.dxe5.
White blundered again with 9.Qa6, and a move such as 9...Nxe5 would have kept you in the game. 9...Bc8?? went wrong again, and after 10.Qa4 you lost on time with the evaluation at -1.9.

review.turning_point: 7.Qxb7?? was a gift. 7...Bc6 would have put the queen in trouble, but 7...Nc6?? let it escape.
review.focus: When your opponent grabs a pawn deep in your camp, as with 7.Qxb7, ask first whether the queen can be trapped. 7...Bc6 was the move to find before 7...Nc6.

review.headline: A Two Knights game that swung back and forth, until a king walk ended in mate on move 17

sections.text: This was a Two Knights Italian with 4.O-O and 5.Re1. Black played 6...Na5??, which gave you +2.1, when 6...Bb6 was the right move. You went for 7.Bxf7+, which kept a smaller edge at +1.5.

After 7...Kxf7 8.Nxe5+ Black went wrong with 8...Ke8??, and the right move was 8...Kg8. Instead of the strong 9.d4, you played 9.Qh5+??, which dropped the evaluation to -6.8. Black missed the answer 9...Nxh5.
After 9...Ke7?? you got another chance. 10.Ng6+ Kd6 11.Qe5+ Kc6 chased the king around the board, but 12.Nxh8?? was a mistake, since 12.d4 d6 13.Qf4 kept the attack going.
You recovered with 13.Qd5+! Kb6 and 14.b4?? Bxf2+ 15.Kh1, then Black blundered with 15...Bxe1??. You finished with 16.Qxa5+! Kc6 17.Qc5#, a mate with the king stuck on c6.

review.turning_point: 9.Qh5+?? nearly threw the game away, but 9...Ke7?? let you back in. The final mate came after 16.Qxa5+!, a capture with check that forced the king forward.
review.focus: At 9.Qh5+ you went for a check before checking what it left behind. 9.d4 Bb6 10.Ng6 kept the initiative without risking the queen.

review.headline: A Wayward Queen game where you were fine until 18...Nxa4 opened the b-file

sections.text: White opened with 2.Qh5, the Wayward Queen, and you replied well with 2...d6. 3.Nf3? was a slip, and 3...g6?! 4.Qg5 Qxg5 5.Nxg5 traded queens. After 5...Be7 you were fine.
The middlegame was about equal for a long time. 8.Nf3 Bg4 9.Nc3 Bxf3 10.gxf3 doubled White's pawns, and 10...c6 and 11...Nbd7 kept things solid. You were around even through 13.b5.
White opened the queenside with 11.b4 and 12.a4, and you kept pace with 12...a5 and 13...Nb6. The position was balanced. 16...Bd8 and 17...Nh5 were reasonable, though a little passive.

Then 18...Nxa4?? was the blunder. The knight on b6 had been blocking the b-file, so moving it let 19.Rxb8 take your rook. The safe move was 18...Kd7. You ended up lost on time with the evaluation at -5.1.

review.turning_point: 18...Nxa4?? was the decisive mistake. The knight was the only thing between White's rook on b1 and your rook on b8, and 19.Rxb8 won it.
review.focus: Before taking a pawn, ask what your piece was doing. At 18...Nxa4 the knight on b6 stood between two rooks, and 18...Kd7 kept the file closed.

review.headline: A Three Knights Petrov where White's 11.Qf3 let your bishop win a piece

sections.text: You played a very solid Petrov Three Knights with ...d6, ...Bd7 and ...Be7, and answered 4.Bb5+ with 4...Bd7. By 9...O-O you had a comfortable, equal position.
sections.line: 4.Bb5+ Bd7 5.d3 Nc6 6.a3 Be7 7.O-O a6 8.Ba4 b5 9.Bb3 O-O

sections.text: White tried 10.Ng5?, and you replied 10...Ng4?, which was a little too fast. 10...Nd4 11.Be3 was cleaner. White then blundered with 11.Qf3??, and the evaluation jumped to +4.6 for you.
You found 11...Bxg5!, which started the sequence. After 12.Bxg5 Qxg5 you were clearly better, and your queen on g5 kept pressure on the kingside.
You finished cleanly with 13...Nf6 and 14...Nxd5. After 15.exd5 Nd4 16.Qg4 White resigned, and you were up a knight with a big attack.

review.turning_point: 11.Qf3?? was the blunder, and 11...Bxg5! won a piece, since after 12.Bxg5 Qxg5 you were a knight ahead.
review.focus: At 10...Ng4 you let the knight on g5 stay. 10...Nd4 11.Be3 kept your position healthier, so first deal with the loose piece.

review.headline: A Colle System where your strange king moves were fine, and White's 16.Bg5 and 22.Rae1 let you win

sections.text: White played the Colle System with 4.Bd3 and 5.c3, and you responded with the unusual 5...Kf8?! and 6...g6?!. The evaluation moved to -1.6, but your position was playable and White did not take advantage.
You held your own. 10.e4 dxe4 11.Nxe4 b6?! 12.h3 Bb7 gave you a solid structure, and White's attack with 13.Qe3 and 14.Qh6+ was not dangerous. After 15.Nxf6+ Bxf6 the game was balanced.
sections.line: 10.e4 dxe4 11.Nxe4 b6 12.h3 Bb7 13.Qe3 c5 14.Qh6+ Kg8 15.Nxf6+ Bxf6

sections.text: White then blundered with 16.Bg5??, and the evaluation was +2.4 for you. You missed 16...Bxf3, playing 16...Bg7?? instead, but the exchange after 17.Qxg7+ Kxg7 18.Bxd8 Raxd8 left you fine.
The decisive error came with 22.Rae1??. You found 22...Rde8!, and 23.Bf3 Rxe1 24.Bxb7 R8e2 won a rook for you. After 36...c1=Q you finished with 39...Qxg2#.

review.turning_point: 22.Rae1?? stepped into 22...Rde8!, and after 23.Bf3 Rxe1 you were up a rook.
review.focus: At 16...Bg7 you missed 16...Bxf3 17.Bxf6 Qxf6. When an opponent blunders, look for the capture that wins a piece before looking for exchanges.

review.headline: A French Defense where 7...Nxd4 helped you, but 8.Nxd4?? gave it back and the clock finished the game

sections.text: Black tried the odd 2...Qh4, and you answered with the strong 3.Nc3! After 3...Bb4 4.Qf3 Nc6 5.Ne2 Nf6 6.e5 Nd5 7.g3 you had a comfortable game with a lead of more than half a pawn.
Black blundered with 7...Nxd4??, and you were at +3.2 for the moment. You should have played 8.Qd3, but 8.Nxd4?? let Black continue with 8...Qxd4, and the evaluation turned to -3.0.
From there you kept fighting. 9.Bd2 Qxe5+ 10.Be2 Nxc3 11.Bxc3 Bxc3+ 12.bxc3 left you worse but with some play, and 14.Rad1 and 15.Rfe1 put your rooks on open files.
19.Bxb5? was another mistake, since 19.Bd3 was safer. After 19...cxb5 20.Qxb7 Qxe1+ 21.Rxe1 Rxb7 you were lost, and the game ended on time.

review.turning_point: 8.Nxd4?? took the knight but lost to 8...Qxd4. The line 8.Qd3 Bxc3+ 9.bxc3 would have kept your edge.
review.focus: After your opponent blunders, slow down and check what the capture opens. At 8.Nxd4 you took the knight without noticing 8...Qxd4, and 8.Qd3 was the safer move.

review.headline: An Englund Gambit that began shakily, until 7...Nxg3! and 8...Nxh1! won a rook

sections.text: You played the Englund Gambit with 1...e5?!, which gives up a pawn after 2.dxe5 Nc6. It is a risky opening against good play, and you started at -1.2. The point is quick development and tricks, and that is how the game turned out.

3...Qh4+ was a little hasty, since 3...d6 4.Nf3 was safer. After 4.g3 Qh5?! you were at -2.0, and 5.Nc3 Nh6 6.Nf3 Nf5? made it -3.2. At that point White was clearly better, but the pieces were still easy to trip.

White then played 7.e3?, which left the g3 pawn loose. You found the best reply, 7...Nxg3!, with the queen on h5 and the knight on g3 aiming at the rook on h1. 8.hxg3 was the way to keep the position together.
8.h3?? lost at once to 8...Nxh1!, and the knight took the rook in the corner. The evaluation went from -1.6 to +2.8 and White resigned.

review.turning_point: 7...Nxg3! was the move that turned the game around. After 8.h3?? Nxh1! you picked up the rook on h1 and White resigned.
review.focus: The gambit works when you find tactics, but your own moves matter too. At 6...Nf5 the quiet 6...Bc5 kept your pieces coordinated, so look for a developing move before an attacking one.

review.headline: A chaotic Sicilian where both sides blundered, and you won with a rook on d8

sections.text: This was a wild game. You opened with 2.Qf3?! and 3.Bc4?!, and Black answered with 4...Bg4??, giving you +1.4. A sensible reply to 4.d4 was 4...cxd4. After 5.Qg3??, it was your turn to give the edge back.

Black missed 6...cxd4 and played 6...g6?? and 7...d5?? instead, so you were suddenly at +1.2 and +1.6. But 7.Bg5? and 8.e5?? gave that advantage back. The right move was 8.Bxf6 exf6, instead of the pawn push.

9.g4?? lost another piece after 9...dxc4, and 11.h6?? sank you to -3.6. Black then blundered with 12...dxc3??, and 13.Nxc3! brought you back to about -0.9. After 13...Qxe5+ 14.Nge2 your pieces were finally out.
Black blundered with 14...e6?? and 15...Bb4??, and you finished with 16.Rd8#. It was a messy game, but you kept going.

review.turning_point: Black's 15...Bb4?? missed the threat, and 16.Rd8# finished the game. Until then both sides had been trading mistakes.
review.focus: At 9.g4 you walked into 9...dxc4 and lost a piece. Before a pawn push like g4, check which of your pieces it leaves undefended; 9.Bb5+ Nc6 10.Bxc6+ was safer.

review.headline: A Clemenz Opening where White's weak pawn moves let you win with 8...Qf2#

sections.text: White started with 1.h3, and after 1...e5 2.e4 d5 3.exd5 Nf6 you were fine. The first real mistake came with 4.f3??, which weakened the king's diagonal. You found the best reply, 4...Nxd5!, and the evaluation went to +2.3.
White made it worse with 5.Bc4??, and 5...Qh4+! forked the king on e1 and the bishop on c4, so White had to play 6.Kf1.
You missed the best move, 6...Qxc4+, and played 6...Nf4??, which still left you at +1.8. After 7.d3 Bc5 you kept developing, and White needed to be careful.
White blundered again with 8.Bxf4??, taking the knight. You finished with 8...Qf2#. It was a short, clean win.

review.turning_point: 5.Bc4?? let in 5...Qh4+!, and White never got the king safe. The game ended with 8...Qf2#.
review.focus: At 6...Nf4 you could have won the bishop with 6...Qxc4+ 7.d3 Qc5. When your opponent's king is stuck in the center, take what comes with check first.

review.headline: A Nimzo-Larsen where an early pawn loss and 13.Qh5 left you in trouble, and the clock ended it

sections.text: You opened with the offbeat 1.b3?! and 2.e4, and the early 3.d4? lost a pawn to 3...Bxe4. After 4.Qe2 Bb7 5.Bg5?! you were at -2.1, because the queen and bishop were rushing without a plan.
The position got sharper with 5...h6 6.Bh4 g5 7.Bg3 Nf6, and you tried to open lines with 9.f4?! and 10.fxg5?!. After 10...hxg3 11.gxf6 the pawns were wide open, but you were still about -3.
sections.line: 5.Bg5 h6 6.Bh4 g5 7.Bg3 Nf6 8.Nc3 h5 9.f4 h4 10.fxg5 hxg3

sections.text: 13.Qh5?? was the big error, taking you to -6.3. The simple 13.Ne4 Bxe4 14.Qxe4 Qxf6 kept things closer. After 13...Qxf6 14.Nf3, Black's 14...Na6? gave you some hope, as the evaluation improved to -3.5.
But 17.Ne5? and 18.Nxf7? went wrong again. 18.Qe2 was the safe move. After 18...Qf2 19.Qe2 Qxf7 you were lost, and the game ended on time.

review.turning_point: 13.Qh5?? turned a difficult position into a lost one. The quiet 13.Ne4 would have kept you in the game.
review.focus: When you are behind, avoid moves that add pieces to a king hunt without support. At 13.Qh5 the queen went alone, and 13.Ne4 Bxe4 14.Qxe4 was the safer way to trade.

review.headline: A London System where 8...Nxf2 gave up a knight, and you fought on until a late mating attack

sections.text: White played a London setup with 2.Bf4, 3.Nf3 and 5.h3, and you responded with 3...Bg4, 4...Nc6 and 6...Ne4. By 7.c3 the position was close to level.
sections.line: 1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 d5 3.Nf3 Bg4 4.e3 Nc6 5.h3 Bh5 6.Be2 Ne4 7.c3

sections.text: 7...e5? was the first slip, since 7...e6 8.O-O Bd6 was safer. After 8.Nxe5 you saw a knight sacrifice, but 8...Nxf2?? simply lost a piece. The best choice was 8...Bxe2 9.Qxe2 Nxe5 10.dxe5.
After 9.Kxf2 g6 10.Nxc6 bxc6 11.Bxh5 gxh5 12.Qxh5, you were down a piece and the evaluation was around -5. You kept playing with 12...Qf6, 13...Rg8 and 14...Rb8, which made White work for the win.
21...Ra7? made things worse, since 21...Qc8 was better. After 22.Bf6? you had a chance with 22...Qc7, but 22...Qa5?? allowed 23.Rb8+, and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 8...Nxf2?? cost you a knight, because 9.Kxf2 simply took it. The solid 8...Bxe2 9.Qxe2 Nxe5 10.dxe5 would have kept the game even.
review.focus: Before a knight sacrifice, count what you will get back. At 8...Nxf2 you gained one pawn for a knight, while 8...Bxe2 first removed the attacking bishop.

review.headline: A Petrov Three Knights where you held a tough game until a king and pawn race, which slipped away at the end

sections.text: You played a solid Petrov Three Knights against a much higher-rated opponent. After 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4 Nc6 6.Bg5 Be7 7.Bb5 Bd7 8.O-O O-O the game was equal, and 9.Nxc6 Bxc6 10.Bxc6 bxc6 left you with a healthy position.
The middlegame was quiet for a long time. 16.e5 dxe5 17.Bxe5 Qxd1?! was a trade of queens that dropped you to about -1.6, and 19.Bxf6 Rxe1+ 20.Rxe1 gxf6 21.Nd5 left your king exposed.

24...Rf5?? was the worst moment, since it allowed a forced mate with 25.Re8#. White missed it with 25.Rf1??, and you got a second chance. You then played the excellent 29...Kg6!, which brought you back to equality.
But 31...Rxf6?? lost the rook endgame, since 31...a4 was better. After 32.Rxf6+ Kxf6 White's king and pawns ran through, White queened with 41.h8=Q, and you resigned after 50.g7.

review.turning_point: 31...Rxf6?? was the game-changing error, because it traded rooks into a lost king-and-pawn ending. 31...a4 would have kept the balance.
review.focus: In rook endings, do not trade into a king and pawn ending without counting it out. At 31...Rxf6 the line 31...a4 kept your pieces on and avoided the lost ending.

review.headline: An Alekhine Defense where you were completely winning, but lost on time on move 29

sections.text: You met the Alekhine with the Two Pawns Attack, 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4, and Black played 3...Nb4. 4.a3?! was a slight inaccuracy, since 4.d4 N4a6 was cleaner. But Black replied 4...Nd3+??, which gave you a huge edge.
You found the best reply, 5.Bxd3!, winning a piece. After 5...d5 6.Nc3 Nc6 7.cxd5 Nxe5 the evaluation was already +5.3.
You kept going. 8.Bb5+ Qd7 9.Bxd7+ Bxd7 won the queen for a bishop, and 10.Qh5?! was a small inaccuracy. 10.d4 Ng6 kept more control, but 11.Qxe5 won another piece anyway.

With a huge advantage you kept taking pawns, with 16.Qxa7, 18.Qxb7, 20.Qxg5+ and 21.Qxg7+. Sadly the clock ran out at move 29, when you were over +9. It was a great game, and the only thing missing was time.

review.turning_point: 4...Nd3+?? and your reply 5.Bxd3! decided the game within five moves. After that, only the clock could stop you.
review.focus: You played accurately, so the lesson is the clock. At 10.Qh5 the quiet 10.d4 Ng6 11.h4 was just as strong; when far ahead, choose simple moves and play them quickly.

review.headline: An Owen Defense where 13.N2f3?? let Black's queen into your position, and 15...Qg2# ended it

sections.text: You answered the Owen Defense with the classical 2.d4 and 3.Nd2, and after 4.Ngf3 c5 5.Be2 Be7 6.O-O Nf6 7.e5 Nd5 you were comfortable at around +0.8.
sections.line: 1.e4 b6 2.d4 Bb7 3.Nd2 e6 4.Ngf3 c5 5.Be2 Be7 6.O-O Nf6 7.e5 Nd5

sections.text: 8.c4 Nf4 was a normal try, but 9.g3?! gave Black the chance for 9...Nxe2+ 10.Qxe2 cxd4 11.Nxd4 d5, and you were suddenly slightly worse at -0.3.
12.cxd5?! Qxd5 opened the position for Black's queen, and 13.N2f3?? was the key error. The best move was 13.Qb5+, which forced matters on the queenside. After 13...Bc5 14.Rd1 you were at -4.6.
15.Nxd4? was the final mistake, since 15.Rd3 Nc6 16.Bf4 kept the game going. After 15.Nxd4? Black played 15...Qg2#, and the game ended.

review.turning_point: 13.N2f3?? was the decisive mistake. 13.Qb5+ would have kept the game balanced.
review.focus: Before developing a knight, check the opponent's queen. At 13.N2f3 Black's queen and bishop were already aiming at your kingside, and 13.Qb5+ should have come first.

review.headline: A short Italian-style game where you punished weak play and finished with 7.Qxf7#

sections.text: Black started with 1...e5?, which gave you a small edge at +1.5. Your 2.e4 was a little inaccurate, since 2.Nxe5 d5 3.d4 kept more of the lead. After 2...Nc6 3.Bc4 d5 the game was still comfortable.
4.exd5 won a pawn and Black replied 4...Nce7?. You found the best move, 5.Nxe5!, which hit f7 and left your bishop pointing at the same square. The evaluation was +3.0 and Black was in trouble.
Black missed 5...Nxd5 and played 5...c5??, which sent the score to +6.6. 6.Qf3? was a bit loose, since 6.Bb5+ Bd7 7.Bxd7+ Qxd7 kept things simpler, but it was still enough.
Black finished the game with 6...Nxd5??, and you found 7.Qxf7# right away, a mate on f7 with the bishop and knight supporting the queen.

review.turning_point: 5.Nxe5! was the key move. It put two attackers on f7, and after 5...c5?? and 6...Nxd5?? the queen finished with 7.Qxf7#.
review.focus: At 2.e4 you gave up some of your edge, since 2.Nxe5 d5 3.d4 was stronger. When the opponent has weakened the center on move one, look first for the capture on e5.

review.headline: A Petrov where 6.Nd5?? gave you a big edge, and you finally won after some shaky moments

sections.text: The game began as a quiet Petrov with 3.d3, 4.Bg5 and 5.Nc3. White then blundered with 6.Nd5??, and you found the best reply, 6...Nxd5!, which won a piece and raised the evaluation to +4.9.
But 7...Qxe7?? let the advantage slip, since 7...Nxe7 8.Qd2 kept the extra piece. After 8.exd5 you were only +1.2, and 8...Bg4 and 9...c6 did not make the position easier.

White's 11.b4? and 12.a3? were mistakes that gave you +1.9 and +1.6, but your 11...a5? and 12...Nb6? let it slip back to +0.1. The better plan was 11...cxd5 12.O-O Be6. After 13.O-O?, your 13...cxd5! got the edge back to +1.2.

White blundered with 16.g3??, and your 16...Nxe2+! brought the evaluation to +8.4. After that you had a huge edge. 29...d3+ and 33...Qf4+ were small slips, and 35...d5?? nearly gave it back, but White answered 36.b5??, and 36...Qxb8! took the queen. White resigned.

review.turning_point: 6...Nxd5! won a piece, but 7...Qxe7?? gave it right back. The later 16...Nxe2+! was the move that made the win straightforward.
review.focus: 7...Qxe7 allowed 8.exd5, which won your knight back. 7...Nxe7 was the safer recapture, so always compare recaptures before choosing one.

review.headline: A Scandinavian where you were doing well through the opening, but 14.Qb3 and 15.Rad1 lost it

sections.text: You met the Scandinavian with 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qd6 4.d4 Bf5, and 5.Nf3 was fine. After 5...Nc6 6.d5 Ne5? you were at +3.0, but 7.Be2?? let a good chunk of that go. 7.Nb5 was the right way to hit the queen.
8.O-O exd5 9.Re1?? was another miss, with 9.Nb5 stronger. Black took with 9...Nxf3+?, and your 10.Bxf3+! recaptured with check from the rook on e1. After 10...Be7 11.Nxd5 you were up to +4.
