You kept the edge through 12.Bf4 Qc5 13.c3 c6, but 14.Qb3?? was the big mistake, dropping from +3.4 to +0.5. The line 14.Re5 cxd5 15.Rxf5 kept the advantage.
15.Rad1?? made it worse, because 15.Re5 Bd3 16.Bg4+ was better. Black missed 15...Qc4 and played 15...Be6??, but 16.Be3?? gave the edge back and you resigned after 16...Qc4.

review.turning_point: 14.Qb3?? let a clearly better position drop to equal, and 15.Rad1?? finished the job. 14.Re5 was the move that kept the pressure.
review.focus: When you are ahead, look at your opponent's threats before you add a quiet move. At 14.Qb3 and 15.Rad1 the rook on e1 stayed passive, and 14.Re5 or 15.Re5 would have kept your pieces active.

review.headline: A Scotch Game where 9.h4 and 10.h5 put you behind, and you turned it around for mate on move 42

sections.text: You played a sound Scotch with 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 and then 5.Bc4?!. After 5...Nxd4 6.Qxd4 Nc6 7.Qd5 Qf6 8.Bg5 Qg6 you had a normal position with the queen active in the middle.
sections.line: 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nge7 5.Bc4 Nxd4 6.Qxd4 Nc6 7.Qd5 Qf6 8.Bg5 Qg6

review.headline: A King's Knight game with wild swings, where you recovered from 4.Nxe5 and won on time

sections.text: Black played 2...h5? and 3...f6??, two weak moves that gave you a +3.0 edge. The right move in reply to 3...f6 was 4.Nh4, but you went for 4.Nxe5?? and 4...fxe5 5.Bxh5+, which dropped to +0.6.
After 5...Ke7 6.d4 Nf6 7.dxe5, Black blundered with 7...Rxh5?? and you were at +5.2. The right move was 7...Nxh5, which would have kept things much closer.
But then 8.Bg5?? gave it away, as 8.exf6+ gxf6 9.Qxh5 was the strong plan. Black missed 8...Rxg5 and played 8...b5??, and you found 9.Qxh5!, which took the rook on h5 at once.

review.focus: You nearly gave away the game twice, with 4.Nxe5 and 8.Bg5. Before a capture, check whether a quieter move such as 4.Nh4 or 8.exf6+ keeps everything defended.

review.headline: A short Hyperaccelerated Dragon where 6.d4 cost you the center, and you resigned early

sections.text: You played the Sicilian from the white side with 2.Nf3 and 3.d3?!, a slow setup that left you at -0.2. After 3...Bg7 4.Be2 Nf6 5.O-O O-O both sides castled and the game was balanced.
6.d4? was the mistake. It opened the center before you were ready, and the evaluation dropped from -0.2 to -1.4. The more patient 6.c3 kept your pieces together and avoided the trade.
After 6...Nxe4 7.dxc5 Nxc5 the knight on c5 was strong, and your 8.Be3?! was a slight inaccuracy at -2.3. You were worse, but the position was far from lost, and there was a lot of play left.
The lesson is that in this slow setup you must keep control of e4. 5.O-O was fine, but 6.d4 left the e4 pawn undefended against the knight on f6.

review.turning_point: 6.d4? was the decisive moment. After 6...Nxe4 the e-pawn was gone and you had to defend the rest of the game.
review.focus: Before pushing 6.d4, count the attackers and defenders of e4. 6.c3 would have kept the pawn defended and your setup intact.

review.headline: A Scotch Gambit where 6.Qf3 let Black take over, and a second error ended the game on move 7

sections.text: You played the Scotch Gambit with 3.Bc4 and 4.d4, and after 4...exd4 5.Nxd4 Black grabbed the e4 pawn with 5...Nxe4. The position was playable for White, but only if you found the right idea.
The right idea was 6.Nxc6, taking the knight on c6 before it could bother your knight on d4. Instead 6.Qf3? hit the knight on e4 but brought the queen out early, and 6...Nd6 pushed the bishop back.
7.Nb5?? was the blunder. 7.Nxc6 was available again and kept the game close, but the knight move left you at -3.6, and you resigned.
In short, you had two chances to take on c6, and each time you chose a different move.

review.turning_point: 6.Qf3? turned a normal opening into a worse position, and 7.Nb5?? made it worse; 7.Nxc6 would still have kept things close.
review.focus: When a gambit line leaves your knight on d4, check the capture on c6 first. At 6.Nxc6 and 7.Nxc6 you could have simplified the position.

review.focus: In sharp Sicilian lines, don't send a bishop to h6 unless the queen is ready to recapture. At 9.Bh6 the calm 9.O-O-O kept the position safe, and you could keep pieces coordinated.

review.headline: A Philidor where 15...g5?? gave you a winning attack, and you finished with 38.Qf7#

sections.text: You played the Philidor with 3.Bc4, and after 4.d3 Nc6 5.c3 Na5 6.Bb3?! Nxb3 7.axb3 you gave up your bishop pair. The game stayed balanced through 8.O-O, 9.Re1 and 10.d4.
Black went wrong with 14...Bg4?, and then blundered with 15...g5??. You found the best reply, 16.hxg4!, and after 16...gxh4 17.Nxh4 h5 you were far ahead at +3.9.

You kept pushing with 18.Nf5, 19.g5 and 20.f3?, a small slip, since 20.b4 was cleaner, After 20...Bf6? and 21.Qb5+ c6 you kept control. 22.Qxb7?? was a mistake, since 22.Qb4 was safer, but Black blundered with 22...Bxg5??, which gave you +8.9.
You found 23.Qxc6+! and then 24.Rd1?? allowed Black a big swing, but 24...Be3+?? gave you the chance to fix it with 25.Nxe3!. The game finished with 38.Qf7#.

review.turning_point: 15...g5?? gave you the chance, and 16.hxg4! opened the h-file with a strong attack. You nearly lost the lead with 24.Rd1??, but Black's 24...Be3+?? gave it back.
review.focus: At 22.Qxb7 you took a pawn and let the queen wander. 22.Qb4 Qxb4 23.cxb4 kept things safe, so count the cost before grabbing pawns with your queen.

review.headline: An Alekhine where Black blundered a knight on move 3, and 25.a6?? and the clock threw away a winning game

sections.text: Black played the Alekhine and you chose the Two Pawns Attack with 2.e5 and 3.c4. Black then blundered with 3...Ne3??, and after 4.fxe3 you were a knight up at +4.9.
You played the follow-up well. 5.d4, 6.Nd2, 7.Qe2 and 8.a3 met Black's checks, and after 8...Bxd2+ 9.Bxd2 you kept the extra piece with a safe position at about +6.3.
You kept growing the advantage with 10.Nf3, 11.g3 and 12.Bg2, then broke open the center with 13.d5 exd5 14.cxd5. By 18.exd6 Rxd6 you were still around +5.9.

The game turned with 22.Qxb7?! and 25.a6??. The right move at 25 was 25.Bxc5 Rxc5 26.Qb4, but 25.a6?? let Black take your queen with 25...Bxb7. After that you were fighting, and you lost on time after 37.Ne5.

review.turning_point: 25.a6?? turned +3.9 into -2.9 in one move, because it allowed 25...Bxb7. 25.Bxc5 Rxc5 26.Qb4 was the move that kept your queen safe.
review.focus: With a winning position, the clock matters as much as the board. At 22.Qxb7 and 25.a6 you went for pawns with your queen exposed, so choose the simple move that keeps your queen safe.

review.headline: An Italian where 9.O-O? and 13.Nd2?? let Black grab pawns in the center

sections.text: You played the classical Italian with 3.Bc4 and 4.c3, then 5.d4 exd4 6.cxd4 Bb4+ and 7.Nc3. This is the main line, and the position was equal.
Black replied 7...Bxc3+?, which helped you, and you found the best reply, 8.bxc3! Black then took the pawn with 8...Nxe4. 9.O-O? was the first inaccuracy, since 9.d5 was stronger.
After 9...d5 10.Re1 O-O 11.Bd3 Nxc3 you had to be careful. 12.Qc2 Ne4 was a normal sequence, and the position was still close to level at +0.1.
Then 13.Nd2?? was a blunder. 13.Bxe4 was the right move, and after 14.Qxe4 you would have kept the balance. 13...Nxd4 won a pawn, and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 13.Nd2?? lost a piece for nothing. 13.Bxe4 would have kept the game level.
review.focus: At 9.O-O you gave away the central initiative; 9.d5 was the move. It attacks the knight on c6 and keeps Black busy, so after a pawn grab look for the central push first.

review.headline: A Sicilian where you survived 8.Qf3?? and won a long game with 56.Qh1#

sections.text: You played the Open Sicilian with 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 and developed with 5.Nc3, 6.Bg5 and 7.Bb5. Then 8.Qf3?? was a blunder, since 8.Qd3 was safe. Luckily Black missed 8...Nxd4 and played 8...Be7??.
11.Bd3?? gave the edge back, since 11.Bxd7 Nxd7 12.Bxe7 was best. After 11...h6 12.Bh4 e5 13.Rb4 a5? you played the strong 14.Rxb7!, winning a pawn.
16.Rb3?? was another slip, since 16.Rxd7 kept the lead, and Black replied 16...h5??. After 17.h4 Ng4 18.hxg5 f5 19.exf5 Bxg5+ you were winning at +4.4.
The finish was straightforward. 21.Rxh5 and 22.Rxg5+ took pieces, and after 44.f8=Q you hunted the king until 56.Qh1#.

review.turning_point: 8...Be7?? let you off after 8.Qf3??, and 14.Rxb7! was your best move. Black's 16...h5?? then gave you a winning attack.
review.focus: At 8.Qf3 and 11.Bd3 you left pieces loose in the middle. Check which pieces are defended before a developing move; 8.Qd3 and 11.Bxd7 kept everything safe.

review.headline: A Philidor where 10.Bxe4?? gave you a big edge, but 15...Qf6 and a resignation ended it

sections.text: You played the Philidor Nimzowitsch with 3...Nf6 4.dxe5 Nxe4 5.exd6 Bxd6, and the position was equal. 6...Qe7?! and 7...f5? were inaccurate, because the simple 7...Nf6 8.Re1 Be6 kept things safe.
After 8.Nc3 O-O 9.Nxe4 fxe4, White blundered with 10.Bxe4??, and you found the best reply, 10...Qxe4!, which took the bishop. The evaluation jumped to +4.5.
You kept going with 11.Re1 Qg6 12.Qd5+ Kh8 13.Nd4 Bh3 14.g3 Nd7, and White's pieces were all over the board. At 15.Ne6 you were at +6.5.
15...Qf6? was a mistake, since 15...Rae8 was stronger, but you were still at +3.6 when the game ended in a resignation. That was an early end to a position that was still good.

review.turning_point: 10.Bxe4?? gave you a winning position, and 10...Qxe4! took it. The only slip was 15...Qf6?, and you were still ahead when the game ended.
review.focus: At 15...Qf6 the move 15...Rae8 16.Be3 Bxe6 kept your advantage. In a good position, keep playing instead of resigning, because the evaluation was +3.6 for you.

review.headline: A Two Knights Knight Attack where 6.Nxf7! and 8.Bxd5+! won a clean game, ending on time

sections.text: You played the Two Knights Knight Attack with 4.Ng5 d5 5.exd5, and Black replied 5...Nxd5?, which gave you +1.4. The best defense was 5...Na5 6.Bb5+ c6.
You found 6.Nxf7!, which forked the queen on d8 and the rook on h8. After 6...Kxf7 7.Qf3+ Qf6? you were at +2.4, and 7...Ke6 had been better.
8.Bxd5+! took the knight with check, and after 8...Ke7 9.Bxc6 Black blundered with 9...Qxf3??. You recaptured with 10.Bxf3! and had a huge edge at +5.5.
You then converted cleanly with 12.Bg5+ and 14.Bxb7, and the position stayed above +5 for the rest of the game. Black lost on time after 24.Rd5.

review.turning_point: 6.Nxf7! started the combination, and 8.Bxd5+! kept it going. After 9...Qxf3?? 10.Bxf3 the game was won.
review.focus: The game had no mistakes by you. Study the idea behind 6.Nxf7: it works because 7.Qf3+ follows with check, and 8.Bxd5+ wins back the knight.

review.headline: A Petrov Italian where you were winning, but 22...Qa5?? walked into mate

sections.text: You played a Petrov Italian with 3...d6?! and 4...Be6, and White replied 5.Bd5??, which gave you +1.3. The best move was 5...Nxd5, but 5...c6?? gave the advantage back, and 6.Bxe6 fxe6 followed.
After 7.Re1, 8.d3 and 10.Bg5 you were slightly worse. White then played 12.d4?, and you found 12...e4!, which opened the position. After 13.c4? O-O! you were at +3.3.
14.Ne5 Nxe5 15.dxe5 Bxe5 won a pawn, and 16.cxd5 Bxb2 17.Nc3 Bxa1 took the rook. You were at +5.4, and 18.Qxa1 cxd5 left you winning.
You kept going with 19...d4 and 21...d2, but 22.Ne6 was a strong reply and 22...Qa5?? lost to 23.Qxg7#. The correct move was 22...Qf6, which kept you ahead.

review.turning_point: 22...Qa5?? turned a +5.7 position into a loss, because 23.Qxg7# was mate. 22...Qf6 would have kept your advantage.
review.focus: With a knight on e6 aiming at g7, you needed to check that square before moving the queen. 22...Qa5 ignored the threat, and 22...Qf6 covered it.

review.headline: An Italian where 4.Nxe5?? began a wild game, and 17.Qxc7?? walked into mate

sections.text: Black played the weak 3...f6?, and you could have punished it with 4.d4. Instead 4.Nxe5?? lost a piece, and after 4...Nxe5 5.Qh5+? g6 you were at -3.8.
You fought back well. 6.Qe2 Bc5 7.Bb3 Ne7? and 8.c3? were a messy sequence, but Black replied 8...d6?? and you found 9.d4!, which regained the lead. After 9...Ng4?? 10.dxc5! dxc5 you were at +2.5.

11.O-O Qd6 12.g3? Be6 kept you ahead, but Black blundered with 13...Qe5??, and your 14.Qb5+?? gave much of it back, since 14.f4 was better. 15.Qxb7! brought the evaluation back to +4.0, and 16.Qxc6 Qh5 left you around +5.7.
sections.line: 11.O-O Qd6 12.g3 Be6 13.Rd1 Qe5 14.Qb5+ Nc6 15.Qxb7 O-O 16.Qxc6 Qh5

sections.text: 17.Qxc7?? was the final blunder. It allowed 17...Qxh2+ 18.Kf1 Qxf2#, a forced mate. 17.Bxe6+ was the move, and it would have kept your large lead.

review.turning_point: 17.Qxc7?? turned +5.7 into a forced loss. Taking the pawn on c7 with the queen left your king without enough defenders.
review.focus: At 17.Qxc7 you grabbed a pawn while Black threatened your king. 17.Bxe6+ Kh8 18.Bxg4 Qxg4 kept your king safe, so check your opponent's threats before grabbing a pawn.

review.headline: A Scotch Game where you built a winning position, then gave it back with 14...d3 under time pressure

sections.text: White played the Scotch with 2.d4 exd4 3.Nf3 Nc6, then 4.a3 Bc5 and 5.Bg5. You were comfortable at about +0.4 after 4...Bc5.
White's play became loose with 6.Bc4 h6 7.Bxf6 Qxf6 8.O-O O-O 9.e5, but you took advantage with 9...Nxe5. After 10.b4 Nxf3+ 11.Qxf3 Qxf3 12.gxf3 you had a clear lead around +3.6.
sections.line: 6.Bc4 h6 7.Bxf6 Qxf6 8.O-O O-O 9.e5 Nxe5 10.b4 Nxf3+ 11.Qxf3 Qxf3 12.gxf3

sections.text: You kept things under control with 12...Be7 and 13...Bf6, and 13.Nd2 Bf6 14.Ne4 was a normal sequence. White's pieces were passive.
14...d3?? gave away a lot of the lead, because it let 15.Nxf6+ gxf6 16.Bxd3 break up your structure. The calm 14...Be5 15.Rfe1 d6 kept the pawn on d4. You resigned after 17.c3.

review.turning_point: 14...d3?? threw away a big edge, dropping from +3.7 to +1.1. 14...Be5 would have kept everything protected.
review.focus: When you are ahead and short of time, choose the solid move that keeps the pawn on d4 protected. At 14...d3 the line 14...Be5 15.Rfe1 d6 kept your advantage.

review.headline: A Two Knights Knight Attack where 6.Nxf7! won quickly and Black resigned on move 8

sections.text: You went for the sharp 4.Ng5 against the Two Knights Defense, a line that asks Black to find the right answer. After 4...d5 5.exd5 Black grabbed the pawn with 5...Nxd5?, which gave you +1.4. The better choice was 5...Na5 6.Bb5+ c6.
You found the key move, 6.Nxf7!, which forked the queen on d8 and the rook on h8 at once. After 6...Kxf7 the king had been dragged into the open.
7.Qf3+ came with check and also hit the knight on d5. The best defense was 7...Ke6, but Black played 7...Kg8??.
You then took the knight with 8.Bxd5+, and Black resigned. It was a clean attack where every move had a purpose.

review.turning_point: 6.Nxf7! was the decisive moment. After 6...Kxf7 7.Qf3+ the black king could not hold the position together.
review.focus: You played accurately, so the lesson is the pattern. After 5...Nxd5, the sacrifice 6.Nxf7 only works because 7.Qf3+ follows with check, so always check the follow-up before you give up a piece.
